en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Pācittiya Offenses in the Vinaya Piṭaka.
5. The Chapter on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa) 1.
The Section on False Speech (Musāvādavagga) 1.
Commentary on the Training Rule on False Speech (Musāvādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā)
Now follows the commentary on those Minor Texts whose collection is well-established in nine sections. 1.
Therein, regarding the first training rule of the Chapter on False Speech (*musāvāda-vagga*), "Hatthaka" is the name of that Elder.
"Sakyaputta" means "the son of the Sakyans. It is said that during the time of the Buddha, eighty thousand men from the Sakyan clan went forth into homelessness, and he was one among them.

"Vādakkhitta" means thrown, cast, sent, or dispatched toward an opponent by means of a debate, having reflected, "I shall engage in a debate"; or it refers to one who has entered into a debate with his own mind.
"Cast down" (*khitto*): wherever there is an argument, it is "cast down in argument" (*vādakkhitto*) because it appears right there. "Having denied, he denies":
perceiving some fault in his own position, he first denies it, saying, "This is not my position.
Then, as he speaks again and again, perceiving its faultlessness, he asserts, "This is indeed my position. "Having asserted, he denies": [this refers to]...

Perceiving a benefit in some particular statement, he claims, "This is my own doctrine," and as he speaks further and further, perceiving a fault therein, he dismisses it, saying, "This is not my doctrine.
He evades one thing with another means; that is, by means of one reason, he evades, conceals, and covers over another reason, [saying], "Form is impermanent..."
Having said, "because it must be known," he further says, "because it is subject to birth," and so forth.
In the *Kurundi*, however, it is stated: "He speaks much else for the purpose of concealing this. The intention here is as follows:
for the sake of concealing both that which is admitted and that which is denied, he speaks much such as, "Who said it? What did he say? In reference to what did he say? and so on.
Furthermore, it is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*: “One who denies what has been admitted, or admits what has been denied, thus evades the matter with prevarication.
“He speaks a deliberate lie” means he speaks a falsehood while being fully aware of it.
“Having made an appointment, he deceives” means [saying], “Let the discussion take place at such-and-such a time or in such-and-such a place,” regarding times such as before the meal, and so forth.
Having made an appointment, he goes either before or after the appointed time and departs, saying, "Look, sirs! The sectarians have not come;
they have been defeated.
Regarding "lying in full awareness": this refers to speaking falsely while knowing it to be so, and while being aware that one is speaking falsely.
3. "Of one who has deception as his primary aim" means: of one who speaks having placed a deceptive mind before him.
"Speech" (*vācā*) refers to the volition (*cetanā*) that originates the utterance included within wrong speech. "Voice" (*girā*) indicates the sound originated by that volition.
"Discourse" (*byappatha*) means the path of speech; for speech itself is called "discourse" because it serves as the path even for others who follow after one's views.
“Division of speech” (*vacībhedo*) means the division of that which is designated as speech; it is speech itself that has reached such a state that it is thus called.

“Vocal intimations” (*vācasikā viññatti*) refers to vocal intimation (*vacīviññatti*). Thus, it should be understood that by the first term, pure volition (*suddhacetanā*) is expressed; by the three middle terms, volition accompanied by the sound originated by that [volition] is expressed;
and by the final term, volition accompanied by intimation is expressed. “Noble-less expressions” (*anariyavohārā*) refers to those of the ignoble.
These are the conventional expressions of foolish worldlings (*bālaputhujjana*).

Having thus shown intentional lying (*sampajānamusāvāda*), he now speaks the words beginning with "What was not seen, I have seen" in order to demonstrate the characteristic of the ignoble conventions (*anariyavohāra*) termed intentional lying mentioned at the end. Therein, "not seen" (*adiṭṭhaṃ*)...
The meaning should be understood according to this method: "the speech of one who says 'I have seen it,' or the volition that originates it, is one ignoble mode of expression.
Furthermore, in this context, what has not been grasped by means of the eye is "not seen" (*adiṭṭha*); what has not been grasped by means of the ear is "not heard" (*asuta*);
and what has been smelled and so forth by means of the nose and other faculties, having been made as if connected to those three faculties and reached—[is "not sensed" (*amuta*)].
It should be understood that "not grasped" means not grasped by the five faculties, and "not cognized" means not cognized by pure consciousness alone.
However, in the Canon, the teaching is given in a coarse manner, stating: "The unseen is that which has not been seen by the eye.
Regarding the seen and so forth, what has been seen by oneself or by another is simply "seen. The same applies to the heard, sensed, and cognized.
This is one method. Another way is this: what one has seen oneself is indeed "seen"; this same principle applies to what is heard and so forth.
However, what has been seen by another stands for oneself in the place of "heard," and the same applies to "sensed" and the rest.
Now, having attributed an offense by means of those ignoble modes of speech, he says, "In three ways," and so forth.

Its meaning is to be understood exactly according to the method stated in the commentary on the fourth *pārājika* rule, beginning with: “For one who speaks a conscious lie, saying ‘I attained the first *jhāna* by means of three modes,’ there is an offense of *pārājika*.
For in that [commentary] it says “I attained the first *jhāna*,” whereas here it says “the unseen has been seen by me”; and in that [case] there is an offense...

Regarding the distinction: "In this case it is an offense of defeat (pārājika)" and "In this case it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)," there is a difference only in the matter (*vatthu*) and the offense (*āpatti*);
the rest has the same characteristic. 9.

As for the meaning of "one who is doubtful about what was seen in three ways," etc., it refers to one who, while committing an offense of defeat (*pārājika-dhamma*), is [doubtful] regarding what was seen.
This should be understood according to the method explained in the commentary on the passage concerning the faults of "being doubtful about what was seen" and so forth.
For here, the difference lies merely in the wording of the text (*pāḷi*), but in meaning there is no discrepancy whatsoever from the Theravāda position.
11. "He speaks impulsively" means that without investigating or reflecting, he says out of haste, even regarding what was seen, "I did not see it."
He speaks. "He says one thing when he intends to say another" means that, due to dullness or stupidity, stumbling over his words, he says "cīra" and so forth when he ought to say "cīvara.
Furthermore, when a novice monk asks, "Venerable sir, have you seen my preceptor?
and [the monk], playing a joke, replies, "Your preceptor must have gone off after yoking a wooden cart," [he is guilty of this offense].
Or, having heard the sound of a jackal, when asked, "Venerable sir, whose sound is this?

he replies, "This is the sound of those who are lifting a wheel stuck in the mud while your mother is traveling in her carriage"—if he speaks thus, neither in jest nor in derision, but says something else, he still incurs an offense.
There is also what is called "filling out the story": for instance, one person, having obtained a little oil in the village...
Having returned to the monastery, he says to a novice: “Where have you been today?
The village was empty,” or, having received a piece of cake placed in a basket, he says: “Today they were distributing cakes from baskets in the village.
This is indeed a deliberate falsehood. The rest is self-evident.

It has three origins: it originates from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind; it is an action (kiriya); it is liberated by perception (saññāvimokkha); it is accompanied by consciousness (sacittaka); it is a fault according to worldly convention (lokavajja); it is bodily action and verbal action; it is an unwholesome state of mind (akusalacitta);

and it is associated with three types of feeling (tivedana). This is the first training rule concerning false speech. 2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Slanderous Speech (omasavāda-sikkhāpada)
12. In the second training rule, *omasanti* means they revile. *Khuṃsenti* means they abuse. *Vambhenti* means they disparage. 13.
*Bhūtapubbaṃ* (formerly) refers to this story which the Blessed One brought up for the purpose of censuring those who speak with contempt.
*Nandivisālo nāma*: *Nandī* is the name of that ox, while its horns (*visāṇāni*) were broad (*visālāni*); therefore, it was called "Nandivisāla."
It is said: at that time, the Bodhisatta was named Nandivisāla. The brahmin nourished him exceedingly with rice porridge, food, and other provisions.
Then, out of compassion for the brahmin, he said, "Go, you," and so forth. He remained right there;
even at the moment of a rootless rebirth-linking (*ahetuka-paṭisandhi*), he followed only what was unpleasant to others, and therefore [he perceived] the fault of the brahmin.

He stood there, desiring to demonstrate [his power]. "He set rolling a hundred yoked carts" means that having arranged them in a row and secured them beneath the trees, making them into a single connected unit, he set rolling a hundred carts filled with bean soup, sand, and so forth;
for although the place where the axle had previously rested was again reached by the axle as it rolled, the Bodhisatta—by means of the first cart—[caused the rest to follow].
In the place where he had halted, he caused the area to move forward by the measure of a hundred carts so that the last cart might be brought to a standstill;

for there is no such thing as slackness in the actions of Bodhisattvas. "He was satisfied because of that" means that Nandivisāla was satisfied because of that Brahmin’s acquisition of wealth and because of his own deed.

15. Regarding the phrase “even by reviling”: here, since he intends to analyze later on with the words, “There are two kinds of reviling—the inferior reviling and the superior reviling”—he says simply “by reviling,” rather than saying as was previously stated, “insulting even with an inferior reviling.
“Of the bamboo kind” means of the carpenter kind; they also say it means of the basket-maker kind.
“Nesādajātī” means those of the hunter caste and so forth.
“Rathakārajātī” means those of the leather-worker caste. “Pukkusajātī” means those of the flower-scavenger caste. “Avakaṇṇaka” and so on are names for slaves;
therefore, it is lowly. “Oññātaṃ” means despised; they also read it as “uññātaṃ. “Avaññātaṃ” means looked down upon.
"Having despised" means having made known [the contempt]. "Contemned" means loathed. "Treated with contempt" means treated with the thought, "What is the use of this?
"Not honored" means not respected. "Carpentry" means the work of a woodcutter.
"Finger-calculation" refers to the counting of hand-gestures. "Arithmetic" refers to other forms of calculation such as the *acchiddaka* (unbroken counting) and so forth.
*Lekhā* means a written mark or letter. The disease of diabetes (*madhumeha*) is called "excessive" (*ukkaṭṭha*) because of the absence of [ordinary] pain.
*Pāṭikaṅkhā* means desirable. Regarding the phrase "with the letter *ya* or with the letter *bha*": having joined the letters *ya* and *bha*, whatever abuse [is expressed by them], that is the term.

Regarding "with a wooden mortar (*kāṭakoṭacikā*)," "wooden mortar" (*kāṭa*) refers to the male organ, and "mortar" (*koṭacikā*) refers to the female organ; whatever abuse is expressed by these is called "inferior" (*hīna*) abuse.
16. Now, having attributed the offense by way of the classification of those [offenses] such as birth and so forth, he says: "One who is ordained [speaks to] one who is ordained," and so on.
In that context, "desiring to revile," "desiring to mock," and "desiring to humiliate" mean desiring to abuse, desiring to disparage, desiring to censure, and desiring to deprive of dignity;
this is the meaning. "By means of what is low, [speaking of] what is low" means [speaking of] one of low birth by means of a word for low birth. By this...
The meaning in all these cases is to be understood through the application of skillful means (*upāya*).

Furthermore, in this context, although one who speaks of an inferior person as inferior speaks the truth, because of his desire to revile, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for every single utterance.
And although one who speaks of a superior person as inferior speaks what is false, because of his desire to revile...
However, by this very training rule (*sikkhāpada*), one incurs an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*), and not by the previous one.
Even one who says such things as, "You are an extreme outcaste," "You are an extreme brahmin," "You are a wicked outcaste," or "You are a wicked brahmin," is also to be dealt with for an offense.

In the section beginning with "There are some here," however, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) because it was stated as something to be avoided. This same method applies to those [other cases] as well.

"Surely... [and so on]... even in the case of those who say "it is not I," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for all four instances. However, when addressing one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), there is an offense of wrong-doing for all four instances as well.
But by means of such words as "You are a thief! or "You are a cutpurse!", there is an offense of wrong-doing for all instances, whether the person is fully ordained or not.

However, if it is done out of a desire for sport, there is an offense of ill-spokenness (*dubbhāsita*) for all instances, whether the person is fully ordained or not. This applies to the desire for sport.

“Nāma” means the intention for joking or laughing. And in this training rule, it should be understood that—with the exception of a bhikkhu—all beings, such as bhikkhunīs and others, stand in the category of those who are not fully ordained (anupasampanna). 35.
Regarding “one who has the welfare [of others] in view,” and so forth: one who explains the meaning of the Pāḷi is “one who has the welfare in view”; one who recites the Pāḷi...
"Having the Dhamma as one's primary concern" means that when one stands by the instruction and speaks in such a manner as "Even now you are an outcaste; do not commit evil;
do not go from darkness to darkness," it should be understood as "having the instruction as one's primary concern. The rest is self-evident. It has three origins:
it originates from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. It is functional (kiriyā), with perception as its liberation (saññāvimokkha).

[The offense] has consciousness, is a world-transgression (*lokavajja*), is bodily action (*kāyakamma*), is verbal action (*vacīkamma*), is unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*), and is painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).

However, the offense of ill-spoken words (*dubbhāsitāpatti*) here arises from speech and consciousness; it is an act (*kiriya*), is liberated by perception (*saññāvimokkha*), has consciousness, is unwholesome consciousness, and consists of two feelings: pleasant and neutral.
The second training rule concerning false speech.
3. Commentary on the third training rule concerning malicious talebearing (pesuñña).
36. Regarding the third training rule: "Of those who have engaged in a quarrel" means of those in whom a quarrel has arisen. "Quarrel" refers to strife.

The preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*) consists of deliberating within one's own faction, thinking: "This was done by such-and-such a person and that by such-and-such; when this is said, we shall say this," and so forth.
Quarrel (*kalaha*) is transgression of body and speech leading to an offense. Dispute (*vivāda*) is contentious talk.
"Of those who have fallen into dispute" means of those engaged in such contention. Slander (*pesuñña*) is malicious speech; it is said to be speech that makes empty the state of being dear.
37. *Bhikkhupesunñe* means in the sowing of dissension among bhikkhus; the meaning is: having heard [something] from one bhikkhu, the sowing of dissension is conveyed by a bhikkhu to another bhikkhu.

38. *Dvīhākārehi* means by two causes. *Piyakamyassa vā* means of one who desires to be dear, that is, one who aspires to his own state of being dear [to others], thinking, "In this way, I shall become dear to him.
*Bhedādhippāyassa vā* means of one who intends to cause a split, thinking, "In this way, he [will be separated] from him..."

“...it will break apart”—this refers to one who desires the division of another by means of another. “Even by birth,” and so forth—all of this follows the same method as stated in the previous training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
Here too, starting with the nun, all those who are not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) are included.
“Neither for one desiring affection nor for one desiring division”: having seen one person reviling and another person forgiving, [one might think], “Oh!”...
“Shameless! He thinks he will speak thus again to such a venerable one as you!”—there is no offense for one who speaks in this way solely for the purpose of censuring evil.

The rest is of plain meaning. It has three origins: it originates from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind; it is an action, it is liberated by perception, it involves consciousness, it is a worldly offense, and it is bodily action.
Vocal action, unwholesome consciousness, and the three feelings.
This is the third training rule on malicious speech.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule on Reciting Verses Together.
44. In the fourth training rule: *appatissā* means those who lack deference. When addressed as "lay followers" (*upāsaka*), they do not even wish to hear the words;

this is the meaning of "disrespectful. Alternatively, the meaning is that they are "without deference," meaning they do not conduct themselves with humility. *Asabhāgavuttikā* means those whose livelihood is dissimilar;
the meaning is that their conduct is not practiced in the same manner as it ought to be among the monks.
45. *Padaso dhammaṃ vāceyyā* (he should recite the Dhamma word by word) means he should recite the Dhamma one word after another;

the meaning is that he should recite it section by section. Since that section-named word is fourfold, the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) is stated as “word, following-word, following-syllable, following-phrase” in order to show that. Therein:
"Word" (*pada*) refers to one intended verse-line (*gāthāpāda*). "Following-word" (*anupada*) refers to the second line. "Following-syllable" (*anvakkhara*) refers to each individual syllable.
"Following-phoneme" (*anubyañjana*) refers to a subsequent phoneme that resembles the preceding phoneme.
Alternatively, any single syllable is a "following-syllable," a collection of syllables is a "following-phoneme," and a collection of syllables and phonemes is a "word. This is the first word.
The distinction here should be understood as follows: the first is simply "pada" (word), while the second is "anupada" (line).

Now, regarding what is called a "pada"—when one who is reciting the Dhamma in verse form, having established it from one side and concluding it from the other, begins each individual word such as "manopubbaṅgamā dhammā" together with a novice, starting from one side and ending at the very same [other] side—[this is a pada].
He brings it to completion. For one who teaches in this manner, the offenses of expiation (*pācittiya*) are to be understood by counting the words.

Regarding "word by word" (*anupadaṃ*): having established them separately, they conclude them together. Thus, when the Elder says, "States are preceded by the mind," the novice, not yet having reached that word, recites the second word, "Mind is supreme, mind-made," together with him; these [words] are established separately.

Having set it forth, they are said to "conclude together. For one who teaches in this manner, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for each syllable counted in succession. Regarding "syllable by syllable" (*anvakkhara*):
when it is being said, "Form is impermanent," he utters "rū"; when told, "Sāmaṇera, say 'Form is impermanent,'" he stands after pronouncing only the sound "rū.
For one who teaches in this manner, there is an offense of expiation for each syllable counted in succession.
These are *pācittiya* offenses. This same principle applies even in the composition of verses. Regarding "elucidation" (*anubyañjana*):
when it is said that "form is impermanent," one utters the sound "feeling is impermanent.
Thus, while reciting this Sutta—"Monks, form is impermanent; feeling is impermanent"—when the Elder says "Form is impermanent," the novice, due to his quick wit...

“Feeling is impermanent”—uttering this word of impermanence while reciting it together with the word of impermanence “form is impermanent,” he utters the speech. Even for one who teaches in this manner, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for each count of the phrasing.
This is the summary here: regarding these words and so forth, for whatever he recites together, he incurs an offense for each such instance.
"Spoken by the Buddha" refers to the entire Vinaya Piṭaka, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the Dhammapada, the Cariyāpiṭaka,
the Udāna, the Itivuttaka, the Jātaka, the Suttanipāta, the Vimānavatthu, the Petavatthu, and suttas such as the Brahmajāla.
"Spoken by disciples" refers to those spoken by disciples included among the four assemblies, such as the Anaṅgaṇa, Sammādiṭṭhi, Anumāna, Cūḷavedalla, and Mahāvedalla suttas.
"Spoken by an Isibhāṣita" refers to the entire Paribbājaka-vagga spoken by external wanderers, such as the questions of the sixteen brahmins who were pupils of Bāvari, and so forth.
"Spoken by a deity" means spoken by deities; it should be understood as consisting of the Devatā-saṃyutta, Devaputta-saṃyutta, Māra-saṃyutta, Brahmā-saṃyutta, Sakka-saṃyutta, and so on.

"Connected with the goal" (atthūpasañhita) means dependent upon the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). "Connected with the Dhamma" (dhammūpasañhita) means dependent upon the canonical text (*pāḷi*); by both of these, it is indeed dependent upon the turning away from the cycle of existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*).

He speaks. Even if he speaks that which is conducive to the turning away from the round (vivaṭṭūpanissita), there is an offense for one who causes another to recite word by word a teaching that has been included in the three councils (tisso saṅgītiyo).
However, even regarding what is conducive to the turning away, there is no offense [if it is] composed in various languages or in the form of verses, stanzas, and so forth.
Even if it is not included in the three councils, there is no offense for the Kulumbasutta, the Rājovādasutta, or the Tikkhindriya.
The *Catuparivaṭṭa*, the *Nandopananda*, and so forth—these are indeed offenses (*āpatti*). The *Apalāladamana* is also mentioned, yet it is prohibited in the *Mahāpaccarī*.

In the *Meṇḍaka* and *Milindapañha*, there is no offense regarding what was stated as the Elder’s own inspired response; however, there is an offense regarding that which was brought forward for the purpose of convincing the King. The *Vaṇṇapiṭaka*, *Aṅgulimālapiṭaka*, *Raṭṭhapāla*, *Gaja*, *Jātaka*, *Āḷavaka*, *Gajjita*, *Guḷhamagga*, *Guḷhavessantara*, and *Guḷhavinayavedalla-piṭakas*.

However, it is stated that these are indeed not the words of the Buddha. They say that what is called the *Sīlūpadesa* was spoken by the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), and in that case, there is an offense.
There are also other works such as the *Maggakathā*, *Ārammaṇakathā*, *Buddhikadaṇḍaka*, *Ñāṇavatthu*, and the *Asubhakathā*;
in those, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhammā*) are analyzed, and in the *Dhutanga-pañha*, the practice path (*paṭipadā*) is analyzed.

Therefore, it is stated that there is an offense regarding those [passages]. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other [commentaries] not included in the Council, it is stated that an offense occurs only in the cases of the *Rājovāda*, *Tikkhindriya*, *Catuparivaṭṭa*, *Nanda*, and *Upananda-kulumpa Suttas*.
Regarding the remainder, the meaning established is this: only that which has been extracted from the word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*) constitutes an offense, and nothing else.
48. "Reciting together" means that even if one takes the recitation together with one who is not fully ordained, there is no offense for speaking together; this is the meaning.

Herein is the analysis: if both the fully ordained and the not fully ordained sit down and cause [the text] to be recited, and the teacher, thinking "I am speaking to those who are seated," speaks together with them, there is an offense for the teacher. [If it is] with one who is not fully ordained...
There is no offense for one who takes [the robe] together with another. The same principle applies if two people standing together take it.
If a young bhikkhu is sitting and a novice (sāmaṇera) is standing, there is no offense for one who says, "I am speaking to the one who is sitting.
If the young one stands and the other sits, there is likewise no offense for one who says, "I am speaking to the one who is standing. If, among many bhikkhus, one...
The novice is sitting; while he is sitting and the teacher is reciting the Dhamma word by word, there is no offense for the teacher because [the novice] is unintentional.

If the novice has left the vicinity and is either standing or sitting, since he is not included among those to whom one is reciting, he is counted as having "taken up the knot of flight" from one direction; therefore, there is no offense.
Even when reciting together with one who is not fully ordained, if one who is fully ordained recites together with that person and speaks along with them, there is no offense.
Even for one receiving a formal recitation (uddesa) from one who is not fully ordained, if they speak together with them, there is no offense; for this too is reckoned as "reciting together."
"Reciting [the text] while causing one who is generally proficient in the text to stop" means:

if even a single line of a single verse does not come out, while the rest does come out, this is called "generally proficient in the text. This principle should be understood in the same way regarding the Suttas.
There is no offense for one who says, "Speak thus to him as he recites," even if they speak only once. "Causing one who is concluding [the recitation] to stop" means...
If one says to someone who is reciting a sutta in the midst of an assembly, "I am suspicious of you," there is no offense for speaking even once together with that person.

However, as for what is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other commentaries—that if one who has been told, "Do not speak with me," nevertheless speaks, there is no offense—that is not found in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*; indeed, its very absence [from that source] is the proof.
It is associated. Why? Because it originates from action (*kiriyasamuṭṭhāna*). Otherwise, it would be neither-action-nor-non-action (*kiriyākiriya*).

The rest is self-evident. Regarding the origin of the training rule on abusive speech: it originates from both speech and the mind of speech; it is action; it is not a liberation through perception; it is without consciousness; it is an offense by formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*); it is verbal action; it is associated with three types of consciousness and three types of feeling. This is the fourth training rule on abusive speech.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule on Sleeping Together (Sahaseyyasikkhāpada) 49.
Regarding the fifth training rule: “with mind unmindful and unaware” is said by way of not having practiced mindfulness and clear comprehension in the preliminary stage;
for when one has crossed over into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), how could there be mindfulness and clear comprehension? “Groaning” means prattling or babbling.
“Chattering like crows” means emitting meaningless sounds from the nose like the cry of a crow. “Lay followers” (*upāsaka*) refers to those lay followers who had risen earlier.
They said this—“Friends, a training rule has been laid down by the Blessed One, Rāhula”—out of respect for the training rule itself;
yet they also spoke thus out of their natural reverence for the Blessed One and out of the Venerable Rāhula’s own desire to train.

When that venerable one arrives at his dwelling place, they prepare whatever small bed or backrest is available and give him either a robe or an upper garment to wrap around his head. This is due to that venerable one’s desire for training:
it is said that when the monks see him coming from afar, they [prepare] a hand-broom and a water-strainer.
And they threw away the rubbish outside. Then, when others asked, "Friends, who dropped this?", some replied, "Venerable sir, Rāhula has been walking about in this place; perhaps he dropped it.
But that venerable one, without saying even once, "Venerable sir, this was not my doing," set it right and [addressed] the monks.

Having asked for forgiveness, he departed. "He made his bed in the privy" means that, cultivating that very same desire for training, he did not go to the presence of the General of the Dhamma, Mahāmoggallāna, the Elder Ānanda, and others, but instead made his bed in the privy used by the Blessed One.
It is said that this hut was fitted with a door, adorned with perfumes, and draped with garlands of flowers.
"It stands like a shrine (cetiyaṭṭhāna), not to be used by others.
(51) "For more than three nights" means that the Blessed One granted a dispensation for three nights for the sake of supporting the novices;
for it is not fitting to ordain sons of good families and then fail to support them. "In the same sleeping place" means lying down together.
“Lying down” (*seyyā*) refers both to the act of reclining known as stretching out the body, and also to the lodging where one lies down.
In that regard, first, to show the lodging, it was said: “Lying down means entirely covered,” and so forth. To show the stretching out of the body, it was said:
“When one who is not fully ordained has already lain down, a bhikkhu may lie down,” and so forth. Therefore, this is the meaning here:
“Having entered a bed known as a lodging, one should arrange, dispose, and prepare a bed known as the stretching out of the body.
By the words “completely covered,” etc., the characteristic of that bed known as a lodging is stated.
Therefore, whatever lodging is entirely covered on top by the five kinds of roofing or by any other means, [that is the type intended].
This is the bed called "completely covered. However, in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), adopting common parlance and for the sake of ease of recitation, it is stated:
"The 'completely covered' means covered with five types of coverings.
Even though this has been said, it is not possible to claim there is no offense even for one staying in a cloth tent; therefore, whatever is capable of providing concealment here—
Both "roofed" (chadana) and "enclosed" (paricchanna) must be understood.
For if only the fivefold roofing were taken, then even a dwelling roofed with grass mats would not constitute a "shared sleeping place.
However, that lodging which is enclosed by a wall or by anything else—even just a cloth—starting from the ground up to the roof, is called "completely enclosed."

Regarding the bed: even if it is enclosed by a wall or similar structure one and a half cubits high at its lowest point without touching the roof-covering, it is considered "completely covered" according to the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā*.

However, for that [bed] where a greater portion of the upper area is covered and only a small part is uncovered, or where a greater portion is enclosed on all sides and only a small part is not, [it is considered completely covered].
If it is unenclosed, this is called "mostly covered and mostly enclosed.
Indeed, if a building possessing these characteristics—even if it is a seven-storied palace, or a four-sided hall with a hundred rooms—is a single precinct, it is reckoned as a single bed.
With reference to that, it was said: "On the fourth day, when the sun has set..."

“If a monk lies down while the sun has not yet set and he is lying down, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya),” and so forth. In that case, it is an offense of expiation by the mere act of lying down.
However, if there are several novices and one monk, there is an offense of expiation for each number of novices.
If they lie down repeatedly, rising again and again, for each such instance of action, there is an offense for the monk.
Regarding the offense: when a bhikkhu repeatedly rises up and lies down, it is an offense for the bhikkhu alone by virtue of his own action.
However, if several bhikkhus and one sāmaṇera all commit an offense together, it is still an offense for the bhikkhus even by virtue of their repeated rising and lying down.
This same principle applies even when both groups consist of several individuals.
Furthermore, in this context, a tetrad concerning "dwelling in one place" and so forth should also be understood.
For whoever, in a single dwelling, shares a sleeping place for three nights with even a single person who is not fully ordained, from the fourth day onward, he incurs a daily offense.
This is likewise the case for whoever, in that very same dwelling, shares a sleeping place for three nights with various persons who are not fully ordained.
It applies also to one who, in various dwellings, shares a sleeping place for three nights with even a single person not fully ordained;
and it applies also to one who, having gone even a hundred leagues in various dwellings, shares a sleeping place with various persons not fully ordained—
from the fourth day onwards, there is an offense for each day.
And this offense of lying down together exists even with an animal, because of the statement: "With the exception of a bhikkhu, everyone else is called 'one who is not fully ordained'.

In that regard, the definition of an animal should be understood by the same method as that stated for the offense of sexual intercourse. Therefore, even if some animal—such as a monitor lizard, a cat, or a mongoose—enters [the bed] along with a bhikkhu...
If one sleeps in a single enclosure area within the dwelling of the Vāsanasenas,
it is considered sleeping together. However, if one enters through the hollow of a beam situated above the wall of a palace built over pillars—
where the upper floor is not connected to the wall— and sleeps inside that beam, [it is not so].
If one goes out through that very opening, there is no offense for the monk lying on the lower floor of the palace.

If there is a hole in the roof, and having entered through it and stayed inside the roof, one departs by that same way, there is an offense for one lying on the upper floor within the interior of the roof, provided they are outside the common access area; however, there is no offense for one lying on the lower floor. If...
Just as if climbing up inside a palace, they enjoy all the floors; they constitute a single area of access, and there is an offense for one who lies down anywhere within them.
When a lodging with half-walls is constructed by way of a common assembly hall, if pigeons and the like enter into the hair-mats and so forth while one is lying down—
They lie down; it is indeed an offense. If they lie down outside the enclosure but within the reach of a shout, there is no offense.

Even if the lodging consists of a hundred rooms in a multi-roomed building that is either circular or square and covered by a single roof, if one enters through a common door and [the rooms] are not separated by individual walls within the vicinity of the rooms, [then there is no offense].
They enter all the huts; even if one person who has not received full ordination is lying down in a single hut, there is an offense for all those lying down in the huts.

If the huts have openings facing each other, then even if the space above the opening is uncovered and high-walled, one lying in the opening does not commit an offense against those lying in the huts. However, if by means of the roof-covering of the huts...
It has a roof connected [to the rest of the structure]; one lying there commits an offense for all [the people inside]. Why?
Because it is entirely covered and entirely enclosed; for its enclosure is indeed the enclosure of the inner chamber itself.
It is by this very principle that the offenses at the four gate-towers of the Lohapāsāda are mentioned in the commentaries.

As for what is stated in the *Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā*: "There is no offense if it is in an unenclosed front area," this was said with reference to the *kathina* enclosure intended as the front area on the ground without a walkway (*jagati*).
And as for what is stated there, "on the ground without a walkway," that refers to the individual dwellings with a single roof in the city of Andhaka.

This is not found in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), nor does it accord with the Canon (*pāḷi*). For even a dwelling ten cubits high does not constitute the measure for a "dwelling" (*jagati*) in this context.
Therefore, that which is stated there in the second training rule—after giving the measurement of a dwelling—"this is what is called a single-roofed enclosed space"—is not to be accepted.
As for those dwellings arranged as one-hall, two-hall, three-hall, or four-hall structures...
In the case of large palaces, it is possible for one who has washed his feet in one place to walk all the way around;

yet even there, he is not exempt from the offense of sleeping together. If, however, a boundary has been demarcated at each respective location, the offense occurs only within a single contiguous area.
In the middle of a plastered pavilion provided with two doors, they build a wall;
having entered by one door, if an unordained person sleeps in one section and a bhikkhu sleeps in the other, there is no offense.
Even if there is a hole in the wall large enough for a lizard or similar creature to enter, and lizards sleep in one section, there is likewise no offense.

For a house with a breach does not become what is called "having a single precinct. If they construct a door by cutting through the middle of the wall, there is an offense because of its status as having a single precinct.
Even if they close that door with a door-leaf and sleep there, it is still an offense.
For by closing the door, the house does not become what is called "having multiple precincts," nor does the door cease to be a door. Indeed, the door-leaf may be opened or closed at will.
It was made for the purpose of use, not for the purpose of interrupting use. However, if they close that door again with bricks, it becomes a non-door;
it remains within the very same previous distinct zone (nānūpacāra). There is a cetiya-hall with a long entrance.
One door is on the inside and one is on the outside; between the two doors, one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna) [enters] into the cetiya-hall.
If one commits an offense while lying down, it is because of the single access (ekūpacāra).
In this regard, as for the question of whether this "single access versus multiple access" distinction is mentioned in the Udosita training rule (*sikkhāpada*), here it is stated:
"A 'bed' (*seyyā*) means entirely covered and entirely enclosed, or mostly covered and mostly enclosed."

Only this much was stated: "The womb with its doors closed is entirely enclosed; therefore, there is an offense for one who lies inside it together [with another], but no offense for one who lies outside. He should be asked:
"But why is there an offense for one who lies outside when the door is not closed? Because the front part is completely covered along with the womb.
“But if the interior of the womb is enclosed, is the roof destroyed? “It is not destroyed;
it is simply that the entire front opening is not covered along with the interior. “Is the enclosure destroyed? Certainly he will say, “It is not destroyed;
the vicinity is enclosed by a door. Even if one goes this far, one will eventually return to the very same distinction between a single vicinity and various vicinities.

Furthermore, if the meaning were easily understood from the mere phrasing alone, then based on the expression "completely covered," a bed would have to be considered "covered" only by one of the five types of coverings and not by another. This being the case, there would be no offense in instances such as beds covered with mats;
consequently, the very purpose for which the training rule was established would be lost. Let it be lost.
Whether it has been stated or not, how is that which has not been stated to be understood? Or who says, "That which has not been stated must be understood"?

For this has indeed been stated among the undetermined rules: "A concealed seat is one that is concealed by a wall, or a door, or a mat, or a screen, or a tree, or a pillar, or a stack of grain, or by anything whatsoever. Therefore...
Just as in that case whatever is covered remains covered, so too should it be understood here. Therefore,
whether the dwelling is small or large, connected with another or unconnected,
long, circular, square, single-storied, or multi-storied— whatever constitutes a single enclosure— [is considered one dwelling].
In all cases, when it is entirely covered and entirely enclosed by any means whatsoever,
or mostly covered and mostly enclosed, there is an offense of sleeping together. Regarding the statement,
"When it is half-covered and half-enclosed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," here [the case] refers to that which is entirely covered and half-enclosed.
In such cases as these, it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that there is only a *dukkaṭa* offense. However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it says:

"In a place entirely enclosed (*sabbacchanne*) or mostly enclosed (*yebhuyyenaparicchanne*), there is a *pācittiya*; in a place entirely enclosed or half-enclosed (*upaḍḍhaparicchanne*), there is a *pācittiya*;

in a place mostly covered (*yebhuyyenachanne*) or half-covered (*upaḍḍhaparicchanne*), there is a *pācittiya*; in a place entirely covered or mostly covered (*yebhuyyenachanne*), there is a *pācittiya*; in a place entirely covered..."
"It is stated: 'If half-covered, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya); if mostly covered and half-covered, there is an offense of expiation;
together with the offense of expiation mentioned in the Pāḷi, there are seven offenses of expiation.

Furthermore: 'If entirely covered and slightly enclosed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); if mostly covered and slightly enclosed, there is an offense of wrong-doing; if entirely enclosed and slightly covered, [there is an offense of wrong-doing].'"

It is said: "There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); when it is mostly covered and slightly uncovered, there is an offense of wrong-doing; together with the [initial] offense of wrong-doing mentioned in the text, there are five offenses of wrong-doing.
"When it is half-covered and slightly uncovered, there is no offense; when it is half-uncovered and slightly covered, there is no offense."
“There is no offense when it is partially covered and partially enclosed;
and here, the description of a *senāmaṇḍapa* applies to that which is entirely covered and entirely unenclosed. By this it should also be understood:
“Just as a foundation does not lose its status as an enclosure. The remainder is self-evident.

The origin of the offense concerning the wool of a goat: it originates from both body and body-and-mind; it is an action (kiriyā); it is not a liberation through perception (no-saññā-vimokkha); it is without thought (acittaka); it is an offense by transgression of the rule (paṇṇatti-vajja); it is bodily action (kāya-kamma);

it involves three types of consciousness (ticitta) and three types of feeling (tivedanā). This is the fifth training rule on sharing a sleeping place. 6. Commentary on the Second Training Rule on Sharing a Sleeping Place.
55. In the second training rule on lying down in a common dwelling (*sahaseyya*): "A guest-house" (*āvasathāgāra*) means a lodging for visitors.
"Has been prepared" (*paññattaṃ hoti*) means it has been set aside having been built out of a desire for merit.
"He approached that woman" means he approached her after hearing from people that a guest-house had been prepared in such-and-such a place. "Fragrant with perfumes" (*gandhagandhinī*)...
The scent of fragrances such as agarwood, saffron, and so forth is "scent-scent" (*gandhagandha*); since she possesses that, she is "possessing scent-scent" (*gandhagandhinī*).
"Having set aside her cloth" means she did so thinking, "Perhaps even while he is seeing this disfigurement of hers, lust might arise in him.
"Having cast down" means having thrown it downward. "Transgression" (*accaya*) means an offense. "He has transgressed against me" means...
It occurs having surpassed and overcome me. The remainder should be understood according to the method stated in the first training rule (sikkhāpada).
This indeed is the distinction: whereas in the first training rule the offense occurs on the fourth day, here it occurs even on the first day.
[This applies] when one has sexual intercourse with a female spirit (*yakkhinī*) appearing in visible form, or with a female animal (*tiracchānagatitthi*).
In this case, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). There is no offense for the others. The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other factors are exactly like those of the first [offense].
This concludes the sixth training rule concerning sleeping on the same bed. 7.
Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Teaching the Dhamma.
60. In the seventh training rule: “Housewife” means the mistress of the house. “At the door of the dwelling” means at the main gate of the residence.
“The daughter-in-law of the house” means the daughter-in-law in that house. “At the door of the chamber” means at the door of the inner room.

“With a clear voice” means with a well-articulated sound. “With an open [voice]” means very distinct and unrestrained. “The Dhamma should be taught” refers to this [Dhamma] distinguished by the refuges, the precepts, and so forth.
The Dhamma should be spoken. "To understand" means to comprehend. "By a wise person in human form" means by a wise man;
even though he has taken on a human form, he is not a *yakkha*, nor a *peta*, nor an animal.
66. There is no offense for one who stands together with a wise person in human form, even if [she speaks] much.
There is no offense for one who teaches the Dhamma. "With five or six words" means there is no offense for one who teaches using five or six words.
In this context, one verse-line constitutes one word; thus, the measure of a "word" should be understood in this way throughout.
If he wishes to speak the Aṭṭhakathā, the *Dhammapada*, or the narratives of the Jātakas and so forth, [he may do so] provided it does not exceed five or six words.
It is appropriate to speak. When speaking together with the Pāḷi, one should speak without exceeding six words—namely, one word from the Pāḷi and five from the Aṭṭhakathā.
For here too, every aspect of the teaching (dhamma) is precisely that which was explained under the heading of "reciting the words" (padasodhamma).
"He teaches in that" means he teaches at that moment; or else, this locative case is used in the sense of the dative.
The meaning is that he teaches it to her. "To another woman" means that having taught one, he teaches yet another who has come along;
thus, while sitting on a single seat, he teaches even a hundred thousand women.
It is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī-aṭṭhakathā*: "To the women sitting together, I shall teach one verse to each of you. This refers to...

If she says, “Listen,” and he teaches, there is no offense. It is permissible to speak after having made the intention and informed her, thinking, “First I will recite one verse for each [woman],” but not afterwards.
Regarding the phrase “he asks a question; being asked a question, he speaks”:
a woman asks, “Venerable sir, what does the Dīghanikāya illuminate? Being thus asked a question...
If a bhikkhu recites the entire Dīghanikāya, there is no offense. The rest here is of obvious meaning. Regarding the origin of the training rule on reciting the words:

it originates from speech and from speech-and-mind; it is an action that is not non-action; it is not a liberation through perception; it is without mental involvement; it is an offense by formal rule (paṇṇattivajja); it is verbal action; it involves three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
This is the seventh training rule concerning the teaching of the Dhamma.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Proclamation of What Has Occurred (Bhūtārocanasikkhāpada) 67.

Regarding the eighth training rule, whatever needs to be said concerning the discussion of the subject matter is entirely according to the method already stated in the commentary on the fourth *pārājika*.
This is the only distinction: in that case they proclaimed what was non-existent (*abhūta*), whereas here it is what has actually occurred (*bhūta*). Even though it has occurred...
It was the worldlings (*puthujjana*) who reported this, not the noble ones (*ariya*). For among the noble ones, there is no such thing as "premeditated speech" (boasting).

However, when others were reporting their own virtues, they did not prevent them; and when conditions arose in that manner, they accepted them, being unaware of the fact that they had arisen in such a way.
But in the passage beginning with, "Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One," it refers to those [who have attained] the superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*).
They spoke in praise [of him], and it should be understood that they reported this.
When asked, "But is it true for you, monks?", they all admitted, "It is true, Blessed One. For even among the Noble Ones (ariya), there exists a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma) that is real.
Then the Blessed One, because he was in the midst of the Noble Ones, did not say, "You foolish men," but rather, "How is it, monks, that you..."

Having said this, he spoke the words beginning with, “For the sake of the belly,” and so forth. In that regard, because the Noble Ones—when questioned by people who had gained faith after hearing from others, “Venerable sir, it is said that you are a stream-enterer,” and so on—did not perceive any danger in what had not yet been prescribed as a training rule, they confessed their own and others’ attainment of distinction due to the purity of their minds.
By those who thus confessed, [the training rules were subsequently laid down].

And even when those others, for the sake of their own bellies, spoke in praise of superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) and thereby procured alms-food, it was as if they themselves had spoken in praise of superhuman states for the sake of their own bellies—even though they accepted that food with a pure mind.
Therefore, by way of a comprehensive principle, [the Blessed One said]: "How indeed, monks, can you...?"
“For the sake of their bellies, you will speak in praise of superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) to householders,” he said.

The remainder is exactly like the case in the fourth *pārājika* rule. In the analysis of the training rule (*sikkhāpadavibhaṅga*), the only difference is that whereas there [in the previous rule] it was a *pārājika* and a *thullaccaya*, here, because the act has actually occurred, it is a *pācittiya* and a *dukkaṭa*. The rest is according to the method already stated.
77. “He reports what is true to one who is ordained”—this is said specifically with reference to a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma).
For at the time of final Nibbāna, or even when being drawn along [to the funeral pyre], it is permissible to report what is true to one who is ordained.

However, it is also permissible to report qualities such as learning, mastery of the scriptures, and virtue even to one who is not ordained. There is no offense for a first offender. “For one who is insane,” etc.
This, however, has not been stated here. Why? Because for those possessed of right view, there is no insanity or derangement of mind.

For it has also been examined in the *Mahāpaccarī*: "If one who has attained jhāna becomes insane when that jhāna has lapsed, even in his case an absence of offense cannot be said on account of 'speaking what is true,' because of the very non-existence of [the state] being true. The rest is self-evident.
This offense called *bhūtārocana* (reporting what has occurred) arises from three origins not previously mentioned: from body, from speech, and from both body and speech.
It is an action (*kiriya*), not associated with liberation through insight (*nosaññāvimokkha*), without consciousness (*acittaka*), and an offense by formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*).
It is bodily action and verbal action; it is associated with two types of consciousness—wholesome and indeterminate—and is associated with two feelings—pleasant and neutral.
The eighth training rule concerning the misrepresentation of what has occurred. 9. Commentary on the ninth training rule concerning the misrepresentation of a grave offense:
In the ninth training rule—“grave offenses” refers to the four *pārājika* rules and the thirteen *saṅghādisesa* rules.

Regarding this passage, it is stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) that "the *pārājikas* were mentioned for the purpose of showing the meaning of the term *duṭṭhulla*, whereas the *saṅghādisesa* is what is intended here. Concerning this, the following investigation arises:
if there were no offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for one who reports a *pārājika*, then just as the sound of "fully ordained" (*upasampanna*) is the same for both monks and nuns, where—
A nun is not intended [by the term]; in that context, with the exception of a monk, the remainder is called "one who is not fully ordained.
Likewise here, although the terms *pārājika* and *saṅghādisesa* are equally grave offenses (*duṭṭhulla*), if the *pārājika* were not intended, then it should have been stated simply as:
"A grave offense is the thirteen *saṅghādisesas*. In that case, it would be so.
“One who has fallen into a *pārājika* offense has fallen away from the state of being a monk; therefore, one who confesses his offense incurs a *dukkaṭa*.
If this were the case, even one who reviles [another] would incur a *dukkaṭa*, whereas he actually incurs only a *pācittiya*.
For it has been said: “A person is impure when he has committed one or another *pārājika* offense; if... [he confesses it]...”
"If one who holds an impure view, having obtained permission, speaks with the intention of reviling, it is an offense of abusive speech (*omasavāda*).
Thus, when the text is examined, even for one who proclaims a *pārājika* offense, only a *pācittiya* is seen.
Although it is so seen, nevertheless, because it is stated in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), the masters of the commentaries alone are the authority here, not [the literal text].
There is another consideration. We have also stated previously: “The Dhamma and Vinaya were spoken by the Buddha, and they are understood exactly as such by his sons,” and so forth.
For the teachers of the commentaries (aṭṭhakathācariyā) know the intention of the Buddha.
This should also be understood by this method. For it is said: “Except by the consent of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. By the consent of the bhikkhus...
Furthermore, the announcement was authorized by the Blessed One for the sake of future restraint and for the purpose of not committing such an offense again;
it was not for the purpose of proclaiming the mere disrepute of that bhikkhu, nor for the purpose of prohibiting his establishment in the Teaching.
Moreover, for one who has committed a *pārājika* offense, there is no such thing as "bhikkhu-hood" simply by virtue of not committing that same kind of offense again.

It exists. Therefore, what is stated in the commentaries—that "the *pārājika* rules were spoken for the purpose of showing the meaning of the term *duṭṭhulla*, whereas the *saṅghādisesa* is what is intended here"—is indeed well-said. 80.
Regarding the passages beginning with "there is the authorization of the monks (*bhikkhusammuti*) as a limit for an offense," this which is called the "authorization of the monks" [is as follows]:
This [rule] has not been mentioned anywhere else; however, because it is stated here, it should be understood that when the Saṅgha sees a monk who repeatedly commits offenses,
it may— out of a desire for his welfare, thinking, "In this way he will attain restraint in the future through shame and dread of blame toward others"—
perform the act after having requested permission three times.
82. "One who reports a non-gross offense commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" means that for one reporting any of the five classes of offenses, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated that even for one reporting a *pārājika* offense, there is only an offense of wrong-doing.
Regarding the phrase "misconduct, whether gross or non-gross, of one not fully ordained," here the first five training rules constitute gross misconduct.

The emission [of semen] is transgression (*ajjhācāra*); the rest are grave offenses (*duṭṭhulla*). However, it is said that for him, the emission of semen, physical contact, a grave offense, and acting for one's own sake constitute transgression. 83. "He reports the matter" means:
"This person has committed the emission of semen; he has committed a grave offense; he has acted for his own sake."

There is no offense for one who says, "He has committed [an offense]; he has committed bodily contact. Regarding the phrase "he reports an offense," there is no offense if one says, "This person has committed a *pārājika*, a *saṅghādisesa*, a *thullaccaya*, a *pācittiya*, a *pāṭidesanīya*, a *dukkaṭa*, or a *dubbhāsita*.
Or if one says, "Having emitted semen, this person has committed a *saṅghādisesa*," and so forth.
However, according to this method, the offense belongs only to one who reports the offense by connecting it with the basis [of the rule]. The rest here is self-evident. It has three origins:

it originates from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. It is an action; it is liberated by perception; it is accompanied by consciousness; it is a worldly transgression; it is bodily action and verbal action; it is an unwholesome state of mind; and it is painful feeling.
This is the ninth training rule concerning the reporting of a grave offense.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule on Digging the Earth (Pathavīkhaṇana-sikkhāpada) 86.
Regarding the tenth training rule: by the words “earth that has been formed” (*jātā pathavī*) and “earth that has not been formed” (*ajāta pathavī*), it shows both formed earth and unformed earth.
“With little stone” (*appapāsāṇā*): the meaning is “that in which there are few stones. Thus is the sense.
It should be observed. In this context, stones are to be understood as those larger than the size of a fist;
pebbles are the size of a fist. Potsherds are fragments of broken vessels. Gravel is coarse sand. Sand is simply fine sand.
"Predominantly dust" means that two of the three portions are dust, while one portion consists of any one of the others, such as stones. "Even when not burnt" means...
It was not burnt in various ways, such as by being placed on a hearth, in a pan for baking, in a potter’s kiln, or in a pit. However, that [earth] does not exist separately;
it should be understood as being one of the types of pure sand and so forth. "For the most part gravel" means there was a greater amount of gravel.
It is said that after having a single basketful brought from the belly of an elephant and washed in a trough, the earth was found to be mostly gravel.
Having understood this, the monks themselves dug a lotus pond.

As for the two phrases in the middle, "little dust, a small amount," these mostly enter into the five [categories] beginning with stone; indeed, this is a demonstration of the subdivisions of those very two.
Regarding the rule, "If one digs oneself, there is an offense of *pācittiya*," here it should be understood that for every blow [with a tool], there is a *pācittiya* offense. Once.
"Having been commanded, he digs even much": even if he digs for the entire day, there is only one *pācittiya* offense for the one who gave the command.
However, if he is lazy, he must be commanded again and again. For each time he commands him and he has him dig, there is a *pācittiya* for every word [of command].
This, first of all, is the commentary on the canonical text (*pāḷivaṇṇanā*).
This, however, is the decision independent of the canonical text: if one says, "Dig a lotus pond," it is permissible;
for only when it has been dug does it truly become a "lotus pond," and therefore this is an allowable expression.
This same principle applies to such phrases as "Dig a reservoir," "a lake," or "a pit. However, one may say, "Dig this spot," or "Dig a lotus pond in this spot."
It is not permissible. It is permissible to say, without specifying, “Dig up the bulb; dig up the root.
It is not permissible to say, “Dig up this creeper; dig up the bulb or the root in this spot.
When those cleaning a lotus pond are able to scoop out thin mud with buckets, it is permissible to remove it, but thick mud is not permissible [to remove].
Mud dried by the sun cracks; in that case, it is proper to remove only that which is not connected to the earth below.
Where water has flowed, there is what is called a "water-film" (*udakapappaṭaka*); it moves when struck by the wind, and it is proper to remove that.
If the bank of a lotus pond or similar body of water has broken and fallen into the vicinity of the water, and if it has been submerged for at least four months, [it is proper to remove it].
It is permissible to cut or break it, but not after four months have passed.
However, if it falls directly into water, it is permissible even if it remains there for more than four months, because it has fallen into water and thus remains in water.
If they dig a trench on a stone surface, and if fine dust falls there first and is then covered by rain, [it is permissible].
After the lapse of four months, it comes to be reckoned as unconsecrated earth.
When the water has dried up, while they are cleaning the drain, it is not permitted to disturb that [earth].
If it was first filled with water and only afterwards did dust fall upon it, it is permitted to disturb it; for even when it rains there, the rain falls only upon the water.
On a stone slab there is fine dust; when it rains, it becomes moist, and even that must not be disturbed for the duration of the four months.
However, if an anthill has arisen on a slope where no work has been done, it is permissible to disturb it as one pleases.
If it arises in the open air, it is permissible to disturb it only after the minimum period of four months has passed. This also applies to the clay of an anthill situated on trees and such.
The same principle applies here. This same principle applies to ant-hills, dung, mouseholes, dogholes, cow-hoof marks, and so forth.

A "cow-hoof mark" (gokaṇṭaka) is said to be the mud where a cow's hoof has been cut into the ground. However, if it is connected to the underlying soil at its base, it is not permissible even for a single day.
Even in a ploughed area, for one who takes up a lump of clay merely cut by a plough, [the same rule applies].
The same principle applies here. An old dwelling may have its roof missing or its roof destroyed;
if it has been abandoned for more than four months, it is considered as having become mere earth. Whatever remains—be it bricks, rafters, or other such materials—is [permissible] when one thinks:
"I am taking the brick, the rafter, the base of the wall, the floor-mat, or the stone pillar."
It is permissible to take [clay] with the perception, "I am taking it. If clay falls along with that [object], there is no offense.
However, for one who takes clay from a wall, there is an offense. If he takes whatever portions are not yet baked, there is no offense.
If there is a heap of clay within the house, and on a certain day they cover the house while it is still wet, if the whole...
After the lapse of four months, it becomes "earth that has arisen" (*jātapathavī*) itself.

If only its upper portion has become fermented while the interior remains unfermented, then whatever portion has fermented may be removed by the stewards using formal terminology; the remainder may be used as one pleases.
For when moistened with water, it becomes a single mass of "earth that has arisen," whereas the other [unfermented portion] does not.
In the open air, there is a mud wall; if it has been standing for more than four months, it is reckoned as "earth that has formed.
In that case, it is permissible to take the soil adhering to it by touching it with a wet hand.
If it is a brick wall, and it stands mostly on a site of gravel, it is permissible to disturb it as one likes. In the open air...
It is not permissible to grasp a pillar of a standing pavilion by shaking it here and there or by shaking up the earth;
it is permissible only to lift it straight up. The same rule applies to one who grasps another dry tree or a dry stump.
When people go about rolling stones or trees on poles for the purpose of construction work, [they do so in this manner].
In that case, if the earth is broken, there is no offense if they proceed with a pure mind.

However, if they intend to break the earth precisely by means of that pretext, it is an offense. The same principle applies to those dragging branches and such, as well as those splitting wood in the earth.
On the ground, it is not permitted to strike or drive anything into it, such as bone needles or thorns.
It is likewise not permitted to urinate with the intention, "I will split the earth by the force of my urine-stream";

if one does so, the earth splits and there is an offense. It is also not permitted to smooth uneven ground with a broom, thinking, "I will make it level"; it must be done only with the edge of the bowl.

Indeed, it must be swept clean. Some people beat the ground with their walking-sticks, scratch it with their big toes, or pace back and forth repeatedly breaking the ground, thinking, "We shall show the place for walking";
all of this is not permitted. However, one who practices the ascetic’s duty for the sake of exerting energy may walk back and forth with a pure mind.
It is permissible [to rub] if they think, "We shall wash our hands," yet it is not permissible if they rub them against the ground.
However, it is permissible for one who does not rub them to place the wet hand on the ground and take up dust.
Some who are afflicted by diseases such as ringworm or scabies rub their limbs and members against broken riverbanks and the like; this is not permissible.
87. “Digs or causes to dig” means that one digs oneself, or causes another to dig, even as much as with a toe or a broom-handle.
“Breaks or causes to break” means that one breaks oneself, or causes another to break, even as much as when throwing out water. “Burns or causes to burn” means even as much as a bowl.
While cooking, one either burns it oneself or causes another to burn it. For as many places where one gives fire or causes fire to be given, there are that many *pācittiya* offenses.
Even when cooking in a bowl, it must be cooked in the very same place where it was previously cooked.
It is not permitted to place fire on ground that has not been burnt. However, fire may be placed upon the rim of the bowl used for cooking.
It is permissible to place [the fire] on top. If one places it on top of logs, that fire, while burning them, goes on to burn the earth;
this is not permissible. The same principle applies to bricks, potsherds, and so forth.
For there too, it is permissible to place it only on top of the bricks and such. Why? Because they are non-fuel (anupādāna). It is not...
For these [materials] are reckoned as fuel for fire. It is not permissible to give fire even to dry stumps, dry trees, and so forth.
However, if one gives it with the thought, "I shall extinguish it before it reaches the ground and then depart," it is permissible.
If he is unable to extinguish it afterwards, there is no offense because it was beyond his power. While walking along carrying a torch in his hand...

If he causes it to fall on the ground while it is burning, there is no offense. It is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that it is permissible to make a fire by placing fuel in the very spot where it has fallen.
And it is stated in that same work that on burnt earth, it is permissible to disturb as much of the area as has been permeated by heat.
However, regarding a monk who is unaware [of the danger] and [uses] a fire-drill set...
Having produced fire and held it up with his hand, he says, "What shall I do? He should be told, "Heat it.
If he says, "My hand is burning," he should be told, "Do it in such a way that it does not burn.
However, he must not be told, "Throw it on the ground. Even if he throws it while his hand is burning, this is because he did not throw it with the intention, "I will burn the earth."
There is no offense. However, it is stated in the *Kurundi* that it is permissible to make a fire at the place where [the earth] has fallen away.
88. Regarding "there is no offense in knowing this," etc., [it means]:
"Know the pit for this pillar; know the great clay; know the husk-clay; give the great clay; give the husk-clay; bring the clay; [bring] the soil."

The meaning should be understood as follows: "Bring it; there is need for clay, there is need for soil; prepare a permissible pit for this pillar; make this clay permissible; make this soil permissible.
Regarding "unintentionally": this refers to one who is rolling stones, trees, and so forth, or who moves about repeatedly striking with a wooden staff.
When the earth breaks, because one did not intentionally break it with the thought, "I shall break it by that means," it is called "broken unintentionally.
Thus, for one who breaks it unintentionally, there is no offense. "By way of non-mindfulness" means:
being distracted, while conversing with someone about something else, one stands scratching the earth with a toe or a walking stick.
Thus, there is no offense for one who scratches or breaks [the earth] while lacking mindfulness. "Without knowing" means:
if one does not know that the covered earth within the dwelling is "unfit earth," but disturbs it with the perception that it is "fit earth";
or if one does not know, "I am digging, breaking, or burning it," but merely uses spades and so forth for the purpose of guarding [the property].
If he sets it aside, or if his hand is burning and he lets go of the fire—there is no offense for one who does not know this. The rest is self-evident. It has three origins:

it originates from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. It is an action; it is liberated by perception; it involves consciousness; it is an offense of formal rule; it is bodily action and verbal action;
it consists of three types of consciousness and three types of feeling. This is the tenth training rule concerning digging the earth.
The first chapter, on False Speech, is completed according to the sequence of the commentary. 2.
The Chapter on Living Plants.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Living Plants.
89. Regarding the first training rule of the *Senāsanavagga*: "Not taking it up" means not accepting his words.

"He struck the boy’s arm" means that, being unable to restrain the raised axe, he struck the boy’s arm right at the root of the breast while the boy was lying in a divine tree-stump mansion obtained from the Great King, beyond the range of sight of ordinary people.
"Cut it down. This is the brief commentary on the passage beginning with "It is not fitting for me [to do so]": it is said that on the fast days in the Himalayas there is an assembly of deities;
there they ask about the "duty of trees"—that is, "Are you established in the duty of trees or not?
The "duty of trees" consists in the tree-deity's refraining from mental malice when the tree is being cut down.
In that regard, whichever deity was not established in the duty toward the tree was not permitted to enter the assembly of deities.
Thus, that deity saw this danger— the condition of not being established in the duty toward the tree— and, following the teaching on the Dhamma previously heard in the presence of the Blessed One,
she recollected the Tathāgata’s past conduct during the time of Chaddanta and other such occasions.
It occurred to her: “This is not fitting for me... [as before] ...I should not take his life. Then she thought:
“What if I were to report this matter to the Blessed One? This reflection arose because she considered: “This monk has a wife and children;
surely the Blessed One, having heard of this transgression of his, will establish a boundary and lay down a training rule.”
"Ahosi. "Sace ajja tvaṃ devate" means "If you, O deity, today. "Pasaveyyāsi" means "you would produce," "you would give rise to.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, in order to instruct that deity, said:
"One who indeed restrains arisen anger, as one would a racing chariot;..."
“Him I call a charioteer; others are merely holders of the reins.
Thus he spoke this verse. At the conclusion of the verse, that deity was established in the fruit of stream-entry. Then the Blessed One, teaching the Dhamma to the assembled company, said:
“He who restrains arisen anger with medicines, as one would [neutralize] the spreading venom of a snake with antidotes...”
"Thus the bhikkhu abandons both this shore and the far shore, just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.
Thus he spoke this verse. Therein, the first verse is included in the *Dhammapada*, the second in the *Sutta Nipāta*, while the narrative background (*vatthu*) is found in the *Vinaya*.
Then, while the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma, [he reached] the dwelling place of that deity.
While surveying the surroundings, he saw a suitable place and said, "Go, devatā, to such-and-such a spot where there is a secluded tree;
approach it. It is said that this tree was not in the province of Āḷavi, but within the enclosure of Jetavana;
because the young deva who had possessed it had passed away, it was called "secluded. From that time on—
Moreover, that deity, having received her favor from the Perfectly Enlightened One, became an attendant of the Buddha.

Whenever there was an assembly of deities, when the high-ranking deities arrived, other deities of lesser rank would withdraw as far as the great ocean, the world-system mountains, and the surrounding mountain ranges.
But this one, remaining seated right in her own dwelling place, listened to the Dhamma. Furthermore—
In the first watch of the night, the monks ask questions; in the middle watch, the deities [ask questions]. Sitting right there, he hears all of that.

Even the Four Great Kings, having come to attend upon the Blessed One, see that deity as they depart and then go on their way. 90. Regarding the phrase “destruction of the forest of beings” (*bhūtagāmapātabyatā*):
here, those that exist and have existed are called “beings” (*bhūta*); they are born, they grow, and they have been born.
"And increased" is the meaning. "Village" (*gāma*) means a heap; a village of beings is a "village of beings" (*bhūtagāma*). Or, beings themselves are the village, thus it is a "village of beings.
This is a designation for established green grass, trees, and so forth. "The state of being drinkable" is "drinkability" (*pātabyatā*);

the meaning is that they are to be enjoyed at will through cutting, breaking, and so on. Regarding that "drinkability of the village of beings," the locative case is used in the sense of the cause (*nimitta*).
The meaning is: "On account of the destruction of the community of living beings" (*bhūtagāma-pātabyatā-hetu*);

it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) on account of the cutting and so forth of the community of living beings. Now, having classified that community of living beings, he says: "The community of living beings consists of the five kinds of seeds," and so forth.

Therein, regarding the phrase "the community of living beings": having raised up the term "community of living beings," he speaks this in order to show what it is that, when present, constitutes a community of living beings.
“It is said in the commentaries: ‘There are five kinds of seeds. Even so, [the definitions] such as ‘or whatever others there are that grow from roots’ and so forth do not harmonize.
For root-seeds and the like do not grow *in* roots and so forth; rather, those things growing from roots and so forth are what constitute seeds.
Therefore, the explanation here should be understood in this way: ‘What is called a group of living beings (bhūtagāma)...’”
This is the term to be analyzed. "Five" is the delimitation of its analysis. "Born from seeds" (*bījajātāni*) is an indication of the phenomena so delimited.
Its meaning is as follows: "born from seeds" means those produced by seeds; this is a designation for trees and the like. According to another method:

they are both "seeds" (*bījāni*) and "born" (*vijātāni*), meaning produced or developed with leaves and roots, thus they are "born from seeds. By this [term], [the inclusion of] moist sand and so forth—
This includes a collection of ginger and other such plants whose leaves and roots have already emerged.
Now, in order to show those seeds by which trees and so forth are born—and are thus called "born from seeds" (*bījajāta*)—he says, beginning with "root-seed" (*mūlabīja*).
Their enumeration is quite evident. In the detailed explanation (*niddesa*), it says: "Or whatever others there are that are born from the root, grow from the root."
Here, by means of that which is produced from a seed, the seed itself is demonstrated; therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows:

moreover, there are other roots as well—distinguished as *ālu*, *kaseruka*, *mālu*, *utpala*, *puṇḍarīka*, *kuvalaya* tubers, *pāṭali* roots, and so forth—from which trees, creepers, climbing plants, and the like are born and produced; those [roots] in which they are both born and produced.

And that, as well as turmeric and so forth mentioned in the Pāḷi—all this is called "root-propagated seed" (*mūlabīja*). The same method applies to "stem-propagated seeds" (*khandhabīja*) and the others.
