Among the miscellaneous stem-propagated seeds, however, the *ambāṭaka*, *indasāla*, *nuhī*, *pāḷibhadda*, *kaṇikāra*, and so forth are stem-propagated seeds;
the *amūlavalli*, *caturassavallika*, *kaṇavīra*, and so forth are joint-propagated seeds (*phaḷubīja*); and the *makaci*, *sumana*, *jayasumana*, and so forth are tip-propagated seeds (*aggabīja*).
The mango, rose-apple, jackfruit, *ṭhiti* (or *ṭhi*), and so forth are to be understood as seed-propagated plants (*bījabīja*). 92.

Now, regarding what was stated—"an offense entailing expiation for the destruction of a living plant"—he says "perceiving a seed as a seed," and so forth, in order to show the distinction between offense and non-offense based on perception, as well as the distinctions within the act of destruction.
In that context, just as [in the case of] boiled rice of *sāli* paddy...
In such passages as "eating," rice-grains that have been cooked into boiled rice are called "boiled rice of rice-grains" (*sālīnaṃ odano*);
in the same way, it should be understood that the category of living beings (*bhūtagāma*) produced from seeds is called "seed" (*bīja*).

However, that which is referred to in such passages as "abstaining from the destruction of seed and plant life" (*bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhā paṭivirato*), where seed has been set aside after being cleared of living beings—that is an object of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭavatthu*). Alternatively, that which is this...
“‘A group of living beings’ (bhūtagāma)”: this is the opening phrase of the analysis of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
Having connected with that, if one perceives as seed what is called a "group of living beings," and having taken up a knife or other tools, one cuts it oneself or causes another to cut it;
or, having taken up stones or the like, one breaks it oneself or causes another to break it; or [uses] fire...
"Having brought it together, one cooks it oneself or has it cooked by another; there is an offense of *pācittiya*.

This is how the meaning should be understood here. However, if one were to take the literal sense [of the rule], it would have to be stated that there is a *pācittiya* for the act of consuming seeds—such as cutting them—that are distinct from living plants (*bhūtagāma*). But this is not so.
This is the analytical explanation here: for one who destroys a grove of living plants (*bhūtagāma*), there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*);
for one who destroys any of the five kinds of seed-plants (*bījagāma*) that have been spared from such destruction, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

This so-called seed-plant and grove-of-living-plants exists both in water and on land. Therein, those in water consist of mustard seeds, clay, sesame seeds, and various other types, whether with leaves or without leaves.
And all species of algae, including even the water-moss (*udakapappaṭaka*), should be understood as "the community of beings" (*bhūtagāma*).
What is called water-moss is hard and rough-colored on the upper surface, while it is soft and blue-colored underneath.
Among these, for that algae whose root has grown down and is established in the earth, the earth is its location; that which moves about in the water [has the water as its location].
Regarding water: if one disturbs it by lifting it up or moving it to another place from wherever it is established on the earth, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
If one disturbs water that is flowing [over] the ground, there is likewise an offense of expiation.
However, it is permissible to bathe by splashing the water here and there with the hands, for the entire body of water is its [proper] location. Therefore, he...
Up to this point, he has been transferred to another status. However, it is not permissible to intentionally lift [the water] out of water without using water;
having lifted it together with water, it is permissible to put it back into the water again.

If it escapes through the opening of the strainer, one must have the water made allowable (*kappiya*) before consuming it. [This applies to] water-lilies, lotuses, and other such aquatic creepers and grasses.
For one who pulls [plants] out from the water, or damages them right there, it is a *pācittiya*.
For one who damages those [plants] uprooted by others, it is a *dukkaṭa*; for they are included within the category of "seed-plantings.

Even a mere bit of moss the size of a sesame seed, if pulled from the water and not yet withered, is included within the category of "tip-seeds" (*aggabīja*). In the *Mahāpaccarī* and other texts, it says: "Anantaka, sesame seeds, water-moss, and so forth..."

It is stated, "These are matters of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," yet no reason for this is seen there. In the *Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā*, it is said, "The community of living beings (*bhūtagāma*) is not complete;

therefore, it is wrong-doing. That too is not consistent, for a *pācittiya* offense is prescribed for a community of living beings, whereas wrong-doing is prescribed for a community of seeds (*bījagāma*).
A "community of living beings that is incomplete" is mentioned neither in the Canon (*pāḷi*) nor in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) as a third category.
[If one says,] "He has arrived," and then [thinks], "Now he will go to that seed-plantation," that too is not proper, because such a seed-plantation has its root in an unreal village.
Furthermore, the characteristic of the Vinaya is this: "In matters of heavy and light offenses, one should abide by the heavy.
Regarding what stands on dry land—there is what is called a "remaining green stump" of trees that have been cut down. Therein [are found] the *kakudha*, *karañja*, *piyaṅgu*, *panasa*, and so forth.
The stump of a tree that grows upward is included within the category of living beings (*bhūtagāma*). The stump of a palmyra, coconut, or similar trees does not grow upward;

it is included within the category of seeds (*bījagāma*). However, the stump of an unfruited plantain tree is included within the category of living beings, while that of a fruited one is included within the category of seeds.
Furthermore, as long as the fruited plantain tree has green leaves, it is included solely within the category of living beings.
Likewise, when a bamboo has borne fruit, it is included among the seed-plant categories. But when it withers starting from the top, it then comes under the category of seed-plant.

Under which seed-plant category? Under the category of *phaḷu*-seed (fruit-seed). What is produced from that? Nothing at all. For if anything were produced, it would come under the category of living beings (*bhūtagāma*).
When trees such as the *Indasāla* are cut down and made into a heap, even though—
From the *rāsikatadaṇḍaka* trees, branches as large as gems emerge; they are included within the category of "seed-plant life" (*bījagāma*) alone.
There, people plant them in the ground for the sake of pavilions, fences, or climbing vines.
Once their roots and leaves have emerged, they again fall under the reckoning of "living beings" (*bhūtagāma*). However, when only the roots remain...
Or, when even just the leaves have emerged, they are indeed included within the category of "seed-plant.
Whatever seeds have been placed on the ground after being sprinkled with water,
or have been set down in pots and the like after moist soil has been added— all these are still merely seeds, even when only roots or leaves have emerged.
Even if both roots and a sprout emerge above ground, as long as the sprout has not yet turned green, they are still merely seeds.

However, when the leaves of mung beans and the like have emerged, or when the rice sprouts have become green with the color of young foliage, they are included within the category of "grove of living beings" (*bhūtagāma*).
In the case of palmyra palms, first the root emerges, resembling the tusk of a boar.
Even when it has emerged, as long as the upper leaf-sheath has not come forth, it remains merely a seed-state (*bījagāma*).
When the coconut husk is split and the sprout emerges like a toothpick, as long as it does not become a blue leaf-sheath resembling a deer’s antler, it remains merely a seed-state.
Even if the root has not yet emerged, once such a leaf-sheath has been produced, it is included within the category of "beings that have no roots" (*amūlaka-bhūtagāma*).
The *ambaṭṭhi* and other such plants are to be distinguished by their similarity to rice and other grains.
As for the *vandākā* or any other plant that grows on a tree and covers it, the tree is its proper location;

for one who damages it or pulls it out from there, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). There is one rootless creeper which, like a finger-ring, winds itself around the trunks of forest thickets.

The determination for this case is as follows: When blue-green algae grows on the front of a house, a gate, a wall, a railing, a shrine, or similar places, it is classified as "seed at the tip" (*aggabīja*) as long as two or three leaves have not yet developed. Once the leaves have grown, it becomes an object for an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
Therefore, it is not permitted to apply lime plaster to such places. [This applies] when [the work is done] by one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).
It is permissible to apply a coating of oil on top of it. If dried moss remains during the hot season, it is permissible to remove it by scrubbing with a broom or similar tool.
Moss on the outside of water jars and such vessels is a matter of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*);
inside, it is not subject to censure. Even the sprouts on tooth-sticks, cakes, and so forth, are likewise not subject to censure. For this has been said: "If..."
"A wall treated with red chalk becomes stained; it should be wiped clean by moistening a cloth and squeezing it out.
Stone, stone-dust, moss, seaweed, *seleyyaka*, and so forth, when they are green and have not yet reached maturity, are grounds for an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
As for the *ahicchattaka* mushroom, as long as it remains a bud, it is a ground for an offense of wrong-doing. From the time it has flowered onwards, it is not an offense.
However, one who takes an *ahicchattaka* from an *allārukkha* tree damages the bark of the tree; therefore, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) in that case.
The same principle applies to the *pappaṭikā* (scale-like growth) of a tree as well.

But there is no offense for one who takes the *pappaṭikā* of plants such as *indasāla* or *kakudha* that remains after it has detached from the tree. The same also applies to *niyyāsa* (resin) that remains after it has detached from the tree on a dry tree.
It is permissible to take what has fallen, but it is not permissible from a living tree. The same principle applies to lac.
For one who shakes a tree and causes a withered leaf or a fully ripened flower such as the *kaṇikāra* to fall, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
The same principle applies even to one who carves letters on soft surfaces such as the trunk of an *indasāla* or *nīhī* tree, or on palm leaves grown there, by means of scratching with the hand.
It is permissible to bend down a branch to give flowers to novices who are picking them. However, one must not infuse water with those flowers.
One who wishes to infuse water should have a novice pick the flowers by lifting him up.
Likewise, one who wishes to eat fruit oneself must not bend down a fruit-bearing branch; rather, one should have a novice pick the fruit by lifting him up. Whatever [is required]...
It is not permissible to take hold of a tree or a creeper and drag it along with novice monks who are pulling it up.
However, for the purpose of encouraging them, it is permissible to grasp the tip [of the branch] as if showing the act of pulling, without actually dragging it.
Regarding those trees whose branches grow, their branches may be made allowable (*kappiya*) for the sake of fanning away flies and so forth.
If one takes [a plant] without having it made allowable (kappiya), there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for anyone who scratches it—even with a fingernail—whether on its bark or its leaf.

This same principle applies to garlic, ginger, and so forth. However, if a root grows on a plant that has been made allowable and placed in a cool spot, it is permissible to cut off the upper portion.
If a sprout grows, it is permissible to cut off the lower portion.
When the root and the sprout have grown, it is not permitted.

"Cuts or causes to be cut" means that even if one is sweeping the ground with a broom or a blade of grass, thinking "I will cut the grass," one either cuts it oneself or causes another to cut it. "Breaks or causes to be broken" means, at the very least...
Even while walking, thinking "let what is liable to break break; let what is liable to split split;
I shall show the place for walking," one intentionally steps with the feet upon grass, creepers, and so forth, either breaking them oneself or having another break them.
For even if a blade of grass or a creeper breaks while one is tying a knot, the knot must not be tied. This applies to palm trees and the like as well.
However, they strike wooden monkeys to prevent thieves from climbing up, and they bind them with thorns; it is not permissible for a bhikkhu to do such things.
If the wooden monkey is merely attached to the tree and does not cause it distress, it is permissible.
It is also permissible to say: "Cut down the tree, cut down the creeper, or pull out the bulb or the root."
Because it is unspecified. However, it is not permissible to say, "Cut this tree," and so forth, after having specified it.

Even when a name is mentioned, such statements as "Cut, break, and uproot the mango tree, the square creeper, the yam tuber, the muñja grass, or the bark of such-and-such a tree" are likewise unspecified.
Only a statement such as "This mango tree... [is considered specified].
For that which is called "determined" (niyāmita) is not permitted.

Regarding the phrase "cooks or causes to cook": even one who merely intends to cook a bowl, if he intentionally sets fire upon grass and so forth, whether he cooks it himself or causes another to cook it—all this is according to the method explained in the training rule on digging the earth.
It should be understood thus. However, it is permissible to say, "Cook the mung beans; cook the black gram," and so forth, provided one does not specify them.
It is not permissible to say, "Cook these mung beans; cook these black grams.
There is no offense in cases such as "Know this," etc., when saying, "Know this root medicine; give me either this root or this leaf."
The meaning should be understood as follows: "Bring this tree or creeper; there is need for this flower, fruit, or leaf," or "Make this tree, creeper, or fruit *kappiya* (made allowable).

To this extent, the protection of the forest-dwelling (*bhūtagāma*) is accomplished. However, when one is about to consume it, one must again have it made *kappiya* for the purpose of protecting the seed-planting (*bījagāma*).
And here, the making allowable (*kappiyakaraṇa*) should be understood according to this sutta: “I allow you, monks, to consume fruit by means of five kinds of ascetic preparations:
that which is prepared by fire, that which is prepared by a knife, that which is prepared by the nail, that which is seedless, and fifthly, that from which the seed has been removed.
Therein, “prepared by fire” means prepared or overcome by fire.
“Burnt” means scorched. “Conquered by the knife” (*satthaparijita*) means conquered, overcome, cut, or pierced by a knife.
The same method applies to what is conquered by the nail (*nakhaparijita*). Seeds that have been extracted from their husks are themselves allowable (*kappiya*).
One who makes something allowable by means of fire may use any kind of fire, such as a wood-fire or a cow-dung fire, or even a mere fragment of iron.
One must make it allowable by means of fire. Furthermore, this must be done by touching only one part [of the object] while saying, "It is allowable.
When using a knife, one must do so by showing the cutting or piercing with the point or the edge of any iron instrument whatsoever—even a needle or a nail-cutter—while saying, "It is allowable."
When making something allowable (*kappiya*) with a claw, it must not be done with a rotten claw.
However, the claws of humans, lions, tigers, leopards, monkeys, and birds are sharp; with these, it may be done. The hooves of horses, buffaloes, pigs, deer, oxen, and so forth, are too blunt;
with these, it must not be done, for even if done, it is as if not done. But elephant claws are not [like] hooves.

If there are those [who are authorized], it is permissible with them. However, those with whom it is permissible to perform [the act] must do so only after having had [the seeds] extracted—even if they were grown right there—or having had them taken away, and having shown [them] either a cut or a perforation, saying, "It is allowable" (*kappiya*).
In that regard, even if there is a heap of seeds as large as a mountain, or if a thousand trees have been cut down and made into a single mass—

Or if a large load of sugarcanes has been tied up and set aside; or if, regarding even a single seed, a tree branch, or a sugarcane, the *kappiya* (formal authorization) has been performed, then everything is considered authorized.

If the sugarcanes and pieces of wood are tied together, and one pierces a piece of wood thinking, "I will authorize the sugarcane," it is indeed permissible. However, if [one pierces] the rope or the creeper by which...
If they are bound together, he pierces them; that is not permitted. When they bring a basket filled with pieces of sugarcane, if one piece is made allowable (*kappiya*), the whole becomes allowable.

When they bring rice mixed with pepper, pakkā, and so forth, even if he pierces a grain of rice when told, "Make it allowable," it is indeed permitted. This also applies to sesame, rice, and the like.
The same method applies here. However, as for grains placed in rice gruel, they do not remain settled as a single mass;
therefore, one must pierce each individual grain and then make it *kappiya* (sanctified). In the case of fruits such as the *kapittha*, the inner pulp moves about, leaving the husk behind;
one must have it broken open and then have it made *kappiya*. If it remains a single mass, it is permissible to perform the *kappiya* rite even within the husk.

"Unintentionally" means: when one is rolling stones, trees, and so forth, or pulling a branch, or walking while striking the ground with a staff and grasses are cut, those are called "cut unintentionally" because they were not cut with the deliberate thought, "I shall cut these.
Thus, for one who cuts unintentionally, there is no offense.

"Without mindfulness" means: he stands distracted by something else, talking with someone, or cutting grass or a creeper with his big toe or his hand; for one who cuts thus without mindfulness, there is no offense. "Not knowing" means:
within this area, he does not know it is a seed-plot or a grove of living beings;
nor does he know, "I am cutting"; he merely [uses] a stake, a bundle of straw, or a hoe, a spade, or a pickaxe.
If he places it there for the purpose of concealment, or if, with his hand burning, he throws it onto the fire, and if the grass therein is either cut or burned, there is no offense.
However, in the commentary on the Pārājika regarding the human form, all the Aṭṭhakathās state:
"If a bhikkhu is overhung by a tree, or has fallen into a pit, and it is possible [to extinguish the fire] from the tree..."
"Even for the sake of one's life, one must not personally cut down a tree or dig into the earth to escape.

However, it is permissible for another bhikkhu to dig into the earth, cut down a tree, or cut a branch from a living tree and roll that tree over to let [the person] out; there is no offense. Regarding this, the reason is not...
Only this single sutta is found: “I allow you, monks, when a forest fire is burning, to set up a counter-fire and to perform a protective rite.
If this were the case, it would be impossible to find any distinction such as, “It is not permitted for oneself, but it is permitted for another.
For one who performs it for his own sake does so out of self-attachment.
If it is argued that there is no offense because one acts with an unwholesome mind while the other acts out of compassion, this too is not a valid reason.
For one may incur this offense even with a wholesome mind. However, since this has been stated in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), it cannot be refuted.
One must seek the underlying logic (*yutti*) here, or else proceed by faith in the teachers of the commentaries. The rest is self-evident.

It has three origins: it originates from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. It is functional (*kiriya*), with perception as its liberation (*saññāvimokkha*), associated with consciousness (*sacittaka*), an offense by rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), verbal action (*vacīkamma*), associated with three types of consciousness, and associated with three types of feeling.
This is the first training rule regarding plants.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Speaking Otherwise (*Aññavādakasikkhāpada*).
94. In the second training rule: "having practiced improper conduct" means having done what should not be done;

it is said that this refers to having committed an offense through the doors of body and speech. "He evades one thing with another" means he evades, conceals, or covers over one statement with another statement.
Now, showing the manner of such evasion, the text says: "Who has fallen [into an offense]? and so forth.

In this regard, the connection of the words is as follows: it is said that having seen some transgression, while being questioned by the Sangha in their midst regarding the offense with the words, "Friend, you have fallen into an offense," he says, "Who has fallen?
When told, "It is you," he says, "What have I fallen into? Then, when told, "A *pācittiya* or a *dukkaṭa*," he asks about the basis [of the offense].
He says, "In what have I fallen? When it is then stated, "In such-and-such a matter," he asks, "How have I fallen? What was I doing when I fell?
Then, when it is said, "By doing this, you fell," he says, "Whom are you speaking of? When it is then said, "We are speaking of him," he says, "What are you saying?"
Furthermore, there is this method of evasive evasion not found in the canonical texts:
when monks say, "A kahāpaṇa coin was seen in your box; why do you act so improperly? he replies, "It was clearly seen, venerable sirs, but that is not a kahāpaṇa;
it is a brass disc. Or, when they say, "You were seen drinking liquor; why do you act thus? [he likewise evades].
When told, "Venerable sir, you were clearly seen," yet saying, "This is not liquor;
it was prepared as medicine, an *ariṭṭha*," or when told, "You were seen sitting on a concealed seat with a woman; why do you do such an unseemly thing?
replying, "By whom it was seen, it was clearly seen; but there is a wise person here who is the second witness—why was he not seen?"
Whether he says, "I have seen nothing like this," when asked, or, being asked, "Have you heard anything?
he inclines his ear and says, "I did not hear," or, when asked about the ear-door, he points to the eye—he should be understood as one who evades the issue with something else.

"Let him be charged with speaking otherwise" means let him be brought to the charge of speaking otherwise; the meaning is "let him be established [in that offense]. "Let him be charged with harassment"—the same method applies here as well.
98. Regarding the offense of expiation for one who speaks otherwise or one who harasses: here, "one who speaks otherwise" (*aññavādaka*) means one who says something different [from what was asked];
this is a name for one who evades with one thing after another. "One who harasses" (*vihesaka*) means one who causes annoyance; this is a name for one who remains silent.
"Expiation" (*pācittiya*) refers to two offenses of expiation stated for these two cases.

100. "When one who speaks otherwise has not been charged" means when the formal act (*kammavācā*) has not been pronounced against the one speaking otherwise. "When one who causes vexation has been charged"—the same method applies here as well.

101. Regarding the phrases "perceiving a legitimate legal act as a legitimate legal act," and so forth: if that legal act which was performed—namely, the act of charging one who speaks otherwise or one who causes vexation—is indeed a legitimate legal act, and if that monk perceives it as a legitimate legal act, and [perceives the person] as one who speaks otherwise and as one who causes vexation...

"He commits [an offense]; then, because of that [act], there is for him an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for speaking otherwise and for harassing"—the meaning should be understood according to this method.
102. "He asks while not knowing" means that he asks, "What are you saying? I do not know," precisely because he does not know whether he has committed an offense or not.
"Or, being ill, he does not speak" means that he has such a disease in his mouth that—
He is unable to speak. Regarding the phrases "quarrel among the Saṅgha" and so forth, the meaning should be understood in this manner:
thinking, "If this is spoken in the midst of the Saṅgha, it will result in a quarrel, a dispute, or a contention for the Saṅgha;
may that not happen," he does not speak. The rest is self-evident.
It has three origins: it originates from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind.

It may be an action (*kiriya*) or it may be a non-action (*akiriya*); for one who evades with something else, there is an action, whereas for one who harasses by means of silence, there is a non-action.
It is liberated by perception, accompanied by mind, a worldly offense, bodily action and verbal action, unwholesome mind, and painful feeling.
The second training rule concerning speaking otherwise. 3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Reviling. 103. Regarding the third training rule:
"the monks reviled Dabba Mallaputta" means [accusing him] with such words as, "Dabba Mallaputta acts out of favoritism," and so forth.
The meaning is: “By speaking thus, they cause that venerable one to be despised by those bhikkhus, they cause him to be looked upon with contempt, or they cause him to be considered as inferior.
Furthermore, the grammatical characteristic here should be understood according to the rules of the science of grammar (*saddasattha*).
There is also a reading *ojjhāpenti*, which has the same meaning. *Chandāya* means by way of desire, that is, through partiality; [it refers to] their own personal friends and associates.
The intention is that he proclaims things as being excellent. "They revile" means they make it known by saying such things as, "Dabba Mallaputta acts out of favoritism," and so forth.
105. Regarding the offense of expiation (pācittiya) for reviling and censuring: here, that speech by which they censure is "censuring" (ujjhāpanaka);
and that by which they revile is "reviling" (khiyyanaka). In the case of such censuring and reviling—there is an offense of expiation in these two instances.
Two *pācittiya* rules have been stated. 106.
Regarding "reproaching" (*ujjhāpanaka*): for the ordained person who has been appointed by the Saṅgha as the assigner of lodgings, or... [etc.
...or the distributor of trifles—these terms are connected with the phrase "desiring to cause embarrassment. It means desiring to speak dispraise or bring infamy.

Regarding the phrase "desirous of doing," in the case of [the rules] beginning with "one who is fully ordained" (*upasampanna*), one must apply a change of grammatical case (vibhattivipariṇāma) to read "of one who is fully ordained. Furthermore,
in the rule "there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for one who reviles or censures," although the matrix word (*mātikāpada*) "one who censures" (*khiyyanaka*) is cited,
it is precisely the commentary (*vibhaṅga*) on this term "one who reviles" (*ujjhāpanaka*) that has already been stated.
It should be stated that, as in the training rule concerning one who speaks otherwise (*aññavādaka*), there is no other distinction;

therefore, it should be understood that this [case] has not been cited separately nor analyzed individually, but rather the conclusion alone has been made together with the others. Regarding the phrases "perceiving a legitimate legal act as a legitimate legal act" (*dhammakamme dhammakammasaññī*) and so forth:
if the formal act (*sammutikamma*) performed for that ordained person is indeed a legitimate legal act, and that monk...

If one, perceiving it as a formal act of the Dhamma (*dhammakamma*), utters censure (*ujjhāpanaka*) or disparagement (*khiyyanaka*), then for that censure and disparagement, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*);
the meaning should be understood according to this method.

Regarding the phrase "he censures or disparages one who is not fully ordained" (*anupasampannaṃ ujjhāpeti vā khiyyati vā*), here [the exception applies to] another who is fully ordained and authorized by the Saṅgha.
"To revile or despise one who is not fully ordained" means to speak disparagingly of him in his presence.

"One who is fully ordained but not authorized by the Saṅgha" refers to one who has not been authorized by a formal act (*kammavācā*), but whose burden has been assigned by the Saṅgha with the thought,
"This is your responsibility," or one who carries that burden himself for the sake of the monks' comfortable dwelling, or where there are two or three monks.
The intention is that they dwell there, or perform such an action therein. Regarding the phrase "one who is not fully ordained, whether authorized or unauthorized by the Saṅgha":

although it is not permissible to grant the thirteen authorizations to one who is not fully ordained, nevertheless, one who received an authorization at the time of full ordination and subsequently remains in the state of being unordained [is included].

With reference to that, it is said: "or one approved by the Saṅgha. However, with reference to a competent novice for whom the responsibility has been assigned by either the Saṅgha alone or by a monk approved by the Saṅgha, saying, "You perform this formal act," it is said:
"or one not approved. The rest here is self-evident.

It has three origins: it originates from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind; it is an action (*kiriya*); it is liberated by perception (*saññāvimokkha*); it involves consciousness (*sacittaka*); it is an offense against worldly convention (*lokavajja*); it is bodily action and verbal action; it is unwholesome consciousness;
and it is associated with painful feeling. This is the third training rule concerning censuring. 4.
Commentary on the First Training Rule on Lodgings (*Senāsana*).
108. Regarding the fourth training rule: “In the winter season” means during the winter period, at the time when snow falls.
“Baking the body” means sitting on beds, chairs, and so forth, and baking the body with the morning sun.

“When the time has been announced” means when the time for any meal, such as rice gruel or solid food, has been announced. “It becomes soaked” means it becomes soaked and drenched by the falling snow.
110. Regarding "at the fixed rendezvous" (*avassikasaṅkete*): this refers to eight months—four winter months and four summer months—since [the rule] was not thus prescribed for the rainy season.
"In a pavilion" (*maṇḍape vā*) means either in a leaf-pavilion or in a wooden-beamed pavilion. "At the foot of a tree" (*rukkhamūle vā*) means beneath any tree whatsoever.
"Where crows or hawks do not drop their dung" (*yattha kākā vā kulalā vā na ūhadanti*) means where...
"These crows, owls, or other birds dwelling in their nests by making their home there do not defile that lodging;

therefore, I allow you to set it down at the foot of such a tree. Consequently, it is permissible to set it down at the foot of a tree where birds, having gone out for their food, rest before departing. However, in which [tree]...
They dwell having made a nest in a tree inhabited by bats; [the bowl] must not be placed at the foot of that tree.
Because of the statement "for eight months," it is likewise not permitted to place it even for four months in those regions where it does not rain during the rainy season.
Because of the statement "in a non-permanent shelter," where it rains in the winter, there...

It is not permissible to leave [a bed or chair] out in the open even during the winter. However, in the summer, when the sky is entirely free of clouds and pure, it is permissible to leave a bed or chair out in the open for some necessary purpose during such a time.
One who lives in the open air must also know the proper conduct; for if he has a private bed, he should [leave it] right there.
One should lie down. When taking what belongs to the Sangha, one should take a bed stripped of its coverlet made of hemp or linen.
If that is not available, an old bed should be taken. If even that is not available, a new-woven or upholstered bed should be taken.

Having taken it, however, one should not even construct a robe-shed, thinking, "I am one who dwells at the foot of a tree in the most austere manner; I am one who dwells in the open air in the most austere manner."
It is not permitted to spread out [the robe] and lie down under a tree or in the open air when it is not the proper time. However,
if even a hut made of a fourfold-layered robe cannot protect one from the elements— such as during a seven-day storm and so forth—
it is permitted for a monk, because he must remain in accordance with his body.
For those dwelling in leaf huts in the forest, people with hearts inspired by their perfection of virtue provide new beds and chairs, saying, "Use these for the communal use of the Saṅgha.
When they depart after staying there, they should send word to the monks who share the same community in a neighboring monastery before leaving;
if there are no such monks, they should leave them in a place sheltered from the rain and then depart. In a place sheltered from the rain...

If there is no tree, one should hang it [on a wall] and then depart. Having taken the broom to the courtyard of the cetiya, or having swept either the courtyard of the dining hall, the courtyard of the Uposatha hall, or any other place such as a cell, a day-quarters, or a fire-hall, and having washed it, the broom should be placed back in the broom-shed itself.
Or, having taken it to one of the places such as the Uposatha hall, etc., [it should be hung there].
The same procedure applies even when sweeping the remaining areas.
However, if a monk wishes to go while sweeping the path to the alms-round, he should sweep it and, if there is a hall along the way, place it there.
If there is none, he should observe whether the clouds have ceased to rise.
One who knows, "It will not rain as long as I am away from the village," should place [the bedding] wherever it is and, upon returning, put it back in its original place.
If one places it in the open air while knowing that it will rain, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
this is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*. However, if it is for the purpose of sweeping here and there...
When the broom has been set aside, it is permissible to sweep each respective place and set it down right there.
One who sweeps the sitting hall should know the proper procedure. This is the procedure: starting from the center, the sand should be cleared toward the foot-stands.
Taking the refuse in one's hands, it should be thrown outside.
111. A *masārakoti* is made by boring holes in the feet of a bed and inserting cross-pieces (*aṭanī*) there.
A *bundikābaddha* is made by fastening the cross-pieces to the bed feet and forming them into the shape of a couch (*pallaṅka*).
A *kuḷīrapādaka* is made with feet resembling those of a crab, a goat, or similar animals; or any bed that has curved legs is called a *kuḷīrapādaka*.
Regarding "with fixed legs" (*āhaccapādaka*): this is stated later in the Canon itself as, "A bed with fixed legs is one made by boring holes into the frame.
Therefore, a bed made by boring holes into the crossbars (*aṭanī*), inserting the leg-shafts there, and placing a pin on top should be understood as "one with fixed legs.
The same method applies to a chair (*pīṭha*). Having wrapped [the material] inside...
"It is bound" means it is bound having been made in the shape of a drum—broad at the bottom and top and narrow in the middle;
they say that they even encircle its middle with the skins of lions or tigers. There is no "unallowable skin" (akappiyacamma) here.
For even a lodging made of gold is permissible; therefore, it is of great value. [Regarding] one who is not fully ordained...
"It is an impediment for him who has it spread" means it is an impediment for the one by whom it was caused to be spread.

"For one who goes beyond the distance of a clod's throw, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)" means that for one who goes beyond the distance of a clod's throw of a man of medium strength, there is an offense of expiation.
Herein, this is the analysis: An elder, having finished his meal duties in the dining hall, commands a junior monk.
“Go and prepare a bed and chair in the daytime resting place. Having done so, he sat down.
The Elder, having wandered about as he pleased, went there and placed either his bag or his upper robe; from that point on, it became an impediment for the Elder.
When he sat down and was about to leave himself, he neither removed it nor had it removed, even beyond the range of a stone’s throw.

[This constitutes] a *pācittiya* offense. However, if the elder, having left his bag or upper robe there, continues walking up and down while saying to the junior monk, "Go," then the junior must point out, "Venerable sir, here are the bed and chair.
If the elder knows the proper conduct (*vatta*), he should say, "You go; I shall put things back in their proper place. If...
If the elder is one who has not fulfilled his duties toward the junior, he may simply rebuke the junior, saying, "Go away, do not stay here; I will allow you neither to sit nor to lie down.

When the junior has obtained permission to rest for a while by saying, "Venerable sir, may you sleep well," and has paid his respects and departed, it constitutes an obstruction for the elder himself.
His offense should be understood according to the same method as previously described.
But if, at the very moment of being commanded, the junior monk says, "Venerable sir, I have some business to attend to,
such as washing my bowl," and the elder, having told him, "You go after making your arrangements," leaves the dining hall and goes elsewhere,
he must be made to pay for the removal of his foot-rest. If he goes and sits down right there, it is according to the previous method.

There is an offense when he has gone beyond the range of a clod-throw. However, if the Elder instructs the novice, then even if the novice has arranged a bed and chair there and is sitting, [the monk] going elsewhere from the dining hall must be dealt with according to the lifting of the *pādukka* (the rule regarding the distance).
Having gone and sat down, when he goes again, he is to be dealt with for an offense upon going beyond the range of a clod-throw. But if, while giving the instruction...
If he instructs, "Having prepared a bed and chair, sit right there," [the monk] may go wherever he wishes and return;
however, for one who departs without restoring them to their original state, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) once the distance of a stone's throw has been exceeded.
When sitting in a gathering in the midst of the community after having prepared beds and chairs, it should be said at the time of departure: "Have the monastery attendants put these away."
For those departing without having entered [the boundary], there is an offense once they have passed beyond the range of a clod of earth.
There is what is called a "great Dhamma-listening" (mahādhammasavana); for that purpose, they bring out beds and chairs from both the Uposatha hall and the dining hall and arrange them.
This is an impediment only for the resident monks. If the incoming monks say, "This belongs to our preceptor, this..."
They take [the seat] thinking, "It belongs to the teacher," and from that moment on, it becomes an impediment for them alone.
When departing, there is an offense for those who do not restore the seat to its natural state and who step beyond the distance of a stone’s throw. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*:
"As long as others have not sat down, the responsibility rests with those by whom it was prepared. Once others have arrived and are seated, the responsibility rests with those who are sitting. If..."

If they depart without having had [the seats] removed or having had them removed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Why? Because it was prescribed as not being a formal instruction (*anāṇatti*).
As long as no one—either the announcer or the preacher of the Dhamma—has arrived when the Dhamma-seat has been prepared, it remains an impediment for those who prepared it;
once he has arrived and is seated, that [impediment] belongs to him. The listening to the Dhamma lasts for the entire day and night.
If another person—whether a steward or a preacher of the Dhamma—stands up and another sits down, the responsibility belongs to whoever arrives last and sits down.
However, the one who stands up must say, "This seat is your responsibility," and then depart.

Even if the first person who sat down stands up and leaves before the other has arrived, provided that the latter is still within the vicinity (upacāra), [the responsibility remains with the one who arrived later].
If the other person comes and sits down, and having stood up departs, he is not to be charged with an offense.
However, if the one who sat down first stands up from his seat before the other has arrived and crosses the distance of a stone’s throw, he is to be charged with an offense.
And in all such cases, the method stated in the Mahāpaccarī is as follows: “For crossing the distance of a stone’s throw, there is a *dukkaṭa* for the first step and a *pācittiya* for the second.”

112. Regarding the passage beginning with "cimilikaṃ vāti": *Cimilika* refers to a covering made for the purpose of preserving the color of the ground that has been prepared with plaster and other materials;
having spread it on the floor below, they spread a straw mat (*kaṭasāraka*) over it.
*Uttarattharaṇa* refers to a bedspread (*paccattharaṇa*) intended to be spread over beds and stools. *Bhūmattharaṇa* refers to [a rug] on the ground...
It refers to a matting made from straw, reeds, or similar materials that is to be spread out. A "mat" (*taṭṭika*) is a mat made from palm leaves or from bark fibers (*vāka*).
A "hide" (*cammakhaṇḍa*) is any kind of skin, including those of lions, tigers, leopards, hyenas, and so forth.
For in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), no specific hide is seen as prohibited for the use of lodgings; therefore, it is only the handling of lion skins and the like that is forbidden.
The prohibition is to be understood as follows: "Foot-wiping cloth" (*pādapuñchanī*) means something made of ropes or rags for the purpose of wiping the feet.
"Wooden bench" (*phalakapīṭha*) means a bench made of wood. Alternatively, it refers to both the wooden plank and the wooden bench;
by this, all wooden articles and the like are included. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated in detail:
“Having placed a bowl-rest, a bowl-cover, a foot-washer, a fan, a palm-leaf fan, any kind of wooden vessel—
even down to a water-pot or a water-conch— in the open air, it is an *dukkaṭa* offense for one who departs.
This method, however, is shown in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* regarding the second training rule concerning boiling dye in the open air.
The dye-vessel, the dye-tub, and the dye-trough—all these should be put away in the fire-hall.
If there is no fire-hall, they should be placed on a sheltered ledge.
If even that is not available, it is permissible to go after having set them down in a place where monks, looking about, can see them.

"Another’s private property": according to the *Mahāpaccarī* and other texts, if trust cannot be placed in someone, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) regarding what belongs to them; however, if trust can be placed in someone, what belongs to them is treated as if it were one's own private property.

113. "He goes after asking permission": if a bhikkhu, a novice, or a monastery attendant is conscientious and regards [the departure] as a personal impediment, and such a person goes after having asked permission, there is no offense for him. While warming [the water],...
"He goes" means he goes thinking, "I will come and remove it after warming it in the sun"; for one who goes in this manner, there is no offense.
"It is obstructed by something" means the lodging has been disturbed by something.
For even if an elder monk comes and takes it away after making [the junior] rise, or if a *yakkha* or a *peta* comes and sits down, or some powerful person [does so], [there is no offense].
If someone comes and takes it, the lodging becomes an impediment; or even if lions, tigers, and the like come and stay in that place, the lodging remains an impediment.
Thus, there is no offense for one who departs without removing [the bedding] when it has been made an impediment by anyone.
"In cases of emergency" means in cases of obstacles to life or to the holy life (*brahmacariya*). The rest is self-evident.

The Origin of the Kathina: It originates from body and speech; from body, speech, and mind. It is functional and non-functional; it is not accompanied by liberation through perception; it is without thought; it is an offense by rule; it is bodily action and verbal action;
it consists of three types of consciousness and three types of feeling. This is the fourth training rule on lodgings. 5. Commentary on the Second Training Rule on Lodgings.
116. In the second training rule on bedding: "Cushion" (*bhisī*) means either a cushion for a bed (*mañcaka-bhisī*) or a cushion for a chair (*pīṭhaka-bhisī*).
Blankets (*cimilika*) and so forth are of the same types as those mentioned in the previous training rule. "Sitting mat" (*nisīdana*) should be understood as one with a border.
"Spread" (*paccattharaṇa*) is stated only as "woolen cloth" (*pāvāra*) and "rug" (*kojava*). "Grass matting" (*tiṇasanthāra*) is a matting made of any kind of grass whatsoever.

This same method applies to a mat of leaves. Regarding the phrase "one who crosses the boundary": here, for one who steps over the first foot [of the boundary], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
upon crossing the second, there is an offense entailing confession (*pācittiya*). The precinct (*upacāra*) of an unenclosed area is defined as two *leḍḍu*-throws from the lodging.
Regarding the phrase "or goes without having asked permission": here, if a monk is present, that monk must be asked for permission; if he is not present...
If a novice is not present, it should be asked of a monastery attendant; if he is not present, of the owner of the monastery who had it built;

or of anyone in that person's family. If even he is not present, one should place a bed on four stones, stack the remaining beds and stools upon that bed, and pile the ten kinds of bedding, such as mattresses and so forth, on top.
Having put away the wooden utensils and the earthenware utensils, closed the doors and windows, and fulfilled the duties for one departing, one should go.
However, if the lodging is leaking and straw or bricks have been brought for the purpose of roofing, if one has the strength, it should be roofed over.
If one is unable to do so, then the beds, chairs, and other furniture should be moved to a place where there is no rain.
Having set it down, one must depart. If it rains all over, one who is able should place it in the house of a lay follower within the village.
If they do not accept it, saying, "Venerable sir, that which belongs to the Saṅgha is burdensome;
we fear fire, smoke, and so forth," then even in the open air, having placed a bed upon stones, the rest should be done according to the method previously described.
Having set it aside and covered it with grass and leaves, it is permissible to go, thinking:
"Whatever part remains there will be of benefit to other monks who come to that place. Regarding the phrases "in the vicinity of the monastery" and so forth:
the "vicinity of the monastery" (*vihārassūpacāro*) refers to the surrounding courtyard (*pariveṇa*). The "attendance hall" (*upaṭṭhānasālā*) refers to the dining hall of the courtyard.
*Maṇḍapa* refers to a pavilion for a *pariveṇa*. *Rukkhamūla* refers to the foot of a tree within a *pariveṇa*. This is the method stated in the Kurundi-ṭīkā.
Although this is what is stated, nevertheless, "vihāra" should be understood as either an inner chamber or any other completely enclosed, well-guarded dwelling place.
"In the vicinity of the vihāra" means in the area near its exterior. "In the assembly hall" (*upaṭṭhānasālā*).
"Or in the dining hall," or "in a pavilion"—that is, in a pavilion for the assembly of many people, whether it is open or enclosed.

There is no need to mention "at the foot of a tree. Regarding the phrase "there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," this refers to one who, having arranged the ten kinds of beds mentioned above in a protected place such as an inner chamber and so forth, departs; for since both the bed and the lodging [are infested] with termites...
It dissolves and becomes just a heap of earth; therefore, an offense of expiation (pācittiya) is stated.
However, for one who departs after having arranged it outside in the assembly hall or similar places, only the bedding itself would be lost;

because the place is not protected, it does not constitute "lodging" (senāsana), and therefore an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is stated here. Regarding "a bed or a chair": since it is not possible [to leave] a bed or a chair...
Because [the bedding] might be suddenly bitten by centipedes, it is stated that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who goes after having spread it out even within the monastery.
However, in the vicinity of the monastery, even those wandering on a tour of the dwellings will see it and put it away. 118.
"Having lifted it up, he goes": here, by one who goes having lifted it up, the entire bed, stool, and door...
Having removed it and gathered it up, one should hang it on the robe-peg before departing. Later, when returning, the monk who is staying there must also do exactly the same:
having spread out the bed or stool again and slept, he should depart after putting it away in that very same manner.
If one has stayed with the bed arranged inside the wall and spread outside the wall, at the time of departure, it must be put back precisely where it was taken from.
The same rule applies even for one who has descended from the upper palace and is living in the lower palace.
Even if beds and chairs have been arranged in the night-quarters or day-quarters, they must be put back in the very place they were taken from at the time of departure.
Regarding the phrase "he goes after taking leave," here is the analysis of what should and should not be asked for leave: first, as for those on the ground...
Whether it be a long hall or a leaf-hut, or wherever a house built against tree trunks serves as a nesting place for termites, one who departs from there must first take leave before departing;
for if that place is not tended for a few days, it remains nothing but a termite mound. However, in the case of a stone floor or stone pillars...

Or, in the case of a lodging made of grass, a rock-cave, or a plastered dwelling where there is no fear of termites, it is permissible for one departing from there to go either after asking permission or without asking; however, asking permission is a duty (*vatta*).
If, even in such a lodging, termites are climbing up from one side, one must depart only after having asked permission. Whoever...
However, when an incoming bhikkhu, having taken up a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha,
lives there following the resident bhikkhu without taking up his own separate dwelling, that dwelling remains an impediment for the resident bhikkhu alone until the former takes it up.
But once he has taken up the dwelling and lives there according to his own authority, from that point on—
It is an impediment only for the visitor. If both [the resident and the visitor] take it after dividing it, it is an impediment for both.
However, it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*: "If two or three persons together designate [a robe], then at the time of departure, everyone must seek permission.
Among them, if one who is departing first goes while making the mental resolve, 'The last one will look after it,' it is permissible."
There is no release through the attention of the last person. Many may send one to spread out [the bedding] and have it prepared;
at the time of departure, either everyone must take leave, or one may be sent to take leave.

Having brought beds, chairs, and so forth from elsewhere and having stayed elsewhere, they must be taken back to that very place at the time of departure. If, while staying after bringing them from another residence, someone else...
If an elder arrives, he must not be turned away; rather, one should say: "Venerable sir, I have brought this from another residence; please restore it to its original state.
When the elder has consented by saying, "I shall do so," it is permissible for the other person to depart.
Even if, after having carried it elsewhere, one uses it as communal property belonging to the Saṅgha, [if it] is lost or worn out...
If it is stolen by thieves, there is no debt; however, for one who uses it as personal property, there is a debt.
But if another person’s bed or chair is used—whether as communal property or as personal property—and it is lost, the debt remains with the user alone.
“Obstructed by something” means [obstructed] by senior bhikkhus, authority, yakkhas, lions, wild beasts, black snakes, and so forth.
If a lodging is obstructed by something or other, he goes away with a sense of concern; standing there, he asks for permission, thinking, "It is obstructed by something;

I shall come back this very day and attend to it. Thus, having gone across a river or to another village with such concern, he stands right where the thought of going arose, and after sending someone, he asks for permission.
Or if he is obstructed or afflicted by something such as a river in flood, a king, or thieves, and is unable to return—there is no offense even for one in such a state.
The remainder is exactly as explained in the first training rule, together with its origin and so forth.
This is the fifth training rule concerning lodgings.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Entering by Pushing In (Anupakhajja-sikkhāpada) 119.
Regarding the sixth training rule: "They encroach" means that having gone there first, they bring their bowls and robes [into the dwelling] and remain obstructing [the space].
"The elder monks are making [the junior monks] leave" means [the elders say], "Friend, it is our turn according to the seniority of the rains."
Having taken [the lodgings], they cause them to be vacated. They intrude upon others' beds: thinking, "Venerable sir, only your bed's place is reached;
the entire monastery is not yours. Now this place has come to us," they enter, arrange beds and chairs, and sit, lie down, or even engage in recitation.
120. They know: "This person is not to be made to rise. Knowing this, it is said in its analysis (vibhaṅga): "He knows him as 'an elder,'" and so forth.
For an elder is not to be made to rise because of his own seniority, and a sick person because of his illness.

However, the Saṅgha [is not to be made to rise] out of regard for the great service rendered by a storekeeper, or by a preacher of the Dhamma, a master of the Vinaya, and so forth, or by a teacher who recites for a group.
Perceiving the excellence of his virtues, he designates and gives a monastery for him to reside in permanently;
therefore, even one to whom it has been given by the Saṅgha must not be displaced.

Although in this case the Saṅgha alone provides suitable lodgings even for the sick, nevertheless, the sick person "should not be troubled, but should be shown compassion, even if he has not been assigned a lodging by the Saṅgha after seeking permission."
It is stated separately in order to show this.
121. Regarding "the vicinity" (*upacāra*): here, first, in a large monastery, the vicinity for beds and chairs extends one and a half cubits all around;
in a small one, it extends one and a half cubits from wherever space permits, for one who enters after having washed their feet and for the purpose of relieving oneself.
The area extending from the stone for washing feet placed at the door to the bed or chair, as far as the place for urination, while one is departing,
is called the "approach" (*upacāra*), measuring one and a half cubits in width.
For a monk who is standing within that approach of either the bed or the chair, or who is entering or departing within that approach, [if he lies down] by encroaching upon it...
If one spreads out a bed or causes it to be spread out with the desire to use it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Regarding the phrase "sits down upon it" or "lies down upon it," the offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) occurs by the mere act of sitting down or by the mere act of lying down.
However, if one performs both actions, there are two offenses of expiation. This applies even to one who sits down repeatedly after having risen.
For each act of lying down, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

Regarding the phrase "if one spreads out a bed or has one spread out within the vicinity (*upacāra*)," and in the subsequent section on offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) beginning with "in the vicinity of a dwelling," just as here [it is an offense] for merely sitting down or merely lying down, so too [it applies].
The classification of offenses as *pācittiya* has been stated regarding both the act itself and the difference in application; in the same way, the classification of *dukkaṭa* is to be understood.
For there is no purpose in living with such a person of dissimilar character in the same monastery or even in the same courtyard;
therefore, his residence in all such places is forbidden. Regarding the phrase "another's private property," here too it refers to the private property of one who is trusted.
If it is exactly like one's own private [dwelling], there is no offense therein.
123. "In times of distress" means: if there is an obstacle to life or to the holy life for one living outside, then for whoever enters during such times of distress, there is also no offense.
The rest is self-evident. This is the origin of the first *pārājika*, an act of volition.
It involves perception as the means of release, possesses consciousness, is an offense against the world, is bodily action, is unwholesome consciousness, and is associated with painful feeling.
This is the sixth training rule, concerning encroaching upon another’s space. 7. Commentary on the Training Rule on Expelling [a Layperson] from a Monastery.

126. Regarding the seventh training rule: "If one causes [a person] to pass through many doors by a single effort"—this refers to palaces of four or five stories, or quadrangles with six or seven gate-towers;

in such dwellings, if one takes hold of [the person] by the hands or by the neck and makes them pass through the interior, one causes them to pass by a single effort, and there is only one *pācittiya* offense. Having set [them down]...
Excepting those cases where one exceeds [the limit] by various means, there are *pācittiya* offenses for each door counted.
The same rule applies even when one does not touch with the hand but says "Go out! and expels them by word alone.
Regarding the phrase "commands another," here there is a *dukkaṭa* offense merely upon the command, such as "Expel this person. If he is commanded once...
If he causes [the monk] to pass through many doors, there is one *pācittiya* offense.

However, if he has been instructed with a specific limitation, such as "expel him through so many doors," or "expel him as far as the main gate," then there are *pācittiya* offenses according to the number of doors.
His requisites (*parikkhāra*) refers to whatever belongs to him, categorized as bowl, robe, water-strainer, spittoon, bed, chair, couch, pillow, and so forth.
Even down to a mere piece of dyed bark—whosoever ejects it or causes it to be ejected incurs *dukkaṭa* offenses according to the number of items.
However, in the case of those who have been bound tightly and left there, it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that there is only a single offense.

127. "Another’s private property": here too, "private property belonging to a person of trust" is exactly like one's own private property. And as it is here, so it is everywhere. Wherever there will be a distinction, we shall explain it there.
128. Regarding the phrases "he expels the shameless one" and so forth:
only one who creates discord and quarrels may be expelled from the entire monastery of the Saṅgha, for such a person, having gained a faction, might even cause a schism in the Saṅgha.
However, those who are shameless and the like should be expelled only from their own place of residence; it is not permissible to expel them from the entire monastery of the Saṅgha.
"Of one who is insane": there is no offense for one who is himself insane. The rest is self-evident. This [offense] has three origins:

it originates from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind; it is an action, released by perception, accompanied by consciousness, a worldly transgression, bodily action and verbal action, unwholesome consciousness, and painful feeling.
The seventh training rule, on expelling.

8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Upper Story of a Gabled House (Vehāsakuṭi-sikkhāpada) 129. Regarding the eighth training rule: "In the upper story of a gabled house" means in a two-storied gabled house whose floor above is not covered, or in a three-storied or higher gabled house.
"He sat down suddenly upon the bed" means he suddenly overpowered and overspread the bed.
He sat down. This accusative case ending has the sense of the locative; the meaning is "he sat on the couch.
As for the word *abhi*, it is merely a prefix used for the sake of poetic embellishment (*padasobhanattha*). *Nippatitvā* means having fallen down or having gone out.
For indeed, no pin had been placed upon it [the couch], and therefore he went out. *Vissaramakāsī* means he made a discordant, distressed sound.
131. "Vehāsakuṭi" means that which does not strike the head of a man of medium height;
by this, the *vehāsakuṭi* intended here is shown, not the definition of a *vehāsakuṭi*.
For any two-storied house, three-storied house, or the like, whose upper floor is not cut off [by the roof], is a *vehāsakuṭi*.
Or it is called a "wooden hut. However, in this context, those that do not strike the head [when one sits] are intended.
Regarding sitting down and so forth, the classification of offenses should be understood according to the application of the method previously explained.
133. "In a non-elevated wooden hut": there is no offense regarding leaf-huts and the like constructed on the ground; for it is not possible there for another person—
To cause affliction. Regarding "where there is a head-collision": even in such a place where there is a head-collision, there is no offense.
For it is not possible to move about in the lower story there without stooping; therefore, because it is a place where one cannot walk, there will be no affliction of others.
"The area below is not used" means that because materials and other things have been stored beneath it, it is not being utilized.

If it is [a floor] covered with planks, there is no offense. "It is covered with wooden planks" means that its upper surface is thickly laid with wooden boards or has been treated with plaster and the like; even in such a case, there is no offense.
"A support has been provided" means that a pin has been fixed into the tips of the legs of the bed or chair, so that they do not slip out even when one sits upon them; in such a case...
There is no offense even for one sitting on a bed or a stool. Regarding "standing upon that":

if one stands upon a bed or a stool with detachable legs and takes hold of a robe or anything else hanging from hooks or similar fixtures above, or causes another to take hold of it, there is likewise no offense for him.
The remainder is self-evident. This origin is from the body and from both body and mind.
It arises from three origins; it is functional; it is not liberation through perception; it is without consciousness; it is an offense by formal rule; it is bodily action;
it involves three types of consciousness; it involves three types of feeling.
The eighth training rule on the upper-story hut.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning a Large Vihāra (Mahallakavihārasikkhāpada) 135.

Regarding the ninth training rule: "As far as the door-frame" (*yāva dvārakosa*). Here, "door-frame" (*dvārakosa*) refers to the space surrounding the wall-panels (*piṭṭhasaṅghāṭa*) measuring the width of the door-panel.
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "One and a half cubits starting from the door-post."
It has been stated [thus]. However, in the *Kurundi* it says: "On both sides of the door, the measure is that of the door-panel (*kavāṭa*).
In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* it is said: "A door-panel may be one and a half cubits, two cubits, or two and a half cubits";
this is well-said. For it was with reference to this very [measure] that the Blessed One also said: "Within arm's reach all around the wooden frame (*piṭṭhasaṅghāṭa*)."

This has been the exposition of the highest limit. "For the purpose of fixing the bolt" means for the purpose of fixing the door-fastening with its panels; the meaning is: for the sake of making the door-fastening with its panels immovable.

This word-commentary (*padabhājana*), "for the purpose of fixing the door," was also spoken with reference to this very same meaning. However, the intended sense here is this: for a door-panel that turns easily...
At the time of opening, one strikes the wall; at the time of closing, one strikes the door-bolt. By that striking, the wall shakes;
then the plaster moves, and having moved, it either becomes loose or falls away. Therefore the Blessed One said: “As far as the door-recess for the insertion of the bolt.

In this regard, although there is nothing stated in either the summary table (*mātikā*) or the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) that “this specific thing must be done,” [the meaning is established by implication].

It is stated [in the Vinaya]; however, in the *Aṭṭhuppatti*, because of the context—"he had it plastered again and again, he had it smeared again and again"—the meaning should be understood as follows:
from the door-bolt to the door-frame, it must be smeared or have it smeared again and again for the purpose of fixing the bolt.
As for what is said in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), "within arm’s reach all around the wooden frame of the wall" (*piṭṭhasaṅghāṭassa samantā hatthapāsā*): therein, for one...

There is a door in the middle; the upper part is a high wall. Its precinct (*upacāra*) extends for the distance of an arm’s reach all around it on three sides, while for a small dwelling (*vihāra*), the precinct extends on two sides.
Even there, whichever wall the opening door strikes against is considered to have an incomplete precinct. However, according to the highest limit:
Plastering within the reach of the hand on all three sides of the door is permitted for the sake of making the door steady.

If there is also a space for plastering on the lower part of that door, it is likewise permissible to plaster that as well. Regarding the phrase "for the preparation of the light-slits" (*ālokasandhi*):
here, "light-slits" refers to the window shutters; these too, when opened, [should not exceed] even a span (*vidatthi*) in width.
They even strike the wall surface beyond that. However, in this context, the practice is to be found in all directions;
therefore, the intention here is that an area equal in width to the door should be plastered or caused to be plastered in all directions for the purpose of preparing the light-opening.

The passage beginning with “white-colored” (*setavaṇṇa*) is not a word-commentary (*padabhājana*) on the matrix (*mātikā*). For by this [statement], it is permitted within the word-commentary itself that there is no such thing as the “heaviness” of a dwelling; therefore, all of this may be done according to one’s convenience.

Having thus shown what must be done regarding plastering work (*lepakamma*), he said “of two or three layers of roofing” (*dvatticchadanassa*) and so forth, in order to show what must be done regarding the roofing (*chadana*).
Therein, “the turn of two or three layers of roofing” means two or three turns of the roofing; a “turn” (*pariyāya*)...
It is called a "boundary" (*parikkhepa*); the meaning is that either two boundaries or three boundaries are to be determined.

"Standing where there is no green" means standing where there is no green (*aharita*). Here, "green" (*harita*) refers to the seven kinds of grain known as the "first fruits" (*pubbaṇṇa*), and the various vegetables known as the "second fruits" (*aparaṇṇa*), such as mung beans, black gram, sesame, horse gram, bottle gourd, pumpkin, and so forth. For this very reason, he said: "Green..."
"Namely, paddy and non-paddy. Regarding the statement,
"If he makes a formal determination while standing on green growth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," here even a field where the seed sown has not yet sprouted,
but will sprout once the rain falls, is still reckoned as green growth.

It moves away. Therefore, one standing even in such a field must not perform the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*); rather, it should be determined while standing only where there is no green growth.

Even there, this is the boundary: sitting on the side of the ridge-pole, or the pinnacle of the gabled roof, or the finial on top, and looking down as far as the edge of the roof's opening, one may determine that portion of ground which one can see.
And one must resolve upon that spot of ground where one stands while looking down at someone sitting above.
It is not permitted to resolve while standing inside [the building], even if it is overgrown with grass. Why? Because [one might think], "This is the place where the monastery will fall.
136. Regarding "covering by way of a path": here, covering by way of a path means covering directly without surrounding it on all sides.
That [roofing] is obtained by means of bricks, stone slabs, and plaster. "Having determined two paths" means:
if the two paths are poorly roofed, even after removing them, one may roof them again and again;
therefore, having determined the two paths as one wishes, and having commanded regarding the third path, "Now roof it in this way," one should depart. "By turns" means...
By way of circumference. Such roofing, however, is obtained with grass and leaves.
Therefore, here too, having determined two alternatives as one wishes, one should command the third alternative thus: "Now, roof it in this manner," and then depart.
If he does not depart, one should remain silent. And all this roofing—
This is to be understood as being "on top of the covering. For they cover it in this way thinking, "A dwelling that is covered layer upon layer remains free from rain for a long time.
"Beyond that" means beyond the three paths or methods—that is, on the fourth path or method.
137. “He shakes handful after handful of grass” means he shakes it repeatedly. The rest here is self-evident. Regarding the six origins:

it is an action (kiriya), not associated with liberation through perception (nosaññāvimokkha), without consciousness (acittaka), an offense by rule (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), consisting of three types of consciousness (ticitta), and three types of feeling (tivedana).
This is the ninth training rule concerning large dwellings (mahallakavihārasikkhāpada).
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Water with Living Beings (Sappāṇaka-sikkhāpada) 140.
Regarding the tenth training rule: "Knowing it to contain living beings" means knowing, in whatever way possible, that "this contains living beings.
"Should sprinkle or cause to be sprinkled" means that one should either sprinkle oneself with that water, or having commanded another, cause them to sprinkle it.
In the Pāḷi, however, the meaning of such statements as “siñceyya (he should sprinkle) means he sprinkles himself” is to be understood according to the method already explained above.
In that regard, for one who sprinkles without interrupting the stream, there is only a single offense regarding a single water-jar; this same principle applies to all vessels.
But for one who interrupts the stream, there is an offense for each individual act. [Regarding] the *mātikā* in the presence of...

If he does so, even if it flows for an entire day, it is a single offense. If he ties it here and there and leads it from one place to another, there is an offense for each individual act of effort (*payoga*).
Even if he throws a load as large as a cart’s worth of grass into the water with a single act of effort, it is a single offense.
For one who throws in each blade of grass or leaf individually, there is an offense for each act of effort. The same applies to clay.
The same principle applies to other materials such as wood, cow dung, and so forth. However, this was not said with reference to a large body of water;

rather, it should be understood that it was said with reference to such water as is consumed when grass or clay is thrown into it, or which becomes turbid, or wherein living creatures die. The rest here is self-evident.

It has three origins: it originates from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind; it is an action (kiriya); it is liberated through perception (saññāvimokkha); it is accompanied by consciousness (sacittaka); it is an offense by formal rule (paṇṇattivajja); it is bodily action and verbal action;
it consists of three types of consciousness and three types of feeling. The tenth training rule concerning living beings is finished.
The second chapter on lodgings is completed according to the order of the commentary.
3. Ovādavagga 1.
Ovādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā 141–144.
Regarding the first training rule of the Bhikkhunīvagga: “They are recipients”—here, it is not that the bhikkhunīs [are the recipients] for them.
They did not give [the instruction]; however, when daughters of noble families who had gone forth from great clans saw their own kinsmen and relatives come into their presence and asked,
"Noble ladies, where can you receive exhortation (*ovāda*), recitation (*uddesa*), and questioning (*paripucchā*)?", they would name the eighty great disciples, saying,

"Such-and-such an elder and such-and-such an elder provide exhortation," and then, following the course of the conversation, [they would describe] the distinctions regarding their virtue, learning, conduct, birth, lineage, and so forth.
They speak of qualities that actually exist. Indeed, it is appropriate to speak of such existing qualities.
Consequently, people with confident hearts brought forth great gains and honors for the elders, consisting of robes and other requisites. Therefore it is said:
"They become recipients of robes... [and] of the requisites."
“Having approached the bhikkhunīs”: it is said that not even a single bhikkhunī went into their presence;
however, with hearts drawn by craving for gain, they went to their dwelling place. It is with reference to this that it is said:
“having approached the bhikkhunīs. Those bhikkhunīs, too, because of their fickle minds, did exactly as they were told.

Therefore it was said: “Then those bhikkhunīs... sat down. “Frivolous talk” (tiracchānakathā) refers to various kinds of useless talk, such as talk about kings and so forth, which is like a bypath even on the way to heaven and the path [to liberation]. “Prosperous” (iddha) means well-flourishing;
the intended meaning is that it is connected with the penetration of characteristics, being coherent in meaning, profound, and rich in flavor.

145–147. Regarding the passage, “I allow you, monks,” it is because those monks, being told, “Do not, O monks, exhort the bhikkhunīs,” might—since they had not yet seen the Truths—conceive resentment toward the Tathāgata and thereby fall into the states of misery.
Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to prevent them from falling into those miserable states, [spoke] by means of another method concerning that exhortation of the bhikkhunīs.
It should be understood that he authorized this formal authorization (*sammuti*) for a monk instructor because he wished to act outside [the monastery].

Having thus authorized him here due to the desire to act outside, he subsequently spoke the words beginning with, “I authorize you, monks, one who is endowed with eight factors,” while actually performing the action.
For these eight factors had never before occurred even in a dream to the group of six monks (*chabbaggiyā*).
In this context, "one who possesses virtue" (*sīlavā*) means that virtue (*sīla*) belongs to him. Now, in order to show what that virtue is and how it is said to belong to him, he says:

"restrained by the restraint of the *pātimokkha*," and so forth. Herein, the *pātimokkha* itself is the restraint; thus it is the "restraint of the *pātimokkha*" (*pātimokkhasaṃvara*). One who is restrained, that is, endowed with, the restraint of the *pātimokkha* is "restrained by the restraint of the *pātimokkha*" (*pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuta*).
“He dwells” means he conducts himself. For this has been said in the Vibhaṅga:
“The Pātimokkha is virtue, the foundation, the beginning, the conduct, the restraint, the control, the liberation, the release for the attainment of wholesome states;
it is restraint as bodily non-transgression, verbal non-transgression, and both bodily and verbal non-transgression.”

Non-transgression. "Restrained" means that by means of this restraint of the Pātimokkha, he is endowed with it, fully endowed with it, approached with it, fully approached with it, possessed of it, fully possessed of it, perfected in it, and equipped with it; therefore, he is called "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha.
"Dwells" means he moves about, conducts himself, protects, maintains, sustains, goes about, and lives; therefore, he is called "dwells."
