"Endowed with proper conduct and resort (*ācāra-gocara-sampanna*)" means he is endowed with conduct that prohibits wrong livelihood—such as not giving bamboo [for begging]—and with a resort that has abandoned places like brothels, such as families possessed of faith.
"Seeing danger in even the slightest faults (*aṇumatta-vajja*)" means seeing danger in even minor faults; it is said that his nature is to view those faults as dangerous.

"Having undertaken, he trains in the rules of training" means that among the rules of training established in three ways—namely, as the training in higher virtue and so forth—he trains by undertaking each respective rule of training, by correctly undertaking it, by grasping it thoroughly, and by not abandoning it.
This is the summary here; however, for one who desires the detailed exposition, it should be taken from the *Visuddhimagga*.

"One who has heard much" (*bahu-suta*) is one who is learned (*bahussuta*). "One who retains what has been heard" (*suta-dhara*) means that what is called his "much hearing" is not merely the hearing itself;
rather, the meaning is that he retains it. "One who has accumulated what has been heard" (*suta-sannicaya*) means that the heard is gathered within him like jewels in a casket (*mañjūsā*).
By this, [it is shown] that whatever he retains as heard, he protects it as if in a casket.
This demonstrates that, like a hoarded treasure, it remains undestroyed even over a long period of time. Now, showing that learning (*suta*) in its essential form, he says, "Those teachings...
and so forth; this follows the same method as explained in the Verañjakaṇḍa. Here, however, is the conclusion:

such teachings are well-learned by him, therefore he is "one of great learning" (*bahussuta*). He is a "retainer" (*dhātā*), therefore he is "one who retains what has been heard" (*sutadhara*). By means of speech...
"Accumulated by the mind, examined with the mind, and well-penetrated by view; therefore, it is an accumulation of what has been heard.
In this context, "accumulated by speech" means made proficient through verbal recitation. "Examined by the mind" means examined with the mind;
when one reflects upon them, they appear as if illuminated by a thousand lamps. "Well-penetrated by view" means [penetrated] both in terms of their meaning and their underlying reasons.
Through wisdom, they are thoroughly penetrated and well realized.
Furthermore, this one called "learned" (bahussuta) is of three kinds: the one who releases from dependence, the one who establishes a community, and the one who instructs the bhikkhunīs.
Among these, by the one who releases from dependence, at the minimum limit of five years since full ordination, two...
The *mātikā* (matrices) should be made proficient and committed to memory for the purpose of reciting the Dhamma on the fortnightly days (*pakkha-divasa*).

From the Suttanta, there should be four recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*) for the purpose of preaching the Dhamma to those who have assembled; one discourse path (*kathāmagga*), such as the *Andhakavinda*, *Mahārāhulovāda*, or *Aṅguttara* [Suttas], for the purpose of providing instruction;

three expressions of thanks (*anumodanā*) for the purpose of giving thanks during communal meals and on auspicious or inauspicious occasions; and [the rules] for the purpose of knowing the Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and other ceremonies.
The determination of what is action and what is not action, and for the purpose of performing the duty of a recluse,

a single meditation subject culminating in Arahantship— either by way of concentration or by way of insight— is what must be mastered. For to this extent one is "learned" (bahussuta) and "four-faceted" (cātuddisa),
and one is permitted to dwell anywhere under one's own authority.
A formal supporter (parisupaṭṭhāpaka) who has been ordained for at least ten years must, at the very minimum, master and recite fluently both Vibhaṅgas in order to guide the assembly in the Vinaya.
One who is unable to do so must, together with three other persons, master those [Vibhaṅgas] that are capable of being exchanged [in recitation].

Furthermore, one must learn what constitutes a valid and invalid legal act (kamma), as well as the conduct prescribed in the Khandhaka. For the purpose of guiding the assembly in the Abhidhamma, however—
If one is a reciter of the Majjhima Nikāya, the *Mūlapaṇṇāsa* should be mastered; by a reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya, the *Mahāvagga*;

by a reciter of the Saṃyutta Nikāya, either the first three sections (*vaggas*) or the *Mahāvagga*; and by a reciter of the Aṅguttara Nikāya, half of the collection (*nikāya*) from either the beginning or the end should be mastered.
For one who is unable [to master so much], it is also permissible to master the portion starting from the *Tikanipāta* downwards. (From the *Mahāpaccarī*)
However, it is stated: "For one learning [the Dhamma], it is permissible to take up either the Catukka-nipāta or the Pañcaka-nipāta.
A reciter of the Jātakas must learn the Jātaka together with its commentary; less than that is not permitted.
It is stated in the Mahāpaccarī that it is also permissible to learn the Dhammapada along with its background stories (*vatthu*). Having compiled these from various sources...
Is a mere basic fifty [of the Dhammapada] sufficient, or is it not? In the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā*, it is rejected with the words, "It is not sufficient";
in the other commentaries, there is no discussion at all. It is not stated in the Abhidhamma that anything need be mastered.

However, for one who has already become proficient in the Vinaya Piṭaka and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, including their commentaries, and who possesses the aforementioned qualities regarding the Suttanta...
One who has no mastery of the texts is not permitted to establish a following.

However, one who has mastered the texts as prescribed in both the Suttanta and the Vinaya is a learned one who establishes a following; such a person is a renowned teacher who travels wherever he wishes and is permitted to establish a following.
Furthermore, the instructor of bhikkhunīs should master the Three Piṭakas together with their commentaries.

If he is unable to do so, he should make the commentary on one of the four Nikāyas thoroughly proficient; for by means of one Nikāya, he will be able to explain questions regarding the remaining Nikāyas as well.
Among the seven treatises (pakaraṇas), he should make the commentary on four of them thoroughly proficient; therein—
For by means of the method already acquired, he will be able to explain the questions in the remaining treatises.

However, since the Vinaya Piṭaka has various meanings and various reasons, it must certainly be mastered together with its commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). To this extent, indeed, a monk who instructs nuns is called "learned" (bahussuta).

The passage beginning with "But both of these... is stated separately because, even when all other nine factors of great learning (*bāhusacca*) are present, it is simply not possible without the Vinaya Piṭaka together with its commentary (*sāṭṭhakatha*).
In that context, "in detail" means together with the two Vibhaṅgas. "Well-received" (*svāgatāni*) means properly received. To show how they are well-received, [the text says]:
“‘Well-analyzed,’ and so forth, was said. Therein, ‘well-analyzed’ means thoroughly analyzed, being free from the faults of misplaced words, omissions, or confusion.
‘Well-proclaimed’ means mastered and brought to the lips. ‘Well-determined according to the Suttas’ means well-determined by way of the suttas to be cited from the Khandhaka and Parivāra.
‘According to the phonemes’ means by way of the completeness of syllables and words.”
And they are well-determined, unbroken, and with syllables that are not distorted. By this, the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) is indicated, for this determination arises from the commentary.
"Possessing beautiful speech" means having words and phrases that are perfectly rounded through speaking according to the rules regarding laxity, emphasis, and so forth.
He is endowed with speech that is polished, distinct, free from indistinctness, and capable of making the meaning known. "Possessed of beautiful speech" means having a sweet voice;
for women delight in excellence of voice, and therefore they despise even speech whose words and phrases are perfectly rounded if it lacks excellence of voice.
He is generally dear and pleasing to the bhikkhunīs; he is dear to all of them.
He is difficult to find; however, he is dear to and pleasing to the majority of wise bhikkhunīs due to his perfection in virtue and conduct.

He is capable of instructing the bhikkhunīs, for he is able to teach such a Dhamma by demonstrating both the scriptural authority and the underlying reason, and by exhorting the bhikkhunīs with the fear of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭabhaya*).

"Clad in saffron robes" means dressed in saffron-colored garments. "A heavy rule" (garudhamma) refers to the fact that, during her time as a householder, she has never previously committed an offense such as physical contact with a monk or sexual intercourse with a female trainee (sikkhamānā) or a novice nun (sāmaṇerī).
For a woman who recalls what was done in the past does not show respect for the teaching of the Dhamma, even toward one established in self-restraint. Now...
Or he arouses his mind toward that very unrighteousness. "One who has twenty years [of seniority]" means one who has been ordained for twenty years or more than that.
For such a person, even if they repeatedly encounter unsuitable objects, does not—as a youth would—suddenly come to the destruction of their virtue;
rather, having reflected upon their own age, [they avoid] what is improper.
He is capable of subduing desire and lust; therefore it is said: “He is twenty years of age or more than twenty. In this context, “virtuous” (*sīlavā*) and so forth constitutes the first factor;
“learned” (*bahussuto*) and so forth is the second; “both of these [qualities] indeed belong to him” and so forth is the third;
“he is of good speech and possesses a refined manner of speaking” is the fourth; and “for the most part [he is able to instruct] the bhikkhunīs... [and so forth].
“It is dear and pleasing” is the fifth; “he is capable of exhorting the bhikkhunīs” is the sixth; “But this is not so,” etc., is the seventh;
and “twenty years of age,” etc., is to be understood as the eighth. 148.

“By a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations” (ñatticatutthena) is exactly as stated previously regarding the matter. “By the heavy rules” (garudhammehi) means by the weighty rules.
For these are called "heavy rules" (*garudhamma*) because they must be accepted by the bhikkhunīs with respect.

Regarding the phrase "one who is fully ordained on one side": here, if one exhorts a woman who has been fully ordained on one side—that is, in the presence of the bhikkhunīs—by means of a heavy rule, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for him.
However, if she has been fully ordained in the presence of the bhikkhus, it is according to the actual status [of her ordination].

149. "Having swept the pariveṇa": if it has not been swept in the morning, or even if it was swept but has become dirty again with grass, leaves, and so forth, or if the sand has been scattered by kicks from feet, it must be swept. For seeing that it has not been swept, [the teacher] thinks:
"The venerable one does not even engage his own dependents, the young bhikkhus, in the performance of duties; he teaches only the Dhamma..."
The bhikkhunīs might become as if unwilling to listen [to what was being said]. Therefore it is said: “Having swept the pariveṇa.
Furthermore, when the bhikkhunīs come from within the village, they are thirsty and weary; they expect drinking water and means to cool their hands, feet, and faces.
If these are not provided, there will be disrespect for the same reasons as mentioned before.
Having brought it forth, they may even become unwilling to listen. Therefore it is said: "having set out drinking water and water for washing.

Regarding the seat: having prepared a seat—be it of various kinds such as low stools, wooden planks, mats, or straw mats, or even just a broken branch—thinking, "this shall be their seat. Furthermore, for the purpose of being released from the offense of preaching the Dhamma:
A second person must be sought. Therefore it is said: “Having taken a second, one should sit down.

“One should sit down” means not at the edge of the monastery, but rather in the middle of the monastery, at the door of the Uposatha hall or the dining hall—in a place where everyone gathers. “All have come” means that all have arrived. “They conduct themselves” means...
They come; the meaning is that they are proficient and have mastered [the texts]. "It should be handed over" means it should be applied. "It should be recited" means the Pāḷi should be spoken.
"For one who is fully ordained for a hundred years," etc., is the demonstration of the Pāḷi to be spoken.
Therein, "proper conduct" (sāmīcikamma) refers to the appropriate duties such as preparing the path, providing seeds, and asking for water.
And herein, the salutation of a bhikkhunī to a bhikkhu means: whether in a village or outside a village,
in a monastery or outside a monastery, in a house or on a carriage road—

even when a royal procession is taking place, or while it is raining and the ground is muddy, or even if she holds an umbrella and a water-strainer in her hand, or is followed by elephants, horses, and so forth.
It must indeed be done. When seeing [nuns] entering for alms on a continuous line, it is appropriate to pay homage at one place, saying, "I pay homage, Venerable Ladies.
If they walk with intervals of twelve cubits between them, they should be paid homage individually.
When seated in a great assembly, it is appropriate to pay homage at that very same spot. This is the method.
And also the act of joining the palms in reverence. However, rising to meet her should be done whenever she is seated;
it should be performed at the appropriate place and time, corresponding to each specific act of respectful service.
"Having honored" means having acted in such a way that the honor is well-rendered. "Having revered" means having generated a sense of respect toward her.
"Having honored" means having made dear through mental respect. "Having worshipped" means having worshipped by performing these very three duties.
"Not to be transgressed" means it must not be overstepped.
Regarding the phrase "in a residence without monks": here, if within half a *yojana* of the nuns' quarters there are those who give the exhortation...
When no bhikkhus reside there, this is called a "residence without bhikkhus. One should not spend the rains retreat there. For it has been said:
"A residence without bhikkhus is one where it is not possible to go for exhortation or for communal living.
Furthermore, it is not possible to go there after the meal, listen to the Dhamma, and then return. If one were to spend the rains retreat there...
If nuns who do not wish [to stay] are told by relatives or supporters, "Venerable ladies, please stay;

we shall bring monks," it is permissible. However, if monks who intend to enter the rains retreat in that prescribed area arrive and stay for even one night in a bower of branches—provided they have not been invited and do not intend to leave—it is permissible on this account as well.
A residence that has monks is suitable for entering the rains retreat.
Those who enter must request the monks on the thirteenth day of the fortnight itself, saying: "Venerable sirs, we shall dwell under your instruction.
However, if the place where the monks reside is half a *yojana* away by the direct route, then for those traveling by that same route—
If there is a danger to life or a danger to the holy life, or if for those traveling by another route the distance exceeds half a *yojana*,
this [rule] remains in force only in a place where no monks reside. However, if within a *gāvuta* from there there is another nunnery in a safe location,
those nuns should request permission from the resident nuns, and having returned, they should then request permission from the monks.
“Venerable sirs, there is an obstacle on our direct path; it is more than half a yojana by way of another route.
However, along the way, about a quarter-league from our residence, there is another nunnery.
We shall stay there, receiving the exhortation from the venerable ladies when they have arrived. This should be accepted by those monks. Then, by those bhikkhunīs...
Having come to that nunnery, the Uposatha should be performed; or, having seen those bhikkhunīs, it is also permissible to go to one's own residence and perform it there.
However, if bhikkhus who wish to enter the rains retreat arrive at the monastery on the fourteenth day, and [the bhikkhunīs...]
When asked, "Noble ladies, will you spend the rains retreat here? they replied, "Yes. Then those [other] nuns said, "In that case, noble ladies, we too shall stay, living under your guidance.
On the second day, however, not seeing any success in their alms-round in the village, they departed, saying, "It is not possible to stay here. Then, on the Uposatha day, those bhikkhunīs...
If, having gone to the monastery, they do not see any bhikkhus, what should be done here?
One should go to where the bhikkhus are residing and enter upon the later rains residence there.

Alternatively, one may stay and dwell with those who have arrived, having formed the intention: "They will come to enter upon the later rains residence," and by means of exhortation. But if [they do not find anyone] even during the later period...
Some arrive, but on the way there is danger from kings, danger from thieves, or famine;
for her who stays in a residence without monks, there is an offense, and for her who goes away after breaking the rains retreat, there is also an offense—she must be protected.
For it is stated that there is no offense for one staying in a residence without monks during times of distress. If she arrives and enters the rains retreat...
If the bhikkhunīs depart again for some reason, they must certainly stay [in retreat]. For this has been said:

“There is no offense if the bhikkhus who have entered the rains retreat have departed, or have left the order, or have died, or have gone over to another faction, or if there are emergencies, or if she is insane, or if she is a first-offender.
However, when it is time for the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā), she should go where the bhikkhus are and perform the invitation ceremony there.
“Every half-month” means every half-month. “Two things are to be expected” means two things are to be desired.

“The inquiry regarding the Uposatha” means the asking about the Uposatha; therein, on the fifteenth-day Uposatha, one should go on the fourteenth day of the fortnight, and on the fourteenth-day Uposatha, on the thirteenth day, and inquire about the Uposatha. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, [it says]: “Of the fortnight...”
It was said: "Having gone on the thirteenth day itself, one should ask: 'Is this Uposatha the fourteenth or the fifteenth?

On the Uposatha day, one should approach for the purpose of receiving instruction; however, from the first day of the lunar fortnight (pāṭipada) onwards, one should go for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.
Thus the Blessed One, not allowing any interval for other activities, [established] for the bhikkhunīs and the bhikkhus... [a continuous practice].
He prescribed that they should go into his presence. Why? Because women are of dull intelligence. For women are of dull intelligence;
therefore, constant listening to the Dhamma is of great benefit.
And this being so, by attending upon the Saṅgha of monks without harboring the conceit, "The Ayyās know only what we ourselves know," they will make their going forth truly fruitful.
Therefore, the Blessed One acted in this way. The bhikkhunīs also, thinking, "We shall practice according to the instructions," all went to the monastery in continuous succession. For it is said:
"At that time, the entire community of bhikkhunīs went for the exhortation. People complained..."
They criticize and complain, saying, “These are their wives; these are their mistresses; now they will take pleasure with them.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One: “Monks, the entire Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs should not go for the exhortation.
If it should go, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). I allow you, monks, [to go] by four or five.”
“Let the bhikkhunīs go for the exhortation. Again they complained in the same manner.
Once more the Blessed One said, “I allow you, monks, to send two or three bhikkhunīs to give the exhortation.
Therefore, the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs should request and dispatch two or three bhikkhunīs, saying: “Come, noble ladies, to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.”
“Venerable ladies, the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha requests the approach for exhortation... [the request for] the approach for exhortation.
Those bhikkhunīs must go to the monastery. Then, having approached and paid homage to one bhikkhu who accepts the exhortation, that bhikkhu should be addressed by one bhikkhunī as follows:
“Venerable sir, the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha [requests the approach for exhortation from] the Bhikkhu-saṅgha...”
She prostrates at his feet and requests the visit for the exhortation, saying: "Venerable sir, may the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs receive the visit for the exhortation.
That bhikkhu should approach the bhikkhu who recites the Pātimokkha and speak to him thus:
"Venerable sir, the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs prostrates at the feet of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and requests the visit for the exhortation; may they receive it, venerable sir."
“The community of bhikkhunīs is to approach for the exhortation. The reciter of the Pātimokkha should ask:
“Is there any bhikkhu appointed as an exhorter of the bhikkhunīs? If there is a bhikkhu appointed as an exhorter of the bhikkhunīs, the reciter of the Pātimokkha should say:
“The bhikkhu named so-and-so is appointed as the exhorter of the bhikkhunīs; let the community of bhikkhunīs approach him.”
If there is no monk appointed as a teacher of the nuns, the reciter of the Pātimokkha should say:

"Which venerable one is able to exhort the nuns? If there is a monk who is able to exhort the nuns and he is endowed with eight qualities, having appointed him, he should be told: "Venerable [Name]..."
“Let the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs approach that bhikkhu who has been appointed as the instructor of bhikkhunīs.
But if no one is willing to instruct the bhikkhunīs, the reciter of the Pātimokkha should say:
“There is no bhikkhu appointed as the instructor of bhikkhunīs; let the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs conduct itself with inspiring confidence. Up to this point—
For thus has the entire Teaching, comprised of the three trainings, been announced.

Having accepted this with the words "Very well," that monk should announce it to the bhikkhunīs on the first day of the fortnight (the *pāṭipada*). The Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs should also dispatch those bhikkhunīs [to him], saying:
"Go, noble ladies, and ask: 'What, noble sir, does the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs receive regarding the approach for exhortation? By them, it should be replied: "Very well, noble sir."
Having accepted [the invitation], they should go to the monastery, approach that bhikkhu, and say: "Venerable sir, will the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs receive the exhortation?
He should reply: "There is no bhikkhu appointed as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs; let the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs conduct itself with inspiring confidence. They should then say: "Very well, Venerable sir."
It should be accepted. This is stated with reference to those who have come together from one side;
however, among them, one nun must both speak and accept, while the other is her companion.
But if either the community of nuns or the community of monks is not complete, or if there is merely a group on both sides, [the procedure is as follows].
It may be just a single person, or a single bhikkhunī sent from many bhikkhunī dwellings for the purpose of receiving exhortation.
In that case, the manner of speech is as follows: “Venerable sir, the bhikkhunīs pay homage at the feet of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and request permission to approach for exhortation;
may the bhikkhunīs, venerable sir, receive permission to approach for exhortation. [Or: “I, venerable sir, [on behalf] of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha...”

May the community of bhikkhunīs, noble sir, receive the opportunity to approach for instruction. "The bhikkhunīs, noble sir, pay homage at the feet of the noble ones..."
“They request the approach for the exhortation, saying: ‘May the noble ones grant the nuns the approach for the exhortation. [The Elder says:

“I, noble sir, pay homage at the feet of the noble one and request the approach for the exhortation. May I, noble sir, receive the approach for the exhortation.”

May it be granted, may it be granted, may it be granted, venerable sir, to the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha, the bhikkhunīs, and this bhikkhunī.”
"And the approaching for instruction.

“A bhikkhunī, venerable sirs, pays homage at the feet of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and requests permission to approach for the exhortation.
May the bhikkhunī, venerable sirs, receive permission to approach for the exhortation.

“The Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, venerable sirs; the bhikkhunīs, venerable sirs; a bhikkhunī, venerable sirs, pays homage at the feet of the Venerable Ones and requests permission to approach for the exhortation. May the bhikkhunī, venerable sirs, receive permission to approach for the exhortation.”
“Venerable sir, the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, the bhikkhunīs, and this bhikkhunī pay homage at the feet of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and the venerable ones;

Having returned on the first day of the fortnight, the receiver of the exhortation should speak in that same manner. “I allow you, monks, to receive the exhortation from those remaining, excluding the fool, the sick, and the traveler.

In this regard, one who is a traveler—whether desiring to go on the fourteenth or fifteenth day of the half-month, or on the first day of the new moon (pāṭipada)—does not receive permission to omit it even if he departs on the second day of the fortnight.
[The Buddha said: “Monks, the exhortation must not be omitted.”
"Whoever should not accept it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Thus, one indeed incurs the offense mentioned.

"Monks, the exhortation must not be left unannounced. Whoever should not announce it, there is an offense of wrong-doing."
Furthermore, it is said:
“Monks, the exhortation must not be declined. Whoever should decline it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
In that regard, one who dwells in the forest should make an appointment for the purpose of returning for the exhortation. For this has been said: “I allow you, monks—”

"I will go to such-and-such a hall, pavilion, or foot of a tree at your village gate;

It is not permitted. For this has been said: “Monks, a bhikkhunī must not fail to go to the appointment.

“Let the noble Saṅgha hear me. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha appoint the bhikkhunī named so-and-so to invite the Bhikkhu Saṅgha on behalf of the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. This is the motion.

Having arranged the upper robe and extended the hands in reverential salutation, he should speak to him thus:

There is no offense for one who speaks [the Dhamma] by way of a *pācittiya* rule. There is no offense for one who speaks another teaching by way of a *dukkaṭa* rule.

Regarding "he asks a question" and "being asked a question he explains": if a bhikkhunī asks a question based on the *garudhammas* or based on the aggregates (*khandhas*) and so forth, there is no offense for the bhikkhu who explains it to her. Regarding "speaking for the sake of another": [this refers to speaking] to the fourfold assembly.

There is also no offense for one teaching these—namely, a female trainee (sikkhamānā) or a female novice (sāmaṇerī). The rest is self-evident. Regarding the origin of the training rule concerning recitation word-for-word:

it originates from speech and from speech-mind; it is an action; it is not released by recognition; it is without mental intention; it is an offense of formal prescription; it is verbal action; it consists of three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The first training rule on exhortation. 2.

153. Regarding the second training rule: "In turn" means by way of sequence; the meaning is "in order. "Of one with higher mind" means of one possessing higher consciousness (*adhicitta*).
The meaning is: "of one who is endowed with the mind of the fruit of Arahantship, which is superior to all minds.
"Appamajjato" means "of one who does not neglect," that is to say, "of one who is endowed with the constant practice of wholesome states through heedfulness.
"Munino" refers to one who, by "knowing both worlds," is thus called a "muni" (sage).
Alternatively, "mona" is said to mean knowledge; because he is endowed with that knowledge, one who has destroyed the taints is called a "muni.

[The phrase] "of that muni" refers to him. "Training in the paths of muna" means training in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—which are the paths of muna consisting of the knowledge of arahantship—or in the three trainings.
And this is stated by way of taking up the preliminary practice; therefore, thus...
The meaning here should be understood as follows: "of one who has attained the state of a sage (muni) by training in this training during the prior stage.

Alternatively, "for such a one" refers to a sage endowed with the characteristic of suchness (tādilakkhaṇa). Sorrows [do not exist] for a sage of this kind.
"They do not exist"—this is the meaning here. "Of one who is calmed" means of one who is calmed through the subsiding of lust and the other defilements.

"In the sky, in the atmosphere" means in the sky known as the atmosphere (*antalikkha*), not in the space cleared by the removal of the *kasiṇa*, nor in the delimitation of form. He even walks back and forth there.
Having heard the conversation of those bhikkhunīs, he thought:
"These bhikkhunīs despise me, thinking, 'He knows only this much. Come now, I shall show them my own power.
Having thus conceived a great reverence for the Dhamma, he attained the fourth jhāna as a basis for direct knowledge; then, emerging from it, he performed such a miracle of psychic power.
He displayed [his powers], saying: “He walks even in the sky, in the firmament... [and so on] ...he even makes himself invisible.

In this context, “he even makes himself invisible” means that he goes even to the point of being unseen. It is said that the Elder [Mahāmoggallāna] recited that very inspired utterance (*udāna*) and much other word of the Buddha in the presence of his own brother-elder.
"Just as a fragrant red lotus might bloom at dawn with its scent unspent,
behold Aṅgīrasa shining forth."
“Like the sun scorching in the sky.
Having been made to recite this verse, he practiced it for four months, yet he was unable to master it.
Then the Elder had him expelled from the monastery, saying, “You are incapable in this Dispensation. Weeping, he stood at the gateway.
He stood there. Then the Blessed One, surveying those beings who were ready to be trained with his Buddha-eye, saw him;
approaching him as if taking a stroll through the monastery, he asked, "Cūḷapanthaka, why are you weeping?
He related the matter to him. Then the Blessed One gave him a piece of clean cloth and said, "This is a 'dust-remover,' a 'dust-remover.'"
"Rub it clean," he said. Having agreed, saying "Very well," he sat down in his own dwelling place and rubbed the other's side.

The place where he had rubbed became black. Seeing this, he was struck with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), thinking, "Even though this cloth is so pure, it has become black because of this physical body. He then applied himself to insight meditation (*vipassanā*).
He began [to practice]. Then the Blessed One, knowing his state of aroused energy, spoke this illuminating verse: "Of one whose mind is exalted.
At the conclusion of the verse, the Elder attained Arahatship. Therefore, the Elder already owned this verse by nature;
he recites that very verse to make known his ownership of it. And another...
Having interspersed it with much of the Buddha’s word, it is therefore said: “He recites that very *udāna* and much other Buddha-word.

(156) “To one who has been fully ordained on one side” means to one who has been fully ordained in the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha; however, for one who exhorts a woman who has been fully ordained in the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). The rest here is self-evident. And this too originates solely from the mastery of the words.
The eighth training rule is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Nuns’ Quarters. 162.
Regarding the third training rule—“if she instructs [the nuns] except at the proper time, there is an offense of *pācittiya*,” and so forth—with respect to these eight [factors]:

It should be understood that for one who exhorts [a nun] by means of the *garudhammas* alone, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*); for exhorting her by means of any other teaching, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

"From one side ordained" (*ekatoupasampannā*) means one who has been ordained in the community of nuns (*bhikkhunīsaṅgha*); however, for one who exhorts a woman ordained in the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*), there is likewise an offense of expiation.
From here on, wherever the term "from one side ordained" is used, this same meaning is to be understood. The rest is self-evident.

The origin of the *Kathina* [offense]: it originates from body and speech, and from body, speech, and mind; it is an action (*kiriya*); it is not liberated by perception (*no-saññā-vimokkha*); it is without thought (*acittaka*); it is an offense of transgression against the rules (*paṇṇatti-vajja*); it is bodily action and verbal action; it involves three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
This is the third training rule concerning the nuns’ quarters. Furthermore, regarding the miscellaneous matter mentioned here in the *Mahāpaccarī*:
if a monk who has not been authorized [to perform the Uposatha] [does so] after the sun has set...
If one approaches the nuns' quarters and instructs them with the eight *garudhammas*, there are three *pācittiyas*.
If one instructs them with another teaching, there are two *dukkaṭas* and one *pācittiya*. How so? There is a *dukkaṭa* based on not being authorized;
a *dukkaṭa* based on going to the quarters and instructing with another teaching; and [a *dukkaṭa*] based on instructing when the sun has set.

"An offense entailing expiation (pācittiya). When one who has been formally authorized goes there after sunset and instructs with the eight weighty rules (garudhamma), there is one non-offense and two offenses of expiation. How so? There is no offense because of being authorized;

there is one offense of expiation based on instructing after sunset, and one offense of expiation based on going and instructing with the weighty rules—thus, two offenses of expiation. For that same person, by another rule...
In the case of one who gives advice, there is one non-offense, one offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), and one offense entailing expiation (pācittiya). How so?

There is no offense because of being duly authorized; there is an offense of wrong-doing based on going and advising by means of another teaching; and there is an offense entailing expiation based on advising when the sun has set.
However, for one who goes during the day and advises—whether authorized or unauthorized—there is an offense based on advising at night.
"Excluding one *pācittiya*, the remainder should be understood as offenses and non-offenses.
The miscellaneous discussion is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Material Gain (*āmisa-sikkhāpada*).
164. Regarding the fourth training rule: *na bahukatā* means not having shown great respect; the intended meaning is that she does not instruct out of respect for the Dhamma.

The meaning of the phrases beginning with “desiring to speak dispraise of the instructor of bhikkhunīs” should be understood according to the method explained under the offense of censuring (*ujjhāpanaka*).

Regarding the phrase “one who is fully ordained but not authorized by the Saṅgha,” here “not authorized” refers to one who has not been entrusted with the responsibility either by another who is authorized or by the Saṅgha.

It should be understood that [the person] has been established [in that role] after having performed [the formal act]. Regarding the phrase "one who is not fully ordained, whether authorized or unauthorized":
here, one who has received authorization during the time he was a bhikkhu but now stands on the level of a novice (sāmaṇera) is to be understood as "authorized";
or, a learned novice established by an authorized Saṅgha is to be understood as "unauthorized. The remainder is self-evident because it follows the method already explained.

It has three origins: it originates from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind; it is an action (kiriya); it is liberated by perception (saññāvimokkha); it is accompanied by consciousness (sacittaka); it is an offense against worldly convention (lokavajja); it is bodily action and verbal action; it is unwholesome consciousness;
and it is associated with painful feeling. This is the fourth training rule concerning material things. 5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Giving of Robes.
169. Regarding the fifth training rule: “In the street” means on a carriage road. “He wanders for alms” means he wanders frequently by way of regular rounds.
“Those who were acquainted” means they were friends known to one another. The rest here is clear from the words;
however, the detailed exposition, along with the origin (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth, should be understood in the same manner as stated under the training rule concerning the acceptance of robes.
For in that case it was a monk who was the recipient, whereas here it is a nun; this is the distinction. The rest is exactly the same.
This concludes the fifth training rule concerning the giving of robes. 6.
Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Sewing Robes.
175. In the sixth training rule: *Udāyī* refers to Lāḷudāyī. *Paṭṭho* means capable; it is said to mean one who is both clever and competent.
*Aññatarā bhikkhunī* (a certain nun) was his former wife. *Paṭibhānacittaṃ* means a cloth-work made by one’s own ingenuity;
it is said that he dyed a robe and, in its center, depicted an unfinished act of sexual intercourse using various colors.
He made it into the form of a woman or a man. Therefore it was said: "having caused a beautiful design to appear in the middle. "As it was sewn together" means exactly as it was stitched. 176.
"A robe" refers to that which can be worn as an undergarment or put on as an upper garment; for thus it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other commentaries. "Sews herself":
here, even for one who is deliberating, "I shall sew," or for one who is cutting [the cloth], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
But for one who sews, it is a *pācittiya* offense. "From needle-point to needle-point" means: each time a needle is inserted and withdrawn after being inserted.
However, if he does not withdraw the entire needle but pierces it a hundred times for the sake of inserting a long thread and then withdraws it, there is only a single *pācittiya*.
"Once commanded" means: once told, "Sew the robe. Even if [the command] is repeated many times...
Regarding "sews": even if one finishes the entire needlework and completes the robe, there is only one *pācittiya*.

However, if one is told, "The work to be done on this robe is your responsibility," and then performs it, there is one *pācittiya* for every stage of the work (*ārāpatha*) for the one who was commanded;
for the one who gave the command, there are many [offenses] even for a single utterance. In the case of repeated commands, [the offense is incurred] again and again.
But there is nothing at all that needs to be said [further].

Even for those who, while their own teachers or preceptors are sewing the robes of their relatives, act as their dependents and sew them thinking, "We shall perform the duties toward the teacher or preceptor, or the duties regarding the kaṭhina," they incur offenses according to the count of the *ārāpa* (the distance of the shuttle). This applies to both the teacher and the preceptor.
If they have their pupils sew a robe for their own relatives, it is a dukkaṭa offense for the preceptor and teacher, and a pācittiya offense for the pupils.

If the pupils have their preceptors and teachers sew a robe for their own relatives, the same rule applies there as well. If a robe belongs to a relative of either the pupils or the preceptors and teachers, [the preceptors and teachers...]
However, if they deceive the pupils and have [the robes] sewn, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for both. Why?

Because the pupils sewed them with the perception that they were unrelated persons, and because the others were directed toward what is not allowable. Therefore, having explained, "This robe is for your mother;
this is for your sister," one should have them sewn.
179. “Another requisite” means anything such as a sandal-bag and so forth. The rest is self-evident. It has six origins:
it is an action, not associated with perception or liberation, without mental concomitants, an offense by formal rule, bodily action, verbal action, threefold in mind, and threefold in feeling.
This is the sixth training rule concerning the sewing of robes.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule on Arrangements (Saṃvidhānasikkhāpada) 181. Regarding the seventh training rule:
"While they were walking behind, thieves plundered them" means that while they were walking behind, thieves stole their bowls and robes.
"They violated them" means those bhikkhunīs were violated by the thieves; the meaning is that they brought about the destruction of their virtue.
182–3. *Saṃvidhāya* means having made arrangements; the meaning is: having made an appointment at the time of departure. Regarding *kukkuṭasampāda*:
here, because a cock, having gone out from one village, goes to another village by foot alone, this is called *kukkuṭasampāda*.
Herein, this is the etymological analysis: they go together (*sampadanti*) there, thus it is *sampāda*. What goes together? Cocks.
The "coming together" (*sampāda*) of cocks is "cock-coming-together" (*kukkuṭasampāda*). Alternatively, *sampāda* means "going";
thus, it is also called "cock-coming-together" because there is the coming together of cocks here. There is also a reading *kukkuṭasampāte*;
in that case, it refers to a village where a cock, having flown up from the roof of one house, lands on the roof of another. This...
It is called "a village within cock's flight. The meaning of the term here should be understood according to the method already stated.
Furthermore, even if this village is of the two kinds mentioned, if it is too close together, no "proximity zone" (upacāra) can be established.
However, in a country filled with such villages where the cry of a cock crowing at dawn in one village is heard in the very next village, [the rule applies] between those villages.
"An offense entailing expiation (pācittiya) within a village" is stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). Although it is so stated,
because of the words, "For every village interval there is an offense of expiation," if there is even a village only a cubit (ratana) apart,
there is indeed an offense for one who enters its boundary established by the people thereof.

In this regard, the determination of the offense is as follows: If, at the time of making the appointment, both [monks] stand in the nuns’ quarters, within the monastery grounds, in a hall for seating, or on the beds of the non-Buddhist sectarians and make their appointment, there is no offense, for this is considered a *kappiya-bhūmi* (a place where things are allowable).

Therefore, they do not say that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) here due to the act of appointing; for one who goes [to the meeting], it remains exactly as the original basis [of the rule].

If, however, they make an appointment within the village—at the door of a nunnery, on a street, or at other places such as crossroads, junctions, elephant stables, and so forth—the monk incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Having made such an appointment, if they depart from the village, there is no offense at the time of departure;
however, upon entering the precinct of the next village, the monk incurs a *pācittiya* offense. In that case as well:
"In the first step there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); in the second step, an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya)," so it is stated in the Mahāpaccarī.

However, after departing from a village, as long as they have not yet entered the precincts (upacāra) of the next village, even if they have made an appointment within that interval, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the monk;
upon entering the precincts of the next village, there is an offense according to the previous method. If they wish to go a great distance...
According to the calculation of the village precincts, there is an offense for every entry [into the precinct], but there is no offense upon passing beyond each respective village.

However, if a bhikkhunī leaves her residence thinking, "I will go to such-and-such a village," and a bhikkhu also leaves the monastery thinking, "I will go to such-and-such a village," with reference to that very same village; [then there is no offense].
Now, if two [monks] meet at the gate of a village and say, “Where are you going?
“To such-and-such a village,” and “We too are going there,” and having made an appointment, saying, “Come now, let us go,” they depart—there is no offense. Why?
Because they had already set out with the intention, “We will go beforehand,” as stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*. That [explanation] is not found in the *Pāḷi*...
This does not agree with the *Sīhaḷa-aṭṭhakathā*.

According to the view that "half-yojana, half-yojana," for one who is traversing each successive half-yojana, thinking, "Now I shall traverse [the next]," there is a *dukkaṭa* offense for the first step and a *pācittiya* offense for the second step.
For in this method, there is an offense upon the act of traversing, but no offense upon the act of entering [the destination].

184. A monk makes an appointment: having seen a nun at a city gate or on a street, he says, "I have gone before to such-and-such a village," to which she replies, "Venerable sir, I have not been there before. He then says, "Come, let us go," or "I shall go tomorrow;
you too should come. A nun makes an appointment: [she goes] within a village for the purpose of worshipping a cetiya.
Seeing a bhikkhu departing from a village, she says, "Venerable sir, where are you going?
He replies, "To such-and-such a village to pay homage at the cetiya. She says, "I too will come, venerable sir," and thus she makes an appointment with the bhikkhunī alone, not with the bhikkhu.
185. Regarding "by a different arrangement": having said, "We will go before the meal," they go after the meal.
Having said, "We will go today," they depart on the following day. Thus, there is no offense only when there is a discrepancy regarding the time;

however, if there is a discrepancy regarding the gate or the path, there is indeed an offense even if [the departure occurs later]. Regarding "in cases of distress": when the country is divided and the people mounted on their chariots are wandering through the provinces—in such cases of distress, there is no offense. The remainder is self-evident.

It has four origins: it originates from body, from body and speech, from body and mind, and from body, speech, and mind; it is functional (*kiriya*); it is not a liberation through perception (*nosaññāvimokkha*); it is without consciousness (*acittaka*); it is an offense by formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*); it is bodily action and verbal action;

it consists of three types of consciousness and three types of feeling. This is the seventh training rule concerning the arrangement [of furniture]. 8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Boarding a Boat.
188. Regarding the eighth training rule: *saṃvidhāya* means having made arrangements out of a desire for sport, by way of worldly pleasure and intimacy with friends.
*Uddhaṃgāminim* means going upstream against the current of a river.
However, since one who sports on a boat that moves upward by means of its own propulsion is said to "embark upon an upstream-going [boat]," therefore for him—

In the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), the phrase "by means of a swift boat" (*ujjavanikāya*) is stated in order to show the meaning itself. "Going downwards" (*adhogāminim*) means going down with the current.

Furthermore, because one who plays in a boat that moves swiftly downward is said to "board a boat going downwards," the phrase "by means of a swift boat" (*ojavanikāya*) is also stated in the word-commentary for that case in order to show the very same meaning.
In this context, there is no offense when they carry [the robe] upwards or downwards for the purpose of reaching a landing place (*tittha*).
"For the sake of crossing across" (*tiriyaṃ taraṇāya*) is an ablative expression used in the sense of the accusative. 189.
Regarding the phrase "from village to village": in the case of a river whose one bank is continuous with villages reachable by the flight of a cock, [there is no offense].
In the case of a forest path that has no villages, when traveling along its side where there are villages, there are *pācittiya* offenses according to the count of intervals between villages;
when traveling along its side where there are no villages, they are according to the count of half-yojanas.

Furthermore, for a path that is one yojana wide, it should be understood that even when traveling through its middle, there are *pācittiya* offenses according to the count of half-yojanas. There is no offense for crossing transversely.
In this case, there is no offense not only for one traveling by river, but also for one who goes from a great port city to Tāmaliptī or Suvaṇṇabhūmi;
for in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), the offense is discussed only in relation to the river, not the ocean. 191. Regarding "by a change of appointment":

here too, there is no offense only through a change of time-appointment; however, for one traveling with a change of landing-place appointment or a change of boat appointment, there is indeed an offense. The remainder, including the origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other factors, is exactly the same as in the first training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
The eighth training rule concerning boarding a boat.
9. Commentary on the ninth training rule concerning cooked food:
In the phrase "while the Great Nāgas were standing," the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative; that is, "among the Great Nāgas."

"Tiṭṭhamānesu" means "while they were staying. Alternatively, the phrase "without having seen" (*adisvā*) should be understood here as a textual ellipsis (*pāṭhaseso*) [to be supplied] after "while the Great Nāgas were staying";
otherwise, the meaning would not be coherent. "Antarākathā" refers to a discourse that has reached the middle point between its commencement and its conclusion, without yet reaching its end.
"Vippakatā" means it is being performed [in progress]. "Saccaṃ" [is the word for "truth"].
"O householder, these great *nāgas*, looking with half-closed eyes as they saw the elders entering, spoke thus after learning what had been heard by them:
'Bhikkhuniparipācita' means prepared by a bhikkhunī; it was accomplished through the manifestation of her virtues."

The meaning is "that which is to be obtained has been done. In the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), however, in order to show both the nun and the manner of her bringing [the donor] to maturity, it is said:
"A 'nun' is one who is fully ordained in both Saṅghas; 'brings to maturity' means those who previously were unwilling to give," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "previously initiated by householders" (*pubbe gihisamārambhā*): here, "previously" (*pubbe*) means first. "Initiated" (*samārambha*) refers to what has been undertaken (*samāraddha*).
This is a designation for what has been prepared. "Gihisamārambha" means the undertaking by householders.

It is stated that for a bhikkhunī, regarding food prepared by householders from the very beginning for her sake, there is an offense for one who eats something other than that alms-food (piṇḍapāta), setting it aside;
however, there is no offense for one who eats that [specific] food. This is said in the word-commentary (padabhājana).
However, because almsfood— even if not actually prepared for the sake of a monk—

by those who have invited their relatives, is in fact considered "prepared" in its essential sense since it may be brought according to one's pleasure, the text says, "Householder-preparation means they are either relatives or those who have invited [one]," in order to demonstrate the actual meaning rather than adhering strictly to the literal phrasing.
195. "Prepared for oneself" means it has been prepared by nature for that very bhikkhu himself, [thinking], "We shall give it to the Elder.
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, without saying "for him or another," it is stated without distinction: "It has been prepared [thinking], 'We shall give it to the bhikkhus.'"
197. "Excepting the five kinds of food, there is no offense in all cases" means that regarding rice gruel, dry food, and fruit, there is no offense even when these have been prepared by a nun.
The rest is self-evident. The origin of the first *pārājika* offense: it originates from body and mind; it is an action; it is liberated through perception; it involves volition;
it is an offense of formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*); it is bodily action; it consists of three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The ninth training rule concerning one who has brought another to maturity. 10. Commentary on the Tenth Training Rule Concerning Sitting in Private:
In the tenth training rule, the entire meaning of the canonical text and its detailed exposition are exactly according to the method already stated for the second *aniyata* offense.
This training rule (sikkhāpada) should be understood as having the same scope (ekapariccheda) as the second *aniyata* offense and the fourth training rule concerning Upananda that follows it;
however, it was formulated separately by way of its specific origin story (*aṭṭhuppatti*).
This is the tenth training rule, concerning sitting in private.
The third chapter, the Bhikkhunī-vagga, is completed according to the sequence of the commentary.
4. The Bhojana-vagga. 1. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Alms-food from a Public Rest House (Āvasathapiṇḍa-sikkhāpada).
203. Regarding the first training rule of the Chapter on Food (*Bhojanavagga*): "Alms-food from a lodging" (*āvasathapiṇḍa*) means alms-food at a lodging (*āvasathe piṇḍo*).

Having constructed a lodging (*āvasatha*) that is enclosed on all sides, provided with beds and chairs as appropriate for travelers, the sick, pregnant women, and renunciants, and consisting of many rooms and a central hall, if alms-food is prepared there out of a desire for merit—namely, everything such as rice-gruel, cooked rice, medicine, and so forth—[this constitutes the offense].
The meaning is that it was set aside for the purpose of giving to this or that [person]. "Even yesterday" means even tomorrow.
"Departing" means going away. "People were complaining": not seeing the sectarians, they complained upon hearing, "Where have the sectarians gone?
or "They have departed after seeing these [monks]. "Feeling remorse" means feeling anxiety; the meaning is that he gives rise to the perception that it is improper.
206. "He is able to depart from that lodging" means he is able to go half a *yojana* or a *yojana*.
"He is not able" means he is not able for just this much. "Indiscriminately" means it is established for all [monks] without specifying a single sect, such as "only for these" or "only for so many.
"As much as needed" means without delimiting even the food itself by saying "there is only this much."
It has been prepared as much as required. "To be eaten once" means it is to be eaten on a single day;
from the second day onwards, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for accepting it, and for every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
Herein, this is the analysis: whether by a single family or by various families acting together, at one place...
Or, regarding invitations arranged at various places without a fixed location—such as "today at one place;
tomorrow at another"—it is not permissible to eat at one such place on one day and then eat either at that same place or elsewhere on the following day.
However, regarding invitations arranged by various families at various locations, it is permissible to eat at one such location on one day and [eat elsewhere] on the second day.
It is permissible to eat elsewhere. However, it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that once the sequence has been exhausted, it is not permissible to start eating again from the beginning.
This same principle applies to a single group or different groups, and to a single village or different villages.
Furthermore, even if food such as rice and so forth has been prepared for one family or for several families together, should there be an interruption due to its exhaustion—

If it is cut off, that too must not be eaten. However, if they stop thinking, "We are unable to give," and then, when a wholesome state of mind has arisen again, they begin to give, it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that it is permissible to eat this once more on that same day. 208.
"There is no offense for one who is ill": there is no offense for one who eats after staying [overnight] while being ill. "Or one who is departing":...
If one who is traveling eats for one day at the place where he has gone on the road and for another day elsewhere, there is no offense for him.
The same rule applies to one who is returning. One who returns after having traveled is also permitted to eat for one day at the place where he has arrived on the road and for another day elsewhere.
If, having eaten with the intention "I shall go," he sets out and the river floods;
Or if there is fear of thieves and the like, he turns back; having ascertained that it is safe, as he proceeds, he is permitted to eat again on another day.
All of this is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other texts. "It has been prepared specifically" means it has been set aside and prepared solely for the sake of the monks.
"Not sufficient for as much as one needs" means it was not prepared for as much as one requires, but only a small amount.
If only a small amount is obtained, it is permissible to eat such [food] even regularly.

"In all cases except for the five kinds of cooked food" means that there is no offense in all other instances, such as the various types of rice gruel, snacks, fruits, and so forth; for it is permissible to eat rice gruel and the like even regularly.
The rest is self-evident. This offense originates from wool: it arises from both body and body-mind.

It is a functional (kiriya) action, not a liberation through perception (no-saññā-vimokkha), without consciousness (acittaka), an offense by way of formal rule (paṇṇatti-vajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), consisting of three types of consciousness, and associated with three types of feeling.
This is the first training rule concerning alms-food from a public rest-house.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Eating in a Group.

209. In the second training rule: "One whose gain and honor have declined"—it is said that even after he had caused King Ajātasattu to be killed, plotted his assassination, and brought about the shedding of blood, he remained concealed and hidden.
But when he employed Dhanapālaka during the very day, he became public knowledge. This was due to the widespread talk: "How did Devadatta employ the elephant?"

Once this became known, it was said: "Devadatta is a wicked man; he did not merely employ elephants, but also had the king killed, dispatched assassins, and hurled rocks. When asked, "With whom did he commit these deeds?
they replied, "With King Ajātasattu. Thereupon, the citizens exclaimed, "How indeed can the king [protect] such a thief, such a thorn in the side of the Dispensation?"
“Having seized him, he will wander about,” they said, and rose up. When the king learned of the agitation in the city, he had Devadatta led out.
From that time forth, he cut off for him five hundred servings of the five sweet foods;
he no longer went to attend upon him, and other people also thought that nothing should be given or done for him. Therefore it is said: “His gains and honor were diminished.”

“Eating after having repeatedly requested [food] from families” means: thinking, “May my group not be split,” and thus supporting his retinue by requesting, “You give food for one bhikkhu; you give for two,” he eats together with his followers at families.
211. “Robes arise in small quantities” means: they do not give robes to those who do not accept food; therefore, robes arise in small quantities.

212. "They invite the robe-making monks with a meal": seeing that [the monks] have been walking for alms in the village and are taking a long time to finish making the robe, they invite them out of a desire for merit, thinking, "By finishing the robe so quickly, they will be able to use it.
215. "From various foreign kingdoms" (*nānāverajjaka*): meaning those who have come from various other kingdoms. There is also a reading *nānāvirajjaka*, which has the same meaning.
217–8. "Eating in a group" (*gaṇabhojana*): regarding the eating of a group. And here, "a group" (*gaṇa*) refers to four or more monks.
Monks numbering more than that are intended here; thus, showing the absolute minimum limit, he said:
"Where there are four monks... this is called *gaṇabhojana* (eating in a group). Furthermore, this *gaṇabhojana* arises in two ways:
either through an invitation (*nimantana*) or through a request (*viññatti*). How does it arise through an invitation? [When] four monks...
Having approached, one invites by saying, "Venerable sirs, I invite you with rice; please accept my rice, desire it, look upon it, consent to it, and partake of it.

Thus, by whatever synonym or in whatever other language, one takes the name of any of the five kinds of cooked food and invites. Being thus invited together as a group, according to the limited time frame, for today...
Or if they go together, take [the food] together, or eat together for their own sake, it is a group meal (*gaṇabhojana*), and all incur an offense.
If invited together, they go either together or separately, but take [the food] together and eat separately, there is still an offense;
for in this case, the act of acceptance itself is the criterion. If invited together, they go together... [or separately].
There is no offense if they do not go separately, do not take [food] separately, or eat either together or separately.
Having gone to four different courtyards or monasteries, those invited separately may go either together or separately, or from one place to another— whether one goes with a son or one with a father—
even if thus invited separately, there is no offense if they go together or separately.
Or let them eat; if they take [the food] together, it constitutes a *gaṇabhojana* (eating in a group), and there is an offense for all. Thus, first, it arises from an invitation.
How does it arise from a request? Suppose four bhikkhus, standing or sitting together, see a lay follower and say, "For us..."
If they should request, "Give food for all four," or if, having seen them separately, they should request thus, "Give to me, give to me"—
whether requesting together or separately— and whether they go together or separately after receiving the food,
or eat together or separately once they have received it; if they take it together, it constitutes a *gaṇabhojana* (group meal) for all of them.
An offense. Thus it arises from solicitation.
"The feet are cracked" means that, as with a large hide, the flesh is visible beneath the skin;
they are thus fissured, and at the mere touch of sand or gravel, they cause pain such that one is unable to wander for alms even within a village.
"In such an illness, it is the time for the sick," thus one may eat; one must not perform the "token-allowance" (*lesakappiya*).
"While a robe is being made" means when, having obtained both cloth and thread, they are making a robe;
for there is no separate time specifically called "robe-making. Therefore, whatever work is to be done regarding that robe, if one performs it—
For in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "At least one who pierces with a needle";
by this, it means one should eat at the time when the robe is being made. In the *Kurundi*, however, it is stated in detail:
whoever arranges the robe, cuts it, lays down the waste-thread, lays down the border-strip for newcomers, sews the returned pieces, fastens the border-strip for newcomers, and cuts along the grain.
He rubs it, he stretches it, he sews what has been brought back there, he makes the thread, he weaves it, he fixes the toggle, he performs the turning-over;
all this is indeed called "making the robe. However, one who sits nearby and recites the *Jātaka* or the *Dhammapada* is not a robe-maker.
With the exception of these, for the rest, there is no offense in eating with a group.
"Half a yojana" means by one who wishes to travel even this much distance. As for one who wishes to go a long way, there is no need to say more.
"By one going" means by one traveling on a journey; it is permissible to eat even within a quarter-yojana (gāvuta) of half a yojana.
"To be eaten by one who has gone" means it is to be eaten by one who has traveled for a single day. The same applies to boarding a ship.

This is the method. However, this is the distinction: it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that even after one has boarded and reached the desired destination, one may continue to eat as long as one does not disembark. "When a fourth person has arrived" is the final limit;
when even a fourth person has arrived and they no longer find sustenance there, that is a "great assembly" (*mahāsamaya*). But where a hundred or a thousand people gather together—
In that regard, there is nothing at all to be said. Therefore, at such a time, one should resolve, "It is the Great Assembly," and eat.

Whoever has entered the state of a wandering ascetic—whether among fellow practitioners of the Dharma or among those of other sects—if a meal is prepared by any of these, it may be eaten under the designation, "the time for the alms-food of recluses."

220. There is no offense regarding "the occasion": there is no offense when any one of the seven occasions applies. Regarding "two or three together": even for those who, having accepted an improper invitation, eat after taking two or three [meals] together, there is no offense.

In this regard, the determination should be understood by way of five tetrads: the tetrad of "not invited as the fourth," the tetrad of "alms-food as the fourth," the tetrad of "one not fully ordained as the fourth," the tetrad of "the bowl as the fourth," and the tetrad of "the sick as the fourth. How so? Here, a certain person...
Four monks invite [him], saying, "Please take food. Of them, three have gone, but one has not.
The lay follower asks, "Venerable sir, where is the one elder? [The reply is: "He has not come, lay follower.

He then brings in someone else who arrives at that very moment, saying, "Come, Venerable sir," and gives food to all four; for all of them, there is no offense. Why? Because of the one who completes the group.
Because of not being invited. For in that case, only three were invited and they accepted; the group was not complete, and the one who would complete the group was not invited.
Thus, because the group is incomplete, this is the "fourth [offense] involving one who was not invited.
Regarding the "fourth [offense] involving an alms-food eater": at the time of the invitation, there was one alms-food eater who did not accept. At the time of departure...
However, when it is said, "Come, venerable sir," if he does not come because he has not consented, yet they take him along, saying, "Come, you shall receive alms," he breaks that group.
Therefore, there is no offense for anyone. In the case of a group of four including one who is not fully ordained—if they have been invited together with a novice, he too breaks the group.
Regarding "with a bowl as the fourth": one person does not go himself but sends a bowl; even so, the group is split. Therefore, there is no offense for anyone [in that case].

Regarding "with the sick as the fourth": they have been invited together with the sick person; therein, there is no offense for the sick person alone, but for the others, he serves as the one who completes the group.
For a group is not split by means of the sick person. Therefore, there is indeed an offense for them. [This is stated] in the *Mahāpaccarī*.
However, this was stated without distinction.
One who has received [the robe] by appointment is liberated by himself; as for the others, because they act as the completer of the quorum, they become liable for an offense.

Therefore, sets of four should be understood according to those such as one who has received [the robe] by appointment through the giving of a robe. But if, even though the four people have departed after having consented, one among them is wise—

A bhikkhu said, "I will split your group; accept the invitation," and then, when they were about to take their bowls for the meal at the conclusion of the rice gruel and solid food, he did not give them [the bowls], but sat down, saying, "First feed these bhikkhus and dismiss them;
I will go later after giving the blessing. When they had finished eating and departed, he said, "Give me the bowls, venerable sirs."
When a lay follower takes a bowl and gives food, and [the monks] eat it and depart after giving a blessing of thanks, there is no offense for anyone.
For regarding the eating in a group, there is no distinction based solely on the five kinds of cooked food.
Even those invited with rice who take gruel incur an offense; yet those two were not taken by them together.
However, in the case of rice gruel and such, there is no misunderstanding, as those items are taken together by them. Thus, one wise person brings about non-offensiveness for others as well.

Therefore, if someone sent for the purpose of an invitation by one wishing to provide a meal for the Saṅgha comes to the monastery and, instead of saying, "Venerable sirs, please accept alms at our house tomorrow," says, "Please accept a meal" or "Please accept a meal for the Saṅgha..."
If he says, “Take it,” or “Let the Saṅgha take the meal,” the distributor of food must be wise.
He must release those who accept invitations from the offense of group-meals, and those who are alms-food eaters from the breach of their ascetic practice (dhutaṅga).
How? First, he should say: “It will not be possible tomorrow, lay follower. [The other replies: “On the following day, Venerable Sir? [He says: “Even on the following day...”
“It is not possible. Thus, even after he has carried it for as long as half a month, he should be asked again: “What did you say?

If he says again, “Take the meal for the Saṅgha,” then one should create a diversion by saying, “Lay follower, first make this flower allowable, and this grass,” and then he should be asked again: “What did you say?”
If he speaks in that same way again, he should be told: "Friend, you will not get alms from the great elders who live on alms;
you will get it from the novices. And if he says, "Venerable sir, did they not feed the venerable ones in such-and-such and such-and-such villages?
Why do I not receive anything? he should be told, "They know how to invite them; you do not."
“How did they invite them, venerable sir? “They said, ‘Venerable sir, please accept alms from us.
If he says the same thing, it is permissible. But if he says again, ‘Please accept a meal,’ he should be told:
‘Friend, you will not get many monks now; you will get only three. [If he asks: ‘But, venerable sir, is it not...’”
“In such-and-such a village and such-and-such a village, they fed the entire Saṅgha of bhikkhus; why do I not receive [an invitation]?
“You do not know how to invite them. “How did they invite them? They said, “Take almsfood.
If he also says, “Take almsfood,” it is permissible. But if he says again, “Only a meal,” [it is not].
If he says this, one should say to him: “Go away; we have no need for your almsfood.
This is our regular alms-round; we shall wander here for alms ourselves. When he has returned after saying, “Wander on, venerable sirs,” they ask him:
“Well, sir, did you get anything? He replies: “What is there much to say about this? ‘The elders tomorrow…’”
“Let us go for alms,” they said. “Do not neglect this now.

On the second day, after the monks had performed the *cetiyavatta* (rites at the shrine) and were standing there, the senior of the Saṅgha should say: “Friends, a foolish man has gone to the village ahead to provide a meal for the Saṅgha;
let us go to that village for alms. The monks [should respond] to the Elder’s words...
One should act thus; one should not be difficult to speak to. Without standing at the village gate, one should wander for alms.
When they have taken the bowls and seated [the monks], one should eat while they are serving the food.
If they set aside the meal in the dining hall and announce it by wandering along the streets, saying, "Venerable sirs, please take your meal in the dining hall," it is not permitted.
Furthermore, if they go here and there with food and say, "Take some food," or if they bring it to the monastery in advance,
place it in a suitable spot, and give it to those who come along,
this is called "brought-along alms" (*abhihaṭabhikkhā*), and it is permissible. However, if they prepare a gift in the dining hall and send it to various cells, saying, "In the dining hall..."

If they say, "Take food," it is not permissible. However, those people who, upon seeing monks going for alms, sweep the dining hall, invite them to sit there, and provide them with a meal, should not be refused.
Furthermore, those who, seeing monks leaving the village after failing to obtain alms, say, "Venerable sirs, please take food," [should not be refused].

It should be refused, or one should not turn back. If they say, "Please turn back, Venerable Sir, take some food," it is permissible to turn back at the words "turn back. If they say, "Turn back, Venerable Sir; food has been prepared at home" or "food has been prepared in the village"—for "at home" and "in the village" refer to anyone's [residence]— [...the text continues... "It is allowable to turn back" means it is permissible to return. Some explain this by connecting it with the words, "Turn back, take the meal," [claiming] it is not allowable to turn back.
The same principle applies even when one sees them setting out from the dining hall (*āsanasālā*) to wander for alms and says, "Sit down, venerable sirs, take the meal.
"Regular meal" (*niccabhatta*) refers to a fixed or constant meal. "Regular meal..."
When they say, “Take [it],” it is permissible to take even many [items] together. This same method applies to *salākabhatta* (tickets for food) and so forth.
The rest here is self-evident.

The origin is from the wool of a sheep (*eḷakaloma*); it is an action (*kiriya*), not released by perception (*no-saññāvimokkha*), without consciousness (*acittaka*), an offense by formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), associated with three types of consciousness (*ticitta*), and associated with three types of feeling (*tivedana*).
The second training rule on eating in a group.
3. Commentary on the third training rule on eating in succession:
“This cannot be insignificant, that these people should treat [us] with such respect...”
“They prepare a meal”: by the manner in which these people respectfully prepare the meal, it is known:
“This gift to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha will not be insignificant; it will not be meager or inferior.
*Kīrapati* means that here “Kīra” is the name of that clansman.
In the sense of being a ruler, however, he is called "the lord of the field" (*kirapatika*).

It is said that as a master and sovereign, he makes his laborers perform work by paying wages according to the system of months, seasons, and years. "Badara fruits were prepared" is said figuratively;
"mixed with badara fruits" means mixed with *badara-sāḷava* (sour plum sauce).
222. "It was brought late" means it was brought past midday. 226.
"I give my portion of food to such-and-such a person"—this is called the assignment of food (*bhattavikappanā*);
it is permissible both in the presence of the recipient and in their absence. If one sees them in person, one may eat after saying, "I assign this to you"; if one does not see them...
One may eat after saying to five fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, "I dedicate this to [so-and-so].

However, in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other such texts, only dedication in the absence of the recipient (*parammukhā-vikappanā*) is mentioned. Since this [latter] is included within the formal acts of the Vinaya (*vinayakamma*), it is not permissible to dedicate to the Blessed One.
For even when the Blessed One is seated in his fragrant chamber (*gandhakuṭī*) or seated in the midst of the Saṅgha...
When the Saṅgha has taken a sufficient number of monks and performed a particular formal act (*kamma*), that act is indeed well-performed;
the Blessed One neither invalidates it nor completes it. He does not invalidate it because he is the Lord of Dhamma, and he does not complete it because he does not fulfill the quorum.
229. "He eats together at two or three invitations" means having placed two or three invitations into a single bowl.
The meaning is: having mixed them together, one eats them as one. Having invited two or three families and having had them seated in one place, they bring food from here and there and pour it over;
they pour out the curry and condiments, and it becomes a single mixture.
In this case, there is no offense—so it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*. However, if the original invitation was the first one, and the subsequent...
The "last" refers to the top; for one who eats starting from the top, there is an offense.

However, having inserted the hand inside, there is no offense for one who eats in whatever manner—whether after taking even a single mouthful out from the time of the first invitation or after the time of having finished eating.
Even if milk or broth is poured over it, by which it is overwhelmed...
In the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "The meal becomes of a single flavor; for one eating from the very beginning [of the dish], there is no offense.
