However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is said: "Having received either milk-rice or sauce-rice and sitting down, others pour more milk-rice or sauce-rice right there upon him; or while he is drinking the milk or the sauce..."

There is no offense. However, while eating, it is permissible for one who has first placed a piece of meat or a morsel of rice into the mouth to eat starting from the tip [of the tongue]. The same rule applies to ghee-mixed gruel.
A lay follower invites a bhikkhu; when he has arrived at his house, the lay follower, as well as his children, wife, brothers, sisters, and so forth, [provide food].

Having brought their respective portions, they place them in the bowl; it is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* that there is no offense for one who eats what was received later without first eating what was given by the lay follower (*upāsaka*).
However, in the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that this is permissible. In the *Mahāpaccarī*, it says: "If they cook separately, [one may eat] from one's own cooked rice..."
"If they bring [food] and give it, then for one who eats what was brought later first, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
However, if there is only a single cooking for all, there is no offense of eating in succession," so it is said.

When a great lay follower has invited [monks] and seated them, if another person takes a bowl, [the food] should not be given. [If he asks], "Venerable sir, why do you not give? [one should reply], "Is it not..."
“If it is said, ‘Upāsaka, you have been invited by us! and he replies, ‘Let it be so, Bhante; whatever has been received, please eat,’ it is permissible to eat.
It is stated in the *Kurundi* that if food is brought by another and given to him, it is permissible to eat even after asking for permission.
When he is departing after giving a blessing (*anumodanā*), those who wish to hear the Dhamma all say, ‘Bhante, please come again tomorrow.’”
They invite [the monks]; it is permissible for them to come on the following day and eat whatever they receive. Why? Because everyone has been invited.
A certain monk, while wandering for alms, receives food; another lay follower invites him and seats him in his house, yet the meal has not yet been prepared. If that monk, having wandered for alms...
If he eats food that has been obtained [as an invitation], it is an offense. If, while sitting without having eaten, he is asked, "Why, venerable sir, do you not eat?
and he replies, "Because I was invited by you," and is then told, "Venerable sir, eat whatever you receive," and he eats, it is permissible.
Regarding "by the entire village": for one who has been invited by the entire village acting together as one, it is permissible to eat anywhere [within that area].
There is no offense. The same principle applies to a group as well. Regarding the statement, "When being invited, he says, 'I will take almsfood'":
this refers to one who, when invited with the words, "Take food," says, "I have no need for your food; I will take almsfood.
On this point, however, the Elder Mahāpaduma said: "One who speaks thus does not constitute an invitation under this training rule."
"He is able [to accept], but since the opportunity for eating has been created, he is neither released from the offense of eating in a group nor from the offense of wandering for alms.
The Elder Mahāsumma said: "At the very moment he is able to invite [the monks], at that very moment there is neither eating in a group nor wandering for alms.
The rest is self-evident.
The origin of the *Kathina* [offense]: it originates from body and speech, and from body, speech, and mind.

Herein, eating is an action (*kiriyā*), while non-distribution is a non-action (*akiriyā*). It is not associated with perception or liberation (*no-saññā-vimokkha*), is without thought (*acittaka*), is an offense by rule (*paṇṇatti-vajja*), is bodily action and verbal action, consists of three types of consciousness, and has three types of feeling.
The third training rule on eating in succession.
4. Commentary on the fourth training rule concerning Kāṇamātā:
"Kāṇamātā" means the mother of a one-eyed woman. It is said that her daughter was indeed beautiful.

"Whosoever sees her, they become one-eyed through passion (*rāga*); the meaning is that they become blinded by passion. Therefore, because she caused others to become one-eyed, she became famous as 'Kāṇā' (the One-eyed).
By virtue of her, even her mother became well-known as 'Kāṇamātā' (the Mother of the One-eyed).
'Āgataṃ' means arrival. 'Kismiṃ viya? means 'Like what?'—the intention is that it is like something shameful."
"To go with empty hands" means that in this journey the hands are empty;
thus, it is said that going on such an empty-handed journey is like something shameful.

"He went to complete exhaustion" means that when the noble female disciple (upāsikā ariyasāvikā) saw the monks, she was unable not to give what she had; therefore, she caused [the food] to be given until everything was gone.

...reached complete exhaustion. Regarding the phrase "with a discourse on the Dhamma": here, even Kāṇamātā, while listening to the Dhamma being taught for her mother's sake, became a stream-enterer at the conclusion of the teaching. "Rising from his seat and departing" means that he rose from his seat and went away.
That man also, having heard that "the Teacher had indeed gone to Kāṇamātā’s residence," brought Kāṇā there.
He placed it back in its original position.
Now, as soon as this matter had arisen, even before the training rule (sikkhāpada) had been laid down, the matter of provisions for the journey (pātheyya-vatthu) occurred;
therefore, in order to show this immediately following, the passage beginning with "At that time" was spoken.
And that lay follower, because he was a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*), caused everything to be given. Therefore it is said: "It went to exhaustion.

233. "Whatever was prepared for the sake of provisions" means whatever was prepared as a gift (*paṇṇākāra*), such as extra sweetmeats, cakes, *sakkhalikā*, and so forth—all of this is here reckoned simply as "baked goods" (*pūva*).
"Whatever was for the sake of provisions for the journey" means for those traveling on the road...
Whatever prepared food for those on the way— whether grain that has been husked or not, sesame, rice, and so forth—
all such things are here reckoned simply as "mantha. If one takes more than that— that is, even if one takes a third bowlful heaped up as a mound—
there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) by the calculation of cakes.
"Having accepted two or three bowlfuls" means having taken bowls filled level with the lower rim of the mouth. Regarding the phrase "two or three bowlfuls were taken by me there":
if two have been taken, one should say, "Two bowlfuls were accepted by me here;
you should take one. If that person, seeing another [offering], says, "The first one who arrived took two bowlfuls..."
One should say: "I have already taken one; do not you take it. This same method applies to the successive announcement by whoever first took one.
However, by one who has himself taken three, upon seeing another, he should simply say: "Do not accept any here.
"Having brought them back to the retiring place" means having carried them to the hall of seats; [this refers to] by one going to the hall of seats.
One should not go to an abandoned hall. One should go to where the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus sits.
However, it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*: "One should go to the assembly hall that is nearest to the place where one has received [the meal].
One should not go elsewhere thinking, 'I will give it to those who are my acquaintances, or my companions, or those of the same school.'"
"It is not permitted. However, if he has a fixed place where he sits, it is permissible for him to go even a long distance. Regarding "it must be shared":
if three bowlfuls have been taken, having set aside one for himself, two must be given to the community of monks (bhikkhusaṅgha).
If two have been taken, having set aside one for himself, one must be given to the community; [this applies] according to friendship.
However, it is not permitted to give [the robe] away. One who has accepted it must not give anything against their will;

it may be done according to one's own preference. 235. "When the journey has been abandoned" means: having seen an obstacle on the way, or due to a lack of need, thinking, "We shall no longer send it;
we shall not go," thus when the journey has been abandoned—that is, cut off. [Regarding] relatives...
"Regarding those who have invited [him to eat]": there is no offense for one who accepts even much from those giving it. However, in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), it is stated:
"Even for them, only a measured amount is permitted from what has been prepared for the purpose of travel provisions or gifts. The rest is self-evident. It arises from six origins:

it is an action (*kiriya*), not involving liberation through perception (*no-saññā-vimokkha*), without mental intention (*acittaka*), an offense by rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), verbal action (*vacīkamma*), associated with three types of consciousness (*ticitta*), and associated with three types of feeling (*tivedana*).
The fourth training rule concerning Kāṇamātā.
5. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Invitation (Pavāraṇā):
In the fifth training rule—“Bhikkhus who have finished eating and are invited”—the brahmin said: "Venerable sirs, please take [some food]."

"Up to as much as you desire"—this refers to the invitation to take as much as one wishes (*yāvadatthapavāraṇā*). And by oneself saying, "Enough, friend, give only a little, a little"—this refers to the invitation involving a refusal (*paṭikkhepapavāraṇā*).

"Neighbors" (*paṭivissaka*) means those living in the surrounding houses. "The sound of crows cawing" (*kākoravasadda*) means the sound of crows crying out after having gathered together. Regarding the phrase "all this is enough," it is permissible to say only "all this is enough" (*alametaṃ sabbaṃ*) without pronouncing the letter *ti*.

238–9. *Bhuttāvī* means "one who has eaten. In this context, since anyone who has swallowed even a single morsel of food—whether it has been chewed or not—is reckoned as "one who has eaten," therefore it is said in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*):
"*Bhuttāvī* means [one who has eaten] of the five kinds of staple foods," and so forth. *Pavārito* means one who has made a refusal; one who has performed the act of declining further food.
And since that [term "invited"] does not refer to a mere refusal, but rather to the state of possessing five factors, it is therefore stated in its word-commentary:
“One who is ‘invited’ (pavārita) is one for whom food is being presented,” and so forth.
In this context, by the phrase “food is being presented,” one who has interrupted his meal is called “invited. And whoever has interrupted his meal has, by that very fact, eaten something.
Regarding that which has not been eaten and that which has been eaten, it is with reference to this that one comes to be designated as "one who has eaten" (*bhuttāvī*);
therefore, we do not see any separate accomplishment of meaning through the word *bhuttāvī*.

However, just as in expressions such as "two nights and three nights" or "five or six utterances," the word *pavārita* serves as a complementary adjunct to the word *parivāra* for the sake of euphonic smoothness (*byañjana-siliṭṭhatā*).
It should be understood that this has been stated.
In such phrases as "food is seen," the meaning is that unfinished food is visible, and that person is one who is currently eating.
In "alms-food is seen," it means that food sufficient for an invitation (pavāraṇa) is visible; that is, any one of the [five] kinds of cooked rice and so forth.

The meaning is that the food must be refused. "Standing within arm's reach" means that after the donor has taken the food sufficient for an invitation, he remains within a space measuring two and a half cubits.
"He brings it forward" means that the donor physically brings that meal toward him. "A refusal is manifested" means that the refusal becomes visible.
The meaning is that if that which has been brought forward, the bhikkhu rejects it either by body or by speech.
In this way, one is said to have "invited" (pavārita) by means of five factors. And this has also been said:
"Upāli, the invitation is recognized through five modes: food is recognized, a meal is recognized, [the donor] stands within arm's reach, he brings it forward, and the rejection is recognized."

In this regard, the analysis is as follows: first, concerning the terms "food" (*āsana*) and so forth, that which one eats and that food brought within arm’s reach which one refuses must be understood as being one or another of these:
boiled rice (*odana*), sour gruel (*kummāsa*), flour (*sattu*), fish (*maccha*), or meat (*maṃsa*).
Therein, what is called "boiled rice" refers to *sāli*, *vīhi*, barley (*yava*), wheat (*godhuma*), millet (*kaṅgu*), and *varaka*.
*Kudrūsaka* is produced from the grains of the seven types of cereal crops. In this context, "rice" (*sālī*) refers to the entire genus of rice, including even *nīvāra*.
"Barley" (*vīhī*) refers to the entire genus of barley. There is no distinction between "wheat" and "godhuma.
"Millet" (*kaṅgū*) refers to the entire genus of millet, including its white, red, and black varieties. "Varaka" includes even the *varakacoraka* variety.
All those derived from it are of white color and of excellent species. “*Kudrūsaka*” refers to black *drava*, as well as all species of grass-grain such as *sāmāka* and so forth.
Here, *nīvāra*, *varaka*, and *coraka* are said to be “grains that conform to [the category of] grain. Whether they are actual grains or grains that conform to grain—
Or, having taken the husked grains from any of these seven kinds of grain mentioned above— whether intending to cook a meal, or rice gruel,
or any one of sour milk-rice preparations (*ambilapāyāsa*) and so forth— they may cook whatever it may be; yet, if at the time of eating,
whether they are eating hot or cold food, a residue (*odhi*) is visible at the place where each morsel was taken, [it is considered impure].

It is considered a portion of rice (*odana-saṅgaha*) and generates an invitation (*pavāraṇa*). If the consistency (*odhi*) is not discernible, it is considered a portion of gruel (*yāgu-saṅgaha*) and does not generate an invitation.
Even if it is rice porridge (*pāyāsa*), or sour gruel mixed with leaves, fruits, and stalks, as soon as it has been taken down from the hearth and is still hot—

When it is hot, one can drink it after having mentally adverted to it; even in the place where it is held by the hand, it does not show its solid mass (*odhi*) and does not produce the need for a formal invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
However, if, once the heat has subsided and it has become cool, it reaches a state of density, it shows its solid mass and again produces the need for a formal invitation.
Its previous thin state does not protect [it from this]. Even if one adds curd, buttermilk, and so forth—
If even a mere handful of rice grains has been placed among many leaves, fruit, and sprouts, and a solid mass (*odhi*) is discernible at the time of eating, it generates an invitation (*pavāraṇa*).

In an invitation where no rice gruel is served, they say, "We shall give rice gruel," and having poured water, sour gruel, milk, and so forth over the cooked food, they give it saying, "Take the rice gruel. Even though it is thin, it certainly generates an invitation. If...
However, if they throw it into boiling water or similar liquids, cook it, and then give it, it is included within the category of *yāgu*.
Even when it is included in that category of *yāgu*, if fish or meat is added— whether to that *yāgu* or to anything else— if even a piece of fish or meat the size of a mustard seed,
or even a sinew, is discernible, it gives rise to an invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
However, pure rice gruel (*suddharasaka*) does not generate an invitation (*pavāraṇā*).

Except for the grains mentioned above, even a meal made from other types of bamboo-grain (*veṇutaṇḍula*), or from any tubers, roots, or fruits, does not generate an invitation, let alone thick gruel (*ghanayāgu*).
But if fish or meat is added to it, it does generate one. [In the] *Mahāpaccarī*...
It is said: “One may even generate an invitation for the sake of flowers. Regarding “rice for the sake of flowers”:
this refers to rice grains that have been steamed by placing them in warm water for the purpose of making flower-shaped snacks. However, if they dry those rice grains and eat them, it is permissible;
they do not fall under the category of *sattu* (flour/grains) nor the category of *bhatta* (cooked food). Furthermore, regarding rice prepared by them...
One indeed performs the *pavāraṇā*. They cook rice with ghee, oil, and so forth, or they make cakes, yet they do not perform the *pavāraṇā*.
Or, parched grain, or flour-meals (*sattu*) and such prepared by them, do not constitute a *pavāraṇā*.
As for what is called *kummāsa*, it is *kummāsa* made from barley; however, *kummāsa* made from other grains such as mung beans does not generate a *pavāraṇā*.
"Sattu" refers to flour made from *sāli* rice, *vīhi* rice, and barley.
Even *kaṅgu*, *varaka*, and *kudrūsaka* grains are roasted, slightly crushed, winnowed to remove the chaff, and then firmly ground again to make a powder.
Even if that [powder] becomes clumped together due to moisture, it still counts as a collection of *sattu*. As for the husked grains of rice from paddy that has been roasted until hard...
If they give [the grain] after pounding it, even that powder counts as a collection of enemies.

However, the grains of rice—or the husks of rice—from rice that has been roasted to a moderate degree, or the grains themselves from such rice, do not constitute an *apavāraṇā* (an offense requiring confession).

But the powder of those grains and so forth does constitute an *apavāraṇā*. Even the broken bits (*kuṇḍaka*) of rice that has been roasted to a harsh degree constitute an *apavāraṇā*. This applies to those roasted to a moderate degree as well.
However, one does not offer *kuṇḍaka* that has been dried in the sun. Nor do they offer parched grains (*lāja*), or rice-flour and other such items prepared with them.
Nor does one offer roasted flour, or any kind of plain snack (*suddhakhajjaka*).
But one may offer a snack filled with fish and meat, or a *sattumodaka*. Fish and meat are well known. However, this is the distinction: even if...
If, while drinking rice gruel, they give him two pieces of fish or two pieces of meat— each the size of a grain of rice— in either a single bowl or separate bowls,
and he refuses some other food sufficient for an invitation (*pavāraṇa*) without having eaten those,
he has not invited himself. Then, if one piece has been eaten and one remains in his hand or in his bowl, and he refuses something else, [he has not invited himself].
He invites [the guest to eat]. Both portions have been consumed; there is not even a mustard seed’s worth remaining in his mouth.
Even if he refuses other food, he does not invite [the guest to stop]. When eating allowable meat, he refuses allowable meat; he has invited [the guest to stop]. When eating allowable meat...
He rejects unallowable meat; he does not invite [others to eat]. Why? Because of its lack of foundation.
For an invitation occurs only when one rejects that which is permissible for a bhikkhu to eat. But knowing this, he rejects it because it is unallowable;
even if he does not know, he is said to reject it only when it stands in a position where it ought to be rejected. Therefore, he does not invite.
But if, while eating unallowable meat, one rejects allowable meat, one invites [the guest to eat it]. Why? Because of its status as the actual substance (*vatthutā*).

For that which is rejected by him is the substance for the invitation; however, although that which he eats stands in the place of what ought to be rejected, while being eaten it does not lose its nature as meat. Therefore, he invites [him to eat it]. While eating unallowable meat...
He rejects unallowable meat; as in the previous method, he does not invite [others to eat it].
Whether eating allowable meat or unallowable meat, if he rejects any of the five kinds of edible food that is allowable, he invites [others to eat it].
That which is produced from corrupting families, medical practice, claiming superhuman states, or acquired wealth, and which is censured by the Buddha—[he rejects such things].
When unallowable food has arisen for the purpose of seeking alms, one rejects it and does not partake.
Whether one is eating allowable food or unallowable food, one rejects the allowable food and partakes [of the other].
The reason why one rejects the unallowable food and does not partake should be understood according to the method stated in all instances.
Thus, regarding the terms "eating" (*āsana*) and so forth, having understood both that which one eats and the food brought within arm's reach that one incurs an invitation (*pavāraṇā*) by refusing,
this is now the analysis for the purpose of knowing how one incurs it:
"In this regard, concerning 'eating' (*āsana*) and 'food' (*bhojana*), whoever has swallowed even a single grain of rice— if, from the bowl, the mouth, or the hand..."
Wherever among the five kinds of food there is even one item, he refuses another of the five kinds of food and then invites [the others].
Where there is no food at all, but only the scent of food is perceived, he does not invite.
When there is no food in his mouth or hands, but there is some in his bowl, yet he has no desire to eat at that seat, he goes to the monastery.
Having entered [the village], if one desires to eat or desires to give to another, and in the meantime rejects food, one has not invited [others to eat].

Why? Because the state of having interrupted the meal has been severed. Even if one, desiring to go elsewhere to eat, swallows some food in the mouth and then goes away taking the remainder, and on the way rejects other food—[in that case too, one has not invited others].
"In that case also, there is no *pavāraṇā*," so it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*. And just as with the bowl, so too with the hand.
Or, if food is present in the mouth and one does not wish to swallow it, and at that moment one refuses another [offering], one does not perform *pavāraṇā*.
For the characteristic stated for one instance must be understood to apply everywhere. Furthermore, in the *Kurundi*:

This principle has already been shown. For it is said therein: "If food has been swallowed in the mouth, and one wishes to give food from the hand to a scavenger, or food from the bowl to a bhikkhu, and at that moment he refuses it, one does not perform the *pavāraṇā*.
Regarding the phrase "standing within arm's reach," if the bhikkhu is sitting, [the limit] begins from the rear edge of his seat.
If [the recipient] is standing, it is measured from the edge of his feet; if he is lying down, it is measured from the far edge of the side on which he lies.
For a donor who is sitting, standing, or lying down, excluding the outstretched hand, that part of the body which is nearest is defined by its near edge;
this space of two and a half cubits is called the "hand-reach" (*hatthapāsa*).
It should be understood thus: for one who refuses food brought while standing [in that position], the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) is fulfilled at that very moment, and not beyond it.
"Brings" means that one standing within arm’s reach extends [the food] for the purpose of taking it.

However, even if a monk sitting immediately next to him does not bring the bowl—whether it is held in his hand, on his lap, or in a stand—but simply says, "Take the food," [the invitation is not fulfilled].

If one says this and the other rejects it, there is no *pavāraṇā*. The same principle applies even if, having brought a food tray and placed it on the ground in front [of the recipient], one says, "Take it.
However, if one lifts it slightly or moves it aside and says, "Take it," then for one who rejects it, there is *pavāraṇā*.
A senior elder seated in his own seat [may accept] from a junior monk seated at a distance...

If he sends a bowl and says, "Take rice from here," but having taken it, the messenger stands silent upon returning, and the junior monk refuses it, saying, "Enough for me," this does not constitute an invitation (*pavāraṇā*). Why? Because the elder is at a distance and the messenger did not bring [the food] to him.
However, if the monk who has returned after taking [the food] says, "Take this meal," [it is an invitation].
If one refuses that [request], the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) is valid.
Suppose at a food distribution, one person takes a rice-basket with one hand and a spoon with the other and serves the monks;
if another person arrives there and says, "I will hold the basket, you give the rice," [and the first person] gives it up as soon as it has been taken—[the invitation remains valid].
The one serving the food prepares it, but the server alone holds it; therefore, it is considered as if it has already been brought [to the recipient].
Consequently, for one who refuses someone wishing to take it out of a desire to give, there is an invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
However, if it has merely been touched by the server and the other person holds it, then for one who refuses someone wishing to take it out of a desire to give, there is no invitation.
But when food has been scooped out with a ladle, there is [an invitation]. For the mere act of bringing the ladle constitutes the "bringing" (abhihāra) for him.
Even when two portions are of equal weight, one who refuses [to take more] still performs the *pavāraṇā*; so it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*.
When food is being given to the monk immediately next to him, the other covers his bowl with his hands; there is no *pavāraṇā*. Why? Because it belongs to another.
Because it has been rejected when brought forward. Regarding the phrase "rejection is evident":

here, for one who rejects what has been brought forward by speech, there is no *pavāraṇā*. However, it should be understood that for one who rejects what has been brought forward by the body—whether by means of the body or by speech—there is *pavāraṇā*.
In this context, "rejection by the body" refers to [gestures such as] a finger, a hand, a fan made of leaves, or the corner of a robe.
Or he moves [the bowl], or makes a gesture with his eyebrows, or looks at him in anger;
verbal refusal means saying "Enough!", or "I will not take it", or "Do not pour it out", or "Go away";
thus, when there is a refusal by any such manner through either body or speech, the invitation (pavāraṇā) takes place.
When one person, fearing that his alms-food might be taken away during the *pavāraṇā*, withdraws his hand and repeatedly pours rice into the bowl of another, saying, "Pour it!
Pour it! Pound it and fill it up!"—how is this to be judged? Regarding this, the Elder Mahāsumma said:
"Because it was spoken for the purpose of preventing the pouring [of food], it constitutes a *pavāraṇā*. However, the Elder Mahāpaduma said: "For one who says, 'Pour it! Fill it up!'..."
Having said, "There is no invitation (pavāraṇā) for anyone," he replied, "He does not invite.
Another, having noticed a monk bringing food, said, "Friend, will you take something from there as well? I will give you something.
Regarding that too, the Elder Mahāsiva said, "'Because it was said, "He will not come here," there is an invitation. The Elder Mahāpaduma..."
However, regarding the statement, "To one who says, 'Will you take it? if one says, 'I have an invitation [to eat] from someone,' and then does not partake," he said this:
Suppose one person brings a sauce containing meat and says, "Take the sauce. If, upon hearing that, one refuses it, there is no *pavāraṇā* (invitation).
But if it is said, "This is fish sauce; this is meat sauce," and one refuses it, there is *pavāraṇā*. [Likewise,] if one says, "Take this,"...

Even when this is said, it is still so. If one separates the meat and says, "Take the meat broth," if there is even a piece of meat the size of a mustard seed in it, the invitation is valid for one who refuses it.
However, if it has been strained, the Venerable Abhaya said, "It is permissible. When someone was asking for meat broth, the Great Elder said, "Wait a moment," and then said, "Friend, bring a bowl."
He said: "How is it in this case? First, the Elder Mahāsumma said: "The departure of the one who brings the food was the first [act] to be interrupted;
therefore, he should perform the *pavāraṇā*. But the Elder Mahāpaduma, having said, "Where is he going? What kind of departure is this?
Even for one who is taking [the food], there is indeed a *pavāraṇā*," replied, "He does not perform the *pavāraṇā*. [This was the view] of Kaḷīra, Panasa, and others.
Having hidden the meat, they cook it; then, taking it, they say, "Take fish curry," or "Take jackfruit sauce.
Even in this case, one does not invite [the donor to choose). Why? Because it was spoken using the name of something that is not subject to invitation.
However, if they say, "Fish soup" or "Meat soup," or "Take this," one does invite. This is called "meat mixed with curd-rice."
Even if one wishes to give it, if one says, “Take the *karambaka* (rice-and-meat porridge),” it is permissible; it does not constitute an invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
However, if it is said, “Meat *karambaka*” or “This,” then it is an invitation. This same principle applies to all [foods] mixed with fish or meat.
Furthermore, if one who is eating at an invitation rejects meat that has been brought to him, thinking, “This was prepared specifically for me (*uddissa kataṃ*),” [it is not an offense].
"He is as if he has invited [the monks]"—this is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*. However, the discussion regarding mixed food is explained thoroughly in the *Kuruṇḍī*.
For it is said there: "A monk who goes for alms, having brought rice-gruel mixed with solid food, says, 'Take the gruel,' but he does not invite [them].
When he says, 'Take the solid food,' then he invites them. Why? Because he did not ask [for permission] regarding that [gruel]."
Because of its presence. This is the intended meaning here:

if one says, "Take it with rice gruel," and therein the gruel is either more abundant or equal [in amount] to the other food, one does not invite [the guest to eat more]. If the gruel is meager and the solid food is more abundant, then one invites them.
And since this is stated in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), it cannot be rejected; however, the reason for this is difficult to see.
If he says, “Take mixed food,” whether the food is abundant, equal, or less, he still invites [the guest] to stop eating.

If, without touching either the solid food or the rice gruel, he says, “Take mixed food,” and therein the solid food is more abundant or equal, he invites him to stop eating. If it is less, he does not invite him to stop. And this—
One should not accept it as *karambaka* (gruel). For *karambaka* may be mixed with meat or not mixed with meat; therefore, when "karambaka" is mentioned, there is no invitation (*pavāraṇā*).

But this [food] is mixed only with cooked rice. Here, the invitation occurs according to the method stated for that. In the case of food with much flavor, one should mention the flavor; in the case of much milk, the milk; and in the case of thick porridge with much ghee, the ghee.
If one gives it separately, saying, "Take this," there is no *pavāraṇā* for one who refuses it.
However, if one who is traveling performs the *pavāraṇā*, he may eat while still traveling.
Upon reaching mud or water, he must have the food declared as leftover (*atiritta*). If, along the way, a river is full, [he should go] to a grove on the riverbank.
One should eat while walking around. If there is a boat or a bridge, one should also eat while walking upon it, and one must not interrupt the journey.

Or, having sat in a vehicle, on the back of an elephant or horse, or in the disk of the moon or the disk of the sun, one who has been invited may continue until midday, even while those [vehicles] are moving.
One should eat while remaining seated. If one who is standing invites [another] to eat, the latter must eat while standing; if one who is seated invites [another], the latter must eat while seated.
One should not cause food to be considered "leftover" by disturbing one's posture. If one who is squatting on the heels invites [another], the latter must eat while squatting on the heels.
However, beneath him there should be a straw mat or something similar.
Or a sitting mat should be given. Having sat upon a bench, one who has been invited to eat may continue eating while turning toward the four directions without moving the seat.
However, having sat upon a couch, one who has been invited to eat is not permitted to shift here or there.
But if they lift the couch along with him and carry him elsewhere, it is permissible. [He may also eat] after lying down.
One who has been invited to eat must eat while remaining in the reclining position. When turning over, one must not pass beyond the spot where one was lying.
"Not left over" (*anatiritta*) means not excessive; the meaning is that it is not more than required.

Since that [food] is either not prepared according to the seven formal procedures of the Vinaya—such as the *kappiyakata* (made permissible) and so forth—or is not in excess for one who is ill, therefore the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) states: "not made permissible," and so on.

It has been stated. In that context, "made unallowable" (*akappiyakata*) refers to whatever fruit, root-tuber, or the like there may be that has not been made allowable by the five monastic modes of making allowable (*samaṇakappa*);
and whatever unallowable meat or unallowable food there may be, that is called "unallowable.
Even if such an unallowable thing has been made "leftover" (*atiritta*) by saying, "This is enough for all," it should be understood as "made unallowable."
"Made without having been received": it is made as leftover by a monk in the same manner as previously described, even though it has not been formally received.
"Made without being spoken over": it is made by one who has come to have it declared allowable (kappiya), yet has neither raised [the food] even slightly nor moved it aside.
"Made outside the reach of the hand": it is made by one standing beyond the reach of the hand of the person who has come to have it declared allowable.

"Made by one who has not eaten": this refers to when one makes food "leftover" by saying, "This is enough for all," while having not yet eaten a meal sufficient to satisfy the invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
"Made by one who has eaten, by one who has finished the invitation, or by one who has risen from his seat": this is self-evident.
"Not said, 'This is enough for all'" means it is so because no verbal expression was made; thus, it is "not said. Thus, by these seven...

Whatever is not made permissible (*kappiya*) by means of the formal acts of the Vinaya (*vinayakamma*), and whatever is not "leftover from one who is ill" (*na gilānātiritta*), both of these should be understood as "not leftover" (*anatiritta*).
However, "leftover" (*atiritta*) should be understood by way of its opposite. Furthermore, in this context, it is said: "it has been prepared by one who has already eaten."

It should be understood that even after one has finished eating, if one eats even a single grain of rice or a piece of meat from the bowl of a fellow monk sitting immediately next to oneself, it is considered as if one had not yet finished.
Regarding the phrase "without having risen from one's seat," this is the analysis for the sake of clarity:
two monks who have been invited to eat together early in the morning may both be eating.

One of them should sit right there, while the other, having brought either regular food or ticket-food, should pour half of it into that monk’s bowl, wash his hands, and then, having had the remainder made allowable by that monk, he may eat it. Why?
Because whatever sticks to his hand is unallowable. But if, first—
If the seated bhikkhu takes [the food] from that bowl with his own hand, there is no need for the act of washing the hands.

However, if while he is eating after having had it made allowable in this way, they pour some more curry or solid food into the bowl, the one by whom it was first made allowable is not permitted to make it allowable again; rather, it must be done by the one by whom it was not yet made allowable.

It must be made by him. And that which has not been made must be made. Regarding the phrase "by whom it was not made": it must be made by whichever other monk did not do it first. Regarding the phrase "and that which was not made":
even by that monk who first made the *kappiya* (ritual preparation), that which was not made must be made. However, it is not permitted to do so in the first vessel; for therein—
What is being made becomes "made together" with what was previously made; therefore, the intention is that it is permissible to make it in another vessel.
However, once it has been made in this way, it is permissible for that monk to eat it together with the food previously prepared.
And when making it allowable (*kappiya*), one should do so not only in the bowl, but also in a pot, a basket, or wherever it may be in front of him.
Except for the vessel that has been tilted down, it may be prepared. Even if a hundred monks have already finished their meal invitation (*pavārita*), it is permissible for all of them to eat;
it is also permissible for those who have not yet received an invitation. However, it is not permissible for the one by whom the *kappiya* (allowable) preparation was made.
Even if a monk who has already finished his meal invitation and entered for alms-food is given a bowl and invited to a celebratory feast where eating is mandatory, [it is still permissible].
They cause [the food] to be set down; it must be eaten only after having had it made "leftover" (atiritta).

If there is no other monk there, one should have it made [leftover] by sending a bowl to the sitting hall or the monastery. However, when making it allowable (kappiya), it must not be placed in the hand of one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna).
If there is an incompetent monk in the sitting hall, one should go there oneself and make it allowable.
Having had it prepared and brought, it should be eaten.

Regarding "the remainder of what was left over by the sick" (*gilānātiritta*): here, "the remainder of what was left over by the sick" does not refer only to that which remains after the sick person has already finished eating;
rather, it refers to anything intended for the sick person with the thought, "Whether today or tomorrow, whenever he wishes, he will eat it."
All that has been brought [to him] should be understood as "leftover from one who is ill.

Regarding the offense of *dukkaṭa* for each swallow among the "timely for a watch" (*yāmakālika*) foods and so forth, that was stated by way of [food] not mixed with [other substances]. However, if they are mixed with food, then for one who receives and swallows them—whether for the purpose of nourishment or not for the purpose of nourishment—it is indeed an offense of *pācittiya*.
241. Regarding "when there is a condition": when there is thirst, there is no offense for one who consumes *yāmakālika* (medicines allowable until nightfall) for the purpose of quenching that thirst;

and when there is a specific illness to be pacified, there is no offense for one who consumes *sattāhakālika* (medicines allowable for seven days) or *yāvajīvika* (medicines allowable for life) for the purpose of pacifying that illness.
The rest here is self-evident.

The Origin of the Kathina: It originates from body and speech; from body, speech, and mind. It is both action and non-action, not involving liberation through perception, without mental concomitants, an offense by formal rule, bodily action, verbal action, consisting of three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
This is the fifth training rule concerning the first invitation. 6.
Commentary on the Second Training Rule Concerning the Invitation.
242. Regarding the sixth training rule: "He practices improper conduct" means he commits a transgression of the formal rule (*paṇṇatti*).
"He harbors a grudge" (*upanandhi*) means that, generating resentment, he binds his own anger toward that person; the meaning is that he repeatedly gives rise to malice.
"A monk who harbors a grudge" (*upanaddho bhikkhu*) refers to that monk who has generated such resentment.
243. "To invite by bringing" means: having brought [the food], one should invite thus, "Come, monk, eat or consume.

However, in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), rather than citing "Come, monks," and so forth, it is stated—"Take as much as you wish"—in order to show the meaning of the invitation to bring [food] as common to all. They know.

"Knowing the state of having been invited. Since that knowledge of his occurs in three ways, the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) is stated by way of the method beginning with, "What is called 'knowing' is either he knows himself," and so forth.
"Looking for an offense" means looking for an accusation, a reproach, or the state of causing embarrassment.
"Accepts: there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" means that when he accepts what has been brought, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the monk who is the donor.
However, all the classifications of offenses for the other [recipient] have been stated in the first training rule;
in this training rule, however, it should be understood that all offenses belong to the donor alone. The rest is as in the first training rule.
Because it has been explained in the aforementioned manner, this is self-evident. It has three origins:

it originates from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. It is an action (*kiriya*); it is liberated through perception (*saññāvimokkha*); it is associated with consciousness (*sacittaka*); it is an offense against worldly convention (*lokavajja*); it is bodily action and verbal action; it is unwholesome consciousness; and it is accompanied by painful feeling.
This is the sixth training rule concerning the second invitation (*pavāraṇa*).

7. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Eating at the Wrong Time (Vikālabhojana-sikkhāpada) 247. Regarding the seventh training rule: "A mountain-top festival" (*giraggasamajja*) means a festival at the summit of a mountain, or a festival in the upper region of a mountain.
It is said that an announcement is made throughout the city, "It will take place on the seventh day," and [the festival] is held outside the city.
On that same stretch of ground, in the shade of a mountain, a great multitude of people gathered;
various kinds of theatrical performances were being staged, and tiered seating was erected for the purpose of watching them.
The group of seventeen monks, though young and having received full ordination before the training rules had been laid down, went there, saying, "Friends, we shall see the performances."
Then their relatives, with hearts full of joy, thinking, “Our noble ladies have arrived,” bathed them, anointed them, fed them, and gave them other foods such as cakes and snacks into their hands.
With reference to them, it was said: “When the people saw the group of seventeen bhikkhus,” and so forth.
248–9. *Vikāla* means when the time has passed. By "time" (*kāla*), the mealtime for monks is intended;

and that, at the very latest limit, is until midday. The intention is that [eating] occurs after that has elapsed. For this very reason, it is said in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) for this term: "Non-time (*vikāla*) means from the passing of midday until the rising of the dawn. Even the time when midday has already arrived is included within the category of "time."
It goes away. From that point on, however, it is no longer possible to chew or eat; one might be able to drink suddenly, but out of scruple (kukkucca) this should not be done.
For the purpose of knowing the time limit, a time-post should be set up, and the meal-duty should be performed only within that time.
Regarding the phrase "the remainder is called *khādanīya* (hard food)":
first, as for that which consists of morning and evening meals such as *sakkhali* cakes, rice, and so forth, there is nothing further to be said there.

Furthermore, whatever belongs to the category of edible food (*āmisagatika*), distinguished by roots and so on—namely, root-hard food, bulb-hard food, sprout-hard food, top-shoot-hard food, trunk-hard food, and bark-hard food.
Leaf-guisants, flower-guisants, fruit-guisants, bone-guisants, flour-guisants, and sap-guisants—these also fall under the category of guisants (*khādanīya*).
However, this is merely an illustration of the scope for the purpose of identifying what belongs to the class of food (*āmisagatika*); [the following] concerns root-guisants (*mūlakhādanīya*).

The roots of radish, the roots of *khāraka*, the roots of *cuccu*, the roots of tobacco, the roots of *taṇḍuleyyaka*, the roots of *vatthuleyyaka*, the roots of *vajakali*, the roots of *jajjharī*—such things as these, being the roots of leaf-vegetables used for soups, belong to the category of food (*āmisagatika*).

In this context, regarding the root of *vajakali*, they cut off the old, withered part and discard it; that [remaining part] lasts for the duration of one's life. Any other such [plant] is also [included].
It should be understood by this same method. Furthermore, it is stated that even the old portions of the roots of *mūlaka*, *khāraka*, and *jajjharī* fall under the category of solid food (*āmisa*).
As for those mentioned in the Canon:
"I allow you, monks, medicinal roots: turmeric, ginger, *vaca*, *vacatta*, and *ativisa*..."

“Kaṭukarohiṇī, usīra, bhaddamuttaka, or whatever other medicinal roots there may be that do not serve the purpose of a chewable food among chewable foods, nor serve the purpose of a soft food among soft foods”—
these are said to be for life-long use. When these are counted according to the method beginning with the “small five roots” and the “great five roots,”...
There is no end to their enumeration. However, their defining characteristic is simply the absence of sufficiency for the purpose of eating (khādanīya) and the purpose of consuming (bhojanīya).

Therefore, whatever root suffices for the purpose of eating and the purpose of consuming for people in various regions by way of their natural diet should be understood as "suitable for the time" (yāvakālika); the other is "for life-long use" (yāvajīvika).
For even after saying much regarding those [plants], one must remain within this very definition (*lakkhaṇa*).

However, when names (*nāma*) are being mentioned, only confusion arises for those who do not know each respective name; therefore, without placing emphasis on the naming, only the definition has been shown.
And just as at the root, so too with the bulb and the rest, the determination is made according to the definition that has been shown.

This is to be understood. Furthermore, regarding that which is described in the Canon as the eightfold [root-vegetables] beginning with turmeric, it is stated that all of them—including their stalks, bark, flowers, and fruits—are "for life.

Within the category of bulbous roots (*kanda-khādanīya*), there are two kinds of bulbs: long and short; the round ones include the bulbs of the *bhisaka* and *kiṃsuka*, etc., while the others include the bulbs of the *uppala* and *kaseruka*, etc.
What they also call a "knot" (*gaṇṭhī*). In that regard, for all bulbous roots (*kanda*), the decayed and withered parts, the outer skin, and the fine rootlets are for life-long use.
However, when young, they are pleasant to eat as fresh food;

these include the *sālakalyāṇī* seedling bulb, the *kiṃsuka* seedling bulb, the *ambāṭaka* bulb, the *ketaka* bulb, the *māluva* bulb, the lotus and white lotus bulbs known as *bhiṣa*, the *piṇḍāluka*, *sālu*, and so forth.

Furthermore, the milk-creeper tuber, the *āluva* tuber, the *sigguka* tuber, the *tāla* tuber, the tubers of the blue lotus, red lotus, white water lily, and *sogandhika* lily, the plantain tuber, the bamboo tuber,
and the *kaseruka* tuber— these and others such as these are, according to the local custom of various regions, tubers that serve as food for humans,
both as hard foods (*khādanīya*) and as soft foods (*bhojanīya*), and they are to be consumed only within the proper time (*yāvakālika*).
The milk-creeper tuber (*khīravallikanda*) is for life if unwashed; if washed, it is for the duration of the day.

However, tubers such as *khīra*, *kākolī*, *jīvika*, *usabha*, *kalasuṇa*, and so forth, are for life. These are included in the Pāḷi under the category of root-medicines by the phrase: "or whatever other roots there are that are medicines."
Regarding edible roots (*mūlālakhādanīya*): the root of the lotus (*padumamūlāla*) is exactly like the root of the white lotus (*puṇḍarīkamūlāla*).

The root of the *eraka* grass, the tuberous root (*kandula*), and so forth—these are roots that pervade various regions as natural food for humans, serving both as edible roots (*khādanīya*) and as soft foods (*bhojanīya*), and they are of the "timely" (*yāvakālika*) category.
The roots of turmeric, ginger, long pepper, the *caturassa* creeper, the *ketaka*, the palm tree, the *hintāla*, the *kuntāla*, the coconut, the betel nut tree, and so on—[are likewise included].

Furthermore, that which lasts for as long as life—everything included—is likewise subsumed under the category of root-medicines in the Canon by the statement: “Or whatever other roots there are that serve as medicines.
Regarding the edible fruits at the top [of trees]: those of the palmyra, hintāla, kuntāla, ketaka, coconut, betel-nut, date-palm, cane, eraka grass, and plantain trees.

The term *kaḷīra* refers to the tips of various plants—such as bamboo shoots (*veṇukaḷīra*), reed shoots (*naḷakaḷīra*), sugarcane shoots (*ucchukaḷīra*), radish shoots (*mūlakakaḷīra*), mustard shoots (*sāsapakaḷīra*), and *satāvarikaḷīra*, meaning the shoots of the seven grains—and so forth.

These are the tips of trees, creepers, and the like that spread throughout various regions for the purpose of being chewed or eaten by people as their customary food; they are of the "timely" (*yāvakālika*) category.
Having cut down the stalks of turmeric, ginger, bamboo, *vacā*, garlic, and *kaḷīra*, as well as the stalks of *tāla*, *hintāla*, *kuntāla*, and coconut,
one who has fallen [into this state] is "one for life" (*yāvajīvika*) with respect to the *jaraṭṭhabuṇḍa* (old stalk).

Among the trunk-vegetables (*khandhakhādanīya*), the trunk of the *sālakalyāṇī* tree that has grown underground, the sugar-cane trunk, and the stalks of blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, and *sogandhika* lotuses [are included].

"Stems" (*khandhaka*) and so forth: in various regions, the spreading stem that serves as food for people—whether for chewing (*khādanīya*) or for eating (*bhojanīya*)—according to their natural dietary habits, is "to-be-taken-at-the-proper-time" (*yāvakālika*).
The leaves and stalks of the *uppalajāti* lotuses, all the stalks of the *padumajāti* lotuses, the *kāravindaka* stalks and so on, and all remaining stems are "to-be-kept-for-life" (*yāvajīvika*).

Among the things to be chewed, the inner bark of the *ucchu* (sugarcane) is one that may be used as a meal at the proper time (*yāvakālika*), and even that is flavorful. All the rest are for life (*yāvajīvika*).

Furthermore, among those three—the heartwood, the trunk, and the bark—it should be understood that they are included in the category of medicinal decoctions (*kasāva-bhesajja*) in the Canon. For this has been said: "I allow you, monks, medicinal decoctions:
neem decoction, *kuṭaja* decoction, *paṭola* decoction, *phaggava* decoction, *nattamālaka* decoction, or whatever other medicinal decoctions there may be..."
“They serve as solid food for the purpose of solid food, not as soft food for the purpose of soft food.
For here, their inclusion is established. And it should be understood that all the aforementioned salts are permissible.
Among the solid foods for the bowl are: radish, *khāraka*, *caccu*, *tambaka*, *taṇḍuleyyaka*, *papunnāga*, and *vatthuleyyaka*.
With the exception of *vajakali*, *jajjharī*, *sellu*, *siggu*, *kāsamaddaka*, *ummā*, *cīnamugga*, *māsa*, and *rājamāsa*— and setting aside the large *nipphāva*— the remaining *nipphāva*,
*aggimantho*, *sunisannaka*, *setavaraṇo*, *nāḷikā*, and the salt-vinegars grown in the earth:
the leaves of these and other such things which serve as staple food for people in various regions as a matter of custom are [to be understood as] edible food (*khādanīya*).
The leaves used for spreading over food are exclusively *yāvakālika* (to be consumed within the same day).
However, the leaf of another plant, which is about the size of a large fingernail and climbs upon trees and shrubs, is *yāvajīvika* (to be kept for life).
The inhabitants of the Island (Dīpa) say that the *brahmī* leaf is also *yāvakālika*. The mango sprout is *yāvakālika*, whereas the asoka sprout is *yāvajīvika*.
Or whatever other leaf medicines there are in the Canon—
“Monks, I allow leaf medicines: neem leaves, *kuṭaja* leaves, *paṭola* leaves, *sulasī* leaves, cotton-tree leaves,
or whatever other leaf medicines there are that are not for the purpose of being chewed as solid food.”
“They spread [their scent] but do not spread for the purpose of being used as food”—these are said to be lifelong (yāvajīvika) plants.
Not only the leaves, but their flowers, fruits, and so forth, are also lifelong. Among the leaves:
the *phaggava* leaf, the *ajjuka* leaf, the *phaṇijjaka* leaf, the *paṭola* leaf, and the *tambūla* leaf.
"Lotus leaf"—thus, by way of enumeration, there is no end [to the varieties].

Among the edible flowers are: the radish flower, the *khāraka* flower, the *caccu* flower, the *tambaka* flower, the *vajakalī* flower, the *jajjharī* flower, the small millet flower, the large millet flower, the *kaseruka* flower, and those of the coconut, palm, and *ketaka* trees.

The flowers of the *taruṇa* tree, the white *varaṇa* flower, the *siggu* flower, the flowers of the *uppala*, *paduma*, and *jātika* varieties, the *kaṇṇika*-sized flower, the scentless flower, the *kaḷīra* flower, the *jīvantī* flower, and so forth—these are the "filling" flowers that serve as food for chewing or eating for people in various regions according to their natural dietary habits; they are *yāvakālika*.
[Likewise] those of the *asoka*, *bakula*, *kuyyaka*, *puṇṇāga*, *campaka*, *jāti*, *kaṇavīra*, *kaṇikāra*, *kunda*, *navamālika*, *mallikā*, and other such flowers.
However, there is no end to the counting of flowers that last for a lifetime. In the Pāḷi, this should be understood as being included within "medicinal decoctions" (kasāvabhesajja).

As for fruits and edible foods, there are fruits such as the panasa, labuja, tāla, nāḷikera, amba, jambu, ambāṭaka, tintiṇika, mātuluṅga, kapittha, lābu, kumbhaṇḍa, pussaphala, timbarūsaka, tipusa, vaṭaṅgaṇa, coca, mocā, madhuka, and so forth—those which, in various regions of the world, are used by people as their natural staple food for the purpose of eating.
And they provide nourishment; all of these are "within the time limit" (yāvakālika). It is not possible to show their limit by way of enumeration of names.
However, those which are mentioned in the Canon—“Monks, I allow fruits as medicine: sour gruel, long pepper, black pepper, and yellow myrobalan”—[are included therein].
“The vibhītaka, the āmalaka, the goṭṭhaphala, or whatever other medicinal fruits there may be that do not serve the purpose of a chewed food among chewed foods,
nor serve the purpose of a soft food among soft foods”— these are called “life-long” (yāvajīvika). Even of these,

it is impossible to show their limit by way of name, such as the unripe fruits of the *acchi*, *bimba*, *varaṇa*, *ketaka*, *kāsmarī*, and so forth, as well as the *jātiphala*, *kaṭukaphala*, cardamom (*eḷā*), and *takkola*.
Regarding edible bones: the seeds of the *labuja*, the seeds of the *panasa* (jackfruit), the seeds of the *ambāṭaka*, the seeds of the *sāla*, the seeds of the young fruits of the *khajjūrī*,
*ketaka*, and *timbarūṣaka*, the seeds of the *tintiṇika*, the seeds of the *bimba* fruit, and the seeds of the various species of *uppala* and *paduma* lotuses—
such as these are used by people in various regions for the purpose of eating or as food, according to their natural dietary habits.

Pharaṇaka bones are those that may be consumed for a limited time (yāvakālika). Bones such as those of the madhuka tree, the punnāga tree, the harītakī and other fruits, the siddhatthaka plant, and the rājika mustard plant are those that may be kept for life (yāvajīvika).
Their inclusion within the category of medicinal fruits (phalabhesajja) should be understood from the Pāḷi.
Regarding the flour for solid food (piṭṭhakhādanīya), there is the flour of the seven grains, of their derivatives, and of other vegetables, as well as the flour of the jackfruit (panasapiṭṭha).
Laba-fruit flour, mango-flour, sal-tree flour, unprocessed palmyra-flour, milk-creeper flour, and so forth— these are flours that,
according to the natural dietary habits of people in various regions, serve as edible or consumable foods for the duration of the day (yāvakālika).
Unprocessed palmyra-flour, milk-creeper flour, and the flours of *assagandha* and other such plants [are also included].
And those which are for life-long use. Their collection [of examples] in the Canon should be understood from the *kasāva* (bitters) and the roots and fruits.
Among the resinous edibles, only sugarcane resin is for a seven-day period. The rest are as follows:
"I allow you, monks, medicinal substances—*hiṅgu*, *hiṅgujatu*, *hiṅgusipāṭika*, sour gruel, *takapatti*, *takapaṇṇi*, and *sajjulasa*."
"Or whatever other resins and medicinal substances there may be"—thus, the exudations mentioned in the Canon are for life.
Among those included by way of the "miscellaneous" category, it is impossible to show their limit by name, such as mango resin, *kaṇikāra* resin, and so forth.
Thus, among these [categories] beginning with roots and fresh foods, whatever is "to be taken at the proper time,"...
In this context, everything is included under the category "the remainder is called ‘hard food’” (*khādanīya*).
Regarding “soft food” (*bhojanīya*), that which was to be stated in the passage beginning with “there are five kinds of soft food” has already been explained.
As for the phrase “he accepts it, thinking, ‘I shall eat it, I shall consume it’”: if a bhikkhu accepts this hard food or soft food at an improper time, for him—
In the case of receiving [the wool], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). The rest here is self-evident.

The origin of this rule concerning sheep’s wool arises from both body and body-and-mind; it is an action, not a liberation through perception, without mental involvement, an offense by formal precept, bodily action, associated with three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
This is the seventh training rule on eating at improper times.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Storing Up (Sannidhikāraka-sikkhāpada) 252.
Regarding the eighth training rule: "Belaṭṭhasīsa" was a great elder (mahāthera) who lived among a thousand jaṭila ascetics.
"He dwells in the forest" means he resides in a certain dwelling within a meditation hall not far from the Jeta Grove. "Dry rice" refers to rice served without curry or condiments.
Rice-gruel. It is said that after eating inside the village, he would later go on alms-round and bring back such rice-gruel;
this was indeed out of fewness of desires, not out of greed for requisites.

It is said that after spending seven days in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the Elder, upon emerging from that attainment, would moisten that alms-food with water and eat it; thereafter, again...
He sits in meditative attainment for seven days. Having thus passed two, three, or even four weeks, he enters the village for alms.
Therefore it is said: "He enters the village for alms after a long time. 253.

*Kāra*, *karaṇa*, and *kiriyā* are one in meaning, namely "doing. That which has the making of a store (*sannidhi*) as its doing is "one who makes a store" (*sannidhikāra*); that very thing is "the making of a store" (*sannidhikāram*).
“Stored up” (*sannidhikāraka*) is a designation for that which has been received and kept overnight.
For this very reason, it is said in its word-commentary: “‘Stored up’ means what was received today [is kept] on the following day.

Regarding the phrase “if he receives it, there is an offense of wrong-doing” (*dukkaṭa*): thus, whatever is stored up—whether it be *yāvakālika* (to be consumed during the day) or *yāmakālika* (to be consumed during the watch of the night)—[if received beyond the proper time, it is an offense].
Or, for one who takes [food] with the desire to swallow it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at the very moment of receiving it.
However, for one who swallows it, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for each individual act of swallowing.
Even if the bowl is not well-washed—such that a streak is visible when rubbed with a finger, or if grease has entered between the rings of a laced bowl—for one who is warming it over heat...
If it drips, or if it is visible when warm gruel has been taken [into the bowl], then for one who eats from such a bowl on the following day, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

Therefore, having washed the bowl, one should ascertain its state of being free from oiliness by pouring clear water back into it or by rubbing it with a finger. For if there is oiliness in the water, or if there is a finger-mark on the bowl—
It is visible; it is difficult to wash out. However, in a bowl with the color of oil, the finger-marks are visible, yet they are not subject to formal designation.
Whatever the monks give away to the novices without attachment, if the novices then store it away and give it [to others], all of it is permissible.
For if one receives it oneself and does not relinquish it, it is not permissible on the following day. From that...
For indeed, for one who swallows even a single grain of rice, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

Among unallowable meats, for human flesh there is an offense of grave misconduct (thullaccaya) together with an offense of expiation; for the remainder, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) together with [an offense of expiation].
For one who swallows a post-midnight medicine when a requisite condition exists, there is an offense of expiation. For one who swallows it for the purpose of food, [there is an offense of expiation].

There is a *pācittiya* offense together with a *dukkaṭa*. If, having been invited, one swallows food that has not been made into *atiritta* (leftover), there are two *pācittiya* offenses for ordinary meat;
for human flesh, two together with a *thullaccaya*; for other unallowable meats, together with a *dukkaṭa*;
and for swallowing food at the wrong time (*yāmakālika*) with the mouth when there is a valid reason, there are two [offenses] if it contains meat, and only one if it is without meat.
For one who swallows for the purpose of food, a *dukkaṭa* offense increases in both cases of mental intention (*vikappa*).

If one swallows at an improper time (*vikāla*), two *pācittiya* offenses increase—one on account of storing (*sannidhi*) natural food and one on account of eating at an improper time—and in the case of unallowable meats (*akappiyamaṃsa*), a *thullaccaya* and a *dukkaṭa* increase.

Regarding foods that may be kept until the watch of the night (*yāmakālika*), there is no offense on account of the improper time, but there is [an offense] on account of not having it made "leftover" (*anatiritta*).
However, at the wrong time, there is no offense in any of the various cases.
255. Regarding "for the purpose of food" in the case of seven-day medicines or lifetime medicines:

for one who accepts them for the purpose of food, there is first a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) on account of the acceptance; but as for the act of consuming them, if it is non-material [medicine], there is a *dukkaṭa* for every single swallow.
Now, if it has been received while mixed with food and then set aside, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for the duration of its original state. 256.
There is no offense regarding what is called "temporary" (yāvakālika) and so forth; this refers to that which is specified in the training rule on eating at the wrong time (vikālabhojana).

It is "temporary" because the various kinds of chewable and edible food (khādanīya-bhojanīya) must be consumed only as long as the time designated as "midday" (majjhantika) lasts. This includes [the category] along with the corresponding drinks (anuloma-pāna).
The eight kinds of drink may be consumed until the watch of the night known as the last watch;
thus, because its time is the watch (*yāma*), it is "time-bound for a watch" (*yāmakālika*). The five kinds of medicine, such as ghee and so forth, may be stored for seven days;
thus, because its time is seven days (*sattāha*), it is "time-bound for seven days" (*sattāhakālika*). With the exception of water, all the remainder may be kept for as long as one lives.
Because it is to be consumed when there is a requisite condition, it is called "as long as life lasts" (*yāvajīvaka*).

In this context, that which is received at the very rising of dawn is "timely for the day" (*yāvakālika*); even if it is stored a hundred times, it remains "timely for the day" as long as the time has not passed.

That which is "timely for the watch" (*yāmakālika*) lasts one day and night; that which is "timely for seven days" (*sattāhakālika*) lasts seven nights; and the other [the *yāvajīvaka*] lasts as long as there is a requisite condition.
There is no offense for one who consumes [it] even for the duration of his life. The rest here is self-evident.

However, in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), at this point there is an extensive discussion on drinks, a discussion on what conforms to the allowable (*kappiyānuloma*), such as the discussion beginning with "Is it allowable to use what is allowable for a watch of the night (*yāmakālika*) by means of what is allowable for the time of the day (*yāvakālika*)?", and a discussion on the grounds of what is allowable (*kappiyabhūmi*); we shall discuss that in the very place where it occurs.

The origin of the offense concerning the wool of a goat: it originates from both body and from body-and-mind; it is an action; it is not a liberation through perception; it is without thought; it is an offense by formal rule; it is bodily action;
it involves three types of consciousness and three types of feeling. This is the eighth training rule concerning the storage of food. 9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Luxurious Foods.

257. In the ninth training rule: “Delicate foods” (*paṇītabhojanāni*) means excellent foods. “To whom would what is well-prepared not be pleasing? means to whom would that which is endowed with excellence not be dear?

“Tasty” (*sādu*) means having a good flavor. 259. Regarding the rule: “Whatever monk, being not ill, should have such delicate foods requested for his own sake and then eat them,” in this context, one who eats after having requested pure ghee and so forth does not incur an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
Regarding the training rules (*sekhiya*), it should be understood that one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for requesting soup and boiled rice;
however, having requested them while they are mixed together, one incurs an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) when eating them—this, it is said, is the intended meaning here.
For this very reason, instead of saying "delicacies" (*paṇītāni*) in the Sutta, it says "delicate foods" (*paṇītabhojanāni*). For if "delicacies" were used, it would refer only to ghee and the like.
When it is said, “exquisite foods,” however, the meaning understood is that foods produced from the seven grains, mixed with exquisite [ingredients], are “exquisite foods.
Now, regarding the rules concerning the offense of a *dukkaṭa* for requesting [food] and so forth, this is the analysis: “Give rice with ghee; give ghee...”

For one who requests, saying, “Give it having poured it out,” “Give it having mixed it with ghee,” “Give it together with ghee,” or “Give both ghee and rice,” there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the request,
an offense of wrong-doing for the acceptance, and an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya) for swallowing it.

However, when it is said, “Give ghee-rice,” since there is no such thing as “ghee-rice” in the same way that there is “rice-rice,” it should be understood that there is only an offense of wrong-doing for requesting curry and boiled rice.
But if, when told, "Give rice with ghee," one gives the rice and then gives butter,
milk, or curd, saying, "Make ghee and eat," or if one gives the raw material, saying, "Take this and make ghee and eat," it remains as it was in the original case.
However, when told, "Give rice with cow-ghee," if one gives cow-ghee, or if [cow-ghee is available]...
If it is not available, he may, in the same manner as before, give cow-butter and so forth, or even the cow itself, saying, "Eat from this with ghee," provided it remains in its original state.
However, if he is asked for cow-ghee but gives goat-ghee and so forth, there is a substitution (*visaṅketa*).
For in that case, something other than what was requested has been given; therefore, there is no offense. This same principle applies to the goat.
In cases such as "Give [me] ghee," if one says, "Give me *kappiya* (permissible) ghee," but gives *akappiya* (impermissible) ghee, it is indeed a breach of convention (*visaṅketa*).

If one says, "Give me *akappiya* ghee," and gives *akappiya* ghee, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) both in the act of receiving and in the act of consumption. Regarding *akappiya* ghee...
If, in the same manner as before, one gives unallowable fresh butter and so forth, saying, "Make it into ghee and eat," it is considered given with unallowable ghee.
If "unallowable ghee" is mentioned, yet one gives allowable [ghee], there is a discrepancy (*visaṅketa*).

If "ghee" is mentioned, yet one gives any other among the remaining items such as fresh butter and so forth, there is likewise a discrepancy. This same principle applies to cases such as "Give me fresh butter" and so on.
For whatever specific thing the communication (*viññatti*) is made regarding, once that very thing—or its source—is obtained, it is considered obtained.
However, if they give something else, whether mentioned in the Canon (*pāḷi*) or not, it constitutes a breach of agreement (*visaṅketa*).

For one who makes a request for ghee or other such items by using words other than those specifically mentioned in the Canon—setting aside the ghee and so forth actually listed in the Canon—it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). And just as in the case of saying, "Give me rice with ghee,"...

It has been stated that when [the request] is made, because there is no such thing as rice with ghee (sappibhatta) in the same way as rice with salted curries (sālibhatta), there is only an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for requesting soup and boiled rice.

This is likewise the case in instances such as "Give me rice with fresh butter" and so forth. For even if one were to explain each item in detail in successive order, this very same meaning would have to be stated;
and since it can be understood even in brief, what is the use of detailed exposition in that regard?
Therefore it was said: "This same method applies to such cases as 'Give me butter,' and so forth.

However, if one has requested [these items] from all [donors], whether at one place or various places, and having received them, pours them into a single vessel, makes them of a single flavor, and then swallows after placing even a drop on the tip of the tongue with the blade of a *kusa* grass, [it is considered eating].
One incurs nine *pācittiya* offenses. And this has also been stated in the *Parivāra*:
"They are bodily, not vocal;
all have different bases."
“One might incur [the offense] simultaneously;
this question has been considered by those who are skilled. 261.
Regarding “one who is not ill but perceives himself as ill”: here, even if one perceives oneself as ill, if one uses the five medicines for the sake of medicine...

If he requests [these], he is to be dealt with according to the Mahānāma training rule (sikkhāpada). However, one who requests the nine kinds of choice foods is to be dealt with by this present training rule.
For bhikkhunīs, however, these are grounds for an offense requiring confession (pāṭidesanīya);
in the case of requesting soup or rice, there is only a dukkaṭa offense for both [bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs] regarding the designation of those in training (sekha). The rest here is self-evident.
It has four origins: it originates from body, from body and speech, from body and mind, and from body, speech, and mind.

It is functional (*kiriya*), not associated with liberation through perception (*nosaññāvimokkha*), without consciousness (*acittaka*), censurable by convention (*paṇṇativajja*), bodily action, verbal action, consisting of three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
This is the ninth training rule concerning exquisite food.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule on Tooth-Sticks (Dantapona-sikkhāpada) 263. Regarding the tenth training rule:
one who regards all four requisites—even a tooth-stick—as nothing but refuse-rags is called a *sabbapaṃsukūlika*.
It is said that such a person makes his bowl from a vessel discarded in a charnel ground, and uses only rags discarded there [for his robes].
Having made a robe, he takes only the beds and benches discarded there and uses them. Regarding the term *ayyavosāṭitaka*:
here, "noble ones" (*ayya*) refers to deceased fathers and grandfathers. "Discarded things" (*vosāṭitaka*) refers to hard and soft foods discarded in cemeteries and such places for their sake;
it is said that people, for the sake of relatives who have passed away, [offer] whatever...
While alive, it was dear; now, having gathered it bit by bit from these places such as the charnel ground, they set it aside, thinking, "May our relatives enjoy it.
That bhikkhu takes it and eats it, and does not desire even when other, more choice food is being offered.
Therefore it is said: "He himself takes and eats what has been discarded by noble ones, whether in a charnel ground, at the foot of a tree, or on a threshold."
"Thera" means firm and solidly built. "Vaṭhara" means stout; the meaning is that this bhikkhu is both stout and has a solid body.
"I think he eats human flesh" means we observe him as one who eats human flesh;
for those who eat human flesh become like this—this is their intention.

264. Regarding the phrase "being scrupulous about using water for rinsing the teeth," those bhikkhus were scrupulous because they had failed to correctly discern the meaning of the rule: "One should not take food into the mouth that has not been given.
However, the Blessed One, like a father admonishing his children, established a supplementary rule (anupaññatti) by way of the matter that had arisen, in order to instruct those bhikkhus.

265. *Adinnaṃ* (not given) means that which has not been given by way of the body, or by what is connected to the body, to one who takes it, whether by means of the body or by what is connected to the body, or by means of relinquishing [the object].
It is with reference to this very point that it is said in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*):
"What is called 'not given' is said to be that which has not been formally accepted. However, in the second *pārājika*, it is said: "'Not given' is said to be that which is possessed by another."
It has been stated. However, the term "given" (*dinna*) is extracted here for the purpose of showing the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) by way of the opposite of that which is "not given" (*adinna*).
Regarding its detailed exposition (*niddesa*), it says: "When another is giving, either with the body, or with what is connected to the body, or with what is relinquished (*nissaggiya*)," and so on;
thus, while standing within arm's reach (*hatthapāsa*), one receives it "either with the body or with what is connected to the body."
When it is being given in this manner— even down to as much as a speck of dust from a chariot— if one, standing within arm’s reach of the aforementioned characteristics,
receives it with the body or with what is attached to the body, then that which is received in this way is called "given.
It is not relinquished by means of such words as, "Take this," or "Let this be yours."
In this context, "with the body" means by any part of the body, such as the hand and so forth.
Even when something is given with as little as a toe, it is called "given with the body"; the same principle applies to receiving.
For whatever is taken with any part of the body is indeed "taken with the body. Even if something being given to one who needs nose-salve is received into the nostril by one who is not ill...
Or he receives it with his mouth. For in this case, the mere intention (*ābhoga*) alone is the measure; this method is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*.
"By means of something connected to the body" means that whatever utensil among spoons and so forth is used, what is given by that becomes "given by means of something connected to the body.
This same method applies to the receiving as well: by means of anything connected to the body, such as a bowl, a vessel, or the like.
What is taken with what is attached to the body is indeed considered "taken. Regarding "by means of what is to be relinquished" (*nissaggiya*):

even if one causes [the object] to be brought while standing within arm's reach after having detached it from the body and from what is attached to the body, it is called "given by means of an act involving what is to be relinquished.
This, for now, is the commentary on the canonical text (*pāḷivaṇṇanā*).
Now, here is the decision not found in the canonical text: Acceptance is valid when five factors are present:
it is the mere utterance of a man of medium strength; the range of the hand is discernible; the delivery is discernible;
and a deva, a human, or an animal gives it by means of the body, by something connected to the body, or by something relinquished.
If a monk receives it with his own body or with something connected to his body, then the receiving is valid through these five factors.
In this regard, the range of the hand (hatthapāsa) for those standing, sitting, or lying down should be understood according to the method stated in the Pavāraṇā-sikkhāpada.
