However, if among the giver and the receiver one is in the air and one is on the ground, then for the one on the ground, [it is valid] by means of the head...
Regarding one situated in the air, except for the outstretched hand used for giving or taking,
the extent of the *hatthapāsa* (the range of the hand) must be delimited by the side of whichever limb is nearest. Even if one person is in a well, another on the bank of the well,
one on a tree, and another on the ground, the extent of the *hatthapāsa* must be delimited in the same manner as described.
If one stands within such a reach of the hand, even if a bird gives [the gift] by taking it with its beak,

or an elephant by taking it with its trunk, the acceptance is valid. Furthermore, if one is seated on the back of an elephant even as large as seven and a half ratanas, and accepts what is being given by that [elephant] with its trunk, it is likewise permissible.

If one person comes before a bhikkhu carrying many vessels of food and curry on his head and stands there saying, "Take [some]," it is not yet considered an *abhihāra* (an offering); therefore, it should not be accepted.
However, if he bends down even slightly, the bhikkhu may extend his hand and accept even a portion from the lower vessel.
Up to this point, all vessels have been accepted; from that point onward, it is permissible to take whatever one wishes—either by setting it down or opening it—and eat.
However, regarding a single vessel such as a food-basket (*bhattapacchī*), there is no need for formal acceptance;
even when carrying food in a carrying-pole (*kāja*), it is permissible if the person lowers the pole and gives it to one.
There is a bamboo pole thirty cubits long, with a jar of molasses tied to one end and a jar of ghee to the other;
if one accepts it, all of it is considered accepted. If someone says, "Take the juice as it drips from the sugar-mill bucket," it must not be accepted because no specific portion is indicated.
However, if [the person] discards the dregs and [offers it] with the hand...
If he gives after pouring it out again and again,
it is permissible. If many bowls are placed on a bed, a chair, a straw mat, a trough, or a plank,
one may stand where the giver is within arm’s reach and, with the intention of receiving, [touch] the beds and so forth even with a finger.
Whether standing, sitting, or lying down, whatever is given into those bowls is all considered accepted.
Even if one sits upon a bed or similar furniture with the thought, "I shall accept [the food]," it is still permissible.
However, if one grasps the bed or similar furniture with the hand and then sits on the bed, there is nothing at all that can be said [in its favor].

On the ground, however, even if [the bowls] are placed touching one another from belly to belly, wherever he sits while touching them with his finger or a needle, there they are considered received as they are being given.
It has been said: "In no case does the receiving of alms succeed if the bowl is placed upon a large mat of straw, a felt rug, or similar coverings."
It should be understood that this was stated with reference to exceeding the reach of one's hand.
However, as long as the object is within the reach of one's hand, it is permissible anywhere except for things grown there;
but in the case of things grown there, such as a lotus leaf or a *kiṃsuka* leaf and so forth, it is not permitted. For that is not reckoned as being connected to the body.

It moves away. And just as in the case of what grows there [on the spot], so too it does not grow at all on a bedstead or similar object set up and bound to a stump, nor on a non-portable plank or a stone;

for these also are included within the category of "what grows there. Nor does the receiving bowl grow even on very fine *tintiṇika* leaves or the like spread upon the ground, for they are not capable of supporting it.
"Capable" means: it grows even on large lotus leaves and the like.
If [the donor] stands beyond arm's reach and offers with a long-handled ladle, one should say, "Come closer and give.
If, having not heard or not heeded this, the donor simply pours it into the bowl, it must be accepted again. The same rule applies even if the donor stands at a distance and throws a morsel of food.
If there is dye powder on the bowl when it is being taken out from the bowl-bag, it should be washed if water is available;
if not, one should go for alms after asking about the dye powder or having received it [in a separate vessel].

If dye falls onto the bowl while one is walking for alms, the alms-food should be accepted after receiving it [into another vessel]. For one who accepts it without having received it [into another vessel], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*vinayadukkaṭa*).
However, there is no offense for one who receives that [food] again and then eats it.

But if, when told "Give it after receiving it," the giver continues to offer the almsfood without having heard or heeded those words, there is no *vinaya-dukkata*; one should receive other almsfood after receiving it once more.

If a great wind blows dust from here and there so that it is impossible to collect alms-food, it is permissible to take it with a pure mind, having formed the intention: "I will give this to one who is not fully ordained.

Having thus wandered for alms and gone to the monastery or the sitting hall, he should give it to one who is not fully ordained; then, having received what was given back by that person or through his trust...
or having received it, it is permissible to eat.
If, while on alms-round, someone gives a dusty bowl to a bhikkhu, he should be told:
“Having received this, you may either take alms-food in it or consume [the food already in it]”; he should then act accordingly. If the dust is on top...
If it bubbles up, one should pour off the sour gruel and eat the remainder. If it has entered inside [the mouth], it should be accepted.

If there is no one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna) present, one may accept it without removing it from the hand; however, if there is someone who is not fully ordained present, it should be taken there and accepted by them.
In the case of dry rice, it is permissible to eat after removing any dust that has fallen upon it. If it is too fine...
If [food] falls together with the portion above, it must be removed; or, having received it, it may be eaten.
When those who are stirring place rice gruel or soup in front [of the bowl], droplets rise from the vessel and fall into the bowl; the bowl is to be accepted.
When those serving with a ladle pour [the food], the first drops fall into the bowl before they reach it; these are well-fallen, because they have been brought [into the bowl].
There is no fault. Even if, while the *caru* porridge is being poured, some of it falls as soot or ash from the *caru* vessel, there is no fault because it has been brought [as an offering].
When food being given to one monk falls from his bowl into the bowl of another, it is considered well-fallen; for that has indeed already been accepted.
If, while they are splitting the branches of a *jajjhari* tree and giving [the fruit] to one monk, drops fall from the branch into the bowl of another, that bowl may be accepted.
Since the fruit falls into the bowl of the one over whom they are splitting it because it was brought there with the intention of giving, there is no fault.
If they give a bowl filled with milk-rice (*pāyāsa*), because of its heat, [drops may fall] below...
If he is unable to take it [with his hand], it is permissible to take it with the rim of the mouth. If he is still unable to do so, it may be taken with a support (a spoon).
If a monk who has taken his bowl in the dining hall and is sitting there falls asleep, and neither perceives the bowl being brought to him nor perceives it being given to him, it remains unaccepted.
However, if he is sitting there having formed the mental intention [to accept it], [it is considered accepted].
It is permissible. Even if he falls asleep after letting go of the stand with his hand and nudging it with his foot, it is still permissible.
However, for one who receives [the alms] by stepping on the stand with his foot—even if he is awake—there is an act of receiving with disrespect;
therefore, this should not be done. Some maintain that receiving in this manner with a stand constitutes "receiving what is connected to the body."
They say that because there is "acceptance" (paṭiggahaṇa), it is therefore not allowable; however, that is merely their words.
In terms of its actual meaning, all of this is indeed connected to the body. This same principle has already been shown regarding bodily contact.
Furthermore, even if something being given to a bhikkhu falls [to the ground], it is allowable for him to pick it up himself and consume it. On this point, here is the Sutta:
“Monks, I allow you to take for yourselves and consume whatever falls while being given, for that has been relinquished by the donors.
Furthermore, this sutta is of interpretable meaning (*neyyattha*). Therefore, the intended sense (*adhippāya*) here should be understood as follows:
whatever is being given, having slipped from the hand of the donor onto clean ground, or onto a lotus leaf, a cloth, a mat, or similar items—
If it falls [into one's own bowl], it is permissible to take it up with one’s hand and consume it.
However, if it falls on dusty ground, it should be consumed after wiping away the dust, washing it, or receiving it with the hands.
But if, while rolling along, it goes into the presence of another monk, it is also permissible for that monk to have it brought back. If that monk...
If he says, “You eat it yourself,” it is permissible for her to eat it as well. However, he who has not been instructed must not take it.
Yet, even one who has not been instructed may take it with the thought, “I will give it to the other”; this is stated in the *Kuruṇḍi*.
Why, then, is it not permissible for him to take it for the other monk? Because it was not authorized by the Blessed One. For the Blessed One [said]: “Personally...”
By saying, "Having taken it, one may consume it," the consumption of that very thing—even if not formally received—is permitted for the person to whom it falls while being given.
Furthermore, by the statement, "That, monks, has been relinquished by the donors," the absence of ownership by another is indicated here.
Therefore, it is not permissible to take it oneself from another and consume it; [this applies] to that...
However, it is permissible by way of an authorization; this, it seems, is the intended meaning here.

And because that [food] is authorized due to its being unaccepted, therefore it is permissible to consume it on the second day even if it was left exactly as it stood, not touched, and covered over by someone; there is no offense on account of storage.
Once accepted, it should be consumed. For it is permitted that he may consume it himself on that very same day, but not thereafter;
this, it is said, is the intended meaning here.
Now the method regarding what is not subject to forfeiture is stated: while they are eating, teeth fall out, nails fall out, or [fragments] from the bowl...
The color fades; all such cases are not subject to the formal rule (*abbhohārika*).
Even when the rind of sugarcane and so forth is split with a knife and the inner pith becomes visible, this is called "newly arisen" (*navasamutthita*); having received it, it may be consumed.
When the knife has been washed and the pith is split, the pith does not become visible, but there is merely the scent of iron; that is not subject to the formal rule. Also, when taking up a knife...
They preserve it; the same principle applies even when it has been split open. For they do not preserve it for the purpose of consumption.
When grinding or pounding root medicines and so forth, their sitting mats, small mats, mortars, pestles, and other tools wear out;
having heated a preservation-axe, they cast it into buttermilk or milk for the sake of medicine.
In that case, a dark-blue stain (*nīlikā*) appears. The determination (*vinicchaya*) is exactly as stated for the knife. However, one must not add it oneself to raw tamarind and so forth.
If one does add it, one is not exempt from the offense of cooking for oneself (*sāmaṃpāka*).
When it is raining, if dirty water from the body or the robe of one walking for alms falls into the bowl, [it is permissible].
That should be accepted. This same rule applies even if it falls while he is eating at the foot of a tree or in other such places.
However, if it rains for seven days and the water is clear, or if it falls from the open air, it is permissible.
When giving rice to a novice, it should be given by one who does not touch the rice already in his own bowl; or else, the novice’s bowl should be accepted [from him]. If it is not accepted...
If, after touching the rice, he takes rice for himself from his own bowl again, it becomes "taken up" (uggahitaka).

However, if, wishing to give, he says, "Sāmaṇera, bring your bowl; take some rice," and the other refuses, saying, "Enough for me," even if [the first] says again, "This was relinquished by me to you," [if the other replies], "It is not for me..."
He says, "The purpose is served by this. Even if one gives it up a hundred times, it remains accepted as long as it has come into one's own hand.
However, if he places it on a stand and, being indifferent, says, "Take it," it must be accepted again.
If, while still having a sense of expectation, he sets the bowl down on a stand and says to a novice, "Take the cake or the rice from here," the novice...

If, having washed his hand, he takes [the food] even a hundred times and places it in his own bowl without touching what is already in his own bowl, there is no need for a further act of formal acceptance (*paṭiggahaṇa*).

However, if he touches what is already in his own bowl and then takes from that [other bowl], it becomes mixed with what belongs to the novice; therefore, it must be formally accepted again. Some, however, say...
“If, while being taken, it breaks off and falls back there, it should be accepted again,” they say.
This should be understood as applying when one has specified the limit, saying, “Take one morsel of food; take one cake; take this much portion of this lump of sugar.
But here, no such limit exists. Therefore, regarding that which belongs to the novice...

When it falls into the bowl, that very act of receiving ceases. However, as long as what has come into the hand is not yet withdrawn by the novice saying "Enough," nor prevented by the monk, it remains the property of the monk alone; therefore, the act of receiving does not cease.
If one puts rice into a vessel for boiling gruel for oneself or for other monks for the sake of anyone, [the same applies].
Having said, “Novice, place your hand over the bowl,” it should be placed into his hand;
for what falls from his hand into the bowl does not render the bowl unallowable on the following day, because it has been relinquished.
If he places it [in the bowl] without doing so, the bowl must be used after making it free of meat, just like an alms-bowl.
The donors placed the bowl of rice-gruel and departed; the young novice was unable to receive it himself.
The monk held out his bowl, and the novice, having placed the neck of the bowl upon the rim of the monk’s bowl, poured it in.
Thus, the gruel contained in the [donors'] bowl is considered received. Alternatively, the monk places his hand on the ground, and the novice...
Having rolled it down, one places it there; this is permissible. The same principle applies to baskets of cakes, after-meal rice, baskets of vegetables, loads, and so forth.
If two or three novices carry a load that is suitable for receiving, or if two or three monks receive what has been lifted by one strong person, it is permissible.
[Likewise] if a jar of oil or a jar of molasses is placed on a leg of a bed or a chair...
Or if they hang a jar of fresh butter [on a peg], it is permissible for a bhikkhu to sit on a bed or a bench; it does not constitute an *uggahitaka* (an object formally accepted).

If two jars of oil are hung on a peg or a hook, with the one above being formally accepted (*paṭiggahitaka*) and the one below being unaccepted (*appaṭiggahitaka*), it is permissible to take the upper one. If the one below is formally accepted and the one above is unaccepted...
If one takes the upper [lamp] while taking the other, the upper one becomes "received.
If there is an oil vessel on a lower stand that has not been received, and while sweeping one strikes it with the broom, it does not become "received.
If one takes what has not been received thinking, "I will take what has been received," and having realized this, puts it back down again, it becomes "received."
It does not exist [there]. Having carried it outside, one perceives it; having carried it out and placed it outside, it should be placed right there—there is no fault.
However, if it was previously left open and placed there, it must not be closed; it should be left exactly as it was before.
If one places it outside, it must not be touched again.
While descending from the lower palace, one perceives the middle of the ladder; because there is no space [to move it], it must be set down after being carried either upward or downward.
If a scum forms on oil and such substances already accepted, or a thick sediment on ginger and such, that arises from that very same source;
there is no further need for an act of formal acceptance.
If one has climbed a palm tree or a coconut tree and, having lowered a cluster of fruit by means of a rope, says, "Take it while standing above," it should not be accepted.
If another person standing on the ground takes hold of the rope-ends, lifts [the fruit], and gives it, it is permissible.
If one causes a large branch with fruit to be made *kappiya* (rendered allowable) and then accepts it, the fruits are indeed considered accepted.
It is permissible to consume [the food] as one pleases.
If, standing outside the enclosure, they cut through the fence and give sugar cane or *timbarūsaka* fruit, it is permissible provided one is within arm’s reach (*hatthapāsa*).
It is permissible for one who takes what has come out without having touched the fence posts; however, if it has come out after being touched, [it is not].
No fault has been pointed out in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). However, we consider that whatever place is struck, [the object] falls of its own accord from there.
Therefore, it is logical for it to go without remaining even in that [place], like goods that have rolled out from a customs house and fallen outside.
Or, they give [the goods] after making [the person] leap over a fence or a wall; but if the wall is not wide, [they do so] within the enclosure.
If one standing outside the outer wall can reach [the object] within arm’s length, it is permissible to take what has been reached even after going a hundred cubits upward.

A monk carries a sick novice on his shoulder; if the novice, seeing various fruits, takes them and gives them while still seated on the shoulder, it is permissible. Another person carrying a monk gives [food] to the monk seated on his shoulder;
this is likewise permissible. A monk goes along holding a fruit-bearing branch for the sake of shade; when the thought arises to eat the fruits—
It is permissible to eat after having had it formally accepted.
If one has it made allowable for the purpose of warding off flies and accepts it, then if he wishes to eat it, only the original acceptance is required; there is no fault for him while eating.
If a bhikkhu places goods that are suitable for acceptance upon people’s vehicles and travels along the road, [the vehicle...]
If it gets stuck in mud, a junior monk may take hold of the wheel and lift it; this is permissible, as it is not considered "taking hold" (uggahitaka).
If he places it on a boat and propels the boat with a rudder or pulls it by hand, it is permissible.
The same rule applies to a raft. Even if it is placed in a barrel or a tub, having had it taken up by one who is not fully ordained—[the non-ordained person]...
It is permissible to cross by taking hold of the arm. If even that is not possible, it is permissible to have one who is not fully ordained take hold of the arm and cross.
Lay followers give rice for the provisions of the monks going on a journey. Novices take the rice from the monks...
They were unable to take rice for themselves, so the monks took their rice.
When the novice’s own portion of rice was exhausted, he cooked a gruel with the remaining rice, set out all the bowls in a row, and poured the gruel into them.
The wise novice took his own bowl and gave it to the Elder. To the Elder...
"Pass the bowl to the one next in seniority"—in this way he passes them all around; when the contents of all the bowls have been eaten by the novice, it is permissible.

Even if the novice is ignorant and begins to drink the rice-gruel from his own bowl himself, it is still permissible for him to drink it even after being requested by the elders in turn, saying, "Friend, give me your rice-gruel. It is permissible for all [to do so].
If one has eaten what belongs solely to a novice (sāmaṇera), one incurs no offense on account of taking what is not given (uggahita-paccaya) nor on account of storing up (sannidhi-paccaya).
However, in this regard, no distinction is seen between those who take oil and such for the sake of their parents, those who take branches and such for the sake of shade, and these [others].
Therefore, the underlying reason must be examined.

If a novice (sāmaṇera), wishing to cook a meal, washes the rice but is unable to rinse it thoroughly, a monk should receive both the rice and the vessel, wash the rice, rinse it thoroughly, and place the vessel on the stove.
He must not light the fire himself; rather, at the time of cooking, he should open [the lid] to ascertain whether it is cooked. If it is undercooked, for the sake of cooking it further...

It is not permissible to cover it [with a lid]. It is permissible for the purpose of preventing dust or ash from falling into it; when it is ripe, it is also permissible to put it away or to eat it, and there is no further need for the act of formal acceptance (*paṭiggahaṇa*).
If a novice (*sāmaṇera*) is capable of cooking but has no time because he wishes to go somewhere, a monk [may take] a vessel of rice-water...
Having accepted it, one should say, "Place it on the hearth, kindle the fire, and go. Thereafter, it is permissible to do everything according to the previous method.
It is permissible for a monk to place a clean vessel on the fire to heat water for the sake of rice-gruel (*yāgu*). When the water is hot...
The novice places the rice grains [into the pot]; from that point on, the monk must not make the fire himself.
Once the porridge has been cooked, it is permissible for him to accept and eat it.
While the novice is cooking the porridge, a monk who is anxious about touching things with his hands may touch the vessel while playing; [he may also touch] the lid.
If one touches it and, having cut off the froth that has risen to the top, carries it away, it is not permitted for him alone to drink;
it is called "badly prepared" (*durupaciṇṇa*). However, if one takes a ladle or a spoon and stirs it without tossing [the contents], it is not permitted for anyone;
it is both "cooked by oneself" (*sāmapāka*) and "badly prepared. If one tosses it, it becomes "taken up" (*uggahita*) as well.

When a bhikkhu has gone for alms and placed his bowl on a stand, if another greedy bhikkhu, playing about, touches that bowl or touches the lid of the bowl, the food obtained by him from there is not allowable.
But if he lifts up the bowl and sets it down, it is not allowable for anyone. As for fruits grown there on a branch—
If one takes hold of it by means of a branch or a creeper and shakes it, the fruit obtained from that is not permitted;

one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa* for improper conduct (*durupaciṇṇa*). However, it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that it is permissible to lean against a fruit tree or to tie a thorn to it, as this does not constitute improper conduct.
However, if one sees mango fruits or the like fallen in the forest, it is permissible to pick them up with the thought, "I will give this to the novice," and then give them.
Even if one sees the remains of a lion's meal or similar food, it is permissible to pick it up and give it to the novice, whether one has formally accepted it or not.
Furthermore, if one is able to purify one's thoughts, it is also permissible to eat what has been obtained from that source.
One does not incur an offense on account of accepting raw meat, nor on account of what has been received [for another].

If, while one is going after having taken oil and other such items for the sake of one’s mother or father, a sickness arises along the way, it is permissible to accept and consume whatever one desires. However, if it was accepted even at the source...
There is [the fault], yet there is no further need for the act of receiving. He brings rice grains to his parents and gives them;

they themselves prepare the gruel and so forth from that very material and give it to him. It is permissible, and there is no fault whether on account of storage (*sannidhi*) or on account of what has been received (*uggahita*).
A bhikkhu may cover [the vessel] and heat water; it is permissible to use it until it is completely exhausted. However, if in this case—

If ashes fall [while cooking], it should be accepted. When one is cooking oil while holding a pan with long tongs, if ashes fall, it should be accepted after having cooked it and removed it from the heat, without letting go of it with the hand.
If even charcoal or wood has been accepted and set aside, only the original acceptance is valid.
A bhikkhu is eating sugarcane, and a novice says, "Give some to me too. When told, "Cut it from here and take it," he takes it;
there is no further need for an act of formal acceptance (*paṭiggahaṇa*) regarding what remains. The same principle applies when one is eating a lump of sugar.
For that which is taken after being cut from the portion already designated is indeed still subject to the original act of acceptance.
When a bhikkhu distributes sugar, having received it, he divides it into portions. Other bhikkhus and sāmaṇeras come and each take one portion with a single act of receiving;
what remains after they have taken their portions is indeed already "received.
However, if a greedy sāmaṇera takes it again and again and puts it back down, the remainder of what he has taken becomes "unreceived."

When a bhikkhu receives a column of smoke and drinks it, his mouth and throat become as if smeared with realgar (*manosilā*). It is permissible to consume what is to be eaten within the proper time (*yāvakālika*); there is no fault in mixing what is to be consumed within the proper time with what is to be kept for life (*yāvajīvika*).

When smoke enters through the openings of the ears, nose, or mouth while one is cooking a bowl or dye, or when one smells a flower or fruit due to a medical condition, it is permissible because it is not subject to the formal rules (*abbhohārika*). When a belch strikes the palate...

If it enters only as far as the interior [of the mouth], it is permissible because it has not yet entered the [proper] domain. However, once it has entered the mouth, there is an offense for eating at an improper time.
If the taste of food stuck between the teeth enters [the throat], there is indeed an offense.
If the food is very fine and its taste is not perceived, it falls under the category of what is not an offense.
When the time has come, after eating a meal in a place where there is no water, one should rinse the mouth by spitting out two or three mouthfuls of saliva and then going to a place with water.

If sprouts of ginger or other such items emerge from what was received and set aside, there is no need to receive them again. If salt is lacking, the function of salting may be performed with seawater.
It is permissible. Salt water that has been received and set aside is considered salt; salt is considered water; juice is considered molasses;
and molasses is considered juice. Only the original receiving of the root substance is permissible. Ice crystals belong to the category of water.
When they clarify water using the *kataka* nut as a purifier, that is not subject to the rules [regarding food], provided it is not mixed with edible food.
It is permissible. That which has been offered by those seeking material goods, such as wood-apple fruits and the like, is permissible only before the midday meal.
If the water in lotus ponds and similar bodies of water is deep, it is permissible;
however, if it clings to the mouth or the hands, it is not permissible, and one must receive it [into a vessel] before using it. In fields, there is deep water in the ploughed areas.
It may be accepted. If, after raining, it enters caves and such places and fills a river, it is permissible.
In the case of Kakudha springs and the like, where the water is covered by flowers fallen from trees—if the flavor of the flowers is not discernible, there is no need for formal acceptance.
If the water is scanty but the flavor is discernible, it must be formally accepted. This applies to mountain caves and similar locations.
The same principle applies even when water is covered by dark-colored leaves.
If flowers with pollen or stalks have been placed in a water-jar, they should be removed; or, having removed them, the jar should be refilled.
If *pāṭali*, *campaka*, or *mallikā* flowers have been placed [in the water], it is permissible for the duration of a single night.
That remains beyond the scope of formal designation; on the second day as well, it is permissible to use it together with food.
If a novice takes water from a vessel scented with flowers set out by a bhikkhu and pours the remainder of what he has drunk back into that very place, it should be accepted.
It is permissible to take water from lotus ponds and the like after clearing away the pollen of flowers settled therein by suppressing it with a jar.
If a tooth-stick has been made allowable (*kappiya*), accepted, and set aside, and one wishes to drink its juice, only the original acceptance (*mūla-paṭiggahaṇa*) is valid.
If it was set aside without being accepted, it must be accepted [again]. Even if the juice enters [the mouth] while one is unaware of it, there is still an offense;
for this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is unintentional (*acittaka*).
Regarding the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), what is permissible and what is not? First, milk is permissible;
whether it be the milk from allowable meat or the milk from unallowable meat, there is no offense for one who drinks it.
Tears, saliva, snot, urine, feces, phlegm, tooth-tartar, eye-secretion, ear-wax, and the salt produced on the body—all of this [is likewise].
It is permissible. However, whatever falls from that place onto the bowl or into the hand must be accepted;
what remains clinging to the fingers is already considered accepted. When one eats hot rice gruel, the sweat following along the fingers becomes a single continuous mass and remains within the gruel;
or when walking for alms, [sweat] from the hand or from the rim of the bowl...
When one descends to the level of the bowl’s base, there is no longer any need for formal acceptance (*paṭiggahaṇa*).

Among the great elements that have been burnt, there is nothing that is not permissible; however, what is poorly burnt is not permissible. What is well-burnt—even human bone—is permissible to grind into powder and apply to a sore.
It is permissible to take and consume the four great repulsive things even by oneself if there is no one to make them allowable (*kappiyakāraka*).
In this context, even if a person is difficult to speak with or incapable, they remain within the category of those who make things allowable provided they are present.
If charcoal is not available, one should burn dry wood and take the charcoal. If dry wood is not available, one may even cut fresh wood from a tree [and use it].
It is permissible to do so. However, this fourfold "great repulsive" (mahāvikaṭa) is permitted only at the very moment of being bitten by a snake;

the rest here is self-evident. Regarding its origin: it originates from body and from body-and-mind; it is an action (kiriya); it is not liberated through perception (nosaññāvimokkha); it is without thought (acittaka); it is an offense by formal rule (paṇṇattivajja); it is bodily action (kāyakamma); it consists of three types of consciousness (ticitta) and three types of feeling (tivedana).
The tenth training rule concerning tooth-sticks.
The fourth chapter on Food is completed according to the sequence of the commentary. 5.
The Chapter on Naked Ascetics.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Naked Ascetics (Acelaka-sikkhāpada) 269.
Regarding the first training rule of the ninth section, the Chapter on the Naked Ascetics (Acelakavagga): "A food distribution hall" (*parivesana*) means a place where food is served.

"One who has entered the wandering life" (*paribbājaka-samāpanna*) means one who has entered the homeless life (*pabbajjā*). "Gives: there is an offense of expiation" (*deti āpatti pācittiyassa*) refers to giving a bowl of rice porridge filled to the brim in a single action.
If she gives [it], there is one *pācittiya* offense. If she gives it after repeatedly cutting off [portions], there is a *pācittiya* for each act of giving.

This same method applies to cakes, meals, and so forth. Regarding "one who perceives a non-Tīrthika as not being a non-Tīrthika": if a mother or father has gone forth among the Tīrthikas, even for one who gives while perceiving them as her mother or father, there is still a *pācittiya* offense.
"Causes to be given" means she causes it to be given by one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).
273. "Having set it down, he gives" means: having placed it in such a vessel, he places that vessel on the ground near them and gives;
or, having had them place their own vessel down, he gives into it;
or, even having placed the bowl on a stand or on the ground, it is permissible to say, "Take from here. If a member of another sect says, "To me..."
"This belongs to such-and-such a person; do not scatter it here"—thus it should be scattered. Because it belongs to another, it is not called a "gift with one's own hand.
The rest here is self-evident.

Originating from wool: it is an action (kiriya), not accompanied by liberation through perception (nosaññāvimokkha), without consciousness (acittaka), an offense by rule (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), threefold in mind (ticitta), and threefold in feeling (tivedana).
The First Training Rule on the Naked Ascetics. 2.
Commentary on the Second Training Rule on Sending Away.
274. Regarding the second training rule: “even when returning” means even at the assembly hall. “The distribution of food” refers to the meal duty. “He did not obtain it” means he did not reach it.

"Improper conduct" refers to the transgression of the doors of body and speech remaining after what has been stated. Regarding the phrase "one who leaves the vicinity of sight or the vicinity of hearing":
if one who is standing or sitting urges [the other] to leave, and it is the one urged who leaves, there is no offense for the former.
However, even though that person leaves, in effect, the other has indeed left.
Therefore, this offense belongs only to the one who incites [the act]. In that regard, if one foot is within the precincts, it is a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing).
Upon crossing the boundary, it is a *pācittiya* (offense requiring expiation). Here, the range of sight in an open space measures twelve cubits, and likewise for the range of hearing.
However, if there are walls, doors, fences, or the like in between, the state of being obstructed by them [is taken into account].
The offense is to be understood by way of transgressing the vicinity of sight.
"There is no other condition whatsoever" means that there is no other cause apart from the aforementioned improper conduct.
277. "He issues a command of wrath": "wrath" (kali) is anger; he issues its command; he issues the order of anger.
Out of anger, having displayed displeasure toward his standing, sitting, and so forth, he speaks unpleasant words such as, "Look at this man's standing, sitting, looking forward, and looking around!
He stands like a stump, sits like a dog, and looks here and there like a monkey," thinking, "Perhaps he will leave, being provoked by this too. The rest is self-evident.

It arises from three origins: it originates from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. It is an action (*kiriya*), liberation through perception (*saññāvimokkha*), associated with consciousness (*sacittaka*), a fault censured by the world (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), verbal action (*vacīkamma*), an unwholesome state of mind (*akusalacitta*), and possesses three feelings (*tivedana*).
This is the second training rule concerning incitement (*uyyojana*).
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Eating Together (*sabhojana*)
279. Regarding the third training rule: *sayanighare* means in a bedchamber.
"Since alms were given to the noble one" means because alms were given; the intention is: "What was to be obtained by your coming has been obtained by you;
go. *Pariyuṭṭhito* means overcome by lust; the meaning is: having the intention for sexual intercourse.

280. "Together with both people" means together with those who share food (*sabhojana*); [the phrase] "in that sharing of food. Alternatively, "together with food" (*sabhojana*) means "possessing wealth" (*sabhoga*).
For a man who is overwhelmed by lust, a woman is his wealth, and for a woman, a man is her wealth. Therefore, in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) on this, it is said:
"It is both a woman and a man," and so forth. "In a large house" means in a large bedchamber.
"Having left the reach of the hand of the wooden frame" means: having left the reach of the hand of that wooden frame which constitutes the interior wall of the bedroom;
the meaning is that she sits in a place near the inner bed.
And such a bedroom exists in places such as the great four-sided hall (*mahācatussālā*). "Having passed beyond the backbone" refers here to passing beyond the middle.

[The text] shows this. Therefore, it should be understood that there is an offense for passing through the middle of even a small bedchamber, regardless of how it was constructed. The rest here is self-evident.
The origin of the first *pārājika* is: an action, released by perception, with consciousness, a worldly offense, bodily action, unwholesome consciousness, and two types of feeling.
The third training rule is on eating with [a person of the opposite sex].

284. Whatever needs to be said regarding the fourth and fifth training rules is exactly according to the method already stated for the two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules. And just as the training rule on eating with [a person], so too these [two] originate from the same basis as the first *pārājika*.
The fourth training rule is on being secluded and concealed; the fifth training rule is on sitting in seclusion.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule on Conduct (Cāritta-sikkhāpada) 294.

Regarding the sixth training rule: “Give the meal, friends,” it is said that this meal had been brought there; therefore, they spoke thus. However, if the meal has not been brought, it is not permitted to speak in this way, for it would constitute a prearranged speech (*payuttavācā*).
295. “Therefore, monks, having accepted it, set it aside”—this, moreover, the Blessed One said for the purpose of protecting the family’s faith.
He said: "If one were to say, 'Divide it up and eat,' there might be a change in the people's confidence.
*Ussāriyittha* means it was brought back; what is meant is that they took him right back to his own house.
298. Regarding the phrase "a bhikkhunī who is present": to what extent is she "present," and to what extent is she "not present"? [She is considered present] within the monastery.

When the thought of visiting families has arisen for one staying in a certain place, from that point onward, whoever he sees—whether to his side or directly in front of him—and to whom it is possible to announce [the visit] with ordinary speech, this person is called "present" (*santa*).
There is no need to search here and there to fulfill the requirement of announcing [the visit]. For whoever must be sought out in such a manner is indeed "absent" (*asanta*). Moreover:
Having seen a monk within the boundary of the service area (*upacārasīmā*), one should go with the intention, "I will ask for permission," and whoever is seen there must be asked for permission.
If one does not see anyone, having entered without asking permission from a non-existent monk, it is said that one has "entered without asking.

302. "Within the monastery grounds" (*antarārāma*) means a dwelling (*vihāra*) is located inside the village; one goes to that. "The house of a supporter" (*bhattiyaghara*) means a house where one has been invited.

Or [he may go] to the house of those who give *salākā-bhatta* (tickets for meals) and so forth. "In times of distress" means that it is permissible to go when there are obstacles to one's life or to the holy life (*brahmacariya*).

The rest here is self-evident. Regarding the origin of the offense (*kathina-samuṭṭhāna*): it originates from body and speech, and from body, speech, and mind; it is functional (*kiriyā*), non-functional (*akiriya*); it is not associated with liberation through perception (*nosaññāvimokkha*); it is without thought (*acittaka*); it is an offense by rule (*paṇṇattivajja*); it is bodily action (*kāyakamma*) and verbal action (*vacīkamma*); it involves three types of consciousness (*ticitta*) and three types of feeling (*tivedanā*).
The sixth training rule on conduct. 7. Commentary on the Mahānāma Training Rule: 303.
Regarding the seventh training rule—Mahānāma was the son of the Blessed One’s younger paternal uncle, and he was only about one month older [than the Buddha].
The noble disciple is established in two fruits. "Medicine is abundant" means that ghee which has been brought and set aside for him is plentiful.
"It may be accepted" means that at a time when there is no illness, it should not be refused; however, if there is an illness, one should consent [to it], thinking, "I shall request it.
"I invite you with these medicines" refers by name to two or three [kinds] among ghee, oil, and so forth.
Or [it may be measured] by way of quantity, such as a *pattha*, a *nāḷi*, or an *āḷhaka*. "Requests another medicine" means:
having been invited with ghee, he requests oil; having been invited with an *āḷhaka*, he requests a *doṇa*. "If there is no need for medicine":
even if one is able to subsist on mixed food, it does not constitute a "need for medicine."
310. Regarding "those who have been invited": this refers to those who have been invited by means of an individual’s private invitation (*pavāraṇā*).

There is no offense in making a request in accordance with their having been so invited. However, when they have been invited on behalf of the Sangha, the limit must indeed be observed. The rest is self-evident. This rule has six origins:

it is an action (*kiriya*), not involving liberation through perception (*no-saññā-vimokkha*), without dependence on the mind (*acittaka*), an offense of formal prescription (*paṇṇatti-vajja*), consisting of bodily action (*kāya-kamma*) and verbal action (*vacī-kamma*), and associated with three types of consciousness (*citta*) and three types of feeling (*vedanā*).
The Seventh Training Rule on Mahānāma. 8.
Commentary on the Training Rule on an Army on March.

311. Regarding the eighth: *abbhuyyāto* means "gone forth against"; the meaning is that he has gone out from the city with the intention, "I will go toward the enemy army. *Uyyuttaṃ* means "one for whom preparations have been made"; the meaning is "departed from the village."
314. "An elephant consists of twelve men": four riders and two foot-guards for each leg;
thus it consists of twelve men. "A horse consists of three men": one rider and two foot-guards; thus it consists of three men.
"A chariot consists of four men": one driver, one warrior, and two wheel-guardians; thus it consists of four men. Four men.
"With weapons in hand" means with weapons in their hands; "four men"—this is what is called an army complete with its four divisions at the very minimum.
For one going to see such an army, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for every step taken.

"Having left the vicinity of sight" means that it is no longer visible because it is obstructed by something, or because one has descended into a depression; or because standing where one is, it is impossible to see it, as one must go elsewhere.
The meaning is: having gone to the place, for every single instance of looking, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
315. "One by one" refers to each individual among the four components, such as elephants and so forth;
it includes even a single elephant mounted by only one man, or even a single man with an arrow in hand. "Arrayed" means that the king goes to a park or a river; in this way, he is said to be arrayed.

316. "In times of distress" means when there are obstacles to the holy life (*brahmacariya*) regarding one's livelihood; there is no offense for one who goes with the thought, "Having gone there, I will release [the wool].

The rest here is self-evident. This offense originates from sheep’s wool—it is an action (*kiriya*), not released through non-intention (*nosaññāvimokkha*), without mental involvement (*acittaka*), a transgression against the world (*lokavajja*), a bodily action (*kāyakamma*), an unwholesome state of mind (*akusalacitta*), and possesses three types of feeling (*tivedana*).
The eighth training rule concerning marching out with an army. 9. Commentary on the Ninth Training Rule Concerning Staying with an Army:
Regarding the ninth: "When the sun has set, he stays with an army"—whether he stands, sits, or lies down.
Even if one assumes any posture in the air by means of psychic power (*iddhi*), it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) alone.
"An army is besieged by a counter-army" means it is besieged in such a way that movement is cut off. "Obstructed" means besieged by an enemy or by a ruler.
The rest is self-evident. This [offense] originates from wool; it is an action (*kiriya*), not involving liberation through perception (*nosaññāvimokkha*).
It is without consciousness, an offense by transgression of the rule, bodily action, associated with three types of consciousness, and associated with three types of feeling.
The ninth training rule: On dwelling in an army camp.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Military Parades.
322. In the tenth [chapter]: "Uyyodhika" means that they fight here, having repeatedly ascended [to their positions];
this is a designation for a place of combat. "Balagga" means they know the excellence of the force here; the meaning is a place for counting the forces. "Senābyūha" means the array of the army;
this is a designation for the encampment of the army. "Three elephants" refers to the rear elephant division (*hatthānīka*).
The twelve persons mentioned previously as "an elephant" constitute three elephants with that one elephant. The same method applies to the remaining cases as well.
The rest should be understood according to the method explained in the training rule on mobilized armies, together with its origin and other details.
This is the tenth training rule, concerning battle arrays.
The fifth chapter, on the Acelakas, is completed according to the sequence of the commentary. 6.
The Chapter on Drinking Liquor.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Drinking of Liquor.
326. Regarding the first training rule of the Surāpāna-vagga: *Bhaddavatikā* is the name of a certain village;
it received this name because it was possessed of a beautiful enclosure (*bhaddikā vati*). *Pathāvino* means travelers.
*Tejasā tejaṃ* means by one’s own power and majesty [to overcome] the power of the nāga. *Kāpotikā* means having a reddish luster with a color like that of a pigeon’s foot. *Pasannā* means clear.

This is a designation for the scum of surā-liquor. "It is unbecoming, monks, for one who has come" means it is said that drinking intoxicants is not fitting for one who possesses the five super-knowledges (pañca-abhiññā). 328.
"Flower-fermented liquor" (pupphāsava) is that made from the juice of madhuka flowers and so forth. "Fruit-fermented liquor" (phalāsava) refers to [liquors made from] grapes and other fruits.
Having crushed them, it is made from their juice. That which is made from the natural juice of *muddika* grapes is called honey-wine (*madhvāsava*);

they say it may also be made from bee-honey. That which is called molasses-wine (*guḷāsava*) is made from sugarcane juice and so forth. That which is called spirituous liquor (*surā*) is made by adding flour and husks;
even that made from the juice of coconuts and the like is reckoned as spirituous liquor, as is that same [juice] when husks have been added.
They say that when the dregs are taken, it is indeed reckoned as *meraya*.
"Even if one drinks with the tip of a blade of kusa grass" means that even if one drinks this *sura* or *meraya* starting from the seed with the tip of a blade of kusa grass, it is a *pācittiya*;
however, for one who drinks a great deal in a single act, there is only one offense. For one who drinks repeatedly, taking sips, there are offenses according to the number of acts.
329. "And it is non-intoxicant but has the color, smell, and taste of intoxicant" refers to salt-sour gruel (*soṇḍikā*) or fermented rice water (*sutta*).
Regarding "in a curry preparation": if they cook a curry by adding a small amount of intoxicant for the purpose of imparting flavor, there is no offense.
The same principle applies to meat preparations as well. However, regarding oil, if it is mixed with intoxicant for the purpose of a medicine for wind-disorders (*vāta*), [there is no offense].
If they cook together, there is no offense provided that the liquor has not yet been removed;
however, regarding that which has had the liquor removed, where the color, smell, and taste of the liquor are still discernible, there is indeed an offense.
Regarding "non-liquor aritta": there is no offense in the case of an *ariṭṭha* that is not liquor—such as an *ariṭṭha* made from the juice of *āmalaka* and so forth.
They prepare it, but it possesses only the color, smell, and taste of liquor, and is not actually liquor; it is with reference to this that it was said.
However, that which has been mixed with the ingredients becomes liquor; from the moment of its being fermented, it is not permitted.
The rest here is self-evident. This offense is originated by wool; it is an action, not a release through perception, without mental involvement, and a transgression according to worldly convention.

Bodily action is unwholesome consciousness; it has three feelings. And herein, one should understand its "state of being without consciousness" (acetanaka) by way of not knowing the object, and its "worldly transgression" (lokavajja) by way of being incurred through unwholesomeness alone.
This is the first training rule on the drinking of fermented liquor.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Tickling with Fingers (Aṅgulipatodaka-sikkhāpada) 330.
Regarding the second [offense]: "With fingers" (aṅgulipatodakena) refers to the touching of the armpits and so forth with the fingers.

"Being terrified" (uttasanto) means being distressed by excessive laughter. "Becoming breathless" (anassāsako) means having the movement of inhalation and exhalation interrupted. [The object of the offense is] one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna).

"By body" means they call out here; even for a nun standing in a place where she has not received full ordination, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who touches her with the intention of sport. The rest here is self-evident.
The origin of this first *pārājika* is: an action, liberation through perception, with consciousness, a worldly transgression, bodily action, unwholesome consciousness, and two feelings.
The second training rule on poking with the fingers.
3. Commentary on the third training rule concerning laughing. 335.
Regarding the third: "Those who do not recognize what has been done" means those who do not understand what has been performed or established by the Blessed One.
336. "In water that is fit for play" means water-sports are being spoken of. "Above the ankles" means at a height measuring above the ankles.

"With the intention of playing" means with the intention of sport. Regarding the phrases "dives" and so forth: for one who descends into the water for the purpose of diving, there is a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) for every step taken.
For each instance of diving and surfacing, there is a *pācittiya* (offense requiring confession). Having dived, while still within the water...
For one who is crossing, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for every hand-span and every foot-span. "Crosses" means to swim across.

For one swimming with the hands, there is an offense of expiation for every hand-span; the same rule applies to the feet as well. For whichever limb one crosses with, for each individual act of that limb, there is an offense of expiation.
Or if one falls into the water from a bank or from a tree...
It is indeed a *pācittiya*. "He plays with a boat" means that he plays with a boat by rowing it with oars, etc., or by pulling it onto the bank; this is a *dukkaṭa*.
In the cases of "with the hand," etc., there is a *dukkaṭa* for every individual act. Some [say] that when a pebble is thrown into the water with the hand...

Regarding the sections on descending and ascending, some say there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); that should not be accepted. For in those cases, because it is a single action, there is only one *dukkaṭa*.

Furthermore, setting aside the acts of emerging and so forth described in relation to water reaching above the ankles, if one descends into water—or does not descend—in any manner whatsoever, or even takes up a single drop of water standing anywhere, [there is an offense].
Even for one playing a game of throwing [dice], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); however, it is permissible to write down characters that indicate the meaning.
This is the analysis in this case. The rest here is self-evident.

The origin of the first Pārājika: it is an action, released by perception, accompanied by consciousness, a world-transgression, bodily action, unwholesome consciousness, and associated with three types of feeling.
The third training rule concerning envy.
4. Commentary on the fourth training rule concerning disrespect:
“How might this discourse be lost? means: how might this Dhamma, its textual tradition, and its lineage be lost? That...
"Or not wishing to train" means: he does not wish to train in that which is called a "formal rule" (paññatta). "In what is not a formal rule" (apaññatte) means:
in what is handed down in the Sutta or the Abhidhamma. 344.
Regarding the phrase "Thus is our teachers' learning," the "teachers' learning" (ācariyuggaha) that is to be censured here should not be accepted; rather, it refers to the lineage (paveṇiyā).

The "approval of the teacher" (ācariyuggaha) must be accepted only when it has been formally received. However, in the *Kurundi*, it is stated: "In the case of a natural offense (*lokavajja*), the approval of the teacher is not permitted;

but in the case of a formal offense (*paṇṇattivajja*), it is permitted. In the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "The approval of teachers who have themselves mastered the Suttas and that which is in conformity with the Suttas is authoritative;
the discourse of those who do not know them is not authoritative. All of this pertains to the tradition (*paveṇi*).
It occurs when one goes after having arrived at a gathering. The remainder is self-evident. It has three origins:

it originates from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. It is an action; it is resolved through perception; it is accompanied by consciousness; it is a worldly offense; it is bodily action and verbal action; it is unwholesome consciousness;
and it is associated with painful feeling. This is the fourth training rule concerning disrespect.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule on Terrifying (Bhiṃsāpana-sikkhāpada) 345.
Regarding the fifth [training rule]: the presentation of forms and so forth should be understood in the same manner as described under the section on human beings. The remainder is self-evident.
The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and other factors are identical to those for the training rule on disrespect (anādariya). This is the fifth training rule on terrifying.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule on Fire (Jotisikkhāpada) 350.
Regarding the sixth [training rule]: *Bhagga* is the name of the country; *Saṃsumāragira* is the name of the city;
*Bhesakaḷāvana* is the name of the forest situated there. Because it was given for the comfortable dwelling of deer, it is called *Migadāya* (the Deer Park).
"Having kindled" means having set it ablaze. "He followed after" means he pursued it.

"Even in the case of a lamp" refers even to the lighting of a lamp. "Even in the case of a fire" refers to making a fire for such purposes as cooking in a vessel or washing clothes. "By such conditions" refers to conditions such as lamps and so forth.
"He himself kindles" means, in this context, starting from the placing of the fire-drill (araṇi) with the desire to kindle a fire.
As long as the flame does not arise, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for all such efforts.
"He picks up a fallen ember" means he picks up a burning ember that has fallen; the meaning is that he places it back in its original position.

Thus, there is an offense of wrong-doing for one who picks up and puts back an ember that has not gone out, but for one who makes an ember that has gone out blaze up again, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
356. “By such a condition”: there is no offense for one who kindles [a fire] by means of any other such condition, excluding lamps and the like.
“In cases of distress”: when there is danger from wicked wild animals or humans, there is no offense even for one who kindles [a fire] therein.
The rest is self-evident. It has six origins: it is an action, not involving volition or liberation, and is without mental engagement (*acittaka*).
It is a formal act (paṇṇatti-vajja), bodily action, verbal action, three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
The sixth training rule concerning fire. 7.
Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Bathing.
364. Regarding the seventh [offense]: "With powder or with clay"—here, from the time of preparing the powder and clay onwards, there is a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) for all such applications.
366. Regarding "he bathes while crossing over": here, it is permissible to bathe even in ditches made by throwing sand into a dry riverbed. Regarding "in cases of distress":
it is permissible for one who is being pursued by bees and the like to submerge himself in water.

The rest here is self-evident. Regarding the origin from sheep’s wool: it is a formal act (*kiriya*), not associated with liberation through perception (*nosaññāvimokkha*), without consciousness (*acittaka*), an offense by rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), consisting of three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
This is the seventh training rule concerning bathing.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Making [Robes] Ugly (Dubbaṇṇakaraṇasikkhāpada) 368–9.
Regarding the eighth rule: "But with the acquisition of a new robe by a bhikkhu"—here, *labho* means "he obtained" (*alabhi*);

*lābho* is simply the act of obtaining. What was obtained? A robe. Of what kind? New. Thus, although one should have said "with the acquisition of a new robe" (*navacīvaralābhena*), there is an elision of the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*).
It was stated [in the rule] as “by the acquisition of a new robe,” meaning “by a newly acquired robe.
The phrase “but in the case of the two middle terms” is a particle (*nipāta*). “By a bhikkhunī” is an indication of the person by whom it was obtained.

However, in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), in order to show what was obtained without regard for the specific phrasing, it was stated: “A robe (*cīvara*) means any of the six types of robes,” and so forth.
"Robe-cloth" (*cīvara*) here should be understood as that which can be worn as an undergarment or as an upper garment;
for this very reason, it is not described as "the last [type] that has reached the stage of being assigned. "Copper-blue" (*kaṃsanīla*) is the blue of a leather-worker.
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "The rust of iron or the rust of copper—this is what is called 'copper-blue'. "Palāsa-blue" is any kind of blue color.
The fifteenth [rule]: "One should take up that which makes it discolored. This was said with reference to the *kappa-bindu* (the allowable mark);

it does not mean discoloring the entire robe with blue or other colors. Furthermore, when applying that allowable mark, after the robe has been dyed, one should apply it to four corners, three, two, or even just one corner, the size of a peacock's eye or the back of a *maṅgula* insect.
Or it may be taken [as a mark]. In the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "It is not permitted on the bowl or on a knot.
However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "It is indeed permitted. But marks such as those resembling a *kappakaṇṇika* or a *kappa* are prohibited everywhere.
Therefore, apart from a single circular dot (*vaṭṭabindu*), no other modification whatsoever should be made as a mark.

371. Regarding the terms *aggaḷa* and so forth: these [items], such as *aggaḷa*, have no need for further formal authorization (*kappa-karaṇa*) once they have been attached to a robe that has already been formally authorized.

The rest is self-evident. This offense originates from wool (*eḷakaloma*); it is a functional-non-functional act (*kiriyākiriya*), not involving liberation through perception (*nosaññāvimokkha*), without mental concomitants (*acittaka*), and an offense by rule (*paṇṇattivajja*).
It is bodily action (*kāyakamma*), associated with three types of consciousness (*ticitta*), and three types of feeling (*tivedana*).
The eighth training rule concerning making [robes] discolored. 9. Commentary on the Ninth Training Rule Concerning Re-assignment (Vikappana) 374. Regarding the ninth [rule]:
"Or what has not been given to him" means that the owner of the robe [says], "Use it or dispose of it as you see fit."

"Or do it yourself"—having spoken thus, it is "what has not been given. Or "without the trust of that person": because of a lack of trust toward the one by whom the formal disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*) was performed.
However, there is no offense for one who uses what has been given by him or with his trust.
The rest here is self-evident, as it follows the method already stated in the commentary on the Thirties. The origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) of the *Kathina* [offense] is from body and speech.
It originates from body, speech, and mind; it is both action and non-action; it is not a liberation through perception; it is without consciousness; it is an offense by formal rule;
it is bodily action and verbal action; it involves three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
This is the ninth training rule concerning the distribution [of robes].
10. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Storing of Robes (Cīvarāpanidhāna-sikkhāpada), §§ 377–81.
In the tenth [rule]: "Storing" (*apanidhenti*) means having set aside, they store away. "With a view to laughter" (*hasāpekkho*) means with the intention of laughter.

"Another requisite" (*aññaṃ parikkhāraṃ*) refers to items not mentioned in the Canon, such as a bowl-bag and so forth. "Having given a talk on the Dhamma" (*dhammiṃ kathaṃ katvā*) means: "By a recluse..."

“Indeed, it is not permissible to be one who has not deposited his requisites. Having thus delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, there is no offense for one who deposits [the items] with the intention, “I shall give them.

The rest here is self-evident. It has three origins: it is an act of volition (*kiriya*), liberation through perception (*saññāvimokkha*), accompanied by consciousness (*sacittaka*), a worldly offense (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), verbal action (*vacīkamma*), unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*), and associated with three feelings (*tivedana*).
The tenth training rule concerning the storing of robes.
The sixth chapter, the Chapter on Drinking Intoxicants, is completed according to the sequence of the commentary. 7.
The Chapter on Living Beings.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Intentional Killing of Living Beings (Sañcicca-pāṇa-sikkhāpada) 382.

Regarding the first training rule of the Chapter on Living Beings with Breath (*sappāṇaka-vagga*): "He was an archer" means that in his time as a householder, he was a master of archery. "Deprived of life" means separated from life.

In the training rule as well, "should deprive of life" means should separate [from life]. However, since this is merely a figurative expression (*vohāra-matta*), there is nothing here [that is actually killed].
When one is deprived of lead ornaments, just as the lead itself is removed, so too when life is taken, that which is called "life" does not remain separately;
rather, it simply passes away. Therefore, to demonstrate this point, the word-commentary states, "he cuts off the life-faculty," and so forth.
And in this training rule, only an animal is to be understood as "a living being."

There is no difference in the offense for one who kills whether the being is small or large. However, in the case of a large being, there is a greater degree of unwholesomeness due to the magnitude of the effort involved.

Regarding "perceiving a living being as a living being": even when cleaning a bed or a chair, if one perceives a tiny insect as a living being and, out of mercilessness, breaks it and removes it, it is an *pācittiya*. Therefore, in such instances—

Having established compassion, one should perform the duties with diligence. The remainder should be understood according to the method already explained in the section on the human being, together with its origins and other details.
This is the first training rule regarding the intentional killing of living beings.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Water Containing Living Beings (Sappāṇakasikkhāpada) 387.
Regarding the second [offense]: "Containing living beings" means water that contains those living beings which die through its consumption.
For one who knowingly consumes such water, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for every act of consumption. Even if it fills the bowl, if it is not strained...

For one drinking with a single act of application, there is one offense. Even for one who rinses a bowl containing food with such water, or cools a bowl of hot rice-gruel in such water, or takes that water with the hand or a cup and bathes, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for every act of application.
This applies even when entering a water-channel or a lotus pond for the purpose of exiting on the other side.
Even when stirring up waves, those who are cleaning a drinking pool or a lotus pond must pour back into the water itself the water they have taken from it.
If there is no water nearby, one should pour eight or ten jars of *kappiya* (permissible) water into a place where the water can remain stable and then pour [the taken water] into that.
One must not pour water onto a hot stone with the thought, "It will roll off and fall into the water."
However, it is permissible to extinguish a stone with *kappiya-udaka* (water for allowable use) and then pour [the remaining water] over it. The rest here is self-evident.

This [offense] has three origins: it is an action (*kiriya*), released by perception (*saññāvimokkha*), accompanied by consciousness (*sacittaka*), an offense of formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), and vocal action (*vacīkamma*);

it consists of three types of consciousness and three types of feeling. And herein, even if one knows that insects and small creatures have fallen [into the water], because of the purity of one's mind—

Just as in the case of lighting a lamp, even though one knows it contains living beings, because it may be used with the perception that it is water, it should be understood as an offense of formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*).
This concludes the second training rule on water containing living beings.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Reopening (Ukkoṭana-sikkhāpada)
392. In the third training rule: *ukkoṭenti* means that they go to the presence of each respective monk and, by saying things such as "the legal act was not performed," they overturn it;

they do not allow it to remain established in its state of being properly established. 393. *Yathādhammaṃ*: the meaning is, "by that very Dhamma which was spoken for the settling of whichever legal issue. *Nihitādhikaraṇaṃ*: a settled legal issue; one that has been resolved by the very Dhamma spoken by the Teacher.
"Legal issue" (*adhikaraṇa*) is the meaning.

395. "Perceiving a legitimate legal act as a legitimate legal act" means that if the legal act by which that legal issue was settled is indeed a legitimate legal act, and one, perceiving that legitimate legal act as being a legitimate legal act, should reopen it—
The meaning is that one incurs an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). By this same method, the remaining phrases are also to be understood. This is the summary here;
the detailed exposition, however, is stated in the *Parivāra* by way of the question: "How many reopenings (*ukkoṭanā*) are there for these four legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*)? and so forth.
In the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), having cited all of that, the meaning of it has been explained. We, however, [shall explain] it right there.
We shall explain [this]. For if we were to bring it here and explain it, there might be even greater confusion; therefore, we have not explained it.

The rest here is self-evident. It has three origins: it is an action (*kiriya*), liberation through perception (*saññāvimokkha*), associated with consciousness (*sacittaka*), a worldly offense (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), verbal action (*vacīkamma*), unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*), and painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
The third training rule on reopening [a settled case].
4. Commentary on the training rule on grave offenses (duṭṭhulla-sikkhāpada). 399.
Regarding the fourth [rule]: "A grave offense (duṭṭhullā āpatti)"—here, by way of enumeration, there are four pārājikas.
These have been shown; however, it is the offense of *saṅghādisesa* that is intended here. For one who conceals it, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
"As soon as the burden is laid down" means at the very moment the burden is laid down. Even if one lays down the burden and subsequently reports it, it does not protect [the offender];
the meaning stated is that there is an offense of *pācittiya* at the very moment the burden is laid down. But if, having thus laid down the burden, [one acts] for the purpose of concealment...

If he reports it to another, and that person in turn reports it to yet another—in this manner, even a hundred or a thousand ascetics would incur the offense as long as the chain is not broken. But when is the chain broken? The Elder Mahāsiva says:
"One who has incurred the offense reports it to one person; that person turns back and reports it to the very first person."
"In this way, the limit is reached," said the Elder Mahāpaduma. However, he further explained: "This refers specifically to the person involved in the case.
One who has committed an offense reports it to one monk; that monk reports it to another; the second monk turns back and reports it to the very person to whom the first had reported it.
When the third person has thus reported it to the second, the limit is reached."
400. “A non-gross offense” refers to the remaining five classes of offenses. Regarding “misconduct, whether gross or not gross, with one who is not fully ordained”:
here, emission of semen and physical contact with one who is not fully ordained constitute what is called “gross misconduct.
The rest in this context is self-evident. This has its origin in the laying down of the burden.

It originates from body, speech, and mind; it is non-action, liberation through perception, accompanied by consciousness, blameworthy according to the world, bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome consciousness, and painful feeling.
This is the fourth training rule on grave offenses.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning those Under Twenty Years of Age (Ūnavīsativassasikkhāpada) 402.
Regarding the fifth training rule: "The fingers will become painful" means that as one writes letters, one thinks, "My fingers will become painful.
"Pain in the chest" refers to the fact that much must be contemplated by one who is learning to count.

They thought, "Because it is hot, his chest will suffer. They thought, "His eyes will suffer," because when one is learning the art of painting, one must look at coins again and again; therefore they thought, "His eyes will suffer.
Regarding "gadflies and so forth": *daṃsa* refers to brown flies. "Suffering" means...
"Painful" means [feelings] that are intense. "Sharp" means coarse. "Bitter" means harsh, or else like a bitter taste due to being unpleasant.
"Disagreeable" means not sweet. "Life-taking" means taking away one's life. 404.
"He establishes a boundary" means he binds a new boundary. However, in the *Kurundi*, it is also mentioned in the context of delimiting by the throwing of water.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) has been stated. "Full twenty years of age" means full twenty years from the moment of conception;
for one who has spent twenty years in the womb is also reckoned as being "full twenty years of age. As it is said:
"At that time, the Venerable Kumārakassapa had received full ordination while being twenty years old from conception. Then..."
It occurred to the Venerable Kumārakassapa: “The Blessed One has laid down this rule:
‘A person less than twenty years of age is not to be ordained. Yet I was ordained at twenty by way of the womb.
Am I ordained, or am I not ordained? They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “Monks, that which is first in the mother’s womb...”
“The mind has arisen; the first consciousness has become manifest. Taking that as its basis, there is birth for him.
Monks, I allow you to grant full ordination at twenty years of gestation.
In this context, one who has dwelt in the mother’s womb for twelve months and is born on the Great Pavāraṇā day is [counted] from that point onward.
When the Mahāpavāraṇā occurs in the nineteenth year, one must wait until that has passed and confer full ordination on the first day of the waxing moon (pāṭipada).
In this manner, the decrease or increase [of the age] is to be understood.
However, the ancient elders, having waited until the full-moon day of the month of departure (nikkhamanīya-puṇṇamāsi) for a novice who is nineteen years old, [conferred ordination].
They confer full ordination on the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipada). Why is that? It is said: in one year there are six Uposatha days falling on the fourteenth.
Thus, over twenty years, four months are lost. Kings, however, postpone the rains retreat every third year.
Thus, over eighteen years, six months are added; therefore, by way of the Uposatha...
Having subtracted four months from the time already elapsed, two months remain; taking those two months, the twenty years become complete.
Thus, being free from doubt, they wait until after the full-moon day of the *nikkhamanīya* (departure) month and confer full ordination on the first day of the following month (*pāṭipada*).
In this context, however, the term "nineteen-year-old" refers to one who will turn twenty years old after the *pavāraṇā* ceremony.

Thus it was said. Therefore, one who has dwelt in the mother’s womb for twelve months becomes twenty-one years old; one who has dwelt there for seven months becomes twenty-seven years and seven months old.
However, one born after six months does not survive. 406.

Regarding the offense of "no offense when one perceives as twenty years old a person who is less than twenty years old": although, for the one conferring full ordination, [the perception may differ],...
There is no offense if the person is one who has not yet received full ordination (*anupasampanna*).
However, if after ten years he confers full ordination upon another, and the quorum of the community is completed by excluding that person, then [the others] are properly ordained.

For him as well, as long as he does not know [of his own status], there is neither an obstacle to heaven nor an obstacle to liberation; but having known it, he must receive full ordination again. The rest is self-evident.

It has three origins: it is a functional (kiriya) action, with perception as its liberation, accompanied by consciousness, an offense by formal rule (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action, verbal action, consisting of three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
This is the fifth training rule concerning those under twenty years of age.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Theft (Theyya-sattha-sikkhāpada) 407.

Regarding the sixth [offense]: *paṭiyālokaṃ* means facing toward the light of the sun; the meaning is "the western direction. *Kammiyā* refers to those who work at a toll-station. 409. *Rājānaṃ vā theyyaṃ gacchanti*:
"They go to steal from the king" means that having stolen from or deceived the king, and having taken something belonging to the king, they depart thinking, "Now we will not give it back to him."
411. Regarding "by a different appointment": there is no offense for one who travels by a different appointment of time or a different appointment of the day.

However, there is indeed an offense if it is by a different appointment of the route or a different appointment regarding the forest. The rest here is of obvious meaning, as it follows the method already stated in the Bhikkhunī-vagga.
This [offense] originates from a caravan of thieves—it arises from body and mind, and from body, speech, and mind; it is an action, and it is liberated through perception.
It is accompanied by consciousness, is an offense by formal rule, is bodily action, is verbal action, consists of three types of consciousness, and consists of three types of feeling.
This is the sixth training rule, on the group traveling together by theft.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule on Arranging Travel Together.
412. Regarding the seventh [offense]: “He sat brooding” means he sat reflecting and reproaching himself.
