“This venerable monk did not expel me” means this venerable monk did not have me turned out; the sense is that he did not take me and go away.
The rest here is to be understood according to the method already stated in the training rule concerning making an appointment with a nun.
"Together with their origin and so forth.
This concludes the seventh training rule concerning appointments.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Ariṭṭha.

417. Regarding the eighth [verse]: "They oppressed the vultures" means *gaddhabādhino*. One whose ancestors were such *gaddhabādhis* is a *gaddhabādhipubbo*; the meaning is: one born into a family of vulture-slayers (*gijjhaghātaka*).

They are called *antarāyikā* because they create obstacles to heaven and liberation. These are fivefold, by way of: (1) kamma, (2) defilements (*kilesa*), (3) karmic result (*vipāka*), (4) slander (*upavāda*), and (5) transgression of the Teacher’s injunction (*āṇāvītikkama*).
Among these, the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantariyakamma*) are known as obstacles of kamma. Likewise is the deed of violating a nun (*bhikkhunīdūsakakamma*).
However, that [the obstruction of the path] creates an obstacle only to liberation, not to heaven. States of fixed wrong view are called "obstructions to defilement" (*kilesantarāyika*).
The states of rebirth-linking for eunuchs, animals, and those with both sexual organs are called "obstructions to fruition" (*vipākantarāyika*).
Slandering the Noble Ones is called "obstruction to reproach" (*upavādantarāyika*); however, that [obstruction] lasts only as long as they do not ask the Noble Ones for forgiveness.
Beyond that: intentional offenses committed are called "obstructions consisting in the transgression of an injunction";
these also [act as obstructions] only so long as one continues to claim the status of a monk, or does not emerge from them, or does not confess them—not beyond that.
In this regard, a monk who is learned and a preacher of the Dhamma may recognize other obstructions, but because he is unskilled in the Vinaya...
He did not know that there was an obstacle consisting in the transgression of the rules of training; therefore, having gone into seclusion, he thought thus:
"These householders, while enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure, are stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners;
even the bhikkhus see agreeable forms cognizable by the eye... [and so on] ...they touch tangible objects cognizable by the body."
“They use soft rugs, coverlets, and so forth; all this is permissible. Why is it that only the forms of women...
[and] the tactile sensations of women are not permissible, while these [other things] are permissible?
Having thus compared like with like, and having unified the enjoyment characterized by desire and lust with the enjoyment devoid of desire and lust, [he compares them] together with coarse wool.

Like one attempting to spin an exceedingly fine thread, or like one trying to join Mount Sineru with a mustard seed, he gave rise to a wicked view and, contradicting the omniscient wisdom [of the Buddha], said:
"Why was the first *pārājika* rule established by the Blessed One with such great effort, as if he were binding the great ocean? There is no fault in this."
By destroying the hope of those individuals capable of progress, he dealt a blow to the Wheel of the Conqueror’s command. Therefore he said:
“Thus do I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One,” and so forth.

In the passage beginning with “likened to a skeleton,” they are likened to a skeleton in the sense of providing little gratification; they are likened to a piece of meat in the sense of being common property to many.

They are like a grass torch in the sense of burning up; like a pit of embers in the sense of great scorching heat; like a dream in the sense of appearing only momentarily; like a borrowed article in the sense of being temporary;
like the fruit of a tree in the sense of crushing all one’s limbs and members;
like a butcher’s block in the sense of hacking; like a spear or stake in the sense of piercing through; and like the head of a snake in the sense of being dangerous and fearful.
This is the summary here. For the detailed exposition, it should be consulted in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
"Thus explained" (*evaṃ byākho*) means "it is indeed thus. The rest here is clear because it follows the method already stated previously.

Regarding its origin: it originates from body, speech, and mind; it is non-action (*akiriya*); it is liberation through perception (*saññāvimokkha*); it involves consciousness (*sacittaka*); it is a transgression according to worldly convention (*lokavajja*); it is bodily action and verbal action; it is unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*); and it is associated with painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
The eighth training rule concerning Ariṭṭha. 9.
Commentary on the ninth training rule regarding association with one who has been suspended. 424–5. Regarding the ninth:

"In accordance with the Dhamma" (*akaṭānudhammena*); here, "conformity to the Dhamma" (*anudhammo*) refers to either the non-failure to acknowledge an offense or the non-failure to make amends for it.

Or, having seen that the one who has been suspended according to the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction—due to an evil view or a failure to relinquish it—has performed the concordant duties (*anulomavatta*), the reinstatement (*osāraṇā*) is carried out; this reinstatement is what is called the "conformity with the Dhamma" (*anudhamma*). One for whom this has not been performed is called "one for whom the conformity with the Dhamma has not been performed" (*akaṭānudhamma*);
the meaning is "together with such a person. For this very reason, its word-commentary says: "one for whom the conformity with the Dhamma has not been performed..."
It is said: "He is suspended, not rehabilitated.
Regarding the phrase "gives or receives": whether one gives or receives much by means of a single act, there is one *pācittiya* offense.
For one who gives or receives after repeatedly interrupting the flow, there are *pācittiya* offenses corresponding to the number of acts.

The rest here is self-evident. It has three origins: it is an action (kiriya), liberated by perception (saññāvimokkha), associated with consciousness (sacittaka), an offense by formal rule (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), associated with three types of consciousness (ticitta), and associated with three types of feeling (tivedana).
This is the ninth training rule concerning sharing with one who has been suspended (ukkhitto).
10. Commentary on the Training Rule on Thorns (Kaṇṭaka-sikkhāpada) 428.
Regarding the tenth [rule]: "A speculative view has arisen"—this has arisen for him as it did for Ariṭṭha, while he was emerging from improper reflection.
"Let him be expelled"—here, there are three kinds of expulsion: expulsion by ceasing co-residence, expulsion by removing the [monastic] emblem, and expulsion by means of a formal act of punishment.

In this context, "expulsion" (*ukkhepanā*) refers to being excluded from communal living due to such things as the failure to acknowledge an offense. "Expulsion by means of the gender" (*liṅganāsanā*) is exemplified by the statement:
"An adulterer must be destroyed; destroy the nun Mettiyā. "Expulsion by means of punishment" (*daṇḍakammanāsanā*) is exemplified by the statement:
"From this day forward, friend novice, you shall no longer represent that Blessed One as your teacher. It is this last type that is intended here.
Therefore he said: “And furthermore, monks, he is to be expelled... ‘Perish! In this context, *carā* means “go. *Pira* means “another,” one who is not of our own kin.
*Vinassā* means “perish”; it means “go somewhere where we do not see you. *Upalāpeyya* means “should win over” (or conciliate).

*Upaṭṭhāpeyya* means “should cause him to wait upon oneself. The rest is to be understood according to the method already explained in the training rule concerning Ariṭṭha, together with its origin and other details.
The tenth training rule concerning thorns.
The seventh chapter, the Chapter on Living Beings, is completed according to the sequence of the commentary. 8.
The Chapter on Fellow Practitioners.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Fellow Monks (Sahadhammika-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā) 434. Regarding the first training rule of the Chapter on Fellow Monks:
"In this training rule"—that which is stated in this training rule—"I will not yet train in that. "An offense of expiation (pācittiya)"—here, however, for every single utterance...

The offense is to be understood as follows: Monks, when a *sikkhamānā* has accepted the exhortation from a *bhikkhunī* with her head bowed, she who desires to train must understand, inquire about, and examine [the matter].

The rest here is to be understood according to the word-meaning in the same manner as it was stated in the training rule regarding the "difficult-to-speak-to" (*dubbaca*). As for the legal decision (*vinicchaya*), it is self-evident.

It has three origins: it is an action (*kiriya*), liberated from perception (*saññāvimokkha*), associated with consciousness (*sacittaka*), blameworthy by worldly consensus (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), verbal action (*vacīkamma*), unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*), and painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
This is the first training rule concerning those who live according to the Dhamma.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Scratching (*vilekhana-sikkhāpada*)

438. Second: “He speaks on the discourse of the Vinaya” means he speaks that which is called the discourse of the Vinaya—a discourse connected with what is allowable and what is unallowable, and with offenses, non-offenses, restraint, and abandonment. “He praises the Vinaya” means he utters the praise of the Vinaya;

the praise of the Vinaya consists of the commentary [given] by way of the word-by-word analysis after laying down the matrix (mātikā) according to the five or seven classes of offenses. He utters that.
"He speaks in praise of the mastery of the Vinaya" means that he speaks of the praise,
the virtue, and the benefit rooted in the mastery of the Vinaya for those who are mastering it.
For one who upholds the Vinaya obtains five benefits rooted in the mastery of the Vinaya, six benefits, seven benefits, eight benefits, nine benefits, ten benefits, and eleven benefits.
The meaning is that he speaks all of them. Which five benefits does he obtain? [He obtains] the well-guarding of his own aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*), and so forth.
For this has been said: "Bhikkhus, there are these five benefits for a person who is a bearer of the Vinaya: his own aggregate of virtue is well-guarded and well-protected;
he becomes a refuge for those overcome by remorse; he speaks with confidence in the midst of the Saṅgha; [his adversaries...]
“He rebukes one who has transgressed in accordance with the Dhamma; he is practicing for the stability of the true Dhamma.
How is his own aggregate of virtue well-guarded and well-protected? Here, a certain bhikkhu, when committing an offense, commits it in six ways:
through lack of shame, through ignorance, through being overcome by remorse, or through the perception of what is unallowable as allowable.
Perception of what is allowable as what is not allowable, and loss of mindfulness.
How does one incur an offense through lack of shame? One who knows full well that something is unallowable nevertheless crushes it and commits the transgression. And this has been said:
"One intentionally incurs an offense; one conceals the offense."
“He goes along a wrong path; such a person is called one devoid of shame. How does one incur [an offense] through ignorance?

For a person who is ignorant—dull-witted and utterly deluded—being unaware of what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, performs what should not be done and fails in what should be done; thus one incurs [an offense] through ignorance.
How does one incur [an offense] through being overcome by remorse? When remorse has arisen concerning what is allowable and what is unallowable, one approaches a master of the Vinaya...

Having asked, if it is allowable (*kappiya*), it should be done; if it is not allowable (*akappiya*), it should not be done. Yet, this person disregards [the rule], thinking "this is permissible," and transgresses it;
thus, through being overcome by remorse (*kukkucca*), he incurs an offense.
How does one incur an offense through the perception of what is not allowable as allowable? He eats the flesh of a deer, thinking it is the flesh of a pig, or the flesh of a leopard...
He eats deer meat [thinking it is] pig meat; he eats what is unfit food [thinking it is] fit food; he eats at the wrong time with the perception that it is the right time;
he drinks what is unfit drink [thinking it is] fit drink. In this way, one commits an offense through the perception of what is unfit as being fit.
How does one commit an offense through the perception of what is fit as being unfit? He eats pig meat [thinking it is] bear meat; he eats deer meat...
One eats what is considered "meat from a lamp"; one eats what is permissible food thinking it is impermissible food; one eats at the wrong time with the perception that it is the right time;
one drinks what is permissible drink thinking it is impermissible drink. In this way, one commits an offense through the perception of the impermissible in what is permissible.
How does one commit an offense through forgetfulness? By reason of sleeping together, being separated from one's robe, [using] medicine, or exceeding the time limit for a robe.
And one commits an offense through forgetfulness. In this way, a certain bhikkhu here commits an offense in these six ways.
However, one who is a bearer of the Vinaya does not commit an offense in these six ways. How does he not commit it out of a sense of shame?
For he thinks: "Look, sirs! This man, though knowing what is allowable and what is unallowable, is transgressing the formal rule."
Even while guarding against this censure by others, she does not fall into it; thus, being modest, she does not fall into it.
Even if she should inadvertently fall into an offense, having confessed one that requires confession and emerged from one that requires emergence, she establishes herself in purity. Then:
"She does not intentionally commit an offense; she does not conceal an offense."
“He does not go upon a wrong path; such a person is called one possessed of shame.
Thus, he is indeed established in this state of shame. How does he not fall away from knowledge?
For he knows what is allowable and what is unallowable; therefore, he performs only what is allowable and does not perform what is unallowable. In this way, he does not fall away from knowledge.
How does one not fall into wrongdoing through the practice of freedom from remorse?

When remorse has arisen concerning what is allowable and what is unallowable, he examines the matter, looks to the matrix, the word-commentary, the intermediate offense, the offense, and the non-offense;
if it is allowable, he performs it, and if it is unallowable, he does not perform it. In this way, one does not fall into wrongdoing through the practice of freedom from remorse.
How does one avoid falling into the perception of what is unallowable and so forth? For he knows what is allowable and what is unallowable;
therefore, he does not perceive what is unallowable as allowable, nor does he perceive what is allowable as unallowable. Furthermore, his mindfulness is well-established:
he determines what must be determined, and he designates what must be designated. Thus, by these six ways, one avoids an offense.
He does not commit an offense. By not committing an offense, he possesses unbroken virtue and purified virtue;
thus his own aggregate of virtue is well-guarded and well-protected.
How is he a refuge for those overcome by remorse? For those who have arisen with remorse while in foreign kingdoms or foreign districts...
Thinking, "It is said that a master of the Vinaya dwells in such-and-such a monastery," monks come into his presence even from afar to inquire about their remorse.
He examines the basis of the formal act (kamma) performed by them, observes the distinctions between offenses and non-offenses, heavy and light offenses, and so forth;
having caused them to confess what requires confession and having had them perform the rehabilitation for what requires rehabilitation, he establishes them in a state of purity.
In this way, it is a refuge for those who are overcome by remorse.

"He speaks confidently in the midst of the Saṅgha": for fear and timidity descend upon one who explains the Dhamma in the midst of the Saṅgha when he is not a master of the Vinaya, but they do not descend upon one who is a master of the Vinaya. Why? Because [he knows]: "If I speak in such a manner, there will be fault."
"Thus there is no fault," knowing this, he speaks.
Regarding the phrase "he refutes adversaries with the Dhamma, having well-refuted them":
here, adversaries are of two kinds—adversaries to oneself and adversaries to the Teaching. In that regard, the Mettiya-Bhummajaka monks and Vaḍḍha...
And the Licchavis accused him with a groundless charge concerning a matter involving defeat; these are called "personal enemies.
Furthermore, whoever else is immoral and of evil character—all such are personal enemies.

However, those with perverted views—such as the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, the novice Kaṇṭaka, the Vesālika Vajjiputtakas, and the Mahāsaṅghikas and others who maintain doctrines such as "inducement by another," "ignorance," "doubt," and "transference"—regard what is not the Buddha’s teaching as "the Buddha’s teaching."
Having spoken thus, he thoroughly refutes those known as the adversaries of the Teaching by means of speech that is consistent with the Dhamma and supported by reason,
ensuring they are so well-refuted that they are unable to establish that which is contrary to the Dhamma.

Regarding the phrase "he is one who practices for the stability of the True Dhamma," here the True Dhamma is threefold, by way of the scripture (*pariyatti*), the practice (*paṭipatti*), and the realization (*adhigama*).
Therein, the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Pitakas is called the True Dhamma as Study (pariyatti-saddhamma).
The thirteen ascetic virtues (dhutaṅga), the fourteen rules of conduct for the Khandhakas, and the eighty-two major rules—this is called the True Dhamma as Practice (paṭipatti-saddhamma).
The four paths and the fruits [of the spiritual life]—this is called the True Dhamma as Realization (adhigama-saddhamma).

In this regard, some elders say that "the study of the scriptures is the root of the Dispensation" based on this sutta: "Ānanda, the Dhamma and Vinaya which have been taught and laid down by me—those shall be your teacher after my passing. Some other elders [say the same] based on this sutta:
"If these bhikkhus, Subhadda, were to dwell rightly, the world would not be empty of Arahants."
Having stated that "the practice is the root of the Dispensation," they said, "As long as five monks who are practicing rightly exist, so long does the Dispensation endure.
But the other elders said, "When the scriptures have disappeared, there can be no realization of the Dhamma even for one who practices well.
[They added: "If there are five monks who observe the four *pārājika* rules..."
Having ordained those faithful sons of good family and granted full ordination (*upasampadā*) in the border regions,
they will complete a group of ten and grant full ordination even in the central regions. By this means,
having completed a Saṅgha of twenty members and performed their own act of rehabilitation (*abbhāna-kamma*), they will cause the Teaching to reach growth, increase, and abundance.
Thus, this holder of the Vinaya is practicing for the long endurance of the Triple Gem in its three aspects;
in this way, it should be understood that this holder of the Vinaya first attains these five benefits.

What six benefits does he attain? The Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, the formal acts of the Saṅgha, the going-forth, and the full ordination are under his authority; he gives dependence and he provides a novice with a teacher.

These nine types of Uposatha— the fourteenth-day, the fifteenth-day, the Uposatha for concord, the Uposatha in the Saṅgha, the Uposatha in a group, the Uposatha for an individual, the recitation of the Suttas, the Uposatha of purity, and the Uposatha by formal determination— all of these depend upon those who hold the Vinaya. Furthermore, these nine types of Pavāraṇā— the fourteenth-day, the fifteenth-day, the Pavāraṇā for concord,
the Pavāraṇā in the Saṅgha, the Pavāraṇā in a group, the Pavāraṇā for an individual, the three-fold, the two-fold,
and the Pavāraṇā for those of the same year of seniority— all of these also depend upon those who hold the Vinaya.
Thus, these belong to him; he is their master.

Furthermore, these four formal acts of the Saṅgha—namely, the act of obtaining permission (*apalokanakamma*), the act consisting of a motion (*ñattikamma*), the act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*), and the act consisting of a motion and a fourth proclamation (*ñatticatutthakamma*)—are dependent upon one who holds the Vinaya.

Moreover, this act of granting the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) and the full ordination (*upasampadā*) to sons of good family by means of being a preceptor (*upajjhāya*) is also [dependent upon one who holds the Vinaya].
This depends entirely upon one who is a master of the Vinaya. Indeed, no one else—not even one who is a master of two Piṭakas—is permitted to do this.
Only such a person may grant formal dependence (*nissaya*) and have a novice (*sāmaṇera*) attend upon him. No one else is permitted either to grant dependence or to have a novice attend upon them.
However, one who desires to have a novice attend upon him should receive the formal going-forth (*upajjhāya*) from a master of the Vinaya and then fulfill the duties of service.
He obtains [the opportunity] to provide for them. And herein, the granting of dependence and the attendance upon the novice constitute a single factor.
Thus, with respect to these six benefits, there are six when combined with one, seven with two, eight with three, nine with four, ten with five, and all of them together—
"Eleven": it should be understood that a person who is an expert in the Vinaya thus obtains five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, or eleven benefits.
Thus, it should be understood that the Blessed One, by pointing out these benefits, speaks in praise of the mastery of the Vinaya.
"Again and again" (*ādissa ādissa*) means having repeatedly determined [the subject] and having distinguished it individually.
"He speaks in praise of the Venerable Upāli" means that, based on the mastery of the Vinaya, he speaks of, extols, and praises the virtues of the Elder Upāli. Why? [It is because he thinks:
"Perhaps even upon hearing my own praise, the bhikkhus will learn the Vinaya in the presence of Upāli."
They would think, "This teaching will endure for a long time; it will continue for five thousand years.

Then, those many bhikkhus—having heard this praise of the Blessed One and thinking, "It seems that neither the experts in the Suttas nor the experts in the Abhidhamma obtain these benefits"—become inspired with zeal to attain the aforementioned benefits. Thus there are many bhikkhus.
The meaning here is: "Elders, novices, and those of middle standing were mastering the Vinaya in the presence of the Venerable Upāli.
The word *idha* is merely a particle. 439–40. Regarding the phrase *uddissamāne*:
it refers to when the teacher is reciting [the text] to his pupil; for that [pupil], in relation to the teacher...

Whether one recites it by one's own preference, or causes it to be recited by requesting a teacher, or whether one memorizes it oneself while another is reciting it—that is what is meant by "being recited.
Therefore, the word-commentary states: "while reciting, or causing to be recited, or performing a recitation.
Regarding the phrase "by minor and secondary matters": by the minor ones...
"And by means of the minor rules. "As far as" (*yāvadeva*) is a statement defining the limit of their application. This is what is meant:

for those who recite, cause others to recite, or rehearse these [rules], they apply to them only so long as there is remorse consisting of anxiety—namely, the thought "Is this allowable, or is it not allowable?"—and affliction consisting of doubt.
And mental remorse indeed arises. Alternatively, "to such an extent" (*yāvadeva*) is an expression of emphasis;
its connection is with the phrase "they lead to," meaning they lead excessively to remorse, vexation, and mental distress.
"He disparages the Vinaya in the presence of one who is ordained" means that, desiring to produce doubt in him regarding that [Vinaya], he does so in the presence of one who is ordained.
He disparages, censures, and reviles the Vinaya. The rest here is self-evident.

It has three origins: it is an action (*kiriya*), liberation through perception (*saññāvimokkha*), accompanied by consciousness (*sacittaka*), a worldly offense (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), verbal action (*vacīkamma*), an unwholesome state of mind (*akusalacitta*), and painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
This is the second training rule concerning disparagement (*vilekhana*).
3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Delusion (Mohana-sikkhāpada) 444.
Regarding the third [rule]: "Every half-month" means every half-month in regular succession.
However, because it is recited on the Uposatha day, it is stated in the word-commentary as "bi-Uposatha. "While being recited" means while it is being recited.
However, because that [offense] is said to be "being recited" while the Pātimokkha is being recited by the reciter, it is stated in the word-commentary as "while [it] is being recited.
And regarding the phrase "who has fallen into an offense therein," this refers to whatever offense one has fallen into when that improper conduct has been committed.
"He should be dealt with according to the Dhamma" means that since the offense was committed through ignorance, there is no release from that offense.
But it should be dealt with in accordance with how the Dhamma and the Vinaya are established.

The meaning is: if he has committed an offense that requires confession, he must be made to confess it; if it is one that requires rehabilitation, he must be rehabilitated. "Well done" means properly. "Having made it a bone" means having made it a matter of necessity;
it is the same as saying "having become one who needs it."
447. In the phrase "Dhammakamme" and so forth, the intended meaning is an act that imposes delusion (*mohāropanakamma*). The rest here is self-evident. It has three origins:

it is a functional action (*kiriya*), with perception as its liberation (*saññāvimokkha*), associated with consciousness (*sacittaka*), a fault according to worldly convention (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), verbal action (*vacīkamma*), an unwholesome state of mind (*akusalacitta*), and painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
This is the third training rule on deluding (*mohana*).
4. Commentary on the Training Rule on Striking (Pahārasikkhāpada) 449.
Regarding the fourth [rule]: "Giving a blow" means that after saying things such as, "Friend, prepare a bench; bring water for washing the feet," they give a blow to those who do not act accordingly.
451. "If one gives a blow, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)": here, even if a blow is given with the intention of striking, [it constitutes an offense].
If he dies, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya). If by the blow his hand or foot is broken, or his head is fractured, it is likewise an offense entailing expiation.
If, with the intention of disfiguring him, thinking, "I will act so that he does not shine in the midst of the Saṅgha," he cuts off his ear or nose, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
452. “To one who is not fully ordained” means: if one strikes a householder or one gone forth, a woman or a man, or even down to an animal, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
However, if with a mind of lust one strikes a woman, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.
453. “Being harassed by anyone” means: being harassed by a human or by an animal. “With the intention of escape” means: [the intention] to free oneself.
Then, desiring his own safety, he gives a blow. "He gives a blow" means that he gives a blow with any one of the following:
the body, an object attached to the body, or an object that can be relinquished; there is no offense.
Even if, on the way, having seen a thief or an enemy wishing to harass him, he says, "Lay follower, stay right here, do not come," and [the other] disregards these words and continues to come...
If one goes after striking [the person] with a club or a weapon, saying, “Go away!”, and that person dies from that blow, there is no offense.
The same principle applies regarding wild animals. The rest here is self-evident. As for its origin and other characteristics, they are similar to the first *pārājika*;
however, this [offense] is of painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
The fourth training rule on striking.
5. Commentary on the fifth training rule on clapping hands. 454.
Regarding the fifth: "clapping their hands" means showing the manner of giving a blow, [whether] with the body or with what is connected to the body.
They cry out. "They cry because they have been struck by blows" means that, being accustomed to blows and having received them before, they now cry out thinking, "They are about to strike me.
They also recite it as "pahārassa muccitā," in which case the meaning is "fearing the blow."
457. Regarding the phrase "he emits an offense entailing expiation" (*pācittiya*):
here, if after emitting he gives a blow, or if a blow falls suddenly upon one who is unable to hold back, there is no *dukkaṭa* because it was not given with the intention of striking.
If anything, such as a hand or other limb, is broken by that blow, there is only *dukkaṭa*.

458. Regarding the statement, "One who intends liberation brandishes a palm-leaf fan," there is no offense for one who brandishes a palm-leaf fan in the manner previously described regarding the aforementioned cases.
Even if one strikes after missing the mark, there is likewise no offense.
The remainder is exactly as before, together with the origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth.

The fifth training rule concerning the *tala-sattika*. 6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Groundless Accusations (Amūlaka-sikkhāpada) 459. Regarding the sixth [rule]: "They accuse" (*anuddhaṃsenti*).
It is said that because they themselves are beset by faults, they [accuse others], thinking: "In this way, monks will not [even... [the rest of the sentence follows].
“[They will] accuse [us], they will not bring it back”—thinking thus, they act as a protection for themselves by accusing monks beforehand with a groundless *saṅghādisesa* offense.
The rest here is self-evident, as it follows the method explained in the thirteenth training rule concerning groundless accusations. It has three origins:

it is an action (*kiriya*), liberated from perception (*saññāvimokkha*), associated with consciousness (*sacittaka*), a worldly transgression (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), verbal action (*vacīkamma*), unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*), and painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
The sixth training rule, concerning groundless accusations, is concluded. 7. Commentary on the Seventh Training Rule, Concerning Intentionality (Sañcicca-sikkhāpada):
464. Regarding the seventh: "upadahanti" means they cause to arise. "He causes remorse to arise; there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)" means...
For every word [spoken], there is an offense. "Of one who is not fully ordained" means of a novice (sāmaṇera).

If he causes remorse by saying things such as, "I believe you were sitting, lying down, eating, or drinking in private with a woman," or "In the midst of the Saṅgha, you did this and that," and so forth—word for word—there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). The rest here is self-evident. The origin (samuṭṭhāna) and other factors are also [as follows].
"These are indeed similar to the rootless offenses.
This concludes the seventh training rule concerning intentional lying.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Eavesdropping.
471. Regarding the eighth [offense]: *adhikaraṇajātānaṃ* means of those legal disputes (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) that have arisen from these [causes] such as quarrels and so forth.
*Upassutiṃ* means the vicinity of hearing; the meaning is: "wherever one stands and is able to hear their words, there. *Gacchati āpatti dukkaṭassa*:
here, for every step taken, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). *Mantentaṃ* means by another.
“While conversing with another”; alternatively, the reading is *mantente*, which has the same meaning.

473. “I shall pacify” means I shall go toward peace; I shall not engage in quarreling. “I shall liberate myself” means that by declaring my state of non-agency, I shall release myself. The rest here is self-evident.
This offense originates from a caravan of thieves—it arises from both body and mind, and from body, speech, and mind; it may be an intentional act (*kiriya*).
By way of going out of a desire to hear; or there may be non-doing by way of not making known [the matter] to those who have come to a place where they are deliberating.
For these three training rules—[concerning] money, speaking otherwise, and eavesdropping—share a single delimitation:
they are resolved through perception, involve volition, are offenses against the world, are bodily and verbal actions, are unwholesome states of mind, and are associated with painful feeling.
The eighth training rule on eavesdropping.
9. Commentary on the ninth training rule on obstructing formal acts.
474. Regarding the ninth: “If we were to know” means if we were to know; the word “ca” (and) is merely a particle.

"Of those that are lawful" (*dhammikānaṃ*): because they are performed according to the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction, they are "lawful" (*dhammika*) since the Dhamma exists within them;
[this refers] to those four lawful sangha-proceedings (*saṅghakamma*). "An offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) is incurred for each word":

here, for every single utterance, there is an offense of expiation. The rest is self-evident. It has three origins: it is an action (*kiriya*), it is liberated by perception (*saññāvimokkha*), and it is accompanied by consciousness (*sacittaka*).
Worldly offense, bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome mind, and painful feeling.
The ninth training rule concerning the warding off of actions. 10.
Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Going Without Having Given Consent.

481. Tenth: “The matter has been announced” means that both the accuser and the accused have related their own accounts, and an investigator has been appointed; even at this point, the matter itself is said to have been announced. The rest here is self-evident.

Originating from the laying down of the burden—it originates from body, speech, and mind; it is both an action and a non-action; it is liberated by perception; it is accompanied by consciousness; it is a worldly offense; it is bodily action and verbal action; it is unwholesome consciousness; and it is painful feeling.
This is the tenth training rule concerning departing without having given one’s consent.
11. Commentary on the Eleventh Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 484.

Regarding the eleventh rule: *yathāmittatā* means “according to friendship”; that is to say, one gives to whoever is a friend. This same method applies to all the following terms. The remainder is self-evident (*uttānattha*), as it follows the same pattern explained under the rules concerning disparagement (*ujjhāpanaka*) and so forth. It has three origins (*samuṭṭhāna*):

it is an action (*kiriya*), it is liberated by perception (*saññāvimokkha*), it involves volition (*sacittaka*), it is a worldly offense (*lokavajja*), it is bodily action (*kāyakamma*) and verbal action (*vacīkamma*), it arises from an unwholesome mind (*akusalacitta*), and it is associated with painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
The eleventh training rule concerning weakness is concluded. 12. Commentary on the Training Rule on Diverting: 489.
Regarding the twelfth [training rule], whatever needs to be said has all been stated according to the same method as in the training rule on diverting in the *Tiṃsaka* [chapter].
This indeed is the distinction: there, because it was dedicated to oneself, it is a *nissaggiya-pācittiya*;
here, because it was dedicated to a specific person, it is a simple (*suddhika*) *pācittiya*. It has three origins:

it is an act (*kiriyā*), free from misconception (*saññāvimokkha*), accompanied by consciousness (*sacittaka*), a worldly offense (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), verbal action (*vacīkamma*), unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*), and associated with three types of feeling (*tivedana*).
The twelfth training rule concerning the dedication [of robes].
The eighth chapter, "On Those in Accordance with the Dhamma," is completed according to the sequence of the commentary. 9.
The Chapter on Jewels (Ratana-vagga).
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Royal Enclosure (Antepurasikkhāpada) 494.

Regarding the first training rule of the Rājavagga: *oraka* means "insignificant" or "meager. *Uparipāsādavaragata* means "having gone to the upper part of the excellent palace. *Ayyānaṃ vāhasā* means "on account of the noble ladies"; because it was made known by them, it is said, "I know. 497.
*Pitaraṃ pattheti* means that, having seen an opportunity, she desires to have him killed. In the phrases *rājantepuraṃ hatthisammadda*, etc., [the meaning is as follows:]...
“Elephant-tread” (*hatthisammadda*) means that there is the treading of elephants here; the meaning is “crowded with elephants.

The same method applies to the terms “horse-tread” (*assasammadda*) and “chariot-tread” (*rathasammadda*). Some read “*sammatta*,” but that should not be accepted. There is also the reading “elephant-tread in the king’s inner palace” (*rañño antepure hatthisammadda*);
in that case, the meaning is the treading of elephants in the king’s inner palace, i.e., an elephant-tread in the king’s inner palace.
"It exists" is what is meant. This same method applies to the remaining phrases as well. "Dilatory objects" (*rajanīyāni*) refers to such forms and so forth within that inner palace. 498.

"Of one anointed on the head" (*muddhāvasittassa*) means of one who has been sprinkled upon the head. "The king has not departed from here" (*anikkhanto rājā ito*) means "one from whom the king has not departed" (*anikkhantarājaka*);
[it refers to] "in that place where the king has not departed," which is to say, in the bedchamber. "Jewel" (*ratanaṃ*) is said to refer to the chief queen; "departed" (*niggataṃ*)...
"Aniggataratanakaṃ" means "that in which a jewel has not been taken out"; that is, one in which a jewel has not been removed from the bedchamber—this is the meaning.

The rest here is self-evident. Regarding the origin of the offense (samuṭṭhāna): it originates from body and speech, and from body, speech, and mind; it is an action (kiriyā) but not a non-action (akiriya); it is not a liberation through perception (nosaññāvimokkha); it is without thought (acittaka); it is an offense by formal rule (paṇṇattivajja); it is bodily action (kāyakamma) and verbal action (vacīkamma); it involves three types of consciousness (ticitta) and three types of feeling (tivedanā).
The First Training Rule on the Inner Chambers.
2. Commentary on the Second Training Rule on Valuables.
502–3. Regarding the second: “having forgotten” means having lost track of. A “full bowl” means five kahāpaṇas from a hundred.
“Kyāhaṃ karissāmī” means “What shall I do? “Having removed the ornament” means having taken off the decoration called the Mahālatā, which was worth nine crores.
504. “Antevāsī” means an attendant. 506.
“The precinct of an unenclosed [monastery]”: here, “precinct” (upacāra) refers to two throws of a clod from the monastery—[the precinct] of a dwelling...
"However, it is like the falling of a pestle or the falling of a mace," as stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*.

Regarding the rule "there is an offense of *pācittiya* for one who acquires [it]," here, for one who acquires or causes to be acquired gold or silver for one's own sake, there is a *nissaggiya-pācittiya*;
for the sake of the Saṅgha, a group, an individual, or a shrine (*cetiyakamma*), there is a *dukkaṭa*; and for the remainder, such as pearls and other gems...
For one who acquires [an item] for his own sake or for the sake of the Saṅgha and so forth, or causes it to be acquired, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Whether it be a permissible object or an impermissible object— even down to a palm-leaf ear-ornament belonging to a mother—
if one has it stored under the pretext of being the property of a storekeeper, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) indeed.
If, however, there is allowable property belonging to one's parents that must necessarily be stored away, it may be taken for one’s own use and then stored.
But if they say, "Store this and give it back [to us]," one should refuse, saying, "That is not permitted.
If they leave after having deposited it with the instruction, "Store this," it is called an impediment (*palibodha*), and one must store it.
It is permissible. When carpenters and others, or royal favorites, are working in the monastery and say, "Please put away our own implements or bedding," one must not do so out of desire or fear;
however, it is permissible to show them a secure place. And when they have departed after having forcibly deposited their items, it is permissible to put them away.
Regarding the phrase "in a monastery or in a dwelling":

here, if there is a great monastery like the Mahāvihāra, one should store [the requisites] after having either collected them oneself or had them collected in such a place as a walled enclosure within the monastery where suspicion might arise that they have been taken by monks or novices. This applies to places similar to the courtyard of the Great Bodhi Gatehouse.
However, it should not be taken up in places where large crowds pass; there it does not constitute an impediment.
But in the *Kurundi*, it is said: "If one person walking along a road sees some goods in a place devoid of people, even when a crowd has gathered, people will suspect that very monk;
therefore, one should descend from the path and sit down. [This applies] when the owners..."
"When they have arrived, it should be pointed out to them. If he does not see the owners, they will do what is appropriate.
Regarding the phrase "having made a mark by means of a form or a sign": here, "form" refers to the goods within the bundle.
Therefore, having opened the bundle and counted [the items], one should observe: "There are so many kahāpaṇas," or "there is this much gold and silver."

"Mark" means a brand or the like; therefore, one must observe everything such as whether the bundle is branded with a clay mark or a lacquer mark, or whether the bundle was made from blue cloth or white cloth, and so forth.
"Monks who are suitable" refers to those who are modest and conscientious; for it is not permitted to place [an object] in the hands of those who are by nature covetous.
Furthermore, one who neither departs from that residence nor sees its owners must not make use of his own robes or other requisites;
however, he may have a permanent dwelling, a shrine, or a lotus pond constructed.
If, after a long period of time, the owner returns, [he should say]: "Lay follower, this was made with your property."
He should be told, "Please give your consent. If he consents, that is well;
if he does not consent, but merely urges, "Give me my wealth," then one must obtain another person's consent and give it.
In such passages as "he takes what is considered a treasure with trust," it is said specifically with reference to what is touched (*āmāsa*); it does not apply to what is untouched (*anāmāsa*).

It is indeed permissible. The rest here is self-evident. It has six origins: it is an action (kiriya), not associated with perception or liberation (nosaññāvimokkha), without consciousness (acittaka), an offense by formal rule (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), three types of consciousness (ticitta), and three types of feeling (tivedana).
This is the second training rule on gems (Ratana-sikkhāpada).
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Entering a Village at an Improper Time 508.
Regarding the third [rule]: "Idle talk" (*tiracchānakathā*) means talk that is like a by-path to the Noble Path. "Talk about kings" (*rājakathā*) means talk connected with kings.

The same principle applies to talk about thieves and so forth. 512. Regarding the phrase "a bhikkhunī who is present": whatever needs to be said here has already been stated under the training rule concerning conduct (*cārittasikkhāpada*). If...
When a large number of people enter a village for some business, they must all ask one another for permission, saying, "I ask for permission to enter the village at an improper time.
If that business is not accomplished in that village and they go to another—be it even a hundred villages—there is no further need to ask for permission. However, if their enthusiasm subsides...
If those going to the monastery wish to enter another village along the way, they must again ask for permission.

Or, having finished their meal duties at a family home or in a dining hall, if one wishes to go out for alms of oil or ghee, one should go after asking permission if a monk is present; if there is none, it is not necessary.
One must go. If one descends to the street and sees a bhikkhu, there is no need to take leave;

one may simply proceed even without asking permission. If the road passes through the middle of a village, and while going along it the thought arises, "I shall go for alms such as oil," if there is a bhikkhu nearby, one should proceed only after taking leave. Without stepping off the path for alms...

However, for one who is traveling, there is no requirement to take leave; the precincts of an unenclosed village should be understood in the same manner as described under the offense of taking what is not given.

Regarding the terms "within a monastery" (*antarārāma*) and so forth, it is not only the case that one may go without asking permission, but also without having fastened the waistband or put on the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*).

There is no offense even for one who is walking [into the village]. "In cases of distress" means: if a lion or a tiger approaches, or if a storm arises, or if some other calamity occurs, there is no offense.
In such circumstances of distress, it is permissible to enter from outside the village into the village. The rest here is self-evident.

The Origin of the Kathina: It originates from body and speech, and from body, speech, and mind; it is functional and non-functional, not involving liberation through perception, without consciousness, an offense by formal rule, bodily action, verbal action, three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
The third training rule on entering a village at an improper time is concluded.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Needle Case.
517–20. Regarding the fourth [offense]: *bhedana* itself is *bhedanaka*; that which possesses this is *bhedanakameva*. *Araṇike* means on the fire-drill wood (*araṇidhanuka*).

*Vidhe* means on the piercing tool (*vedhaka*). The rest here is self-evident. It has six origins: it is a volitional act (*kiriya*), not accompanied by liberation through perception (*nosaññāvimokkha*), without consciousness (*acittaka*), an offense by rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), verbal action (*vacīkamma*), associated with three types of consciousness (*ticitta*), and associated with three types of feeling (*tivedanā*).
The fourth training rule concerning the needle-case.
5. Commentary on the fifth training rule concerning beds:
Regarding the fifth—“cutting down” is exactly as described by the method already stated.

525. Regarding the phrase "having cut it, he uses it": here, if he does not wish to cut it, he may bury it in the ground and show the measurement above, or he may use it after turning it face up, or he may lift it and place it on a balance-frame, making a mark, and then use it—all of this is permissible.
The rest here is self-evident. It originates from six origins (of offenses).
The fifth training rule concerning couches. 6.
Commentary on the sixth training rule concerning stuffed with cotton.

526. Regarding the sixth: "That which is stuffed with cotton here" is *tūlonaddha*; it means that after inserting cotton, it is covered on top with a piece of cloth. The rest here is self-evident. It has six origins.
The sixth training rule concerning what is sewn with cotton.
7. Commentary on the Seventh Training Rule Concerning the Sitting Mat (Nisīdana).
531–4. Regarding the seventh: "A sitting mat was permitted"—where was it permitted? It was permitted in the Chapter on Robes (Cīvarakkhandhaka) in connection with the matter of superior food.
For it is said there: “I allow you, monks, a sitting mat for the protection of the body, the protection of the robes, and the protection of the dwelling.
“Just like an old leather-worker”: the meaning is, as if he were an old tanner.
For just as a tanner, thinking “I will stretch out this hide,” rubs and pulls it here and there, so too—
He [prepared] that sitting cloth (*nisīdana*). Regarding it, the Blessed One spoke thus: “A ‘sitting cloth’ is said to be that which has a fringe (*sada*)”;
having spread it like a rug (*santhata*), one cuts two slits in one corner at a place measuring one span (*vidatthi*) by the Sugata’s measure, and three fringes (*dasā*) are made;
because of those fringes, it is called “with a fringe. The rest here is as follows:
This is self-evident. It has six origins.
The training rule on sitting mats is the seventh. 8.
Commentary on the Training Rule on the Itch-Covering Cloth.
537. Regarding the eighth [offense]: "The itch-covering cloth was permitted. Where was it permitted?

In the Cīvarakkhandhaka, in the section concerning Belaṭṭhasīsa. For it is said there: "Monks, I allow an itch-covering cloth for one who has an affliction such as an itch, a pustule, a discharge, or severe scabies."
539. “For one below the navel and above the kneecaps”: for that bhikkhu [below] the navel and [above] the kneecaps.
*Kaṇḍu* is itch. *Piḷakā* refers to small red pustules. *Assāva* is the oozing of impurity due to conditions such as fistula-in-ano, fistula-in-ano with discharge, or diabetes.
Or, "a disease of severe itch" refers to a disease consisting of large pustules. The rest here is as follows.
This is indeed clear. It has six origins.
The eighth training rule concerns the itch-covering cloth. 9.
Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Rainy-Season Robe.
542. Regarding the ninth [training rule]: "The rain-cloak was permitted"—where was it permitted? In the Chapter on Robes (Cīvarakkhandhaka), in the account concerning Visākhā.
For it is said there: "I allow you, monks, the rain-cloak. The rest here is self-evident. It has six origins.
This is the ninth training rule concerning the rain-cloak.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule of the Elder Nanda 547.
Regarding the tenth: "four-finger-breadth" means a measurement less than four finger-breadths. The rest is self-evident. It has six origins.
This is the tenth training rule, that of the Elder Nanda.
The ninth chapter on the Jewels (Ratana-vagga) is completed according to the sequence of the commentary.
The passage beginning with "Uddiṭṭhā kho" and so forth is exactly as previously stated.
[End of] the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The Commentary on the Minor Rules (Khuddakavaṇṇanā) is completed.
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa) is finished. 6. The Section on Offenses Entailing Confession (Pāṭidesanīyakaṇḍa).

1. Commentary on the First Rule of Confession (Pāṭidesanīya Sikkhāpada) The rules of confession (pāṭidesanīya-dhammā), which follow immediately after the minor rules (khuddaka), have now been established; here follows their commentary.

552. Regarding the first *pāṭidesanīya*: at the time of returning means at the time of returning after having wandered for alms. "He took them all" means he took everything. "Trembling" means shaking. "Go away" means depart. 553–5.
"It is blameworthy, friend," and so forth, is the demonstration of the manner in which it should be confessed. "A carriage road" (*rathikā*) means a street.
"A cul-de-sac" (*byūha*) means a street where people go back and forth without crossing through. "A crossroads" (*siṅghāṭaka*) means a place where roads meet, whether four-cornered or three-cornered.
“House” means a family home. For one who takes [food] while standing anywhere among these, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at the time of taking;
for each swallow, there is an offense entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*). The same rule applies to one who takes [food] from elephant stables and so forth.
If a nun stands on a carriage road and gives [the food], and the monk takes it even while standing inside a monastery or similar place, there is indeed an offense.
Regarding the statement, “having entered among the houses,” the offense here should be understood as occurring by way of the nun giving while standing within the inhabited area (*antaraghara*);
however, the location where the monk stands is not a determining factor.
Therefore, even if a monk standing on a street or similar place receives from a nun who is standing within a monastery or similar area and giving, there is no offense at all.

If one accepts for the purpose of food that which is to be consumed within a watch of the day, that which is to be consumed within seven days, or that which is to be consumed for life, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
"For every swallow, there is an offense of wrong-doing"—this was said with reference to [medicine] unmixed with solid food;
however, if it is mixed, when it has become of a single flavor, it is indeed an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya). "By one fully ordained together" means in the presence of the nuns.
For one who has received full ordination. However, for one who has received full ordination in the presence of the bhikkhus, it is exactly as in the original case.
556. "Causes to give but does not give herself" means that if she causes an unrelated woman to give by means of someone else, there is no offense for the one who receives it.

"Gives after having set it aside" means that having placed it on the ground, she gives it saying, "Venerable sir, this is for you"; regarding what is given in this manner, [he says] "Excellent, sister."
Having accepted it, it is permissible to eat it either by that very nun herself or by having someone else accept it on her behalf.
Regarding "a trainee nun (sikkhamānā) or a novice nun (sāmaṇerī)": there is no offense for one who accepts [the gift] from those giving to these two. The rest here is self-evident.

This offense originates from wool; it is an action, not involving liberation through perception, without mental intention, a fault of formal rule, bodily action, consisting of three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
The First Pāṭidesanīya. 2.
Commentary on the Second Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 558.
Regarding the second: “Withdraw for a moment, sister,” and so forth, is a demonstration of the manner in which she should be dismissed.
561. Regarding "she causes her own meal to be given [to others] but does not give it herself":

even if she gives her own meal herself, there is no offense under this training rule (*sikkhāpada*), but there is an offense under the preceding training rule. Regarding "she gives the meal of others but does not cause it to be given":

even if she were to cause it to be given, there would be an offense under this training rule. However, for one who gives [it herself], there is neither an offense under this [rule] nor under the preceding one.
This is an offense. The rest here is self-evident. As for the origin of the *kaṭhina*:

it is a functional-non-functional [action], not involving perception or liberation, mindless, an offense by rule, bodily action, verbal action, associated with three types of consciousness, and associated with three types of feeling.
This is the second *pāṭidesanīya*.
3. Commentary on the Third Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule 562.
Regarding the third [rule]: *ubhatopasannaṃ* means "confident in both," that is, confident in both the layman (*upāsaka*) and the laywoman (*upāsikā*).

It is said that in that family, both of them were indeed stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*). *Bhogena hāyati* means "it declines in wealth"; for even if such a family possesses eighty million pieces of gold—
It exists, yet it surely diminishes in wealth. Why? Because there, neither the female lay follower nor the male lay follower protects the wealth.
569. "Giving after bringing out from the house" means they bring it to the sitting hall or the monastery and give it.
Even if they first bring it out and place it at the gate before a monk has arrived, and then give it to him once he has reached it, it is permissible.
However, the *Mahāpaccarī* states that it is not permissible [to accept] food being given after seeing a bhikkhu and having it brought out from inside the house.

The rest here is self-evident. The origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) regarding wool is: an action (*kiriya*), not involving liberation through perception (*no-saññā-vimokkha*), without consciousness (*acittaka*), an offense by rule (*paṇṇatti-vajja*), bodily action (*kāya-kamma*), verbal action (*vacī-kamma*), three types of consciousness (*ticitta*), and three types of feeling (*tivedana*).
The Third Pāṭidesanīya. 4.
Commentary on the Fourth Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule. 570.
Regarding the fourth [rule]: "They are obstructed" means they are opposed.

573. “Having informed five” means that even if one has made an announcement to any of the five fellow practitioners, thinking, “I will send for some fresh or cooked food,” it is as if no announcement were made at all.
“Excluding the monastery and its precincts” means excluding both the forest dwelling (āraññaka-senāsana) and its precincts; from the precincts...

It should be understood that even if one has informed [the monastery] after seeing a monk on the road as he departs, or after he has arrived at the village, it is as if no information was given at all.
As for the instruction, "If there is danger, it should be declared as such," why must it be declared?
It is for the purpose of avoiding the reproach: "They do not tell us when bandits are living in the monastery."
Why should it be said that "thieves are people who frequent this place"? It is for the purpose of avoiding the statement, "They have us seized by their own attendants.
When rice-gruel has been announced, its accompaniment is brought; having thus announced the rice-gruel, [one asks] "What?"

Thinking, “When pure rice gruel has been given, we shall give even cakes, meals, and so forth as an accompaniment to this gruel,” whatever they bring is all done with full awareness (*paṭisaṃvidita*). The same method applies to the phrases “with food done with full awareness” and so on. [The phrase] “having made such-and-such a family known, he goes taking hard foods and so forth” means: The meaning is that when a donor intends to give food, thinking, “I will give this to the Saṅgha,” and the Saṅgha, having received it, distributes it among the monks, or when a donor intends to give medicine, thinking, “I will give this to the Saṅgha,” and the Saṅgha, having received it, distributes it among the monks, or when a donor intends to give a robe, thinking, “I will give this to the Saṅgha,” and the Saṅgha, having received it, distributes it among the monks—this is called “making the family known.
Having heard [the announcement], it is permissible for others to bring their own gifts of merit along with him.
It is stated in the *Kurundi* that if they bring either cakes or cooked rice after having made a formal acknowledgment (*paṭisaṃvidita*) regarding the rice-gruel, this too is permissible. 575.
"For one who is ill": there is no offense even if it has not been formally acknowledged for one who is ill; or, if it has been formally acknowledged for the one who is ill...
Or "the remainder" (*sesaka*): if food has been brought after making a formal announcement for the sake of one person, it is permissible for others to eat that remainder.

If much food has been brought after making a formal announcement for four or five people, and they wish to give some to others as well, this too is simply the remainder of what was announced, and it is permissible for everyone. Now, if there is even more...
It is permissible even on the second day for that which was set aside after releasing the storage restriction. The same rule applies to what remains from what was brought for one who is ill.

However, as for that which was brought without having been announced at all, it should be sent outside the monastery to have it announced before being brought back, or the monks should go and take it on the way. Also, [as for that which was brought] through the middle of the monastery...
Or, if forest-dwellers and the like bring [food] from the forest and give it, one must have it made known in the same manner as before.

"Grown there" means grown right within the monastery itself; there is no offense for one who consumes roots, edible fruits, and so forth, if they have been made permissible (*kappiya*) by another and given.
However, if they carry that [food] to the village, cook it, and then bring it back, it is not permitted.
It must be made known [to the Sangha]. The rest here is self-evident.

The origin of the *Kathina* rule: it is an action/non-action, not associated with perception or liberation, without mental concomitants, an offense by formal rule, bodily action and verbal action, involving three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
This is the fourth *Pāṭidesanīya*.
The explanation of the Pāṭidesanīya rules in the *Samantapāsādikā*,
the commentary on the Vinaya, is finished.
The Section on the Pāṭidesanīyas is completed.
7. The Section on Training (Sekhiyakaṇḍa) 1. Explanation of the Chapter on Being All-Round (Parimaṇḍalavagga):
Those training rules which have been studied by one who has trained himself, such a person as that [should practice them].
These have now been spoken; this is the sequence for their commentary.
(576) In that context, *parimaṇḍala* means circular all around.
"The navel-circle and the knee-circle" refers to one who covers from the navel-circle above down to the knee-circle below, [ensuring] that below the knee-circle, from the shin-bone...
It has been stated that one should put on the lower robe after letting it down only eight finger-breadths from the waist;
for anyone who lets it down further than that, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Furthermore, as it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that when sitting, a space of four finger-breadths below the kneecaps remains covered, so too, for one putting on the lower robe in this manner, the robe must be of the proper measure.
In this regard, the measurement is as follows: five fist-lengths in length and two and a half cubits in width.
However, if such [a robe] is not obtained, even a measurement of two cubits in width is permissible for the purpose of covering the kneecaps;
for it is possible to cover the navel even with a robe of that size. In that case, even a single-layered robe, when worn in this manner, covers the area where it should be worn.
"It does not stay; rather, it stays doubled over.

Regarding the rule, "If one wears the lower robe hanging down, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," here it is not only for one who wears it hanging down both in front and behind that there is a *dukkaṭa*;
however, as for others, [it says]: "Now at that time, the group-of-six monks were wearing the dress of householders..."

The faults regarding the wearing of the lower robe (*nivāsana*) have been stated in the Khandhaka in such a manner as: "They wear it like an elephant’s trunk, like a fish’s tail, like a four-cornered cloth, like a palm-leaf fan, or like a hundred-fold fold.
For one who wears it in those ways, there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
None of these faults apply to one who wears it evenly all around in the manner already described. This is the summary here; however, the details will be made clear in that very same place.

"Unintentionally" means: it is no offense for one who, not intending to hang [the robe] in front or behind while putting it on, thinking instead, "I shall put it on perfectly circular," puts it on in a non-circular manner due to a lapse of attention. "Out of forgetfulness" means:

there is no offense for one who puts it on in that way because his mind is preoccupied with something else. "Not knowing" refers here to one who does not know the proper procedure for wearing the lower robe (*nivāsana-vatta*).
There is no offense. For the practice of wearing the lower robe must be properly learned; failing to learn it constitutes disrespect.

However, this applies to one who intentionally neglects it; therefore, there is no offense for one who, even though they have learned the practice, does not know whether they have put it on correctly or incorrectly. But according to the *Kurundi*, "to wear it all around..."
"There is no offense for one who does not know," it is said.

However, for one who has dry shanks or whose calves are large and fleshy, it is permissible to lower [the robe] even more than eight finger-breadths below the kneecaps in order to achieve a proper appearance.
"For one who is ill" means that if there is a wound on the shank or the foot, it is permissible to put it on after either raising or lowering it.
"In times of distress" means that wild beasts or thieves are pursuing one; in such circumstances of distress, there is no offense.

The rest here is self-evident. The origin of the first *pārājika* is: an action, liberation through perception, with consciousness, a worldly offense, bodily action, unwholesome consciousness, and painful feeling.
The Elder Phussadeva says: "Without consciousness, an offense by rule, and threefold feeling."

He said: But because it was stated [in the Vinaya] that "it is dependent on disrespect," the Elder Upatissa said: "It is a worldly offense (*lokavajja*), an unwholesome state of mind (*akusalacitta*), and a feeling of suffering (*dukkhavedanā*). 577.
Regarding the instruction "one should wear the robe all around": at that time, the group of six monks (*chabbaggiyā bhikkhū*) wore the robes like householders (*gihipāruta*).

Having avoided the various kinds of lay dress mentioned in the phrase “wearing [it] on,” one should wear it all around, making both corners even, fulfilling the duty of wearing [the robe] according to the method stated here.
And these two training rules are stated without distinction; therefore, whether in the monastery or in the village, it must be worn all around.

"It must be worn as an undergarment and it must be used as an upper robe. The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other details are to be understood according to the method explained in the first training rule, together with the Elder’s tradition (*theravāda*).
"Having uncovered the body" means having uncovered even the navel or the chest. "Well-covered" means not covered [only] up to the head.

Then, having fastened the neck-tie, having covered the neck with the cloth against the wind, having brought both ears level and tucked them in, and having covered [the body] down to the wrists, one should walk within an inhabited area. In the second training rule:
starting from the nape of the neck, the head; starting from the wrists, the hands; and starting from the flesh of the calves...
One should sit with the feet uncovered.
579. "Having approached for the purpose of staying" means that there is no offense for one who sits with the body uncovered, whether during the night or the day.
580. "Well-restrained" means not playing with the hands or feet; the meaning is "well-behaved."
582. "With downcast eyes" means having the eyes cast downward. "Looking only a yoke's length ahead":
for a well-trained, noble steed looks only a yoke's length ahead—that is, at a portion of ground measuring four cubits in front;
one should walk looking only this much. "Whoever, out of disrespect, looks here and there" refers to one who looks toward various directions.
If he walks looking at a palace, a gabled chamber, or a street, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
However, it is permissible to stand in one place and look for the absence of dangers such as elephants or horses. One who sits must also sit with eyes cast down. 584. *Ukkhittakāya*:
by means of lifting; this is an instrumental expression used in the sense of a characteristic state (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇa*), whether on one side or on both sides.
"Or having lifted up the robe" means that one should not walk in such a manner starting from within the boundary markers (indakhīla).
However, when sitting, even while taking out the spittoon, one must take it out without lifting up the robe.
This is the first section.
2. Commentary on the Chapter on Loud Laughter (Ujjagghikavagga) 586.
*Ujjagghikāya*: laughing with a loud laugh. Here, the instrumental case is used according to the method already stated.
588. *Appasaddo antaraghare*: "making little noise within an inhabited area. To what extent is one considered to be making little noise? Within a house measuring twelve cubits, at the beginning...
When they are seated thus—the senior of the Saṅgha in the middle, the second senior at one side, and the third senior at the other end—the senior of the Saṅgha consults with the second senior;
the second senior hears both his voice and discerns the meaning of what is said.
But the third senior hears only the sound and does not discern the meaning. At this point, there is little noise.
If, however, the third elder defines [the object], there is a great noise. 590.
"Having exerted the body" means having made it motionless; one should walk and sit with an upright body and an even posture. 592.
"Having exerted the arm" means having made it motionless.
594. "Having held the head up" means having placed it straight and motionless.
The second chapter.
3. Explanation of the Chapter on the Hands on the Hips.
596–8. “Leaning on a staff” (*khambhakata*) means having performed a lean by placing the hand on the hip. “Veiled” (*oguṇṭhita*) means having covered [the head] including the head itself.

600. Regarding “squatting” (*ukkuṭikāya*): here, “squatting” refers to walking while lifting the heels and touching the ground with the tips of the feet, or lifting the tips of the feet and touching the ground with the heels. The word expressing the instrument (*karaṇa*) here has the very characteristic already stated.
601. Regarding "with the cloth draped": here, even the *āyoga*-draping is indeed a "cloth-draping. 602.
"Carefully" means having established mindfulness (*sati*). 603.
"Even while [food] is being poured out" means even while the alms-food is being given; "perceiving the bowl" means having formed the recognition that it is a bowl.

604. "With equal curry" (*samasūpaka*) means that where the curry is one-fourth the measure of the cooked rice. Regarding "mung bean curry" (*muggasūpa*) and "black gram curry" (*māsasūpa*), it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that curries made from peas (*kulattha*) and so forth are also included here.

Regarding "various flavors" (*rasarasa*), with the exception of the two types of curry, the remaining items—such as *oloni* greens, vegetable soups, lentil soup, meat broth, and so forth—are what is meant by "various flavors."
These things should be understood. There is no offense for one who takes even a great deal of that flavorful [food].

605. "Level-full" means equally full, equally filled. Regarding the statement, "If he receives almsfood piled up like a stupa, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," here "piled up" means having exceeded the rim-line inside the mouth of the bowl.
“Made” means placed in the bowl, prepared, or filled. Without taking it as being thus made, it should be understood as having a measure equal to the rim-line inside the mouth [of the bowl].
Regarding that, the Elder Abhaya said: “‘Heaped up’ means made with the five kinds of soft food. However, the Elder Cūḷanāga, the Tripitaka Master, said:
“Almsfood (piṇḍapāta) includes rice gruel, boiled rice, hard food, a lump of powder, a tooth-stick, and even a thread for wiping the mouth.”
Having spoken this sutta, he said that even a mere thread of cloth (*dasikasutta*) offered as a stupa-ornament (*thūpīkata*) is not permissible.
Hearing their argument, the monks went to Rohaṇa and asked the Elder Cūḷasumana: "Venerable sir, by what authority is alms-food offered as a stupa-ornament prohibited?
They then related the dispute to the elders. Having heard it, the elder said: "Alas! Cūḷanāga has fallen away from the Teaching."
“I have been teaching him the Vinaya for seven years and never spoke thus; from whom did he receive this that he speaks in such a way?
The monks requested the Elder, “Please tell us now, venerable sir, by what has it been determined?
“By the *yāvakālika* (food allowable at the proper time), friends,” the Elder replied. Therefore, whatever constitutes edible food, whether rice-gruel, boiled rice, or various fruits—
It should be taken up exactly level with the rim. This applies only to a bowl that has been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhānupaga*); for any other, even a bowl heaped up like a stupa is permissible.
However, for food to be kept until the watch of the night, for seven days, or for life-long use, these are permissible even when heaped up in a bowl that has been formally determined.
It is also permissible to take food in two bowls, fill one of them, and send it to the monastery.
In the *Mahāpaccarī*, however, it is stated: "Whatever cakes, sugar-cane pieces, fruits, and so forth, when being placed into the bowl, fall back down, that is not called 'heaped up' (*thūpīkata*).
If they give almsfood after setting aside a cake-ornament (*pūvavaṭaṃsaka*), it is indeed 'heaped up.
But if it is given after setting aside flower-ornaments, *takkolaka*-berries, bitter fruits, and so forth as ornaments..."
It is not "heaped up" (thūpīkataṃ). If one takes food after placing a bowl or a plate on top [of the almsbowl] and filling it, it is not called "heaped up.
It is also stated in the *Kurundi*: "If they place it in a dish or on a leaf and set that upon the mouth of the bowl, a separate vessel is permissible."
In this case, there is no offense because the sick person did not come; therefore, even for one who is sick, it is not permissible to treat [the food] as a heap.
However, in all instances, it is not permissible to accept it at all. But once accepted, it is indeed properly accepted, and it is permissible to consume it.
Thus ends the third section.

4. Commentary on the Chapter on Respectful Conduct (Sakkaccavagga) 606. Regarding the term *sakkaccaṃ* (respectfully): here too, the offense occurs only at the moment of receiving [the food] disrespectfully; once it has been received, however, it is indeed properly received. Both terms—*sakkaccaṃ* and *pattasaññī* (perceiving it as being in the bowl)—are to be understood according to the method already explained.

608. Regarding *sapadānaṃ* (in regular succession): this means without skipping from place to place, but rather following the proper sequence. What should be said concerning *samasūpakaṃ* (equal curry) has already been stated.
610. *Thūpakato* means from the top; the meaning is "from the middle. 611.
*Paṭicchādetvā dentī* means they give after having concealed the condiment during times such as the Magha festival. There is nothing further to be said regarding the act of solicitation (*viññatti*).
614. Even in the training rule concerning the perception of fault (*ujjhānasaññī-sikkhāpada*), one who is ill is not exempt.

615. "Not too large" means that the peacock's egg is too large and the hen's egg is too small; [the proper size] is the measure between those two. "Chewable food" (khajjaka): here, everything including root-vegetables and so forth is to be understood.
The fourth chapter. 5. Commentary on the Chapter on Mouthfuls (Kabaḷavagga).
617. *Anāhaṭe* means not brought forward; the meaning is that it has not been conveyed to the door of the mouth.
618. *Sabbaṃ hatthaṃ* means the entire hand. 619. Regarding *sakabaḷena*:

here, when preaching the Dhamma, one may speak after placing a myrobalan fruit (*harītaka*) or licorice root (*laṭṭhimadhuka*) in the mouth. It is permissible to speak as long as there is something in the mouth provided that the speech does not become incomplete.
620. *Piṇḍukkhepakaṃ*: tossing up morsels again and again.
621. *Kabaḷāvacchedakaṃ*: cutting off mouthfuls again and again.
622. *Avagaṇḍakārakaṃ*: making cheek-puffs like a monkey.
623. *Hatthaniddhunakaṃ* means repeatedly shaking the hand.
624. *Sitthāvakārakaṃ* means repeatedly scattering grains of rice.
625. *Jivhānicchārakaṃ* means repeatedly protruding the tongue.
626. *Capucapukārakaṃ* means making the sound *capu capū* repeatedly.
The fifth chapter.
6. Explanation of the *Surusuru* Chapter.
“Making the sound *surusuru*”: this means making the sound *surusuru* repeatedly. “*Davo*” is a term for mockery;

it refers to the Three Jewels by way of some such method as: “What a Buddha! A stone Buddha, a half-witted Buddha! What a Dhamma! A cow-Dhamma, a foolish Dhamma! What a Saṅgha! A herd of deer, a herd of cattle! and so forth.
The meaning is that it must not be done.
628. *Hatthanillehakaṃ*: having licked the hand repeatedly. For one who is eating, it is not even permitted to lick [the food] as much as a finger’s breadth.
However, in the case of thick gruel, molasses, milk-rice, and so forth, [one may lick] after taking [the food] with the fingers; the fingers—
It is permissible to eat after having placed [the food] in the mouth. The same principle applies to licking the bowl or licking the lips.
Therefore, one must not lick the bowl even with a single finger, nor should one lick even a single lip with the tongue;
however, it is permissible to take hold of the flesh of the lip itself and place it inside [the mouth].
631. *Kokanada*: thus it is named. *Kokanada* refers to a lotus; that palace was shaped like a lotus, and therefore they gave it the name *Kokanada*.
"With a hand that is not impure [with food], [one should take] a water-pot"—this is rejected on account of its repulsiveness.
Therefore, whether it belongs to the Saṅgha, to an individual, to a householder, or to oneself—even if it is a conch—[it should be taken].
