Neither a saucer nor a bowl must be taken up at all; for one who takes them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
However, if a portion of the hand is not smeared with food, it is permissible to take hold of it by that part. 632.
"Having scooped out" means having removed the rice grains from the water and made them into a heap in one place, [and then taking] the water...
"He discards it. Or, "having broken it up," means having broken up the rice balls and made them into liquid consistency, he discards it.
"In a receptacle" means that while receiving it with a bowl, he discards it in the bowl. "Having carried it out" means having carried it outside, he discards it;
for one who discards it in this manner, there is no offense.
634. “A white umbrella” (*setacchatta*) refers to a pale-white umbrella covered with cloth. “A palm-leaf umbrella” (*kilañjacchatța*) refers to an umbrella made of *vilīva* grass.
“A leaf umbrella” (*paṇṇacchatța*) refers to one made from any kind of leaves, such as palmyra leaves and so forth.
“Circularly bound” and “bound with strips” are stated for the purpose of showing the framework (*pañjara*) common to all three types of umbrellas; for they are indeed circularly bound.
And there are those [umbrellas] bound with tickets. Furthermore, even that which is made by means of a frame of leaves born there, having a single-leafed canopy, is indeed an umbrella.
One who has any such umbrella in his hand is "umbrella-in-hand" (*chattapāṇi*).
While he is holding that umbrella, or carrying it on his shoulder, or placing it on his thigh, as long as it is not released from his hand, for that long—
It is not permissible to teach the Dhamma [to one holding a sunshade]; for one who teaches it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) according to the method already stated.

However, if another person holds the sunshade for him, or if he is standing on a sunshade-stand, as soon as the sunshade is removed from his hand, he is no longer considered "one with a sunshade in hand" (*chattapāṇi*).

It is permissible to teach the Dhamma to such a person. Furthermore, the section concerning the Dhamma here should be understood according to the same method stated under the training rule regarding the recitation of the Dhamma (*padasodhamma*).

635. Regarding the phrase *daṇḍapāṇissa*: here, a "staff" (*daṇḍa*) is defined as one measuring four cubits for a man of medium height; however, the state of being "staff-in-hand" (*daṇḍapāṇibhāva*) should be understood in the same manner as that explained for "umbrella-in-hand" (*chattapāṇi*).
636. The same principle applies to "sword-in-hand" (*satthapāṇi*). For even one who stands with a sword girded on does not come under the designation of "sword-in-hand.
637. Regarding "weapon-in-hand" (*āvudhapāṇi*): although it is stated here that "a weapon (*āvudha*) is called a bow (*cāpa*) or a slingshot (*kodaṇḍa*)," nevertheless...
All varieties of bows, together with varieties of arrows, should be understood as "weapons.

Therefore, it is not permitted to teach the Dhamma to one who stands or sits while holding a bow together with an arrow, or a bare bow, or a bare arrow, or a strung bow, or an unstrung bow. However, if his bow is even around his neck...
"It is tied on; as long as one has not yet grasped it with the hand, it is indeed permissible to teach the Dhamma.
The sixth chapter.
7. Explanation of the Chapter on Sandals (Pāduka-vagga).
638. "Having stepped upon" means having stood having stepped on the sandals themselves without inserting even a finger's breadth between the toes and the ends of the umbrella-staff.
"Having put them on" means having stood after putting them on. The same rule applies to shoes (*upāhanā*) as well.
Here, however, "having taken them off" refers to one who has stood after removing the sandals that are fastened at the heel.

640. Regarding the phrase "one who has gone by vehicle": here, even if one is being carried by two people using their joined hands, or is being carried on a bamboo pole after being placed upon a cloth, or is seated on an unsuitable vehicle such as a palanquin, or even if one is seated on a mere wheel that has been set aside, one is reckoned as "one who has gone by vehicle.
However, if both [the giver and the recipient] are seated in the same vehicle, it is permissible.
Even when sitting separately, it is permissible for one seated in a higher vehicle to teach one seated in a lower vehicle; it is also permissible when both are of equal status.
It is permissible for one seated in a front vehicle to teach one seated in a rear vehicle. However, it is not permissible for one seated in a rear vehicle—even if that vehicle is higher—to teach.

"641. To one who has gone to bed": even if [the listener] is lying on a mere straw mat or on the natural ground, it is not permitted for [the teacher], standing or sitting on a high couch or chair or on a spot of ground, to teach [him].
However, it is permitted for one who has gone to bed to teach another who has gone to bed while lying down on a higher level or on an equal level.
And likewise, [it is not permitted] for one lying down to teach one who is standing or sitting.
It is permissible [to teach] while standing to one who is sitting, or while sitting to one who is standing or sitting. It is permissible for one who is standing to teach only to one who is standing.

642. "In the cross-legged posture": it is not permissible to teach one who is not ill and is sitting in any kind of cross-legged posture—whether the *āyoga*-crossed posture, the hand-crossed posture, the cloth-crossed posture, or any other cross-legged posture.
643. "To one whose head is wrapped": to one whose head is wrapped such that the hairline is not visible, either by wrapping it with cloth or with a turban (*moḷi*) and so forth.
644. “Oguṇṭhitasīsassā” means one who has covered his head.
645. “Nisinnenā chamāyaṃ” means by one sitting on the ground. “Āsane nisinnassa” means by one sitting even on a seat made by spreading out cloth or grass.
647. “Chapakassā” means of a caṇḍāla. “Chapakī” means a caṇḍālī woman. “Nilīno” means having concealed himself. Where...
"Indeed, he who is named 'Hi nāma'— thinking, 'Since all this has been made into a final end,
it shall fall right there,' and having uttered these words, 'This entire world has fallen into confusion and is without boundaries,' he fell from the tree right there between those two.
Having fallen, he stood before both of them and recited this verse:"
“Both do not know the meaning... [etc. ...we shall split him like a jar.
In this context, “both do not know the meaning” means that both persons do not know the meaning of the text (*pāḷi*). “They do not see the Dhamma” means they do not see the text. Who are these two?
“The one who recites the mantra and the one who studies it by unlawful means.”
Thus he established both the brahmin and the king in a state of unrighteousness.
Then the brahmin recited the verse beginning with "The rice...". Its meaning is as follows: "O sir, I know that 'this is unrighteous';
nevertheless, for a long time, together with my sons, wife, and attendants, I have eaten the cooked rice belonging to the king."
"Sucimaṃsūpasecano" means one for whom there is a mixing of pure meat as a condiment, prepared from various kinds of transformations;
thus he is "sucimaṃsūpasecano. Therefore, regarding the phrase "tasmā dhamme na vattāmi":
because I have eaten the king’s rice in this way and obtained many other gains, therefore I do not abide in the Dhamma, being bound by my belly; I do not [practice] the Dhamma.
"Unaware. For I know that this Dhamma is praised, extolled, and lauded by the Noble Ones.
Then Chapaka addressed him with two verses beginning with "Fie upon it! The meaning of these is as follows:
"O Brahmin, fie upon that acquisition of wealth and acquisition of fame which you have obtained."
Why? Because this gain obtained by you is a livelihood through unrighteous conduct both now and, in the future, by way of being a cause for falling into the states of misery.
What is the use of such a livelihood as results in falling into the states of misery in the future, or through unrighteous conduct in this present life? Therefore it was said:
“Fie on that gain of wealth, O brahmin, and fie on that gain of fame, if one’s livelihood comes about through falling into ruin or through practicing unrighteousness!
“Go forth, Great Brahmā!”—O Great Brahmin, flee swiftly from this direction! “And others too who cook living beings.”
Other beings also cook and eat; it is not you alone and the king.

Do not think, "An unrighteous act committed by me will not strike back like a pot [against a stone]," for if you do not renounce this life and continue to practice such unrighteousness, then that very unrighteousness, being thus practiced, will shatter you just as a stone might break a water-pot; it will destroy you in that way.
Therefore we say this to you:
“Wander forth, Great Brahmā, even while other beings are cooking;
do not practice unrighteousness, lest you shatter us like a pot.”
"From a high seat": it is not permissible to teach one who is seated on a raised place, even if it is merely a spot of ground that is elevated.

648. "One standing [should not teach] one sitting": even if a junior bhikkhu has gone to attend upon an elder and is standing, and the great elder, seated on his seat, asks a question, he should not speak. However, out of respect, the junior bhikkhu should rise for the elder.
It is not permissible to say, "Ask [me]," but it is permissible to say, "I am speaking to the bhikkhu standing nearby.
Regarding the phrase "not by one walking behind": if a person walking in front asks a question of one walking behind, the latter should not speak.
It is permissible to say, "I am speaking to the bhikkhu behind me. Together with...
However, it is permissible to recite the Dhamma one has already mastered. It is permissible to speak [the Dhamma] to one who is traveling at the same pace. 650. Regarding "not on a by-path":
here too, if both are traveling at the same pace on a cart-track, whether each is on a single wheel-track or on a by-path, it is permissible.
651. Regarding "unintentionally": if, while going to a concealed place, excrement or urine is discharged suddenly, it is called an act done unintentionally; there is no offense.
652. Regarding the phrase "not on green [grass]," even if the root of a living tree visible in the earth moves, or a branch touching the ground moves, all of it is reckoned as "green.
It is permissible to sit on the trunk and drop [the excrement] in a place that is not green.
If one is looking only at the non-green area and suddenly steps out, it is permissible in the case of illness.

It is permissible if it remains as it was. "Made where there is no green growth" means that even if one makes it in a place where no green growth is available by placing a bundle of grass or a bundle of straw, and later green growth covers it over, it is still permissible.
Furthermore, it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that here "saliva" includes mucus as well.
653. The phrase "not water" is stated with reference specifically to water used for consumption;

however, there is no offense regarding water that is not for consumption, such as water in a latrine or in the ocean. When it rains from the sky and there is a flood of water on all sides, it is permissible to leave [the monastery] even while looking for a place free of water.
It is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*: "At such a time, [one may go to] a place free of water..."
“It is permissible for one who has not obtained [the requisite] to perform it. The remainder of all the training rules is already clear in meaning.
This is the seventh chapter.
However, here is this supplementary note for the purpose of illustrating their origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth: those connected with loud laughter and high-pitched voices...
There are four [offenses]: speaking with food in the mouth is one;

and those connected with sitting on the ground, sitting on a low seat, standing behind, and walking along a path are five—these ten training rules (sikkhāpada) originate from formal admonition (samanubhāsana). They arise from body, speech, and mind; they are actions (kiriyā);

they are released through perception (saññāvimokkha); they involve the mind (sacittaka); they are offenses against worldly convention (lokavajja); they consist of bodily and verbal action (kāyakamma-vacīkamma); they are unwholesome states of mind (akusalacitta); and they result in painful feeling (dukkhavedanā).
The training rule concerning the solicitation of rice and curry originates from theft and a caravan; it arises from body and mind, and from body, speech, and mind.
It is an action, liberated by perception, associated with consciousness, a worldly offense, bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome consciousness, and painful feeling.
The eleven training rules concerning one who holds a sunshade, a staff, a weapon, or a sword; one who wears sandals or shoes; one who uses a vehicle, a bed, or a reclining posture;
and one who is wrapped in a turban or covered with a veil—these originate from the teaching of the Dhamma.

They arise from speech and mind; they are both actions and non-actions; they are liberated by perception; they involve the presence of consciousness; they are offenses against the world; they are verbal actions; they are unwholesome states of mind; and they result in painful feeling.
The remaining fifty-three training rules originate from the first *pārājika*.

Among all the *sekhiya* rules, there is no offense on account of illness except for three training rules: [the rule regarding] alms-food placed in a heap, and [the rules regarding] covering curry or sauce with rice when one perceives it as a complaint; in these three, there is no sick person [as an exemption].
The commentary on the *sekhiyas* is finished.
The Section on the Training Rules is finished. 8.
The Seven Methods for Settling Legal Issues (Sattādhikaraṇasamatha). 655.
Regarding the methods for settling legal issues: “seven” is the numerical limit of those rules. They are fourfold.
They settle and resolve legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*); thus they are called "settlements of legal issues" (*adhikaraṇasamatha*).
Their detailed exposition is stated in the *Khandhaka* and the *Parivāra*; we shall explain their meaning right there. The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus ends the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The commentary on the Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga is finished.
Just as this commentary has been completed without obstacle,
may all living beings likewise attain peace without obstacle.
May the True Dhamma endure for long! May the rain fall in due season, and may it long satisfy the people!
May the deity nourish [them] according to the Dhamma, and may the king protect the earth!
The Mahāvibhaṅga is finished.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Analysis of the Bhikkhunī Rules 1.
The Section on Defeat (Pārājikakaṇḍa) [Commentary on the Analysis of the Bhikkhunī Rules]
The sequence for the commentary on the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga* follows immediately after that which was compiled for the *Bhikkhuvibhaṅga*.
Therefore, from this point onward, there shall be a word-by-word explanation of the previously unexplained terms.
This is the commentary on the *pārājika* rules. 1. Commentary on the First *Pārājika* Training Rule:

At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī... [pe] ...as for the passage beginning "Sāḷha, the grandson of Migāra": The commentary on the *pārājika* rules begins here. Regarding the first *pārājika* training rule:
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī... [pe] ...[the section concerning] Sāḷha, the grandson of Migāra. Herein:
*Sāḷha* is his name; however, he was the grandson of Migāra’s mother, which is why it is said, “Migāra’s grandson.
*Navakammika* means one who supervises new building work. *Paṇḍita* means endowed with wisdom (*paṇḍicca*). *Byatta* means endowed with proficiency (*veyyattika*).
*Medhāvinī* refers to one who possesses, in the grasping of the textual tradition (*pāḷi*), wisdom preceded by mindfulness, and in the grasping of the meaning (*attha*)...

Endowed with mindfulness preceded by wisdom (*paññā*). "Dexterous" (*dakkhā*) means skillful; the meaning is that she performs what must be done swiftly without faltering. "Unwearying" (*analasā*) means free from laziness.
"Appropriate to those [tasks]" (*tatrupāyāya*) means possessing the means for those various duties. "With inquiry" (*vīmaṃsāya*) means with the investigation of the tasks to be performed.
"Endowed with" (*samannāgatā*) means associated with [those qualities]. "Able to do" (*alaṃ kātuṃ*) means capable of performing this or that.
"To perform work" means to be capable of arranging it thus and thus, thinking, "Let this be done in such and such a way.

"To know what has been done and what has not been done" means to recognize both what is completed and what is unfinished. "Those two" refers to both of them; the meaning is that both Sundarīnandā and Sāḷha.
"At the mealtime" means at the place where food is distributed. "In the corner" means shown as having been made like a corner.
"In the deep [water]. "My cry will be shrill" means my voice will be distorted; it will be a sound of distress—this is the meaning.
"Looking back" means gazing after. "What am I? means "Who am I? "Weak with old age" means frail because of aging.
"Sick in foot" means afflicted by a disease of the feet.
657–8. *Avassutā* means "lustful" due to lust for physical contact; the meaning is "soaked" or "moistened.
In the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), however, taking that very lust as the basis, it is said "infatuated" (*sārattā*) and so forth.
Therein, *sārattā* means well-colored by the lust for physical contact, just as a cloth is colored by dye. *Apekkhavatī* [means] on account of that very lust...
She is possessed of longing directed toward that man. "With a mind bound" means her mind is, as it were, bound and fixed upon him by that lust.
This same method applies to the analysis of the second phrase as well.
"Of the male person" means of the person designated as a man. "Below the collarbones" means beneath the collarbones. "Above the kneecaps" means...
"Above the kneecaps. In the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), however, it is stated according to the sequence of the words as "below the collarbone and above the kneecaps.
Here, the "upper robe" (*ubbhakappara*) is also included within the "kneecaps" (*ubbhajāṇumaṇḍala*).

The remainder should be understood according to the method explained in the *Mahāvibhaṅga*. "Taking the former ones as a basis" refers to the four offenses involving defeat (*pārājika*) that are common to [all bhikkhunīs].

"Upādāya" means "depending upon. As for the term "ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā," this is merely the name of this *pārājika* offense; therefore, it has not been analyzed in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*). 659.

Having thus analyzed the prescribed training rule according to the sequence of its words, [the text now] addresses the classification of the offenses by way of the distinctions such as "one who is lustful" (*avassuta*) and so forth.
In order to demonstrate this, he said, "When both are lustful," and so forth.
Therein, "when both are lustful" (*ubhato-avassute*) means when there is a state of being lustful on the part of both the bhikkhunī and the man due to the passion for bodily contact.
"She touches body with body" means that the bhikkhunī, with her body as it has been defined, [touches] any part of the man's body, or the man, with any [part of his body].
If with the body one touches the body of a bhikkhunī as it was delimited, in either case it is a *pārājika* offense for the bhikkhunī.
"With the body, [touching] what is connected to the body" means, in the manner already described, with one's own body, [touching] what is connected to the body of a man.
Regarding "touches": here, whether one touches it oneself or consents to his touching it, it is a *thullaccaya* offense. [This applies to] what is connected to the body.
They call it "the body" because it is connected to the body of a man in the manner already described. Regarding the phrase "she touches":
here too, whether she herself touches him or consents to his touching her, there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).
The analysis for the remaining terms should be understood by this same method.
But if there is both a monk and a nun, and the nun touches him while the monk remains motionless yet consents with his mind,
the monk is not to be dealt with for an offense. If the monk touches her while the nun remains motionless and merely accepts it with her mind,
even though she does not move a limb of her body, she commits a *pārājika* offense in a case where a *pārājika* occurs.

In a case of a grave offense (thullaccaya), one should be dealt with according to a grave offense; in a case of an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), one should be dealt with according to an offense of wrong-doing.

Why? Because it is stated: "If she consents to physical contact. This is the explanation found in the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā). However, since the status of being originated by action (kiriya-samuṭṭhāna) is not seen [in that context], it should be understood that it was stated there according to the predominant method.

660. *Ubbhakkhakan* means above the collarbones. *Adhojāṇumaṇḍala* means below the kneecaps. And here, even what is below the navel is included by the term "below the kneecaps. 662. Regarding the phrase *ekatova assute*:
although it is stated here without distinction as "on one side," nevertheless, it should be understood that this classification of offenses applies only when the nun herself is lustful (*avassuta*).
Herein, the detailed analysis from the beginning is as follows: the nun is lustful through passion for physical contact, and the man also...
Likewise: when there is bodily contact with a part of the body below the collarbone and above the kneecaps, it is a *pārājika* offense for the nun.
Whether the nun has lust for bodily contact, while the man has lust for sexual intercourse, or affection rooted in the household life, or a pure mind—[in such cases] it is only a *thullaccaya*.
[But if] the nun has lust for sexual intercourse, while the man has lust for bodily contact...
Whether it be lust for sexual intercourse, affection based on domestic life, or a pure mind, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For a bhikkhunī, whether there is affection based on domestic life or any one of the four types mentioned regarding a man, it is likewise an offense of wrong-doing.
For a bhikkhunī with a pure mind, regardless of which of the four types mentioned regarding a man occurs, there is no offense.
If, however, there is both a monk and a nun, and both have lust for physical contact: for the monk it is a *saṅghādisesa*;
for the nun it is a *pārājika*. If the nun has lust for physical contact, while the monk has either lust for sexual intercourse or worldly affection:
for the nun it is a *thullaccaya*; for the monk it is a *dukkaṭa*. If both have either lust for sexual intercourse or worldly affection...
Or, for both, it is indeed a *dukkaṭa* offense. For whichever of the two has a pure mind regarding that [act], for him there is no offense regarding that.
If both have pure minds, there is no offense for either. 663.
Regarding "there is no offense if unintentional," etc.: if they touch [the body] by mistake, or if they are engaged in something else, thinking, "This is a man..."
There is no offense even if there is touching, provided she does not know [it is a man] or, even if touched by him, does not consent to that contact.
The remainder is clear in all respects.
The origin of the first *pārājika* is: an action, liberation through perception, with consciousness, a worldly offense, bodily action, unwholesome consciousness, and two feelings.
The First Pārājika. 2. Commentary on the Second Pārājika Training Rule (Sikkhāpada). 664. Regarding the second Pārājika: *Kacci no sā* means "Is it not she?

*Kacci nu sā* means "Could it be she? *Avaṇṇo* means a lack of virtue (*aguṇa*). *Akitti* means blame (*nindā*). *Ayaso* means failure of reputation (*parivāra-vipatti*); or it refers to censure in one's absence (*parammukha-garahā*).
665. “A concealer of a *vajja*”: this too is merely a name for this *pārājika* offense; therefore, it is not examined in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*).
The rest here is self-evident. 666. “Or she herself reports it”: she who has fallen into a *pārājika* offense reports it herself.
“One of the eight *pārājikas*” refers to one of the four shared with monks and the four that are unshared.
And this *pārājika* offense was formulated later; therefore, it is stated as "of eight" in the *Vibhaṅga*.

However, because it forms a pair with the preceding [offense], it should be understood that it is placed in this section. "As soon as the burden is laid down" means at the very moment the burden is laid down.
A detailed discussion on this point, however, is found in the *Sappāṇaka-vagga*, under the training rule concerning what is indecorous (*duṭṭhulla-sikkhāpada*).

It should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. For while there was a *pācittiya* offense in that case, here it is a *pārājika*; this alone is the distinction. The remainder is exactly the same.

Regarding the term "one who conceals a fault" (*vajjapaṭicchādikā*), this too is merely another name for this *pārājika* offense; therefore, it was not examined in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*).
The rest here is self-evident.

Originating from laying down the burden: it originates from body, speech, and mind; it is non-action (akiriya); it is liberation through perception (saññāvimokkha); it is associated with consciousness (sacittaka); it is a worldly offense (lokavajja); it is bodily action (kāyakamma) and verbal action (vacīkamma); it is unwholesome consciousness (akusalacitta);
it is painful feeling (dukkhavedanā). This concludes the second Pārājika. 3. Commentary on the Third Pārājika Training Rule (Sikkhāpada)
669. Regarding the third [case]: "By means of the Dhamma" means by means of the factual basis (*vatthu*). "By means of the Vinaya" means having accused and having reminded.

However, the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) was stated merely to show the underlying intention (*adhippāyamatta*) that "one who has been suspended by whatever Dhamma and whatever Vinaya is rightly suspended.
"By means of the Teacher’s instruction" refers to both the perfection of the motion (*ñatti-sampadā*) and the perfection of the proclamation (*anusāvana-sampadā*). [This is] in the word-commentary.
Regarding this, "by the teaching of the Victor" (*jinasāsana*) and "by the teaching of the Buddha" (*buddhasāsana*) are stated merely as synonyms.

As for the phrases "the Saṅgha or a group," etc.: he does not accept, does not follow, and does not show regard for that Saṅgha by which the formal act (*kamma*) was performed, nor for the group consisting of several individuals therein, nor for a single individual, nor for that formal act itself.
The meaning is "one who produces. "Companions" refers to monks who share the same communal life (*samānasaṃvāsaka*).

He does not have them with him; in this context, "communal life" (*saṃvāsa*) consists of: "the same formal act (*ekakamma*), the same recitation of the scriptures (*ekuddesa*), and the same training (*samasikkhatā*).

Those for whom the communal life is common are "those who share the same communal life" (*samānasaṃvāsaka*). Monks of such a kind are "companions" (*sahāya*) to a monk in that communal life by virtue of their state of traveling together.

They are called [bhikkhus]. Now, that communal life (*saṃvāsa*) by virtue of which they were said to be "of the same communion" (*samānasaṃvāsaka*) does not exist for that suspended person (*ukkhitaka*) with them.
And with those [bhikkhus] with whom he has no such communal life, he has not made those bhikkhus his own companions. Therefore it is said: "Bhikkhus of the same communion are called 'companions'."
"He has nothing in common with them; therefore, he is called 'one who has no companions'.
The remainder is of clear meaning because it follows the method already explained in the training rules concerning schism in the Saṅgha (*saṅghabhedasikkhāpada*) and others.

The origin of the offense through formal admonition (*samanubhāsanasamuṭṭhāna*): it originates from body, speech, and mind; it is non-action (*akiriya*); it is released by perception (*saññāvimokkha*); it involves consciousness (*sacittaka*); it is a worldly transgression (*lokavajja*); it is bodily action and verbal action; it is unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*); and it is associated with painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
The Third Pārājika.
4. Commentary on the Fourth Pārājika Training Rule. 675.
Regarding the fourth: “Lustful” (*avassutā*) means being lustful through the passion for physical contact, by way of worldly pleasure and intimacy with friends.

The same method applies to the second phrase as well. Regarding the expressions "taking hold of a man's hand" and so forth, that which is taken by a person with the hand is called "taking hold of a man's hand. The same method applies to "taking hold of the corner of the outer robe" (*saṅghāṭikaṇṇa*) as well.

Furthermore, in the phrase "taking hold of the hand," both "taking hold of the hand" and other forms of taking hold that do not fall within the scope of an offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*) are grouped together here.
It should be understood that this is stated as "having taken the hand. For this very reason, its word-commentary says:
"'Or he should consent to the taking of the hand'—'the hand' means from the elbow down to the fingertips;
if he consents to the grasping [of her] above the collarbone or below the knee for the purpose of engaging in unrighteous conduct, there is an offense of thullaccaya."
It has been stated. And here, "unrighteous conduct" (*asaddhamma*) should be understood as physical contact, not sexual intercourse.

For there is no grave offense (*thullaccaya*) for an act bordering on sexual intercourse. Furthermore, the statement, "a wise man capable of engaging in physical contact," is also a supporting proof in this context.
[As it is said: "Though he had three wives, he did not engage in sexual intercourse with them."
Three types of men and three types of ignoble paṇḍakas—
one should not engage in sexual intercourse with these at the organ;
there would be a cutting off [of the vow] on account of the act of sexual intercourse.
"This question was pondered by the wise.
If it is argued that this contradicts the *Sedamocaka-gāthā* spoken in the *Parivāra*, it is not so;

for it is a preliminary stage to sexual intercourse. Indeed, in the *Parivāra* itself it is said: "The preliminary stage of sexual intercourse is to be known," and thus "bodily contact [is] praise or blame..."

"Vulgar speech, serving one’s own desires, and procuring [sexual intercourse]"—thus, the five training rules beginning with the emission of semen are stated to be the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*) of sexual intercourse (*methunadhamma*). Therefore, bodily contact (*kāyasaṃsagga*) is a condition (*paccaya*) because it is a preliminary stage of sexual intercourse.
Thus, in the phrase "it may be a condition for sexual intercourse," this is the method [of interpretation].
The meaning is to be understood. By this same method, the analysis for all the phrases is to be understood.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "or she might go to a rendezvous," its word-commentary states: "She comes to such-and-such a place. The meaning is that she goes to a location bearing such a name. 676.
One who fulfills the eighth ground becomes a non-recluse (assamaṇī), whether in direct order or in reverse order, or by skipping intervals.
By whichever means she fulfills the eighth ground, she indeed becomes a non-recluse (*assamaṇī*).
However, she who fulfills even a hundred times one ground or seven grounds does not become a non-recluse; having confessed the offenses committed, she is released.
Furthermore, in this context, the offense should be understood as being subject to counting. For it has been said: "There is an offense that, once confessed..."
“An offense that has been confessed is not counted; an offense that has not been confessed is counted. Herein, this is the analysis:
if one makes an effort, thinking “I shall not commit it again,” and then confesses, that confession is counted and enters into the reckoning; it does not become a factor for a *pārājika*.
Therefore, if one who has committed one offense makes an effort, confesses, and then commits it again through the influence of the defilements, [it is counted].
If she confesses in this way, even though she has fulfilled eight grounds, she does not become one who has committed a *pārājika*.
However, if she has fallen into an offense and, while still intent on committing another ground, confesses with that same determination, her offense is not subject to counting;
although confessed, it remains unconfessed and does not enter into the count of confessions, as it remains a factor for a *pārājika*. This concerns the eighth ground.
When she has reached full maturity, she becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.

The remainder is self-evident. This is the origin by relinquishing the burden (*dhuranikkhepa-samuṭṭhāna*). It originates from body, speech, and mind; it is an action (*kiriya*); it is liberated through perception (*saññāvimokkha*); it involves consciousness (*sacittaka*); it is a transgression against worldly convention (*lokavajja*); it is bodily action and verbal action; it is an unwholesome state of mind (*akusalacitta*); and it is associated with two types of feeling (*dvivedana*). This is the fourth *pārājika*.

"Venerable ladies, the eight rules entailing defeat (pārājika) have been recited"—this refers to the four rules common [to both nuns and monks] prescribed with reference to monks, and these other four;
thus, by way of the method for reciting the Pātimokkha, the meaning here should be understood as: "Venerable ladies, the eight rules entailing defeat have been recited.
The remainder is exactly according to the method stated in the Mahāvibhaṅga.
The commentary on the section on the offenses involving defeat (*pārājika*) within the analysis of the nuns (*bhikkhunīvibhaṅga*) in the *Samantapāsādikā*,
the commentary on the Vinaya, is completed.
The section on the offenses involving defeat is finished.
2. The Section on Saṅghādisesa (Exegesis of the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga) 1.
Exegesis of the First Saṅghādisesa Training Rule Now, this [rule] shall follow immediately after the Pārājika rules.
Commentary on the Unelucidated Meaning of the *Saṅghādisesa* Section.

678. *Udositam* means a storehouse for goods. *Māyyo evaṃ avaca* means "Noble lady, do not speak thus. *Apināyyā* means "perhaps, Noble Lady? *Accāvadatha* means "speak beyond [the bounds]"; it is synonymous with "you revile. 679.
*Ussayavādikā* refers to those who dispute out of a sense of personal grievance (*mānussaya*) or out of a sense of anger (*kodhussaya*). For, in terms of its actual meaning...
She is one who engages in legal suits; therefore, it is said in the word-commentary: “One who engages in legal suits is called *ussayavādikā*.
And here, “legal suit” (*aḍḍa*) refers to a judicial decision, which those gone forth also call a “legal matter” (*adhikaraṇa*).
“Or she seeks a second [party]” means she seeks a witness or a companion; there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). “Or she goes” means...

Whether it be a monastery or a path for alms-round, wherever she stands and the thought arises, "I will initiate a lawsuit," then for every step she takes as she goes to the presence of the judges, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"She informs one" means that out of two people, anyone who informs the judges on behalf of either one. "She informs the second" follows the same principle here as well.
Now, here is the detailed explanation for the sake of clarity:
if, anywhere—even if it is merely at the nuns' quarters—a nun sees a legal officer and reports her own case, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the nun.
If a lay follower reports his own case, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) for the nun. First, the lay follower reports his own case...
For the nun, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If she then reports her own conversation [to another], it is a serious offense (*thullaccaya*).

If a nun says to a lay follower, "You yourself should report the conversation between me and you," whether he reports his own conversation first or that of the nun, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the first report and a serious offense for the second report. The lay follower...
If he says to a bhikkhunī, "Tell me your case and mine yourself," the same rule applies here as well.
If a bhikkhunī has a kappiyakāraka (a lay attendant) speak for her, then in that case either the kappiyakāraka may first report the bhikkhunī’s case,
or the other [the monk] his own, or the kappiyakāraka both theirs, or the other both theirs.
How should she report it? Whether she reports it correctly or incorrectly, at the first report the nun incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense;

at the second, a *thullaccaya*. However, whether it was reported correctly or incorrectly, once both sides have been heard and the judges have rendered their decision, that is called the "conclusion of the trial" (*aḍḍapariyosāna*). At the conclusion of that trial, even if the nun is victorious...

Even in the case of defeat, it is a *saṅghādisesa*. However, if the legal case has already reached its conclusion and has been previously heard by the judges, and those judges, upon seeing both the nun and the litigant, say, "There is no need for you to speak;
we know what has transpired here," and they themselves decide and deliver [the verdict], then even at the conclusion of such a lawsuit, there is no offense for the nun.

"First-offense" (*paṭhamāpattika*) means that the offense occurs for this person at the very first instance; the meaning is that it must be committed at the very moment of transgression. That is what is meant by "first-offense.

In the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), however, it is stated—"she commits it simultaneously with the misconduct regarding the matter (*vatthujjhācārā*)," without waiting for a formal admonition—in order to show the mere underlying intention (*adhippāyamatta*). This is the meaning here: simultaneously with the misconduct regarding the matter, whatever nun...
She does not incur it at the third formal admonition; this is called a "first offense" because it is incurred right from the beginning along with the transgression of the matter itself.
It is "entailing expulsion" (*nissāraṇīya*) because it causes one to be expelled from the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs; that which entails such expulsion is *nissāraṇīya*.
In the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), however, it is stated "she is expelled from the Saṅgha" merely to show the underlying intention. In that context, she who has incurred [the offense]...
The meaning should be understood as follows: "A bhikkhunī is expelled from the Saṅgha; therefore, it is called 'expulsion' (nissāraṇīya).
For that very rule (dhamma) is not expelled from the Saṅgha by anyone. Rather, by means of that rule, the bhikkhunī is expelled;
therefore, because it causes her to be expelled, it is "expulsion" (nissāraṇīya).
"She goes being dragged" means that she goes into the presence of the judges when she is summoned— either by the men conducting the lawsuit coming themselves,
or by their sending a messenger saying, "Come. Then, whether the litigant states his own case first or the nun does so,
there is no *dukkaṭa* for stating it first, nor is there a *thullaccaya* for stating it second.
Even when the case has been decided by the ministers and the conclusion of the trial has reached its midpoint, there is no offense. Even if the judge says to the nun,
"Speak for both myself and yourself," and she speaks, yet after hearing her words the judge reaches the conclusion of the trial,
there is still no offense.
"He asks for protection" means he asks for legitimate protection; there is no offense. Now, in order to show how the protection requested becomes legitimate, it says:
"He points out [the danger] without specifying. In this regard, concerning the past, there is pointing out with specification and there is pointing out without specification;
concerning the future as well, there is pointing out with specification and there is pointing out without specification.
How is there a specific declaration concerning the past?
Suppose in a bhikkhunī’s dwelling place, village boys, ruffians, or anyone else commits misconduct, cuts down trees, takes fruits and flowers, or seizes requisites.
Then a bhikkhunī approaches a legal official and says, "Such-and-such was done in our dwelling place."
She speaks. When asked, "By whom?", she specifies, "By so-and-so and by so-and-so. Thus, there is a specific disclosure concerning the past;
this is not permissible. If, having heard that, those judges impose a penalty upon them, the entire liability falls upon the nun.
Even if her intention is merely, "They will take the penalty," the liability still falls upon her alone. But if [she says], "If they impose a penalty upon him..."
If he says, "Take it," and five māsakas' worth is taken, it is a *pārājika* offense.
However, when asked, "By whom? one should say, "It is not permissible for us to say 'by so-and-so';
you yourselves will know that. We merely request protection; grant us that, and have the stolen goods brought back. Thus...
Pointing out [the goods] without specifying [the owner] is permissible.
If, after this has been said, those judges seek out the perpetrators and inflict punishment upon them, even if the entire property is taken by the nun, there is neither debt nor offense for her.
Furthermore, upon seeing them carrying away requisites, it is not even permissible to say "thief, thief" out of a desire to cause them harm.
Even when this has been said, whatever punishment they impose is entirely the responsibility of the nun.
However, it is permissible to say to one who obeys her own instructions, "He took these requisites from me; have him bring them back, and do not punish him.
If they engage in gambling for the sake of slaves, slave-girls, or similar things, this is called "unlawful gambling" (*akappiya-aḍḍa*) and is not permitted.

How is there a specific declaration concerning the future? In the same manner already described, when others have committed misconduct and so forth, a bhikkhunī says to the judges: "They are doing this and that in our dwelling place;
grant us protection so that they may not do it again in the future. And when it is asked, "By whom was this done?", she replies, "By such-and-such a person and by such-and-such a person."
He declares it. Thus, there is a specific declaration concerning the future; that too is not permissible.
For when punishment is imposed upon them, the entire responsibility falls on the nun, just as in the previous case. The rest is exactly the same as before.
However, if the judges [should declare]: "For those who commit such misconduct in the nuns' quarters, this is the punishment..."
Having had the drum beaten with the proclamation, "I shall do so," they seek out those who do not comply with the command and inflict punishment;
yet for the nun, there is neither liability nor offense.
This same principle applies to monks as well as to the rule stated for nuns; for even in the case of a nun, it refers specifically to intentional disclosure.

It is not permissible. Whatever penalty they impose when it has been thus described becomes the responsibility of the one who incited them. For one who causes a penalty to be taken according to the stated method, there is a *pārājika* offense.

However, if one speaks without specifying [the individuals], even though knowing that "they will impose a penalty," and they subsequently seek out those people and indeed impose the penalty, there is no fault. Regarding those cutting trees and so forth within the monastery boundary (*vihārasīma*):
It is not permissible to take axes, hatchets, and so forth, and pound them with stones.
If the edge becomes blunted, it should be made sharp again and then given back. It must not be done to run after them and seize their requisites;
for the mind changes rapidly, and once the intention to steal has arisen, one might even go to one's ruin. The rest is self-evident.

The origin of the *Kathina* [offense]: it is an act (*kiriya*), not associated with liberation through perception (*no-saññā-vimokkha*), without consciousness (*acittaka*), an offense by rule (*paṇṇatti-vajja*), bodily action (*kāya-kamma*), verbal action (*vacī-kamma*), consisting of three types of consciousness (*ti-citta*), and three types of feeling (*ti-vedanā*).
This is the first training rule in the group of seventeen. 2. Commentary on the Second *Saṅghādisesa* Training Rule.
682. Second: "Fine goods" (*varabhaṇḍa*) refers to precious items such as pearls, gems, and beryl. 683.

"Without having asked permission" (*anapaloketvā*) means without having sought leave. "A guild" (*gaṇa*) refers to groups such as the Malla guild or the Bhaṭiputta guild. "A religious association" (*pūga*) refers to a group of Dhamma teachers.
"A company" (*seṇi*) refers to companies such as the perfumers' company or the cloth-dealers' company. For wherever kings [deal] with guilds and the like...
They hand over villages and market towns [with the words], "You yourselves should govern here," and thus they become the masters in each of those places.

It was with reference to them that this was said. And in this matter, even if one has already obtained permission from the king or from the guilds and so forth, the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs must still be asked for permission.
With the exception of those who are *kappanti* (permitted), it is not permissible [to ordain] those who have previously gone forth among other sectarians or among other bhikkhunīs.
"Excepting one who has reached the end of her probationary period": the rest is self-evident.

Regarding the origin of the offense for ordaining a female thief: when the bhikkhunīs have departed on some business, she does not go to the *khaṇḍasīma* (partial boundary) but instead ordains her own circle of dependents right where she is sitting; [this offense arises] from speech and mind.
It originates as follows: for one who ordains [a woman] by going to a broken boundary (khaṇḍasīma) or to a river, it originates from body, speech, and mind.

By way of ordaining without having asked permission, it is an action that is non-informative (kiriyākiriya), characterized by perception (saññāvimokkha), accompanied by consciousness (sacittaka), an offense against the rules (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), vocal action (vacīkamma), three types of consciousness (ticitta), and three types of feeling (tivedana).
The Second Training Rule. 3. Commentary on the Third Saṅghādisesa Training Rule: 692.
Regarding the third rule—“crossing over the enclosure”—if she crosses over even one foot, it is a thullaccaya (grave offense).
With the second step, as soon as it has been crossed, there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense. Regarding "the vicinity of an unenclosed village":
here, if one crosses the place suitable for an enclosure with one foot, there is a *thullaccaya* offense; with the second step, as soon as it has been crossed, there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense.

Furthermore, in this case, there is no offense for one departing from her own village on account of going to another village; however, there is an offense for one who, having departed, goes to another village.

For every step, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). When she has merely crossed the boundary or the precincts of the other village with one foot, there is a serious offense (*thullaccaya*);
when she has merely crossed with the second foot, there is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
The same rule applies even if, having departed from there, she enters her own village again. However, if [the boundary] is by way of a broken wall or a gap in the fence...
Or, if it is possible to enter only the area of the bhikkhunī’s dwelling, then for one entering in that manner, it is considered as having entered a *kappiya-bhūmi* (an allowable ground);
therefore, it is permissible. Even if she enters by means of the back of an elephant or by psychic power (*iddhi*), it is likewise permissible;
for here, only walking on foot is intended. For this very reason, he said: "for her who steps across with the first foot," and so forth.
If two villages are connected by a boundary wall that encloses a bhikkhunī-vihāra, then after walking for alms in the village where the vihāra is located, one may re-enter the vihāra;
if there is a path through the middle of the vihāra leading to the other village, it is permissible to go.
However, one must return from that village by the same path. If [one goes] by way of the village gate...
Having gone out, she returns; the classification of the offense is to be understood in the same manner as before.

When a nun who has gone out from her own village with other nuns for some business returns at the time of re-entry, if an elephant is released or there is a public proclamation, and the other nuns enter the village hastily, [the offense applies] until another nun arrives.
One should stand outside the village gate. If [the person] does not come, the companion nun is said to have departed, and it is permissible to enter.

Previously there was a large village with a bhikkhunī monastery in its center. Later, four people having acquired that village, each built a separate enclosure with a fence, divided it up, and took possession;
thus, from the monastery, one must go to a [different] village.
It is permissible. It is not permissible to enter another village from that point, whether by the gate or through a breach in the wall.
It is permissible to return again to the monastery itself. Why? Because the monastery is common to the four villages.
Regarding the phrase "the inner robe becomes wet": it refers to where, when one is dressed in such a way that the three circles [of the body] are covered, the inner robe becomes moist.

When a bhikkhunī, during the rainy season, descends by a ford or a non-ford and crosses anywhere, even if her inner robe becomes moistened to the extent of a single finger’s breadth, it is [an offense]. The remaining characteristics of a river will be clarified in the discussion on the signs of a river.
Having descended by a ford or a non-ford into such a river as this, at the time of crossing, first—
For one who lifts one foot and places it on the bank, there is a *thullaccaya* offense; when the second foot is lifted, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.
There is no offense if she goes by means of a bridge. There is also no offense for one who, having descended on foot, ascends the bridge at the time of crossing.
However, for one who has gone by bridge but then walks on foot at the time of crossing, there is indeed an offense. This also applies to travel by vehicle, boat, through the air, and so forth.
The same principle applies. However, there is no offense for one who steps from this shore directly onto the other shore.
It is permissible for two or three women to go to a place for washing clothes and wander between both shores while performing duties such as gathering wood.
But if, in that situation, anyone quarrels and goes to the other shore, there is an offense. If two cross together and one [leaves] in midstream...
If, after quarreling with her on the river, she turns back and returns to this very bank, there is an offense.
But if the other woman remains at the place where she departed, then even for one going to the opposite bank, there is no offense.
If she has descended into the water to bathe or to drink and then climbs back out onto that same bank, there is no offense.

Regarding the phrase "until sunrise": if, while performing recitation, meditation, or some other task, she forms the intention, "I will go to my companion before sunrise," and the sun rises while she is still unaware of it, there is no offense.
However, if she intends, "I will remain right here until sunrise," or...
If one remains in a portion of the dwelling without effort [to leave], and does not come within arm’s reach of a companion, it is a *saṅghādisesa* offense at the rising of the dawn.
For in this case, the arm’s reach itself is the measure; once the arm’s reach is exceeded, even a single room does not provide protection.
Regarding the phrase "in a forest where there is no village," the definition stated here is precisely that which was said: "Having gone out beyond the threshold post, all this is forest."
The forest (*arañña*). This, however, is called "without a village" (*agāmaka*) solely because of the absence of a village, not because of its similarity to the Vindhya wilderness.
When one has entered such a forest and left the range of sight, even if the range of hearing still exists, there is an offense.
For this very reason, it is stated in the Commentary: "If, while nuns are entering the courtyard of the Great Bodhi tree, one remains outside..."
"She too incurs an offense. The same rule applies to those entering the Lohapāsāda or entering a pariveṇa.
When women are worshipping the Mahācetiya, if one goes out by the northern gate, she too incurs an offense.
When women are entering the Thūpārāma, if one remains outside, she too incurs an offense. And here, "the range of sight" means where the companion stands.
He sees. However, if there is even a screen of cloth between them, one is said to have abandoned the range of vision.

The range of hearing is that place where, standing, one hears the sound of someone calling out "Venerable Lady," just as one would hear the sound of those lost on the road or the sound of announcing the hearing of the Dhamma. Even at a distance in the open air, it is called the range of vision. In such a case...
If she leaves the vicinity of the dwelling, she does not guard [the robe]; as soon as she has left it, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
If one woman traveling along a path lags behind, and the other, being determined, follows after her thinking, "I will catch up now," there is no offense.
If the women ahead go by another path, they are said to have departed; in that case, there is likewise no offense.
When two women are walking together, if one is unable to keep up and thinks, "Let her go on," and she falls behind, while the other thinks,
"Let her stay behind," and continues on, there is an offense for both. However, if among those walking,
the one in front takes another path and the one behind also takes another, and each stands where the other has departed, there is no offense for either.
693. “Having gone over to another faction” means having gone over to a sectarian order (*titthāyatana*); the rest is self-evident. The origin of the first *pārājika*:
it is an action, liberated by perception, with consciousness, an offense of formal rule, bodily action, associated with three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
This is the third training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
4. Commentary on the Fourth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule 694–8.
Regarding the fourth [rule]: “A footstool” (pādapīṭha) means a support for placing washed feet. “A foot-slab” (pādakaṭhalikā) means a support for placing unwashed feet.
“Without knowing the consent of the group” means without knowing the consent of that very group performing the act. “While conducting oneself according to the proper conduct” (vatte vattantiṃ).
It is practiced while engaged in the forty-threefold duties of hospitality. The remainder is self-evident.

The origin of the offense through laying down the burden arises from body, speech, and mind; it is functional (kiriyā), non-functional (akiriya), with perception as its liberation, accompanied by consciousness, a worldly transgression, bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome consciousness, and painful feeling.
This is the fourth training rule.
5. Commentary on the Fifth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule 701. Regarding the fifth [rule]:

concerning the phrase "lustful on one side," it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that "the lustfulness of the bhikkhunī is to be understood. However, this is not stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*; the latter accords with the canonical text (*pāḷi*).

The remainder is self-evident. This originates from the first Pārājika; it is an intentional act, free from delusion regarding perception, involving volition, a worldly transgression, bodily action, an unwholesome state of mind, and two types of feeling.
The Fifth Training Rule. 6.
Commentary on the Sixth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule.

705–6. Regarding the sixth: "From whom you... means "because you. To whom do the offenses beginning with "if she incites [her], there is an offense of wrong-doing" and ending with the Saṅghādisesa belong? They belong to the one who incites. And this has been stated in the Parivāra as well:
“He neither gives nor receives; therefore, no recipient exists.
He incurs a grave offense, not a light one, and that is due to the cause of consumption.
This question was pondered by those skilled in wisdom.”

This verse was spoken with reference to this instigator; however, the classification of the offense for the other [participant] is explained in the first training rule (*sikkhāpada*). The rest is self-evident. It has three origins:

it is an action (*kiriya*), liberated by perception (*saññāvimokkha*), accompanied by consciousness (*sacittaka*), a worldly transgression (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), verbal action (*vacīkamma*), unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*), and associated with three feelings (*tivedana*).
This is the sixth training rule.
7. Commentary on the Seventh Saṅghādisesa Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 709.
Regarding the seventh [rule]: the meaning of the term *yāvatatiyaka* (up to the third time) is to be understood according to the method already stated in the Mahāvibhaṅga.

The remainder is self-evident. Its origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) is: an act (*kiriya*), liberation through perception (*saññāvimokkha*), accompanied by consciousness (*sacittaka*), a worldly offense (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), verbal action (*vacīkamma*), unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*), and painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
The Seventh Training Rule.
8. Commentary on the Eighth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule: 715.
Regarding the eighth [rule], "in some legal matter" means in one of the four [types of legal matters]. In the word-by-word commentary, however...
The statement beginning with “*Adhikaraṇaṃ nāma cattāri adhikaraṇānī*,” etc., was spoken solely to show the classification of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*).
The remainder, including the origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth, is self-evident.
This concludes the eighth training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
9. Commentary on the Ninth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule 723.

Regarding the ninth [rule]: "In association" (*saṃsaṭṭhā*) means being mixed together. "In an improper manner" (*ananulomika*) means by means of bodily or verbal conduct that is not in accordance with those who have gone forth.

"In association" refers to [associating] with householders through such bodily acts as pounding, cooking, grinding scents, weaving garlands, and so forth; and through such acts as carrying messages, returning messages, acting as a go-between, and so forth.

And they are associated by means of speech. They have an evil reputation, thus they are "evil-repute" (pāpasaddā). They have an evil report—meaning a report concerning their livelihood—thus they are "evil-report" (pāpasilokā).
The rest is self-evident, along with [the sections on] origin and so forth.
This is the ninth training rule.
10. Commentary on the Tenth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule 727.
Regarding the tenth: *evācārā* means "of such conduct. The meaning is: "your conduct is of such a kind;

[we too] are of such conduct. This same method applies everywhere. *Uññāya* means by way of contempt, knowing [them] as inferior. *Paribhavena* means [thinking], "What will these women do? [i.e., treating them with disregard].

"Thus, by way of knowing through contempt. "Impatience" (*akkhanti*) means the state of not enduring; the meaning is "by anger. "Frivolity" (*vebhassiya*) means by the state of excessive talkativeness;
the meaning is "by intimidating others through the manifestation of one's own strength. "Weakness" (*dubbalyā*) means by your own state of weakness.
In all cases, the sense of a conjunction should be understood as "and by contempt and by disdain."
"Live apart" means "be without [others]. The rest is self-evident, together with its origins and so forth.
This is the tenth training rule.
"Noble ladies, the seventeen *saṅghādisesas* have been recited. Here, immediately after the six that entail immediate offense:

Having included these three training rules—sañcaritta (mediating between couples) and the two duṭṭhadosa (corrupt offenses)—from the Mahāvibhaṅga, there are nine *paṭhamāpattika* (offenses involving immediate transgression).
Following the four *yāvatatiyaka* (offenses requiring a third admonition), one should understand that there are eight *yāvatatiyaka* offenses by including four more from the Mahāvibhaṅga as well.
Thus, all of them have been recited by way of the Pātimokkha recitation procedure.
"Venerable ladies, these are the seventeen *saṅghādisesa* rules"—thus should the meaning be understood here.
The rest is self-evident, except for the probation (*pakkhamānatta*), which we shall explain in detail in the *Khandhaka*.
[End of] the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The commentary on the Seventeen [Offenses] is finished. The Section on Formal Meetings (Saṅghādisesa) is finished.
3. The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiya), [Commentary on the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga].
Commentary on the First Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule:
The thirty rules involving forfeiture have been proclaimed for the bhikkhunīs;
now follows the sequence of their detailed exposition.

733. *Āmattikāpaṇa*: "Amattā" refers to vessels; those who sell them are called *āmattikā*. Their shop is an *āmattikāpaṇa*; the meaning is that they will display it there. 734. *Pattasannicayaṃ kareyya*:

"He should make a hoard of bowls" means he should keep a store of bowls; the meaning is that he should set aside a bowl for more than one day without having formally determined its use (*adhiṭṭhahitvā*) or assigned it to another (*avikappetvā*).
The remainder should be understood according to the method explained in the Mahāvibhaṅga.
This indeed is the distinction: there, a ten-day period of exemption is granted; here, there is not even a single day. The remainder is exactly the same.

This too is an offense originating from the *kaṭhina*—it originates from body and speech, and from body, speech, and mind; it is non-action (*akiriya*), not involving liberation through perception (*nosaññāvimokkha*), without mental intention (*acittaka*), an offense against the rules (*paṇṇattivajja*), bodily action, vocal action, consisting of three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
This is the first training rule.
Commentary on the Second Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 738.
Regarding the second [term]: *duccoḷā* means having disfigured robes; the meaning is "having worn-out robes. *Apayyāhi* means "even from the noble ladies" (*api ayyāhi*).
740. *Ādissa dinnaṃ* ("given specifically"): even after saying, "Let those who have assembled divide it," one says, "This I give to the community, this I give to you."
Whether it has been given after having spoken [the words], or placed at the foot [of the recipient] out of a desire to give, even that is called "given specifically.

All of this constitutes "out-of-season robe-cloth" (*akālacīvara*). However, what is obtained by saying, "I give it to the Noble Lady," must be brought back exactly as it was given. The rest is self-evident.

It has three origins: it is an action (*kiriya*), liberated from perception (*saññāvimokkha*), accompanied by consciousness (*sacittaka*), a worldly offense (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), verbal action (*vacīkamma*), unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*), and possesses three feelings (*tivedana*).
The Second Training Rule.
Commentary on the Third Nissaggiya-Pācittiya Training Rule, §§ 743–5.
Regarding the third: *handā* means “take. *Sāmaṃ acchindati* (she herself takes back) refers to one who, having given one [piece], takes back another.

It is an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*); if there are many [items], there are many [offenses]. If one seizes them all at once after they have been gathered and stored together, there are offenses according to the number of objects (*vatthu*).
However, in the case of those stored after being tied up, there is only one offense. The rest is self-evident. It has three origins (*samuṭṭhāna*):

it is an act (*kiriya*), it is liberated by perception (*saññāvimokkha*), it involves volition (*sacittaka*), it is a worldly transgression (*lokavajja*), it is bodily action (*kāyakamma*), it is vocal action (*vacīkamma*), it is unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*), and it is associated with painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
The Third Training Rule.
Commentary on the Fourth Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule 748.
Regarding the fourth: “by purchase” means by means of the price. “I have no need for ghee, friend; I have need of oil”—this is...
It is said that she spoke thus, thinking, "Having given the ghee that was brought, she will bring oil as well.
*Viññāpetvā* means having made known;
or it means having requested, saying, "Bring such-and-such. 752. *Taññeva viññāpetīti*: That which was first requested is not sufficient; therefore, again—
The meaning is that she asks for that very same thing. "And she asks for something else" means:

if ghee has already been requested first, but because the physician says, "A double portion must be cooked," there is a need for oil, she then asks for something else by saying, "I have need of oil as well.
"By showing the advantage" means: if ghee worth one kahāpaṇa has been brought, with this...
"Double the oil is obtained from the root, and by that too this task is accomplished; therefore, bring the oil.
Having thus shown the benefit, he makes the request. The rest is self-evident.

It has six origins: it is an action, not associated with perception or liberation, without consciousness, an offense by formal rule, bodily action, verbal action, three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
The Fourth Training Rule. Commentary on the Fifth Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule: 753.
Regarding the fifth rule—“This trainee is not mine”—it is said that this daughter of good family, having been told this, [thought]: “Surely she was told this...”
Thinking, “Except for oil, my own family home will also bring ghee for me,” she said this.
“Having caused it to be procured” means having made it known; the rest is exactly like the fourth [offense] in all respects.
This is the fifth training rule.
Commentary on the Sixth Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule:
758. Regarding the sixth [rule]: *chandaka* is a designation for requisites taken after having generated consent and approval in others by saying, "We shall perform such-and-such a Dhamma-duty;
give what you are able. *Aññadatthikena*: [refers to] for another purpose.
"Given for another purpose" means given with reference to something else. "Belonging to the Sangha" means dedicated to the Sangha. 762.
"He diverts the remainder" means that having exchanged what was given for its specific purpose, he diverts the surplus for another purpose.
"Having informed the owners" means: "This was given by you for the sake of robes; we already have robes; [we need] oil and so forth..."
Having thus requested, “But there is a need,” he brings it forward. “In times of distress” means in such calamities;
when nuns abandon the monastery and depart, in such emergencies it is permissible to have whatever is needed purchased. The rest is self-evident.

This rule has six origins: it is an action and non-action, not involving perception or liberation, without mental intention, an offense by formal precept, bodily action and verbal action, consisting of three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The Sixth Training Rule.
Commentary on the Seventh Nissaggiya-Pācittiya Training Rule: 764.
Regarding the seventh—*saññācikenā* means by what has been personally requested. This alone is the point of distinction here; the rest is exactly the same as the sixth.
The Seventh Training Rule.
Commentary on the Eighth Nissaggiya-Pācittiya Training Rule: 769.
Regarding the eighth—*mahājanikena* means by what has been assigned to a group. This alone is the distinction here.
The eighth training rule.
Commentary on the ninth Nissaggiya Pācittiya training rule: 774.
Regarding the ninth training rule—the phrase *saññācikenā* (by means of deception) is additional here.
The Ninth Training Rule.
Commentary on the Tenth Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule: 778.

Regarding the tenth—*pariveṇaṃ undriyati* means the courtyard is destroyed; the meaning is that it collapses. And this phrase, *puggalikena saññācikena*, is the only difference [from the previous rule]. The remainder is exactly as before.
The Tenth Training Rule.
Commentary on the Eleventh Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule: 784.

Regarding the eleventh rule—*garupāvuraṇaṃ* means a cloak for use during the cold season. *Catukkaṃsaparamaṃ*: here, a *kaṃsa* is worth four *hāpaṇas*; therefore, it is stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) as "worth sixteen *hāpaṇas*."
The eleventh training rule.
Commentary on the twelfth Nissaggiya Pācittiya training rule: 789.
Regarding the twelfth—“a light cloak” (*lahupāvuraṇa*) refers to a cloak for use during the hot season. The remainder of this and the two preceding training rules is self-evident.

Originating from chance: it is an action, not associated with liberation through perception, without consciousness, an offense by way of formal rule, bodily action, verbal action, consisting of three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
This is the twelfth training rule.
"Venerable ladies, the thirty offenses entailing relinquishment and confession have been recited. Herein, [they are found] from the Cīvara-vagga in the Mahāvibhaṅga.

Excluding the two training rules concerning washing and receiving, the first section is to be completed by means of the training rule on exchanging after determining an out-of-season robe as an in-season robe,
and by means of the training rule on exchanging after bartering, as well as the training rule on a robe that has been lost. Furthermore,
excluding the first seven training rules of the Section on Wool, [the remaining] seven rules concerning "for other purposes" (aññadatthika) [are to be included].

Having inserted [the relevant rules], the second section (vagga) is to be completed. From the third section, having removed these three—the first bowl rule, the rainy-season robe rule, and the wilderness training rule—the third section is to be completed with the rules concerning the accumulation of bowls, heavy coverings, and light coverings.
Thus, twelve training rules for bhikkhunīs are prescribed unilaterally, and eighteen are prescribed bilaterally.
Thus, for all [the rules] by way of the recitation of the Pātimokkha, the meaning here should be understood as: "Venerable ladies, the thirty Nissaggiya Pācittiya rules have been recited.
The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
[End of] the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The commentary on the Thirty [Nissaggiya rules] is finished.
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa) is finished.
4. The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa): Commentary on the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga.
1. The Garlic Chapter (Lasuṇavagga).
1. Commentary on the First Training Rule on Garlic:
Following the Thirty [rules], there are the Dhammas, comprised of one hundred and sixty-six [rules].
Now, there is also a commentary on those [rules] that have been recited together. 793.
Regarding the first training rule of the Garlic Chapter: "two or three bundles" means two or three small packets;
this is a designation for garlic bulbs with the seeds fully developed. "Without knowing moderation" means without knowing the proper measure.
While the field-guard was trying to stop him, he caused much garlic to be carried away.
"A certain swan-birth" means a golden swan-birth. That swan possessed the memory of his former births;
thus, out of affection from the past, he would come and give each of them a leaf, which was indeed gold, capable of withstanding heating, hammering, and cutting.
795. *Māgadhakaṃ* means what is grown in the Magadha country. For here, by "garlic" (*lasuṇaṃ*), only garlic grown in the Magadha kingdom is intended;
and even that must be *bhaṇḍikala*-garlic, not that which has one, two, or three cloves. However, in the *Kurundi*, without specifying the place of origin, it is stated:
"That which is called *māgadhaka* is *bhaṇḍikala*-garlic. Regarding the phrase "with every swallow": if here—
If she chews two or three morsels at once and swallows them, it is one *pācittiya*.
However, for her who breaks them apart and eats each kernel individually, there are as many *pācittiya* offenses as there are instances of that action. 797.
The distinction between onions and so forth should be understood either by their color or by their kernels. First, by color, the onion is—
The *paṇḍu* is white in color; the *bhañjanaka* is red in color; the *haritaka* is the color of green leaves.
As for the seeds (*miñjā*), the *palaṇḍuka* has one seed, the *bhañjanaka* two, and the *haritaka* three. The *cāpalasuṇa* is seedless, for it has only a mere sprout.
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other texts, it is said that the *palaṇḍuka* has three seeds.
It is stated: "Two for *bhañjanaka* (onion), one for *haritaka* (green vegetable). These [plants], beginning with onions, are permitted by their very nature.

However, in the case of soups, seasonings, and so forth, even the Magadhan variety is permitted. For that [Magadhan onion] is allowed in any context whatsoever—whether in bean soups and the like being cooked, or in preparations of fish and meat, or in oils and the like, or in *badara-sālava* (jujube salad) and the like, or in sour vegetables, or in *uttaribhaṅga* (after-meal refreshments).
It is even permissible to put it into rice-gruel. The rest here is self-evident.

This offense has its origin in wool; it is an action, not involving liberation through perception, without mental concomitants, a fault by way of formal rule, a bodily action, associated with three types of consciousness, and associated with three types of feeling.
This is the first training rule on garlic.
2. Commentary on the Second Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 799.
Regarding the second [rule]: *sambādheti* means in a concealed place. To show its specific divisions, however, it is said: "both armpits and the urinary organ.
Even a single hair means by means of a knife, tweezers, or a razor—whichever [is used].

Whether by a single application or multiple applications, for one who causes [hair] to be plucked—whether one or many—the offenses are Pācittiyas according to the number of applications, not according to the number of hairs.
801. "On account of illness" means there is no offense for one who causes it to be plucked on account of illnesses such as scabs, itch, and so forth. The rest is self-evident.
It has four origins: it originates from body, from body and speech, from body and mind, and from body, speech, and mind.

It is functional (*kiriya*), not associated with the deliverance through perception, without consciousness, an offense by formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), bodily action, verbal action, three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
This is the second training rule.
3. Commentary on the Third Training Rule (Tatiya-sikkhāpada) 803–4. Regarding the third rule:

"Striking with the palm" means striking the opening of the urinary tract with the palm. "Even as much as with a lotus leaf"—here, even if the leaf is large, for one who strikes with even the stamen, there is indeed an offense.
805. "On account of illness": it is permissible to strike [the area] in order to treat a boil or a wound. The rest is self-evident. This is originated from the first *pārājika* offense.

— It is a functional state (*kiriyā*), liberation through perception (*saññāvimokkha*), accompanied by consciousness (*sacittaka*), an offense against worldly convention (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), unwholesome mind (*akusalacitta*), and associated with three types of feeling (*tivedana*).
This is the third training rule.
4. Commentary on the Fourth Training Rule.
806. Regarding the fourth [verse]: "The former king’s concubines" means the concubines of the king during his former life as a householder.
"She goes after long intervals" means she goes only after a long time has passed. "Can you bear it? means "Are you able?
When asked, "Whose work is this?", even though it had not been told, he said, "This is my work," thinking: "Even if this is not disclosed, they will suspect me."
807. *Jatumaṭṭhaka*: [This refers to] smooth rods made of lac. This is stated by way of illustration;
however, for anyone who inserts anything whatsoever as a rod, there is indeed an offense. Therefore he said: "Even if she inserts only a lotus leaf into the urinary tract.
And this too is considered excessive; even for one who inserts only a mere filament, there is indeed an offense. The rest...
This is self-evident. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and other details are exactly the same as those stated for the "striking the palm" rule.
This concludes the fourth training rule (sikkhāpada). 5. Commentary on the fifth training rule.
810. Regarding the fifth [offense]: "beginning a very deep water-cleansing" means performing a washing with water after having inserted it to the very end.

812. "She exceeds even by the breadth of a hair-tip" means that for one who inserts it even by the breadth of a hair-tip beyond two finger-joints in depth—whether it be the third or fourth finger-breadth in width—it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). For this has been said:
In the *Mahāpaccarī*: "One is not permitted to take three joints from a single finger, nor is one permitted to take even a single joint from three or four fingers.
The remainder is self-evident. The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other factors are also exactly as stated for the *talaghātaka* [offense].
This is the fifth training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
6. Commentary on the Sixth Training Rule 815.
Regarding the sixth [rule]: *bhattavissaggaṃ* means the performance of the meal duty.
*Upaṭṭhahitvā pānīyena ca vidhūpanena ca* means standing nearby while fanning, having taken a water vessel with one hand and a fan with the other; this is the meaning.
