"Accāvadati" means that she oversteps the conduct of one who has gone forth by speaking of household matters, saying, "In the past you used to eat like this," or "I attend to you in such a way.
(817) "Any kind of drink" refers to either pure water or any one of the following: buttermilk, curd, whey, milk, and so forth.
"Any fan whatsoever" means even a corner of a robe. "Stands within arm's reach": here, the offense of *pācittiya* is stated solely on account of the location.
However, regarding the cause of striking, an offense of *dukkaṭa* is prescribed in the *Khandhaka*. 819.
"Gives or causes to be given" means she gives water or soup and so forth, saying, "Drink this," or "Eat with this"; [or] a palm-leaf fan...
If she gives it saying, "Eat this seed," or if she causes both to be given by another, there is no offense.
"She instructs one who is not fully ordained" means she instructs a female novice for the purpose of attending [to her]; there is no offense. The rest is self-evident.

This offense originates from wool; it is an action, not released through recognition, without mental state, an offense of formal rule, bodily action, consisting of three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
The Sixth Training Rule. 7. Commentary on the Seventh Training Rule. 822. Regarding the seventh:
“If one receives [food] with the intention ‘I shall eat,’ it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). This refers to the wrong-doing of the preliminary action.
Therefore, it is not only at the time of receiving [the grain] that [the offense occurs]; rather, after having received it, it also occurs when bringing it from the forest, when drying it,
on the day before threshing when preparing the hearth for roasting, when preparing the pan, when preparing the ladle,
when gathering wood and making a fire, when putting the grain into the pan, and even when striking with the ladle for the purpose of threshing.

Even during the preparation of the mortar, pestle, and so forth, and during the acts of pounding, winnowing, washing, and so on, there are *dukkaṭa* offenses for all these activities up until the point when one chews with the teeth after placing it in the mouth for the purpose of swallowing.
At the time of swallowing, however, there are *pācittiya* offenses according to the number of times one swallows.
In this case, both the request and the food are the criteria. Therefore, having requested it oneself, [if one causes another]...

There is an offense even for one who causes [the food] to be fried, pounded, or cooked and then eats it. There is also an offense for one who, having requested it from another, performs the frying and so forth herself and then eats it.
However, it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*: "In the case of raw grain, there is a *pācittiya* offense even for one who eats it after requesting it from her own mother;
if obtained without being requested, [one may perform] the frying and so forth oneself."
“There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who eats after having roasted [the grain] herself or having had it roasted by another.

Even for one who eats what was obtained through a request made by another, whether she herself performs the roasting and so forth, or has it performed by that same person, or has it performed by someone else, there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing.
Furthermore, it is said: “For one who eats what was obtained through a request made by another, having herself performed the roasting and so forth, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).”
"But for one who causes [food] to be fried and so forth and then eats it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

This contradicts what precedes and follows it, for there is no distinction between the act of frying and so forth and causing it to be done. In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated without qualification:
"For one who eats what has been requested by another, there is an offense of wrong-doing."
823. Regarding "on account of illness": there is no offense in requesting grain for the purpose of sudation treatments and the like.
However, it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that "it is permissible to accept what is obtained without being requested for the sake of new construction work.
"Requests for other food" refers to items such as mung beans, black gram, and so forth, or gourds, cucumbers, and the like, excluding the seven types of grain.

There is no offense for one who asks for anything else whatsoever at a place where she has been invited by relatives. However, raw grain is not permitted at a place where she has been invited by relatives.
The rest is self-evident. This [offense] arises from four origins:

it originates from body, from body and speech, from body and mind, and from body, speech, and mind; it is an action (kiriya), not dissociated from perception (nosaññāvimokkha), without mental involvement (acittaka), an offense of formal rule (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), and vocal action (vacīkamma); it consists of three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The Seventh Training Rule. 8. Commentary on the Eighth Training Rule: 824.

Regarding the eighth—*nibbiṭṭharājabhaṭo*: one who has been assigned as a royal tax-laborer (*rājabhaṭa*) is called a *nibbiṭṭharājabhaṭa*, meaning one for whom a wage (*keṇi*) has been paid by the king. One...
"Having received the office from Keṇiya" means that he obtained it from him;
"thinking, 'I shall ask for that very same path of hire,' and 'having given the fee to the king, I shall ask for that very same office again,'" while he was reflecting thus.
"He rebuked" means he threatened those bhikkhunīs, saying, "Do not do so again."

826. "She discards herself" means that for one who discards all four items in a single action, there is only one offense; for one who discards them separately, there are offenses according to the number of items.
The same principle applies to commanding [another to discard them]. Regarding the discarding of a tooth-stick as well, it is a *pācittiya* for a bhikkhunī.
For a bhikkhu, it is a *dukkaṭa* in all cases. The remainder is self-evident.
Originating from chance: it is neither action nor non-action; it is not a liberation through perception; it is mindless; it is an offense by formal rule; it is bodily action and verbal action;
it consists of three types of consciousness and three types of feeling. This is the eighth training rule. 9. Commentary on the Ninth Training Rule.

830–2. Regarding the ninth [offense]: whatever constitutes the enjoyment or use of humans—whether it be cultivated fields, or groves such as coconut plantations—in any place where cultivated greenery grows, the classification of the offense for one who discards these things there should be understood according to the same method as before.
This applies whether she is sitting and eating in a field or a grove, or chewing sugarcane and the like.

While walking, if one discards things such as leftover water or food scraps on a green area—even if it is merely a coconut shell that has been emptied after drinking water—it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for the nun; for the monk, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Furthermore, in a ploughed field where seed has been sown, it is an offense of wrong-doing for everyone as long as the sprout has not yet emerged. Regarding fields where no seed has been sown...
It is permissible to discard [the seeds] in the corners of fields and the like, or in the boundaries of fields where crops have not yet grown;

it is also permissible in places where people discard rubbish. Regarding "abandoned fields": when people have harvested the grain and departed, it is called an abandoned field, and it is permissible there.
However, in a place where the previously harvested grain and so forth has been reaped again...
They guard it thinking, "He will get up"; in this case, it remains exactly as the original state. The rest is self-evident. It has six origins:
it is functional and non-functional... [etc. ...and associated with three feelings.
This is the ninth training rule.
10. Commentary on the Tenth Training Rule (Dasama-sikkhāpada) 835.

Regarding the tenth: "Whatever dance" means whether it be dancers such as actors and the like, or those intoxicated with drink—even down to peacocks, parrots, monkeys, and so forth—all this is indeed dancing.
"Whatever song" means whether it be the song of actors and the like, or that of the Noble Ones (ariya).
At the time of the Parinibbāna, whether it be a well-performed song accompanied by the qualities of the Triple Gem,
or the chanting of Dhamma by unrestrained monks— all this is indeed singing. Whatever is "instrumental music" (*vādita*),
whether it be played on stringed instruments and the like, or played on a hollow drum (*kuṭabheri*), or even played on a water-drum (*udakabheri*)— all this is indeed instrumental music.
836. "Going to see, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" means that there is an offense of wrong-doing for each step taken.

If she stands where she sees or hears [the performance], then by a single act of looking, she sees [the dance] and hears the singing and instrumental music of those very same people, there is only one offense of expiation (pācittiya).
However, if, after looking in one direction, she sees the dance, and then again from another [direction]...
Having looked on, she sees them dancing or singing while others play instruments; these are separate offenses.
A bhikkhunī herself is not permitted to dance, sing, or play an instrument, nor is she permitted to tell others, "Dance! Sing! Play!
Even to say, "Give an offering to the cetiya, lay followers," or "We shall perform service for your cetiya," [is not permitted].
When this is said, one may not even accept it by saying "Very well. It is stated in all the commentaries that in every such case, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
For a bhikkhu, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). However, when it is said, "Let us perform service for your cetiya," it is permissible to say, "Performing service is indeed excellent."
837. "Standing in a monastery" means that having stayed in a monastery, whether she sees or hears dancing and so forth inside the monastery or outside the monastery, there is no offense.

"If there is business to be done" means that having gone for the sake of tickets for meals and so forth, or for some other business, she sees or hears [such things] at the place where she has gone; there is no offense. "In times of distress" means being afflicted by such a calamity.
If she enters a place of assembly, there is no offense for her as long as she sees or hears [the act] after having entered in this manner. The rest is self-evident.

This offense originates from sheep’s wool; it is an action, not involving liberation through perception, without mental intention, a worldly transgression, a bodily deed, an unwholesome state of mind, and associated with three types of feeling.
This is the tenth training rule.
The First Chapter on Garlic.
2. The Chapter on Darkness. 1.
Commentary on the First Training Rule.
839. Regarding the first training rule of the *Andhakāravagga*: "Unlit" (*appadīpeti*) means not illuminated by even one of the following: lamps, the moon, the sun, or fire.

For this very reason, it is stated in its word-commentary (*padabhājana*) as "in the absence of light" (*anāloke*). "Should converse" (*sallapeyya vā*) means she should engage in talk concerning domestic matters. 841.

"With indifference toward the Worthy One" (*arahopekkhā*) and "engaged in something else" (*aññavihitā*) means: not having a desire for the enjoyment of privacy, but rather being engaged in something other than the enjoyment of privacy.
He asks after a kinsman, or he consults regarding a gift or an act of honor. The rest is self-evident.

Its origination is from a caravan of thieves—it originates from body and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. It is an action; it is liberated by perception; it is accompanied by consciousness; it is a worldly offense;
it is bodily action and verbal action; it is unwholesome consciousness; and it is associated with two feelings.
The First Training Rule. 2. Commentary on the Second Training Rule: 842.
Regarding the second [rule]—the phrase "in a concealed place" is the only difference. Everything else is exactly the same as the preceding one.
The Second Training Rule.
3. Commentary on the Third Training Rule:
Regarding the third [rule]—“in the open air” (ajjhokāse) is the difference; all else is exactly the same.
The Third Training Rule. 4. Commentary on the Fourth Training Rule: 850–3.
Regarding the fourth—*nikaṇṇikaṃ* means the root of the ear; it means one should whisper into the root of the ear.

"Being mindful that there is something to be done" means for the purpose of bringing back items such as tickets for meals (*salākabhatta*), or for the purpose of putting back away what has been poorly placed in the monastery.
The rest is self-evident. The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other factors are exactly like those of the preceding [rules].
This is the fourth training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
5. Commentary on the Fifth Training Rule 854. Regarding the fifth rule:

"They were cleaning the house"—it is said that they thought, "No physical or verbal transgression is seen in this elder nun; let us clean the house first," and while cleaning the house, they saw her. 856. "If she passes beyond the shelter from rain":

for one who passes beyond it with the first foot, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); for one who passes beyond it with the second foot, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). The same method applies when passing beyond the precincts.

858. “Because of illness” means: she is so ill that she is unable to ask for leave. “In case of an emergency” means: when a fire has broken out in the house, or there are thieves; in such a calamity, she departs without asking for leave—there is no offense.

The rest here is self-evident. The origin of the *Kathina* rule: it originates from body and speech, and from body, speech, and mind; it is both action and non-action, not involving liberation through perception, without mental intention, an offense by formal precept, bodily action, verbal action, associated with three types of consciousness, and associated with three types of feeling.
This is the fifth training rule.
6. Commentary on the Sixth Training Rule 860. Regarding the sixth:

“should sit down” (*abhinisīdeyya*) means she should sit. For one who departs after having sat down, there is one offense; for one who departs without having sat down but after having lain down, there is one offense; for one who departs after having both sat down and lain down, there are two offenses. 863.

“In a permanent arrangement” (*dhuvapaññatte*) means in that which has been permanently arranged for the sake of the bhikkhunīs. The rest is self-evident. It originates from the *kaṭhina* [rules]... [and so forth] ...it is associated with three feelings.
The Sixth Training Rule.
7. Commentary on the Seventh Training Rule: 864.
Regarding the seventh as well, everything should be understood in the same manner as stated for the sixth.
The Seventh Training Rule. 8. Commentary on the Eighth Training Rule:
869. Regarding the eighth—everything is self-evident. It has three origins:

it is an intentional act (*kiriya*), it is liberated by perception (*saññāvimokkha*), it involves consciousness (*sacittaka*), it is a worldly offense (*lokavajja*), it is bodily action (*kāyakamma*), it is verbal action (*vacīkamma*), it is unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*), and it is accompanied by painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
The Eighth Training Rule. 9. Commentary on the Ninth Training Rule: 875.
Regarding the ninth—*abhisapeyya* means one should take an oath. *Abhisapati with hell* means: "May I be reborn in hell."
She reviles her in such a manner as: "May I be reborn in Avīci! May she be reborn in hell! May she be reborn in Avīci! and so forth.

To "curse by means of the holy life" means to revile her in such a manner as: "May I become a housewife! May I wear white garments! May I become a female wanderer! Or may she become someone like that!
For each individual utterance, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya), except for...

However, for one who reviles both the Niraya hell and the holy life with speech such as "you bitch, you sow, you one-eyed one, you cripple," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for each word. 878.
"With the aim of the meaning" refers to one who is expounding the commentary (aṭṭhakathā). "With the aim of the Dhamma" refers to one who is reciting the canonical text (pāḷi).
“With the intention of instructing”: there is no offense for one who speaks while standing on the ground of instruction, saying, “Even now you are like this; it would be well if you desisted.
If you do not desist, you will certainly, by performing such deeds again, be reborn in hell or be reborn in the animal realm. The rest is self-evident.

It has three origins: it is an action, it is liberated by perception, it is associated with consciousness, it is a worldly offense, it is bodily action, it is verbal action, it is an unwholesome state of mind, and it is painful feeling.
This is the ninth training rule.
10. Commentary on the Tenth Training Rule.
879. Regarding the tenth: everything is self-evident. Its origin through the laying down of the burden arises from body, speech, and mind;
it is an action, liberated by perception, associated with consciousness, a worldly offense, bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome action, and a feeling of suffering.
This is the tenth training rule.
The second chapter: The Chapter on Darkness (Andhakāravagga). 3. The Chapter on Nakedness (Naggavagga).
1. Commentary on the First Training Rule (Sikkhāpada).
883–6. Regarding the first training rule of the *Naggavagga*: “*brahmacariyaṃ ciṇṇenā*” means by one who has practiced the holy life (*brahmacariya*);
or alternatively, it means by the practice of the holy life. Thus, the accusative case should be understood as expressing either the sense of the instrumental or the sense of the genitive.
“*Acchinnacīvarikāyā*” (by one whose robe has been stolen) is said with reference to the rain-bath robe (*udakasāṭikā*), not any other robe.
Therefore, there is no offense for one who bathes naked when her bathing-cloth has been torn off or lost.
Even if the bathing-cloth robe is of great value and it is impossible to go outside while wearing it, it is likewise permissible to bathe naked. The rest here is self-evident.

The origin of the offense regarding the wool of a sheep: it is a functional (kiriya) action, not associated with liberation through perception (nosaññāvimokkha), without consciousness (acittaka), an offense by way of formal rule (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), consisting of three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
This is the first training rule.
2. Commentary on the second training rule.

887. Regarding the second [offense]: everything is self-evident. It has six origins; it is functional (*kiriya*), not associated with liberation through perception (*no-saññā-vimokkha*), without consciousness (*acittaka*), an offense by designation (*paṇṇatti-vajja*), bodily action (*kāya-kamma*), verbal action (*vacī-kamma*), associated with three types of consciousness, and associated with three types of feeling.
This is the second training rule (Sikkhāpada). 3. Commentary on the Third Training Rule.
893–4. Regarding the third [offense]: “one who is without obstacles” means one who is free from even a single obstacle among the ten obstacles.

“As soon as she has laid down the burden” means that even if she sews it later after having laid down the burden, there is indeed an offense; this is the meaning. The rest is self-evident. The origin (samuṭṭhāna) of the laying down of the burden is:

non-action (akiriya), release through perception (saññāvimokkha), with consciousness (sacittaka), a worldly transgression (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), unwholesome consciousness (akusalacitta), and painful feeling (dukkhavedanā).
The Third Training Rule. 4.
Commentary on the Fourth Training Rule: 898–9.
Regarding the fourth [rule]—*pañca ahāni* means five days; *pañcāham* means for five days; *pañcāhikam* means pertaining to five days. The distribution of the outer robes (*saṅghāṭī*).

“Moving about with the *saṅghāṭi*”: the meaning is the exchanging of the five robes that have received the name *saṅghāṭi* either by way of being used or by way of being dyed, in the sense of being stitched together. For this very reason, the word-commentary says, “on the fifth day, five robes,” and so forth.
Regarding the phrase “there is an offense of *pācittiya*”: here, there is one offense for one robe, and five offenses for five robes.
900. “In times of distress” means: when a highly valuable robe cannot be used due to fear of thieves and the like;
in such a misfortune, there is no offense. The rest is self-evident. The origin of the rule regarding the *kaṭhina* (the robe-making ceremony) is:
non-action, not involving liberation through perception, without mental intention, an offense by formal precept, bodily action, vocal action, three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
The Fourth Training Rule. 5. Commentary on the Fifth Training Rule: 903.
Regarding the fifth—*cīvarasaṅkamanīyaṃ* means a robe that should be transferred; the meaning is a robe taken from another's possession without asking permission, which must then be returned.
906. "In times of distress" means: if thieves carry off what is uncovered or unworn, there is no offense for one who wears it in such times of distress.

The rest is self-evident. Regarding the origin of the rule (Kathina-samutthāna): it is an action that is not non-action; it is not characterized by perception or liberation; it is without mental intention; it is an offense by formal rule (paṇṇattivajja);
it is bodily action and verbal action; it involves three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The Fifth Training Rule.
6. Commentary on the Sixth Training Rule. 909–10.
Regarding the sixth: “another requisite” refers to anything whatsoever, such as a bowl-stand and so forth, or ghee, oil, and so forth.
"Another. Regarding "benefit": she asks, "How much do you wish to give as the price?
and they reply, "It is this much. If she then says, "Wait a moment; the cloth is currently expensive;
when the cotton arrives in a few days, it will be of equal value," and thus prevents the transaction, there is no offense. The rest is self-evident.

It has three origins: it is a functional action (*kiriya*), liberation through perception (*saññāvimokkha*), associated with consciousness (*sacittaka*), a worldly offense (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), verbal action (*vacīkamma*), unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*), and possesses three feelings (*tivedana*).
This is the sixth training rule.
7. Commentary on the Seventh Training Rule.

911. Regarding the seventh [offense]: "They departed" means that even while waiting for others to arrive, they went here and there thinking, "Surely he will come for us too. "She should ward off" means she should prevent it. 915. Regarding the benefit (*ānisansa*):

There is no offense for one who wards off [the distribution] by showing a benefit, saying, "One cloth is not enough for one person; wait for now, it will appear in a few days, and then we shall share it. The rest is self-evident.

It has three origins: it is a functional (kiriya) action, with perception as its liberation, associated with consciousness, an offense by rule, bodily action, verbal action, consisting of three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
This is the seventh training rule.
8. Commentary on the Eighth Training Rule.
In the eighth [offense]: "Actors" (naṭā) are those who perform plays. "Dancers" (naṭakā) are those who dance.

"Acrobats" (laṅghakā) are those who perform feats of leaping on bamboo poles, ropes, and the like. "Sorcerers" (sokajjhāyikā) are illusionists. "Water-pot jugglers" (kumbhathūṇikā) are those who play with small pots;
some also call them "bimbisaka-performers. "He incurs an offense of expiation" (deti āpatti pācittiyassa).
In this case, the offenses are to be understood according to the counting of robes. The rest is self-evident.

It has six origins: it is an action, not involving liberation through perception, without mental involvement, an offense by formal rule, bodily action, verbal action, associated with three types of consciousness, and associated with three types of feeling.
This is the eighth training rule.
9. Commentary on the Ninth Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 921–4.
Regarding the ninth: "When there is a weak expectation of robe-cloth" means when the expectation of receiving robe-cloth is weak. As for "the benefit":
although they say, "Venerable lady, we are not able [to give]," [one thinks], "But now their cotton will arrive; they are faithful and devoted."
There is no offense for one who prevents [the gift] by showing the benefit in this way: "A man will come; he will certainly give it. The rest is self-evident.

This training rule has three origins: it is an action, it is liberated from perception, it involves a conscious state of mind, it is a worldly offense, it is bodily action, it is verbal action, it is unwholesome consciousness, and it is associated with three feelings.
This is the ninth training rule.
10. Commentary on the Tenth Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 927.
Regarding the tenth [rule]: "They shall not grant the suspension of the Kathina"—of what kind should the suspension of the Kathina be granted, and of what kind should it not be granted?
That for which the benefit rooted in the spreading (*atthāra*) is great, while that rooted in the suspension (*ubbhāra*) is small—such a case should not be granted.
However, for one for whom the benefit rooted in spreading [the cloth] is small and the benefit rooted in taking it up is great, such a person should be given [the cloth].
Even if there is no benefit, it must still be given for the sake of protecting the faith. 931. Regarding "benefit":

there is no offense for one who refuses [the cloth] after pointing out a benefit such as, "The Bhikkhunī-saṅgha’s robes are worn out; there will be a great gain resulting from the benefit of the Kathina ceremony. The rest is self-evident.

It has three origins: it is a functional action (*kiriya*), liberation through perception (*saññāvimokkha*), associated with consciousness (*sacittaka*), an offense against worldly convention (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), verbal action (*vacīkamma*), unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*), and possesses three feelings (*tivedana*).
This is the tenth training rule.
The third chapter, the Chapter on Nakedness (*Naggavagga*), is concluded.
4. The Chapter on Lying Down (Tuvaṭṭavagga) 1.
Commentary on the First Training Rule (Paṭhamasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) 933.
Regarding the first training rule of the Chapter on Lying Down: "tuvaṭṭeyyuṃ" means they would lie down. The rest is self-evident.

The origin of the offense regarding the wool of a goat: it is a functional (kiriya) action, not associated with liberation through perception, without consciousness, an offense by way of formal rule (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action, associated with three types of consciousness, and associated with three types of feeling.
This is the first training rule.
2. Commentary on the Second Training Rule (Dutiyasikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā) 937.

Regarding the second [rule]: "Those who have one common covering and one common upper garment" (*ekattharaṇapāvuraṇā*) means those who lie down after spreading out one end of a portable rug, blanket, mat, or similar item, and putting on the other end as an upper garment. This is a designation for those who lie down in this manner.
940. “Having shown the demarcation” means that there is no offense for those who lie down after placing either a saffron robe, a walking staff, or even a waistband in between.
The rest is self-evident. This offense has its origin in wool;

it is a formal act (kiriya), not released by confession (no-saññā-vimokkha), without a mental component (acittaka), an offense of transgression by rule (paṇṇatti-vajja), bodily action (kāya-kamma), associated with three types of consciousness (ticitta), and associated with three types of feeling (tivedana).
The Second Training Rule. 3. Commentary on the Third Training Rule: 941.

Regarding the third [rule]: “of noble and distinguished standing” means she is called “noble” because she has gone forth from a distinguished family and because of her excellence in virtuous qualities.
*Sambhāvitā*: "Possessed by envy" means overcome by envy; the meaning is "overpowered. *Saññattibahulā*: those who have much persuasion;
the meaning is "those who spend the day persuading the great multitude. *Viññattibahulā*: those who have much entreaty.
"Entreaty" (*viññatti*) should be understood as making known [one's purpose] through various methods such as reasons and examples, not merely begging.

943. Offenses are to be understood by counting the turns while walking back and forth (*caṅkamana*). In the cases of "standing" and so forth, they are counted by the number of applications (*payoga*). In the cases of "reciting" and so forth, they are counted by the number of phrases (*pada*) and so on.

The rest is self-evident. It has three origins: it is both action and non-action; it is resolved through perception; it is associated with consciousness; it is a worldly offense; it is bodily action and verbal action; it is unwholesome consciousness; and it is painful feeling. This is the third training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
4. Commentary on the Fourth Training Rule 949.
Regarding the fourth [rule]: "When there is an obstacle" means when any of the ten kinds of obstacles exist.
"Having sought, she does not obtain" means she does not obtain another attendant. "If she is ill" means if she herself is ill. "In times of distress" means in such a state of calamity.
There is no offense if [the condition] exists. The remainder is self-evident.

This origin is through the laying down of the burden; it is non-action, liberation through perception, accompanied by consciousness, a worldly transgression, bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome thought, and painful feeling.
This is the fourth training rule.
5. Commentary on the Fifth Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 952.
Regarding the fifth rule—concerning the phrase "orders another"—if she is ordered, "Throw her out," and she passes through many doors in a single effort, it is a single offense.
However, if she is ordered, "Pass through this door and that door," [it is a separate offense for each].
If he exceeds [the limit], there are offenses according to the number of doors. The rest is self-evident. It has three origins:

it is an act of doing (*kiriya*), liberation through perception (*saññāvimokkha*), and accompanied by consciousness (*sacittaka*); it is a worldly offense (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), and verbal action (*vacīkamma*); it is an unwholesome state of mind (*akusalacitta*) and painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
This is the fifth training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
6. Commentary on the Sixth Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 955.

Regarding the sixth: everything is self-evident. Its origin is through formal admonition (samanubhāsana). It is non-action (akiriya), release through perception (saññāvimokkha), accompanied by consciousness (sacittaka), a worldly offense (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), unwholesome consciousness (akusalacitta), and painful feeling (dukkhavedanā).
This is the sixth training rule.
7–9. Commentary on the Seventh, Eighth, and Ninth Training Rules (Sikkhāpada). 961.

Regarding the seventh, eighth, and ninth [rules], everything is already clear. All three originate from the wool of a sheep (*eḷakaloma*); they are formal actions (*kiriyā*), not involving liberation through perception (*no-saññā-vimokkha*), unintentional (*acittaka*), offenses by way of formal rule (*paṇṇatti-vajja*), bodily actions (*kāya-kamma*), and possess three types of consciousness and three types of feeling (*ticitta-tivedanā*).
These are the seventh, eighth, and ninth training rules.
10. Commentary on the Tenth Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 973.
Regarding the tenth: "Confined" (*āhundarikā*) means crowded or obstructed.
975. Regarding "merely having laid down the burden": even if one departs after having laid down the burden, it is indeed an offense.
The meaning: there is no offense for one who travels five *yojanas* after having performed the invitation (*pavāraṇā*). There is simply nothing to be said regarding the six [cases].
However, if she goes three [yojanas] and returns by that same path, it is not permitted; it is permitted to return by a different path. Regarding the nine hundred and seventy-six [rules]:
among the ten kinds of obstacles (*antarāya*), if she has set out thinking, "I will go elsewhere," but a river is in flood...
If one has arrived [at a destination], or if there are robbers on the road, or if a storm arises, it is permissible to turn back. The rest is self-evident.

The origin of the first *pārājika* offense is: non-action (*akiriya*), liberation through perception (*saññāvimokkha*), with consciousness (*sacittaka*), a worldly transgression (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), unwholesome mind (*akusalacitta*), and painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
The tenth training rule.
The fourth section: On Rubbing.
5. The section on picture galleries.
1. Commentary on the First Training Rule (Paṭhamasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) 978.
Regarding the first training rule in the Chapter on Painted Halls (Cittāgāravagga): "A royal residence" (*rājāgāra*) means a king’s pleasure house.
"A painted hall" (*cittāgāra*) means a picture gallery for recreation. "A park" (*ārāma*) means a pleasure grove. "A garden" (*uyyāna*) means a pleasure garden. "A lotus pond" (*pokkharaṇī*)...
[He goes] to a pleasure lotus pond. For that very reason, it is said in the word-commentary (padabhājana): "Wherever [it may be], for the king to play," and so forth.
Regarding the offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for going to see [it]: here, the wrong-doing is according to the number of steps taken.
However, regarding the phrase "if she sees while standing in one place": if she stands in exactly one spot and sees all five [lotuses] without lifting her foot, [there is no offense].
There is one *pācittiya* offense. However, for one who sees while looking toward various directions, there are separate offenses for each instance.
For a bhikkhu, however, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense in all cases.
981. "Standing in the monastery" means that they are building royal palaces and so forth within the monastery grounds; for one who sees these, there is no offense. While walking...
Or, if she sees them while on the road as she is coming or going for the purpose of alms-food and so forth, there is no offense.
"Having gone because of some business": if she goes into the presence of a king due to some business and sees them, there is no offense.
"In times of distress": if she enters [the house] because she is threatened by someone and sees them, there is no offense. The rest is self-evident.

The origin [of the offense] concerning Eḷakaloma: it is a functional (kiriya) action, not associated with liberation through perception (nosaññāvimokkha), without consciousness (acittaka), a worldly transgression (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), an unwholesome state of mind (akusalacitta), and possesses three types of feeling (tivedana).
This is the first training rule.
2. Commentary on the Second Training Rule.
982. Regarding the second [offense]: the offenses are to be understood by counting the applications in the acts of sitting down and lying down. The rest is self-evident.

Originating from wool: it is an action, not involving liberation through perception, without mental intention, an offense by formal rule, bodily action, consisting of three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
This is the second training rule.
3. Commentary on the Third Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 988.
Regarding the third: "To twist and turn" means that for as much as is pulled by the hand, there is one offense when it is wound around the paste.

However, prior to the spinning, starting from the initial separation of the cotton, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for every application according to the number of times the hand is obstructed.
989. *Kantitasutta* means that one weaves a thread of cotton or the like after having spun it together, or one re-weaves what has been poorly woven.

The rest is self-evident. It originates from sheep’s wool; it is an action (*kiriyā*), not associated with perception or liberation (*no-saññā-vimokkha*), without consciousness (*acittaka*), an offense by formal rule (*paṇṇatti-vajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), and possesses three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The Third Training Rule. 4.
Commentary on the Fourth Training Rule: 992.

Regarding the fourth rule—in phrases such as “rice gruel” and so forth—for all prior preparations beginning with the pounding of rice, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) according to the number of preparations. For rice gruels and boiled rice, there are offenses of expiation (*pācittiya*) according to the number of vessels; for hard foods (*khādanīya*) and so forth, they are according to the number of items.

993. Regarding "rice-gruel and drinks": when rice-gruel or meals for the Saṅgha are being prepared by people for the sake of the Saṅgha, there is no offense for one who cooks anything at all as an assistant to them.
It is permissible to act as an assistant in the worship of a cetiya and offer perfumes and other such items. Regarding "one's own attendant":
even if one’s mother or father comes, [it is permissible] for anything whatsoever...
Having had a fan or a broomstick made and placed in the service area, it is permissible to cook anything at all.
The rest is self-evident. The origin and other factors are exactly like those of the third rule.
This is the fourth training rule.
5. Commentary on the Fifth Training Rule 996. Regarding the fifth [rule]:
"In the absence of an obstacle" means when ten kinds of obstacles are absent. Having set aside her burden and deciding later, she decides only after having already incurred an offense. 998.
"Having sought, she does not find" means she does not find companion bhikkhunīs. The rest is self-evident.

Originating from laying down the burden: non-action, liberation through perception, accompanied by consciousness, a worldly offense, bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome consciousness, and painful feeling.
This is the fifth training rule.
6. Commentary on the Sixth Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 999.

Regarding the sixth [rule]: everything should be understood according to the method already explained under the training rule concerning householders (*āgārika*) in the section on the naked ones (*naggavagga*).

However, this is the distinction: that [previous rule] has six origins (*samuṭṭhāna*), whereas this one—because it is stated as "with one's own hand" (*sahatthā*)—has the origin of wool-removal (*eḷakaloma*).

It is a functional state (kiriyā), not associated with liberation through perception (no-saññā-vimokkha), mindless (acittaka), an offense by way of formal rule (paṇṇatti-vajja), bodily action (kāya-kamma), consisting of three types of consciousness, and associated with three types of feeling.
This is the sixth training rule.
7. Commentary on the Seventh Training Rule.

1007. Regarding the seventh [offense]: "again by way of another method" means on a subsequent occasion. "In cases of distress" (*āpadāsu*) refers to situations such as when thieves steal even well-secured, high-value robes after they have been removed from the body;
in such cases of distress, there is no offense for one who wears them without having formally relinquished them.

The rest is self-evident. The origin of the *Kathina* rule: it originates from body and speech, and from body, speech, and mind. It is both action and non-action, not characterized by liberation through perception, and is without mental intention (*acittaka*). It is an offense of formal prescription (*paṇṇattivajja*), consisting of bodily action and verbal action. It involves three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The Seventh Training Rule. 8. Commentary on the Eighth Training Rule: 1008.
Regarding the eighth—*anissajjitvā* means not having given [the item] for the purpose of guarding it; the meaning is: not having requested permission by saying, "Please look after this."
"Having sought [a caregiver] but not finding one" means she does not find a person to look after her. "When she is ill" means when she is unable to speak.
"In times of distress" refers to such situations as when the kingdom is falling apart and they depart, abandoning their residence;
in such calamities, there is no offense. The remainder is self-evident. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and other factors are exactly the same as those of the preceding training rule.
The Eighth Training Rule. 9.
Commentary on the Ninth Training Rule. 1015–6. Regarding the ninth:

"External and unbeneficial" refers to various types such as the arts of elephants, horses, chariots, archery, and swordsmanship; the practice of *āthabbana* (Atharvanic magic); the use of stakes; the employment of spells for subjugation (*vasīkaraṇa*), causing emaciation (*sosāpana*), incantations (*manta*), and medicinal applications (*agada*).

"Causing injury to others. "Paritta" (protection) includes all types, such as the *yakkha*-paritta, the *nāga*-maṇḍala, and so forth. The rest is self-evident. Regarding the origin of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*):

it originates from speech and from speech-mind; it is an action (*kiriyā*), not accompanied by liberation through perception (*no-saññā-vimokkha*), without consciousness (*acittaka*), an offense by formal precept (*paṇṇatti-vajja*), verbal action (*vacī-kamma*), associated with three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
This is the ninth training rule.
10. Commentary on the Tenth Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 1018.

In the tenth [rule], the word "should cause to recite" (*vāceyya*) is the specific distinction; the remainder should be understood according to the method already stated for the ninth rule, together with its origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other factors.
This concludes the commentary on the tenth training rule.
The fifth chapter, the Chapter on Painted Halls (Cittāgāravagga).
6. The Chapter on Monasteries (Ārāmavagga).
1. Commentary on the First Training Rule (Paṭhamasikkhāpada).

1025. Regarding the first training rule of the Ārāma-vagga: “For one who crosses the enclosure” and “for one who enters the precincts,” herein there is a *dukkaṭa* for the first step and a *pācittiya* for the second step.
1027. “Looking back at the heads”: if she enters while looking back at the heads of the nuns who are entering first, there is no offense.
“Wherever there are nuns”: wherever nuns have entered first and are engaged in recitation, paying homage to a cetiya, and so forth...
They are doing so; it is permissible to go there thinking, "I shall go into their presence. "In times of distress" means she is being oppressed by someone;
in such times of distress, it is permissible to enter. The rest is self-evident.

Originating from the laying down of the burden—this is a non-intentional action (akiriya), with consciousness as its liberation (saññāvimokkha), accompanied by thought (sacittaka), an offense by rule (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), and verbal action (vacīkamma); it consists of three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The First Training Rule. 2. Commentary on the Second Training Rule. 1028. Regarding the second [rule]:
"Venerable Kappita" refers to this elder who was among the thousand matted-hair ascetics. "He gathered" means he moved [the bowl].

"Saṃhaṭo" means transferred. "Kāsāvaṭo" refers to barbers who perform their work after having put on a yellow robe; it was with reference to them that this was said. The rest is self-evident. It has three origins:
it is an action, it is liberated by perception, it involves the mind, it is a worldly offense, it is bodily action, it is verbal action, it is unwholesome consciousness, and it is painful feeling.
This is the second training rule.
3. Commentary on the Third Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 1036.

Regarding the third rule: "With the intention of instructing" means that there is no offense for one who speaks while standing on the side of instruction in the manner of saying, "Now you too are foolish and incompetent," and so forth.
The remainder is self-evident. The origin (samuṭṭhāna) and other factors are exactly the same as those of the preceding training rule.
The Third Training Rule. 4.
Commentary on the Fourth Training Rule: 1037.
Regarding the fourth [rule]—everything is self-evident. It has four origins: from body, from body and speech, and from body and mind.
It originates from body, speech, and mind. Because an offense occurs when one who has been invited eats without asking permission, it may be both an act and a non-act;
because an offense occurs when one who has been dismissed from the meal eats—whether having requested what is permissible or not—it is an act.
It is not to be released through recognition, is without mental concomitants, is an offense of formal rule, and is an action of body and speech.
Three minds, three feelings.
The fourth training rule.
5. Commentary on the fifth training rule.
1043. Regarding the fifth: *kula-macchara* is stinginess regarding families; one who possesses such stinginess regarding families is a "family-stingy woman" (*kulamaccharinī*).
Alternatively, she is a family-stingy woman because she is stingy toward the family. "Disparagement of the family" means saying of that family:
"They are faithless and lack confidence. "Disparagement of the bhikkhunīs" means saying: "The bhikkhunīs are immoral and of evil character."
1045. "Existing" refers to an existing fault or disadvantage belonging either to a family or to the bhikkhunīs. The rest is self-evident.

This offense has three origins: it is an action (kiriya), liberation through perception (saññāvimokkha), accompanied by consciousness (sacittaka), a worldly transgression (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), unwholesome consciousness (akusalacitta), and painful feeling (dukkhavedanā).
The Fifth Training Rule. 6.
Commentary on the Sixth Training Rule. 1048. Regarding the sixth:

"For the purpose of exhortation" means for the sake of the heavy rules (*garudhamma*). "For the purpose of communal living" means for the sake of requesting the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, has already been stated in the commentary on the training rule concerning the exhorter of bhikkhunīs.

The origin of the offense regarding the wool of a goat: it is a functional (kiriya) action, not associated with liberation through perception, without consciousness, an offense by way of formal rule (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action, consisting of three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
This is the sixth training rule.
7. Commentary on the Seventh Training Rule.

1053. Regarding the seventh [offense]: "Having sought, he does not obtain" means he does not obtain a bhikkhunī. The rest is self-evident. The detailed explanation for this is also stated in the *Bhikkhunovādaka*.

It has its origin in the laying down of the burden; it is non-action, liberation through perception, associated with the mind, a worldly offense, bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome thought, and painful feeling.
This is the seventh training rule.
8. Commentary on the Eighth Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 1056. Regarding the eighth:

by the terms “a single legal act” (*ekakamma*) and so forth, only the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies are mentioned. The remainder is self-evident. The detailed exposition of this rule has already been stated in the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga*.
Its origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) is: non-performance, release through perception, involving the mind, a worldly offense, bodily action, unwholesome consciousness, and painful feeling.
The Eighth Training Rule. 9. Commentary on the Ninth Training Rule: 1058.
Regarding the ninth—everything is quite clear. The detailed explanation for this one as well has already been stated in the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga*.

Originating from laying down the burden: non-action, liberation through perception, associated with consciousness, a worldly offense, bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome consciousness, and painful feeling.
This is the ninth training rule.
10. Commentary on the Tenth Training Rule.
1062. In the tenth [offense]: *pasākheti* means "he spreads apart the lower body. For it is called the *pasākha* because, like a branch of that tree, both thighs extend out from it;
therefore, it is called the *pasākha*. 1065. Regarding the words "break," etc.: if he commands all of them, saying, "Break it! Cut it!
and the other does exactly so, he incurs six offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) and six offenses of expiation (*pācittiya*). Furthermore, if he commands thus: "Lay follower..."
"Do whatever is to be done here, do it all," and he performs all of them, including the causing of schism and so forth;
for each single utterance, there are six *dukkaṭa* offenses and six *pācittiya* offenses, making twelve offenses in total.

However, if he commands him by saying only once, "Do this"—referring even to the causing of schism and so forth—and he performs all of them, then [the offense applies] only to that which was commanded.
If one performs it, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya). In the remaining cases, there is no offense. The rest is self-evident.

The origin of this rule regarding the *kaṭhina* robe is as follows: it is an action that may or may not be performed; it is not a liberation through perception; it is without mental intention; it is an offense by formal precept; it is bodily action and verbal action; it involves three types of consciousness and three types of feeling. This is the tenth training rule.
The sixth chapter: The Chapter on Parks (Ārāmavagga).
7. The Chapter on Pregnant Women (Gabbhinivagga).
1. Commentary on the First Training Rule (Paṭhamasikkhāpada).
1069. Regarding the first training rule of the section on pregnant women: "one who has conceived" means one in whom a being has entered the womb.
This is the first training rule.
2. Commentary on the second training rule.
1073–4. Regarding the second [offense]: “*Pāyantim*” means one who is nursing at the breast. “*Mātā vā hoti*” means she is either the mother of the child whom she nurses or his nurse.
The rest is self-evident. Both [offenses] have three origins:

they are courses of action (*kiriya*), liberated from perception (*saññāvimokkha*), accompanied by consciousness (*sacittaka*), offenses of formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), and verbal action (*vacīkamma*); they possess three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The Second Training Rule. 3. Commentary on the Third Training Rule: 1077.
Regarding the third—why did he cause the formal authorization for training (*sikkhāsammuti*) to be given? [Because] "women are fickle; there are two..."
"Without training in the six dharmas, one who attempts to fulfill the precepts will become weary;
but having trained, he will not be weary later, and will reach deliverance," [the Buddha] thus caused [him] to undertake [the vows].
"For two years, I undertake the undertaking of abstaining from taking life, without transgressing it. This is that [vow].
"Abstinence from taking life" is the training rule (sikkhāpada) that has been prescribed;
the meaning is: "I undertake and observe that training rule of abstinence from taking life, having made a commitment not to transgress it for two years. This same method applies everywhere.
These six training rules must indeed be given even to one who has gone forth at sixty years of age; one who has not trained in these [rules] should not be ordained.
The Third Training Rule. 4. Commentary on the Fourth Training Rule: 1084.

Regarding the fourth—everything is quite clear. However, if the formal authorization for ordination (*vuṭṭhānasammuti*) has not been granted previously, it must indeed be granted even at the ordination hall (*upasampadamāḷaka*). These two are also called "great trainee nuns" (*mahāsikkhamānā*).
The Fourth Training Rule. 5. Commentary on the Fifth Training Rule: 1090.

Regarding the fifth—although there is no offense for one who ordains a girl less than twelve years old while perceiving her to be of full age, she nevertheless remains unordained. The rest is self-evident.
The Fifth Training Rule. 6. Commentary on the Sixth Training Rule: 1095.

Regarding the sixth—after granting the formal authorization for training (*sikkhāsammuti*) to a married girl who is ten years old, it is permissible to confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon her when she has reached twelve full years of age.
The Sixth Training Rule. 7. Explanation of the Seventh Training Rule.

1101. Regarding the seventh: everything is self-evident. The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth are also exactly the same as those stated for the second [rule] in all cases. This, however, is the distinction: wherever there is a formal agreement (*sammuti*), there is both performance and non-performance.
The Seventh Training Rule. 8. Commentary on the Eighth Training Rule: 1108.

Regarding the eighth—*na anuggaṇhāpeyya*: she should not cause [another] to assist by saying, "Noble lady, give her the recitation and so forth"; thus, she should not cause assistance to be rendered through recitation and the like.
"Having sought another" means that after seeking another, she does not find one; she herself becomes ill and is unable to give the recitation and so forth.
For her, there is no offense. The rest is self-evident. This is an offense originating from the laying down of the burden (dhuranikkhepa):
it is non-action, released by intention, involving consciousness, a worldly transgression, bodily action, verbal action, an unwholesome state of mind, and painful feeling.
The Eighth Training Rule.
9. Commentary on the Ninth Training Rule: 1113.
Regarding the ninth—“one should not attend upon [her]”—this refers to [attending by providing] powder, clay, tooth-sticks, and water for rinsing the mouth. Thus...
One should not attend upon him for any such purpose. The rest is self-evident. The origin of the first *pārājika* offense is:
non-action, liberation through perception, with consciousness, a worldly transgression, bodily action, unwholesome mind, and painful feeling.
This is the ninth training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
10. Commentary on the Tenth Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 1116.
Regarding the tenth: "Neither should she take it away herself" means she should not go taking it with her.

"Nor should she have it taken away" means she should not command another, saying, "Noble lady, take this and go. The rest here is self-evident. This offense is originated by the act of relinquishing one's responsibility (*dhuranikkhepa*).
— non-action, liberation through perception, accompanied by consciousness, blameworthy according to worldly standards, bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome mind, and painful feeling.
This is the tenth training rule.
The seventh chapter, the Section on Pregnant Women, is concluded.
8. The Chapter on the Maidenhood (Kumāribhūtavagga) 1–2–3.
Commentary on the First, Second, and Third Training Rules (Sikkhāpada). 1119.
The first, second, and third training rules of the Chapter on the Maidenhood [are to be understood] by means of three training rules concerning those who have entered the household life (gihigata).
They are similar. However, those two who were the very first *sikkhamānās* should be understood as having already exceeded twenty years of age.

Whether they have entered the household life (*gihigatā*) or not, they should be called simply *sikkhamānās*; they should not be called "those who have entered the household life" or "maidens" (*kumāribhūtā*).

Having granted the authorization for training (*sikkhāsammuti*) to one who has entered the household life when she is ten years old, her full ordination (*upasampadā*) takes place when she is twelve years old.
It should be performed. Having granted her the formal authorization (*sammuti*) at the age of eleven, it should be performed at the age of thirteen;
or, having granted the authorization at the ages of twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, or seventeen, the full ordination (*upasampadā*) should be performed at the age of twenty.

From the age of eighteen onwards, however, she may be called either "one who has gone to a householder" (*gihigatā*) or "a maiden" (*kumāribhūtā*); yet, while she is a maiden, she is not [considered] one who has gone to a householder.
They should not be called "those who have gone forth as householders"; they should simply be called "maidens.

Furthermore, it is not permissible to call a *mahāsikkhamānā* (a senior trainee nun) "one who has gone forth as a householder," nor is it permissible to call her "a maiden"; however, by virtue of having been granted permission for training, it is permissible to call all three of them "trainees" (*sikkhamānā*).
The first, second, and third [rules]. 4–5–6.
Commentary on the Fourth, Fifth, and Sixth Training Rules. 1136.
Regarding the fourth, fifth, and sixth, everything is already clear. All are originated by three [modes]. The fourth...
It is functional, liberation through perception, associated with consciousness, censurable by rule, bodily action, verbal action, threefold in mind, and threefold in feeling.

The fifth [category] is neither-functional-nor-non-functional, liberation through perception, associated with consciousness, censurable by rule, bodily action, verbal action, threefold in mind, and threefold in feeling. And herein, that which is to be delimited by the Saṅgha...
It has been stated; the meaning is that it must be examined. The sixth [factor] is:

action (*kiriya*), liberation through perception (*saññāvimokkha*), accompanied by consciousness (*sacittaka*), blameworthy according to worldly standards (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), verbal action (*vacīkamma*), unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*), and painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
Furthermore, as for what is stated here as "having delimited" (*paricchinditvā*), the meaning is "having examined" (*upaparikkhitvā*).
The Fourth, Fifth, and Sixth Training Rules.
7. Commentary on the Seventh Training Rule.

1150. Regarding the seventh: everything is self-evident. It is originated by the laying down of the burden; it is an action, free from [wrong] perception, accompanied by consciousness, a world-transgression, bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome consciousness, and painful feeling.
The Seventh Training Rule. 8. Commentary on the Eighth Training Rule: 1154.
Regarding the eighth as well—everything is entirely clear. The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth are also exactly the same as in the preceding [rule].
The Eighth Training Rule. 9. Commentary on the Ninth Training Rule: 1158.
Regarding the ninth—by making an appointment at a "dwelling place of sorrow," she causes sorrow to enter within men.
"Abodes of sorrow" means that which is an abode of sorrow. For this very reason it is said: "Those called 'abodes of sorrow' produce suffering for others.
Alternatively, just as the owners of a house [are associated with] the house, these women also enter into sorrow when they do not obtain union with men.
Thus, because that which enters them becomes their abode, they are "abodes of sorrow. Therefore it is said: "They enter into sorrow. "Not knowing" means...
“They come in such a way, not knowing [the danger]. The rest is self-evident. It has three origins:

it is an action (kiriya), liberation through perception (saññāvimokkha), associated with consciousness (sacittaka), an offense by formal rule (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), three types of consciousness (ticitta), and three types of feeling (tivedana).
This is the ninth training rule.
10. Commentary on the Tenth Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 1164.

Regarding the tenth rule: *anāpuccha* means without having asked for permission. The nuns must ask permission on two occasions—both at the time of going forth (*pabbajjā*) and at the time of full ordination (*upasampadā*). However, in the case of monks, it is permissible even if they have asked only once.
1165. *Ajānantī* means not knowing the presence of her mother or other relatives. The rest is self-evident. This is the heading for a new class of offenses (*samuṭṭhāna*).
It has four origins: it originates from speech, from body and speech, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. How so?
In cases such as the formal act of rehabilitation (*abbhāna-kamma*), when those sitting within a partial boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*) for some business say, "Call the trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*);
we shall ordain her right here," and they thus perform the ordination; in this way, it originates from speech. Starting from the dwelling...
Having said, "I will confer full ordination," it arises from body and speech for one who goes to a demarcated boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*).
For one who commits a transgression after knowing the established rule in both instances, it arises from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind.

Because it is the conferring of full ordination without having obtained permission, it is a *kriyākiriya* (action-inaction), not involving liberation through perception (*nosaññāvimokkha*), without consciousness (*acittaka*), and an offense by rule (*paṇṇattivajja*).
Bodily action, verbal action, the three types of consciousness, and the three types of feeling.
The tenth training rule.
11. Commentary on the eleventh training rule.

1167–8. Regarding the eleventh [offense]: “By giving consent while on *pārivāsa* (probation)” means by the giving of consent by one who is undergoing probation. In this context, there are four kinds of being on probation:
probation of the assembly (*parisapārivāsiya*), probation of the night (*rattipārivāsiya*), probation of consent (*chandapārivāsiya*), and probation of intention (*ajjhāsayapārivāsiya*).
Among these, “probation of the assembly” refers to when monks have gathered for some business, and then—
Either a cloud arises, or a tumult breaks out, or people come swarming over;
the monks rise up without having relinquished their consent, thinking, "We have no space here, we shall go elsewhere. This is the "setting aside of the assembly.
Although it is a setting aside of the assembly, because the consent has not been relinquished, it is permissible to perform the formal act (*kamma*).
Again, monks having assembled at night, thinking, "We shall perform the Uposatha and other duties," request one [monk], saying, "Let us listen to the Dhamma until everyone has assembled.
While that monk is still delivering a discourse on the Dhamma, the dawn breaks.
If they had sat down intending, "We shall perform the Uposatha on the fourteenth day," but it turns out to be the fifteenth, they must perform it accordingly.

It is permissible. If those who have sat down to perform the fifteen-day observance fail to perform the Uposatha on the first day of the fortnight (the *pāṭipada*), it is not permissible for them to perform the Uposatha;
however, it is permissible for them to perform other business of the Saṅgha. This is called "postponement by night" (*rattipārivāsiya*).
Furthermore, if monks have sat down thinking, "We shall perform some business of the Saṅgha, such as a formal act of rehabilitation (*abbhāna*) and so forth," and therein one [monk]...
A monk who recited the *nakṣatra* (astrological) texts spoke thus: "Today the constellation is ominous; do not perform this work.

Following his words, they relinquished their intention and remained sitting right there. Then another person arrived and said, "The opportunity has passed by while you were waiting for the constellation," and added, "What is the use of the constellation? Go ahead! This...

There are two kinds of *pārivāsiya*: that which is set aside by consent (*chandapārivāsiya*) and that which is set aside by intention (*ajjhāsayapārivāsiya*). Regarding this *pārivāsiya*, it is not permissible to perform a formal act (*kamma*) without bringing back the purity of consent (*chanda-pārisuddhi*).
"When the assembly has risen" means when the assembly has risen either by relinquishing consent through body or speech, or merely by the act of relinquishing consent.
1169. There is no offense if the assembly has not risen: there is no offense if [the formal act] is performed while the assembly has not dismissed its consent and has not risen.

The rest is self-evident. This [offense] has three origins: it is an action, it is liberated by perception, it involves consciousness, it is an offense of transgression, it is bodily action, it is verbal action, it consists of three types of consciousness, and it consists of three types of feeling.
The Eleventh Training Rule. 12.
Commentary on the Twelfth Training Rule. 1170. Regarding the twelfth:
“the dwelling place is not approved” means the residence is insufficient. The rest is self-evident. The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other factors are exactly the same as in the preceding rule.
The Twelfth Training Rule. 13.
Commentary on the Thirteenth Training Rule:

1175. Regarding the thirteenth—“one year, two”: she ordains two [novices] within one year, with a single year intervening. The rest is self-evident. The origin and other details are also similar to what has been stated.
The Thirteenth Training Rule.
The Eighth Chapter: On Maidens.
9. The Chapter on Umbrellas and Footwear.
1. Commentary on the First Training Rule (Paṭhamasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) 1181.
Regarding the first training rule of the Chapter on Umbrellas (Chattavagga): "If one carries [it] even once, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

Even if one carries it for an entire day while traveling on a road, provided it is done in a single continuous motion, there is only one offense. If, however, having reached mud or similar terrain, one takes off the sandals...

If she goes while still carrying the sunshade, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Moreover, if she sees a road or similar obstacle and, having lowered the sunshade, goes while still wearing her sandals, it is likewise an offense of wrong-doing.
If she lowers the sunshade, takes off the sandals, and then puts them back on again, there is another offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Thus, the offenses should be understood according to the number of applications. The rest is self-evident.
The origin of the offense regarding the wool of a goat is: an action; not associated with liberation through perception; without consciousness; an offense by formal rule; bodily action;
consisting of three types of consciousness; and having three types of feeling.
This is the first training rule.
2. Commentary on the Second Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 1184.

Regarding the second [rule]: "Traveling by vehicle"—here too, for one who has alighted and boards again and again, the offenses should be understood according to the count of each individual act. The remainder is exactly as explained in the method stated for the first [rule].
This concludes the second training rule.
3. Commentary on the Third Training Rule (Tatiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) 1190.

Regarding the third [rule]: "They were scattered" means the gems were strewn about. Here too, for one who wears them after having removed them, there are offenses according to the number of applications. The origins and so forth are exactly as previously stated; the only difference here is that it involves an unwholesome mind.
This concludes the commentary on the third training rule.
4. Commentary on the Fourth Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 1194.

Regarding the fourth [rule]: among head-unguents and so forth, the number of offenses should be understood according to the specific item worn. The remainder is exactly as explained in the method stated for the third [rule].
This concludes the fourth training rule.
5. Commentary on the Fifth Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 1199.

Regarding the fifth: "With perfumes and cosmetics" means with both perfumes (*gandha*) and cosmetics (*vaṇṇaka*). The remainder is self-evident. The origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other factors are exactly the same as for the third rule.
Thus ends the commentary on the fifth training rule.
6. Commentary on the Sixth Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 1202.
Regarding the sixth: everything is exactly as stated for the fifth.
This is the sixth training rule.
7. Commentary on the Seventh Training Rule (Sattama-sikkhāpada) 1208–9.
Regarding the seventh rule—“If she causes herself to be massaged, there is an offense of *pācittiya*”: here, if she is massaged without releasing her hand, there is only one offense;
if she is massaged by repeatedly releasing her hand, there are offenses according to the number of applications (*payoga*). The same applies to being rubbed (*sambāhana*).

This is the method. "To one who is ill" means even to one afflicted by the fatigue of traveling on a journey. "In times of distress" refers to situations such as trembling of the body due to fear of thieves and so forth.
The remainder is self-evident. The origin and other characteristics are exactly like those of the third [offense].
This is the seventh training rule.
8–10. Commentary on the Eighth, Ninth, and Tenth Training Rules (Sikkhāpada). 1210.

Regarding the three training rules beginning with the eighth, the only difference [from the preceding] is that they apply to a trainee nun (sikkhamānā), a novice nun (sāmaṇerī), and a female householder (gihinī); the rest is exactly as stated for the seventh rule.
These are the eighth, ninth, and tenth training rules.
11. Commentary on the Eleventh Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 1214.
Regarding the eleventh: “In front of a bhikkhu” means directly facing him. This, however, should be understood as stated with reference to the immediate vicinity (upacāra).
The rest is self-evident. Origin: from body and speech; from body, speech, and mind.
And it arises from: non-intentional action, neither-perception-nor-liberation, mindless, an offense by rule, bodily action, verbal action, three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
This is the eleventh training rule.
12. Commentary on the Twelfth Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 1219–23.
Regarding the twelfth: *anokāsakataṃ* means not having made an opportunity [for questioning] by saying, "I shall ask at such-and-such a place.

For this very reason it is said: "*Anokāsakatan ti anāpucchaṃ*" (Not having made an opportunity means without asking permission). *Anodissa* means [not specifying], "I shall ask at such-and-such a place."

Having thus not fixed [the specific offense], but merely saying, "There is something to be asked; I ask you, Venerable Sir," the rest is self-evident. Regarding the origin of the offense of reciting the words:

it originates from speech and from speech-and-mind; it is functional (kiriyā) and non-functional (akiriya); it is not liberation through perception (nosaññāvimokkha); it is without thought (acittaka);
it is an offense by rule (paṇṇattivajja); it is verbal action (vacīkamma); it involves three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The Twelfth Training Rule. 13.
Commentary on the Thirteenth Training Rule. 1226. Regarding the thirteenth:
“Crossing over the enclosure”—if she crosses with one foot, it is an *dukkaṭa*; if with the second foot, it is a *pācittiya*. The same method applies to the precinct as well.
Regarding "one whose robe has been snatched away" and so forth, it should be understood that the word "robe" (*cīvara*) refers specifically to the *saṅkaccika* robe.
Regarding "in cases of distress": if the *saṅkaccika* is of great value, and a misfortune arises while she is walking after having put it on, there is no offense in such cases of distress.
The rest is self-evident. This offense originates from wool; it is an action (*kiriya*), not involving liberation through perception (*no-saññā-vimokkha*).
It is without thought, an offense by way of formal rule, bodily action, associated with three types of consciousness, and associated with three types of feeling.
This is the thirteenth training rule.
The ninth chapter, the Chapter on Umbrellas and Footwear, is concluded.
"Ladies, the one hundred and sixty-six *pācittiya* rules have been recited.
Herein, among all the minor rules (*khuddaka*), there are ninety-eight for *bhikkhunīs* and ninety-two for *bhikkhus*, making eight hundred and eighty training precepts (*sikkhāpada*) in total.

From these, the entire section on *bhikkhunīs*, as well as eating in succession (*paramparabhojana*), eating what is not left over (*anatirittabhojana*), and [eating] what has been brought by one who has not [first] had enough left over...

The invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), requesting fine food, the training rule concerning naked ascetics (*acelaka*), concealing a grave offense (*duṭṭhulla*), ordaining one who is less than twenty years of age,
traveling along a highway in company with a woman, entering a king’s inner palace,
entering a village at an improper time without asking permission from a monk who is present, and the sitting mat and the rainy-season robe— these are the twenty-two training rules (*sikkhāpada*).
It should be understood that, having set aside the remaining one hundred and sixty-six training rules, they have been recited by way of the recitation of the Pātimokkha.
Therefore he said: "Venerable ladies, the one hundred and sixty-six Pācittiya rules have been recited...
thus do I remember this."
In this regard, here is the summary of the determination of their origins:

the festival on a mountain top, the rule concerning picture galleries, the female waist-band, women’s ornaments, scents and cosmetics, scented sesame oil, and being rubbed or massaged by nuns and so forth—these ten training rules are unintentional offenses of worldly transgression (*lokavajja*).
This, however, is the intended meaning here: even without...

Because they must be committed by means of the mind, they are "without mind" (*acittaka*); however, because when the mind is present they must be committed through unwholesome [states of mind], they are "worldly offenses" (*lokavajja*).
The remaining ones are "without mind" and are exclusively "offenses by rule" (*paṇṇattivajja*). These include:

the disrobing of a female thief, traveling between villages, the training rule concerning the monastery, the seven rules starting from the beginning of the section on pregnant women, the five rules starting from the beginning of the section on unmarried girls, and the rule concerning association with men.

The giving of consent for one on probation (*pārivāsiya-chandadāna*), ordination every year (*anuvassa-vuṭṭhāpana*), and ordination at intervals (*ekantarika-vuṭṭhāpana*)—these nineteen training rules (*sikkhāpada*) are intentional offenses that are merely formal transgressions (*paṇṇattivajja*). All the remaining ones are intentional offenses that are natural transgressions (*lokavajja*).
Thus it is stated in the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga* of the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The Commentary on the Minor Section is finished.
The Chapter on Offenses Entailing Expiation is finished.
5. The Chapter on Offenses Entailing Confession (Commentary on the Analysis for Bhikkhunīs).
The Commentary on the Training Rules for Confession (Pāṭidesanīya):
The eight training rules known as the Pāṭidesanīyas, which follow immediately after the Khuddaka-vagga, have been included here in brief.
This brief explanation has been set forth for them.
For regarding those things specified in the Canon such as ghee, oil, and so forth, it is an offense entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*) for one who eats having had them specifically requested.
However, in all cases other than those mentioned in the Canon, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). The rest here is self-evident. Thus, it is eightfold.
Furthermore, this offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya) has four origins: it originates from the body, from body and speech, from body and mind, and from body, speech, and mind;

it is an action (kiriya), not associated with liberation through perception (no-saññā-vimokkha), without mental concomitants (acittaka), an offense by formal rule (paṇṇatti-vajja), bodily action, vocal action, consisting of three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
The commentary on the Pāṭidesanīya rules is finished.
The Section on the Pāṭidesanīyas is finished.
Now, as for the training rules (sekhiyā) that have been recited, those rules are seventy-five in number.
Immediately following those, the wise know that the detailed exposition of their meaning—
which was stated in the Mahāvibhaṅga under the heading of "Matters Relating to Beings"—
is exactly the same in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga as well.
Therefore, for that reason, a separate commentary on the meaning of those individual factors was not stated there;
however, whatever was stated there has indeed been stated here.
Thus ends the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The commentary on the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga is finished.
May those who have reached the path that destroys all taints see Nibbāna, just as this commentary, which destroys all taints, has been completed.
The Commentary on the Twofold Analysis is completed.
